item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia fears military ‘miscalculation’ near Sabah amid US-China rivalry
item.description:
Malaysia faces a growing risk of miscalculation near its state of Sabah as US-China rivalry drives more military activities into the waters around Borneo, its defence minister has warned, bolstering the government’s push for higher spending on its armed forces.

The concern is particularly acute for Malaysia, a South China Sea claimant that has long sought to keep close economic ties with China while avoiding alignment with either Beijing or Washington and is feeling further unease over the expanding US-Philippine military presence just north of Sabah.

Malaysian Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin told This Week in Asia that Putrajaya did not regard the Philippines, the United States, China or any other country as a specific threat, but said the increase in military activities across the region had created a more complex and potentially combustible security environment.
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia faces a growing risk of miscalculation near its state of Sabah as US-China rivalry drives more military activities into the waters around Borneo, its defence minister has warned, bolstering the government’s push for higher spending on its armed forces.

The concern is particularly acute for Malaysia, a South China Sea claimant that has long sought to keep close economic ties with China while avoiding alignment with either Beijing or Washington and is feeling further unease over the expanding US-Philippine military presence just north of Sabah.

Malaysian Defence Minister Mohamed Khaled Nordin told This Week in Asia that Putrajaya did not regard the Philippines, the United States, China or any other country as a specific threat, but said the increase in military activities across the region had created a more complex and potentially combustible security environment.

“When you have more military assets operating within a relatively confined geographical space, the possibility of miscalculation, misunderstanding or even a small incident escalating into something more serious naturally increases,” he said.

“Geographic proximity is therefore an important consideration for us,” Khaled added. “Even if an incident does not directly involve Malaysia, any escalation in areas close to us could have wider implications for our security and for stability in the South China Sea.”

His remarks provide the clearest explanation yet from Malaysia’s defence establishment of the thinking behind Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim’s push for higher military spending, after Anwar publicly singled out the expanding US-Philippine military presence on Balabac Island, just north of Sabah.

Anwar said on Tuesday during an engagement session at the Finance Ministry for the 2027 budget that Malaysia might need to spend “hundreds of millions, or even a billion ringgit” to strengthen Sabah’s defences, arguing that the country needed adequate capabilities as the strategic environment around the state changed.

“This is no longer an ordinary region. It is increasingly becoming a focal point of tensions between two major powers, the United States and China,” state news agency Bernama quoted him as saying.

Balabac, at the southern tip of the Philippine province of Palawan, lies 50km (31 miles) from the Malaysian islands of Banggi and Balambangan. The latter hosts a maritime radar installation covering much of northern Sabah.

Crowded waters

In 2023, Balabac was one of four Philippine military sites added to the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement (EDCA) between Manila and Washington, bringing the total to nine.

The US Defence Department said in April that year the expanded network would strengthen interoperability between the two allies and allow them to respond more readily to shared challenges across the Indo-Pacific, including humanitarian disasters.

Balabac sits between the South China Sea and the Sulu Sea, close to Malaysian territory, where US forces have shown their prowess with their military hardware in recent months.

During the annual Balikatan exercises in May involving troops from the Philippines, the US and other countries, US soldiers fired a rocket from an M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) on the island. The US Army said HIMARS deployed there could be used to protect shipping entering the Sulu and Celebes seas.

Although Anwar stressed that relations with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr’s government were “very good”, he said Malaysia was “naturally somewhat concerned”, citing both Balabac’s proximity and Manila’s long-standing territorial claim over Sabah, according to the Bernama report.

The Philippines reaffirmed its sovereignty claim over Sabah in February, saying existing legislation continued to preserve Manila’s claim to parts of North Borneo.

Georgi Engelbrecht, senior analyst for the Philippines at the International Crisis Group, said Balabac was becoming an increasingly important part of Manila’s defence planning because of the Balabac Strait, a critical passage between the Sulu Sea and South China Sea.

But he said Malaysia had little reason to regard the Philippine infrastructure itself on the island as a direct threat.

“It is the cooperation with the US [and the Philippines] that makes Malaysia reflect,” Engelbrecht told This Week in Asia.

“For now, both forces are conducting exercises and strengthening alliances. But it is not impossible [that] US forces near Malaysia make some politicians and thought leaders in Kuala Lumpur uncomfortable.”

He said the unease stemmed partly from the proximity of US forces and fears of conflict, particularly as Chinese vessels, including People’s Liberation Army ships, also operated around Palawan.

The Sabah dispute itself was unlikely to disappear, Engelbrecht said, noting that Philippine politicians periodically revived the issue and that it remained embedded in domestic politics.

“The concern is no longer the legacy of Lahad Datu, but how this dormant dispute might be resurfacing amid growing great power competition,” he said.

In 2013, followers of the self-proclaimed Sultanate of Sulu landed in the coastal town of Lahad Datu in eastern Sabah to press their territorial claim, triggering weeks of fighting that killed over 50 militants and 10 Malaysian security personnel.

Florence Principe Gamboa, a Philippine-based analyst and fellow at research firm Verve Research, said Balabac had been part of Philippine defence modernisation even before it was designated an EDCA site.

Its location close to the West Philippine Sea, Manila’s term for parts of the South China Sea within its maritime jurisdiction, and the Philippine-held Kalayaan Island Group had long made it strategically important, she said.

US support was increasingly vital to Manila’s maritime security, Gamboa said, while also providing “a counterweight to maritime coercion” for other regional states confronted by China’s growing assertiveness.

“It also complicates navigating great power competition, especially for states like Malaysia that prioritise non-alignment and neutrality, given their strong economic ties with China,” she said.

Bigger arsenal

Malaysia was already planning to increase defence spending before the latest concern over Balabac.

Khaled said the country intended gradually to raise defence expenditure towards 1.5 per cent of gross domestic product by 2030, describing the increase as part of its long-term defence modernisation plans. In comparison, Malaysia allocated about one per cent of its GDP on defence spending in 2025.

Malaysia allocated 21.74 billion ringgit (US$5.4 billion) to the Defence Ministry under its 2026 budget, including 6 billion ringgit for the acquisition of strategic assets.

Khaled cautioned, however, against interpreting the planned increase purely as a response to the US-Philippine build-up.

Cyber and electromagnetic threats, along with mass misinformation campaigns, had also transformed Malaysia’s security requirements, demanding investment in capabilities beyond conventional weapons platforms, he said.

When asked about the higher defence spending, Malaysia-based defence analyst Zaki Salleh argued that Sabah urgently needed stronger maritime surveillance, including radar, drones and patrol aircraft, as well as better air defences and rapid-response capabilities.

He said Malaysia should acquire another three Anka-S medium-altitude long-endurance drones, continue procuring its next batch of littoral mission ships and establish an army aviation helicopter squadron in Sabah.

Military bases, maintenance facilities and resilient communications infrastructure in the state also required improvement, Zaki said.

Ian Storey, a principal fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute, said Malaysia faced three pressures: intensifying great-power rivalry, recurring South China Sea tensions and Malaysia falling behind some of its neighbours in military capabilities.

He said Kuala Lumpur should invest in longer-range, longer-endurance surveillance drones and eventually heavier fighter aircraft, while noting that Malaysia’s traditional reluctance to confront China meant its surveillance drones would probably remain unarmed.

We do not want developments in the region to be framed as Malaysia choosing one side against another

Mohamed Khaled Nordin, Malaysian defence minister

China asserts sweeping sovereignty across much of the South China Sea, overlapping with the maritime claims of the Philippines, Malaysia, Vietnam and Brunei.

Malaysia has generally adopted a less confrontational posture towards China than the Philippines over territorial disputes, even while rejecting Chinese claims that overlap its exclusive economic zone and continuing oil and gas operations in disputed waters, according to analysts.

Khaled said Malaysia’s move towards enhancing its defence would not change that approach.

“We do not want developments in the region to be framed as Malaysia choosing one side against another,” he said. “Our concern is about maintaining regional stability and ensuring that strategic competition between major powers does not create unintended consequences for Asean countries.”

item.title: [SCMP] In Singapore’s battle of casinos, Marina Bay Sands holds winning hand against Sentosa
item.description:
At Singapore casino Resorts World Sentosa’s Lunar New Year lucky draw for high rollers earlier this year, the biggest prize was a bottle of Martell Cognac. Across the harbour at rival Marina Bay Sands, the top sweepstakes winner walked away with a new Mercedes-Benz CLA 200 worth much more.

It is one of the incidents that has made the casino duopoly in one of the world’s top gambling venues more lopsided in the past few years. That is putting pressure on the Sentosa Island resort, whose gaming licence is due for renewal in the coming months.

The Southeast Asian financial hub has seen a strong post-Covid rebound in tourist arrivals and an increase in wealthy gamblers from neighbouring countries and China. It has also taken some business from Macau, which has been affected by Chinese government crackdowns on casino junkets and illegal money-exchange activities.
item.content:encoded:
At Singapore casino Resorts World Sentosa’s Lunar New Year lucky draw for high rollers earlier this year, the biggest prize was a bottle of Martell Cognac. Across the harbour at rival Marina Bay Sands, the top sweepstakes winner walked away with a new Mercedes-Benz CLA 200 worth much more.

It is one of the incidents that has made the casino duopoly in one of the world’s top gambling venues more lopsided in the past few years. That is putting pressure on the Sentosa Island resort, whose gaming licence is due for renewal in the coming months.

The Southeast Asian financial hub has seen a strong post-Covid rebound in tourist arrivals and an increase in wealthy gamblers from neighbouring countries and China. It has also taken some business from Macau, which has been affected by Chinese government crackdowns on casino junkets and illegal money-exchange activities.

The gains in Singapore have been heavily skewed towards Las Vegas Sands’ Marina Bay Sands. Its casino revenues for the first half of 2026 topped US$2.1 billion, while Resorts World Sentosa’s comparable numbers were less than a third of that.

The struggle to attract more high rollers even in Singapore’s growing wealth hub underscores the challenges facing Resorts World Sentosa’s operator, Genting Singapore.

Back in November 2024, Singapore’s Gambling Regulatory Authority called the Sentosa resort’s tourism performance “unsatisfactory”, and granted it a two-year casino licence that took effect in February 2025 instead of the usual three years.

“This is a soft threat” to pressure Resorts World Sentosa to improve its performance, said Zheng Feng Chee, a consumer analyst at DBS Group. “In reality, there are very few casinos that have the financial muscle to buy them out.”

The agency says it is assessing Resorts World Sentosa’s renewal application, and will announce its decision before the licence expires in February 2027.

The regulator’s evaluation takes into account the entire integrated resort’s performance. Last year, it renewed Marina Bay Sands’ casino licence for another three years.

Genting Singapore said in April that it had “maintained close engagement” with authorities and believed the group was “well positioned for the next assessment cycle.”

A Resorts World Sentosa representative said the integrated resort had over the past 18 months added new attractions and experiences, and had been “enhancing” its hospitality and gaming offerings.

Its goal was to position itself “for sustainable growth over the next decade”, the representative said, adding that “the early signs of progress are encouraging”. Marina Bay Sands declined to comment for this article.

No match for Sands

The competition between the two casinos is likely to remain intense.

“I see them losing the battle, and even more market share,” said Ben Lee, managing partner at IGamiX, a Macau-based consulting firm, of Resorts World Sentosa.

Lee said it simply had not been able to match the “luxuriate experience” of Marina Bay Sands, which has been a big draw for so-called VIPs – the biggest spenders and most highly coveted casino customers.

Singapore’s casino industry has been heavily reliant on foreigners ever since Resorts World Sentosa first opened its doors in early 2010, with Marina Bay Sands launching shortly after.

Singapore citizens and permanent residents have to pay S$150 (US$120) per day to enter either casino, while tourists can go in for free after showing their passports.

Gamblers from China have been flocking to Singapore, which offers visa-free entry to tourists from the mainland. Concerns that their personal data could be shared with Chinese authorities have also made some high rollers wary of gambling in Macau, and they see Singapore as a more discreet alternative to protect their privacy.

These days, the crowd at Resorts World Sentosa’s VIP club is far smaller than that at Marina Bay Sands, according to people familiar with both casinos. In 2023, the Sentosa casino had a larger share of the VIP market, but that tumbled to around 20 per cent in the first quarter of this year before rebounding recently to 36 per cent, according to DBS research.

While there are fewer high rollers compared to so-called mass gamers, the former make outsize contributions to casino revenues and profits.

To become a VIP, gamblers typically have to deposit or spend at least S$100,000 for starters, then accumulate more spending by making bets and playing games over a fixed period to secure a club membership. Benefits include access to private gaming suites, complimentary hotel stays, dining privileges and invitations to exclusive events.

Some members of Resorts World Sentosa’s casino club for VIPs have complained to the integrated resort’s management about what they consider as the Sentosa property’s dated infrastructure, its unresponsiveness to feedback, and even the process of exchanging cash and chips, according to people familiar with the matter.

Rolling out revamps

In addition to more generous lucky draw prizes, the VIP club at Marina Bay Sands offers perks and freebies that include suite stays with a butler service, tickets to musicals and dining credit at restaurants. Its integrated resort – which is one of the world’s most profitable – includes three 57-storey hotel towers with a large boat-shaped rooftop, an art museum and shopping centre.

Resorts World Sentosa clawed back some high rollers’ market share in the recent second quarter, after Marina Bay Sands posted weaker VIP revenue. The latter said that was partly because some of its high-value customers went to the World Cup, which drew spending away from casinos.

Genting Singapore is majority-owned by Malaysian leisure, real estate and hospitality group Genting, which is controlled by 75-year-old billionaire Lim Kok Thay. Last year, he became the Singapore unit’s acting chief executive officer following a series of leadership reshuffles.

In addition to its casino and multiple hotels, Resorts World Singapore operates Universal Studios Singapore, a large water park and other Sentosa attractions. The casino generates most of the integrated resort’s revenue and profits.

The Sentosa venue is in the midst of a S$6.8 billion revamp that includes building an all-suite luxury hotel, expanding its oceanarium and adding Super Nintendo World to Universal Studios Singapore. The improved version of the resort is to be completed by 2030.

Marina Bay Sands, meanwhile, has kicked off its own US$8 billion makeover and expansion that will add another 55-storey hotel tower and a live entertainment arena.

Marina Bay Sands had “made the property more premium, more appealing to higher-value customers,” said Vitaly Umansky, Hong Kong-based senior analyst of global gaming at Seaport Research Partners. “Resorts World has a lot of wood to chop in order to try to gain back some of that market share.”

item.title: [SCMP] Will Putin’s Kuril Islands visit push Japan closer to Ukraine?
item.description:
Japan is weighing how far to push back after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a disputed island last week, as analysts debate whether tougher measures would have much impact on Moscow.

Some observers urged Japan to recall its ambassador, impose additional sanctions and deepen cooperation with Ukraine to show it would not be “bullied”, while others said Tokyo had little economic leverage left given already weak bilateral ties and its reliance on Russian natural gas.

Putin made his first-ever visit to one of four disputed islands, collectively called the Northern Territories by Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia, last Thursday.
item.content:encoded:
Japan is weighing how far to push back after Russian President Vladimir Putin visited a disputed island last week, as analysts debate whether tougher measures would have much impact on Moscow.

Some observers urged Japan to recall its ambassador, impose additional sanctions and deepen cooperation with Ukraine to show it would not be “bullied”, while others said Tokyo had little economic leverage left given already weak bilateral ties and its reliance on Russian natural gas.

Putin made his first-ever visit to one of four disputed islands, collectively called the Northern Territories by Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia, last Thursday.

Japanese media reported that senior foreign ministry officials discussed possible responses on Friday, including tougher sanctions and the temporary recall of Japan’s ambassador.

On Tuesday, Japan’s envoy to Moscow Akira Muto was summoned to the Russian foreign ministry after Tokyo protested against Putin’s visit.

During the meeting, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin warned that his country reserved the “right to take appropriate countermeasures” against Japan, given Tokyo’s continued policy of sanctioning Moscow and its support for Kyiv, according to the Russian foreign ministry.

The Japanese embassy in Moscow said Muto “appropriately explained” Tokyo’s stance in the 20-minute session with Galuzin.

Putin travelled to Iturup Island – known as Etorofu in Japan – where he visited a fish-processing plant and met local residents.

Japan claims the Soviet Union illegally seized the islands – Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group – soon after Japan’s surrender at the end of the second world war in 1945. Russia maintains that the action was legitimate, however.

Describing Putin’s visit as “grave” and “absolutely unacceptable”, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi warned last Thursday that the visit would harden anti-Russian sentiment in Japan and make restoring relations more difficult in the medium to long term.

That same day, her Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi summoned Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to lodge a formal protest, making it clear that Tokyo considers the island an inherent part of Japanese territory both historically and under international law.

On Tuesday, the Russian ministry said in a statement that Galuzin had “conveyed a strong protest” to Muto over Takaichi’s and Motegi’s “anti-Russia” remarks.

Adding that the Southern Kurils were “transferred to our country following World War II”, the statement said that “any attempts by the Japanese side to directly or indirectly call this obvious reality into question are categorically unacceptable and illegitimate”.

Closer to Kyiv?

In addition to recalling its ambassador to Russia and imposing additional sanctions, Japan could respond by deepening cooperation with Ukraine, said James Brown, a professor of international relations specialising in Russian affairs at Temple University’s Tokyo campus.

Takaichi has yet to have a face-to-face meeting with President Volodymyr Zelensky, even though both leaders attended the Group of 7 summit in France in June.

“A face-to-face meeting, especially if it entailed a visit to Kyiv by Takaichi, would send a strong message that Japan will not be bullied by Russia into changing its foreign policy,” Brown said, adding that Putin’s visit came as Japan had been exploring tentative re-engagement with Russia.

This included sending a delegation from the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry to Moscow in May, and restarting foreign ministry-backed student visits in July.

“This tentative re-engagement, which was always controversial, is now likely to be curtailed,” Brown added.

A face-to-face meeting [with Ukraine’s president] … would send a strong message that Japan will not be bullied by Russia

James Brown, international-relations professor

Michito Tsuruoka, a professor of policy management at Keio University, said Tokyo’s priority should be showing Russia that it cannot pressure Japan into changing its policies.

“Strengthening support to Ukraine would be a possible response, though whether the prime minister is interested in this remains unclear,” he said.

There does not appear to be a consensus within the Japanese government on how to handle relations with Russia, according to Tsuruoka.

“Different actors have different views on what Russia is and they see different aspects of [the country] and their meaning to Japan,” he added.

While the economy ministry sees Japan’s northern neighbour as an important energy source – more so given recent developments in the Strait of Hormuz – Tsuruoka said the defence ministry was increasingly concerned about deepening Russia-China and Russia-North Korea ties and the Russian military’s increasing activities near Japan.

“A new consensus needs to be built,” Tsuruoka said.

The Strait of Hormuz has been all but closed since the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran in late February. Before the conflict, Japan was importing over 90 per cent of its crude oil, and a portion of its liquefied natural gas (LNG), through the strait.

Last month, Japan’s defence ministry said that a Russian military IL-20 reconnaissance aircraft had intruded into its territorial airspace over disputed islands, with Russia conducting large-scale live-fire naval drills involving 60 warships and 13,000 troops nearby less than two weeks later.

‘No economic leverage’

Artyom Lukin, a professor at the Far Eastern Federal University in Vladivostok, questioned Japan’s ability to impose any significant economic penalties on Moscow over Putin’s visit.

“Russia-Japan economic ties have already been reduced to a bare minimum because of the Ukraine conflict,” he said, noting that bilateral trade is now largely limited to Russia supplying LNG and seafood while importing Japanese vehicles.

“Japan cannot halt LNG imports from Russia’s Sakhalin Island because it is difficult to find viable alternatives, especially amid the continuing crisis in the Middle East,” Lukin said.

There were also no alternatives to some Russian seafood delicacies, he added, saying: “For the Japanese, seafood specialities are far more important than Ukraine and the Kuril Islands combined.”

Should Japan ban car exports to Russia, Russians would likely respond by buying from China and South Korea instead, according to Lukin.

“In a nutshell, Japan has no economic leverage over Russia,” he said, adding that Tokyo’s main response would be “rhetorical”.

Japan’s bilateral trade with Russia hit roughly US$8 billion last year, dwarfed by its trade with China at about US$300 billion. Over the same period, Japan’s Russian LNG supplies ticked up 2 per cent from 2024 levels to about 5.8 million tonnes, making up about 9 per cent of Japan’s total annual LNG imports.

By comparison, Japan imports roughly 11 per cent of its LNG from the Middle East, according to Reuters.

While Japan could “theoretically” step up military activities near Russia, Lukin said Tokyo was unlikely to do so as it needed those resources to deal with the challenge posed by China.

In its latest Defence White Paper issued earlier this month, Tokyo repeated and reinforced its stance that China’s rapid and opaque military expansion was its “greatest strategic challenge”.

Takaichi took advantage of Putin’s trip to score an easy win “with her hardcore nationalistic audience”, according to Lukin, who said Moscow had always maintained that its sovereignty over Iturup and Kunashir – the larger of the disputed islands – was non-negotiable.

“Russia was only ready to negotiate the two smaller islands, Shikotan and Habomai,” he said. “Takaichi is not naive. I guess she fully realises that Russia is never going to return Iturup to Japan.”

Bilateral relations were already in the doldrums but could worsen, Brown said, citing Japanese concerns over Russia’s possible provision of military technology to North Korea in exchange for Pyongyang’s assistance in the Ukraine war.

“If Russia [strengthens] this support by meaningfully enhancing the North’s ballistic missile and nuclear capabilities, it would lead to even greater tensions between Tokyo and Moscow,” Brown said.

Analysts say Tokyo is concerned that Russian technology transfers will accelerate North Korea’s nuclear, ballistic missile and hypersonic weapons programmes, threatening the regional security balance.

item.title: [SCMP] Southeast Asia’s landmine clearers face closure as global aid shifts to new wars
item.description:
En Poy was minding cattle in a former Khmer Rouge stronghold in Cambodia when he set off his first landmine.

The blast from the rusty relic he picked up cost him an arm and an eye. It also inspired his career with non-profit organisation Cambodian Self Help Demining, which clears landmines and unexploded ordnance across the country, deadly remnants of wars from the last century.

Groups like Poy’s that rely on foreign aid are struggling as donors shift funding for humanitarian demining towards active conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, and to more recent wars, like in Syria and Afghanistan. Today’s conflicts are also driving higher defence spending, leaving less money for aid.
item.content:encoded:
En Poy was minding cattle in a former Khmer Rouge stronghold in Cambodia when he set off his first landmine.

The blast from the rusty relic he picked up cost him an arm and an eye. It also inspired his career with non-profit organisation Cambodian Self Help Demining, which clears landmines and unexploded ordnance across the country, deadly remnants of wars from the last century.

Groups like Poy’s that rely on foreign aid are struggling as donors shift funding for humanitarian demining towards active conflicts in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, and to more recent wars, like in Syria and Afghanistan. Today’s conflicts are also driving higher defence spending, leaving less money for aid.

President Donald Trump’s dismantling of the US Agency for International Development and a 90-day freeze on foreign aid last year worsened the problems, though American demining support to Cambodia has restarted.

Cambodia’s predicament shows that dangers remain even when fighting ends.

Demining groups say that without international support, Southeast Asia’s unfinished work clearing landmines and unexploded bombs will continue to endanger communities, maiming and killing people and slowing development for years to come.

Poy was wounded in a second landmine explosion that pierced his face and body with shrapnel and killed three of his colleagues. He now educates fellow Cambodians in high-risk areas on how to avoid such dangers.

But he is not sure how long that will last.

“If one day donors stop funding my organisation, I would definitely be sad because we haven’t finished our job,” he said. “There are still a lot of landmines left over.”

Deadly legacy

The Vietnam war bled into neighbouring Cambodia and Laos, triggering strife that lasted long after the Americans fled the fall of Saigon, including the Khmer Rouge’s reign of terror, which killed about 1.7 million Cambodians.

Cambodia is one of the world’s most land-mined countries. Laos is the most heavily bombed country per capita in history and Vietnam still battles the fallout of chemical weapons.

Since the wars ended, landmines and unexploded ordnance have killed about 90,000 people and wounded almost twice as many across the three countries.

Leftover weapons lie beneath fields and forests, blocking construction of roads and schools. They are deadly discoveries, mistaken for toys by children who account for more than 40 per cent of the civilian casualties recorded globally since 1999 by the Landmine and Cluster Munition Monitor, formed by non-profit organisations to track such issues.

Demining is slow and painstaking work. Teams first survey and map contaminated areas. Then step-by-step they clear vegetation, using metal detectors and specialised equipment to locate explosives and destroy them. Progress is measured in metres a day and work often stops in wet weather.

“These things don’t really become less dangerous with time. They become more dangerous as they deteriorate,” said Charles Ray, a Vietnam war veteran who became the first post-war US consul general in Ho Chi Minh City and later ambassador to Cambodia.

By funding demining, the US proved it cared, Ray said. “We’re not just this behemoth that comes in with our military machine and breaks things, we can also help nations rebuild,” he said.

Funding for humanitarian demining amounted to US$4.3 billion from 2020 to 2024, according to the landmine monitor.

National contributions from affected countries made up about a fifth and foreign aid provided the rest, with most of the funds from the US, Germany, the European Union, Norway, and Switzerland, the landmine monitor said.

Recent conflicts have created unprecedented demand for demining as contaminated areas expand, Maria Vardis of the UN Mine Action Service said.

Ukraine received a third of all humanitarian demining funding in 2024, more than any other country, the landmine monitor found. Other active conflict zones, like Yemen and Gaza, received increased funding, while demining efforts in Syria, Sudan and Afghanistan have also ramped up, while some Asian nations are getting less funding.

Germany is considering reducing foreign aid in favour of defence spending and military support to Ukraine.

At the same time, more landmines are being planted and bombs dropped in other conflicts such as the civil war in Myanmar and border conflicts between Cambodia and Thailand.

“Funding does fluctuate year to year, but in the big picture, even in the face of cuts by many governments, the big crises continue to be funded, but smaller and older mine action projects are struggling,” Vardis said.

Yo-yo aid

Under Trump, US demining aid to Southeast Asia has yo-yoed. That has “set a really dangerous precedent for what can be done,” Danae Hendrickson of the US-based advocacy group Legacies of War said.

Last year, the US approved US$56.5 million for war-legacy programmes in Vietnam, according to congressional documents, compared with US$197 million allocated in 2024. In July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced US$130 million in demining help for Southeast Asia, without giving details.

Last year’s freeze briefly halted war-legacy projects in Vietnam and weakened Hanoi’s confidence in US commitments, said Nguyen Khac Giang, a visiting fellow at Singapore’s ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute.

“The lasting damage is to the hard-earned trust between the two former enemies,” he said.

A US State Department representative said American help was “not charity” and that humanitarian demining aid would continue to serve US interests around the world.

Between 1992 and 2025, about 1.2 million mines and 3.2 million other explosive remnants of war were found in Cambodia, according to the Cambodian Mine Action and Victim Assistance Authority.

The country still had 1,749 sq km (675 square miles) of uncleared land as of last year.

Thousands or even millions more weapons might still be out there, said Bill Morse, president of the Landmine Relief Fund, which supports Cambodian Self Help Demining.

Barely an hour from the famed Angkor Wat temple complex in Siem Reap, deminers with South Korean, Swiss and American flags on their uniforms and helmets recently inched through a minefield, clearing the land one painstaking step at a time.

They found a Soviet-designed anti-personnel landmine. Another unit nearby was dispatched to destroy a mortar round and a rocket-propelled grenade at a cassava farm just off a highway leading to a new Chinese-funded airport.

The group may have to stop their work by September due to sharp cutbacks in donations. “We have simply run out of donors,” Morse said.

“If people want to pull their money away, that’s a decision that they have to make,” he said. “But when they do, people will die here.”

item.title: [SCMP] China becomes first nation to recover orbital launch rockets with 2 distinct paths
item.description:
In a global first, leading Chinese commercial rocket company LandSpace has recovered a stainless-steel booster after an orbital launch, marking a major step in the country’s efforts to develop lower-cost, reusable rockets.

Previous reusable boosters deployed in such launches have been made from aluminium alloys, which can be more expensive to develop due to higher design and raw material costs.

China is also the first country to succeed in orbital launch recovery down distinct technological pathways, pulling off a dual-track strategy that even the United States – which pioneered reusable rocket technology – has yet to execute.
item.content:encoded:
In a global first, leading Chinese commercial rocket company LandSpace has recovered a stainless-steel booster after an orbital launch, marking a major step in the country’s efforts to develop lower-cost, reusable rockets.

Previous reusable boosters deployed in such launches have been made from aluminium alloys, which can be more expensive to develop due to higher design and raw material costs.

China is also the first country to succeed in orbital launch recovery down distinct technological pathways, pulling off a dual-track strategy that even the United States – which pioneered reusable rocket technology – has yet to execute.

The Zhuque-3 is China’s first commercial rocket to both reach orbit and have its first stage recovered.

LandSpace also became the fourth entity – after US companies SpaceX and Blue Origin, and state-owned China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) – to achieve controlled recovery of a reusable vehicle from an orbital launch.

Like SpaceX’s Falcon 9 and Blue Origin’s New Glenn, Zhuque-3 uses landing legs to recover its rockets.

But last month, China was the first to recover a booster on an orbital launch with a different technique, after the first stage of CASC’s Long March 10B was recovered using a unique sea-based net capture system.

SpaceX’s Super Heavy booster, which is also made of stainless steel, is awaiting US Federal Aviation Administration approval for its first recovery flight to send the Starship into orbit.

The Super Heavy will also attempt a non-leg-based orbital recovery using mechanical “chopstick” arms mounted on a tower to catch the booster.

Wednesday’s milestone is just the start of China’s reusable rocket recovery efforts, while the US already has hundreds of successful booster recoveries and reuses under its belt.

The 66-metre (217-foot) Zhuque-3 rocket, powered by liquid methane and oxygen, lifted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Centre in the Gobi Desert at 7.35am on Wednesday, according to state news agency Xinhua.

The rocket delivered a Honghu-3 internet satellite into its designated orbit, while its first stage returned to Earth and touched down vertically at a recovery site in Minqin county, Gansu province, about 390km (242 miles) southeast of the launch pad.

“This mission marks China’s first successful recovery of a first-stage reusable launch vehicle using landing legs, and also China’s first successful land-based recovery of a first-stage orbital-deployed launch vehicle,” LandSpace said.

“LandSpace will continue to advance the iteration and engineering verification of reusable technology, helping my country further improve its low-cost, high-frequency and highly reliable space transport capabilities,” the company added in a social media post.

Dong Kai, the rocket’s deputy chief designer, told the LatePost news outlet on Wednesday that LandSpace aimed to reuse the recovered rockets as soon as possible, adding that he hoped to launch Zhuque-3 10 times a year.

Wednesday’s launch was LandSpace’s second attempt to put Zhuque-3 into orbit and recover its first stage.

During the rocket’s maiden flight in December, the second stage reached orbit but the first stage erupted in a dramatic fireball during its final powered descent towards the landing pad.

After that mission, Zhuque-3 project chief Dai Zheng told state broadcaster CCTV that the recovery had failed because the first stage’s engine had not reignited when it was about 3km above the ground as required.

LandSpace said on Wednesday that, following the first attempt, the rocket was optimised for reusable flight by reducing the number of landing ignition engines, improving the on-board autonomous safety control system, and enhancing thermal protection for re-entry.

Now, Zhuque-3 is China’s second orbital rocket to demonstrate first-stage recovery. The first was the state-developed Long March-10B, whose first stage was captured by a huge net on an offshore platform after launching from Hainan province in July.

The two rockets have broadly similar payload capacities and are in about the same class as SpaceX’s workhorse Falcon 9. In expendable configuration, the Long March-10B and Zhuque-3 can carry about 22 and 21 tonnes to low Earth orbit, respectively. With their first stages recovered, the figures fall to about 16 and 18 tonnes.

Unlike the stainless steel design of the Zhuque-3, the Falcon 9 is made using an aluminium-lithium alloy. Dong said that the welding process for stainless steel was easier than for aluminium alloy, adding that the material was also cheap and had good heat resistance.

Recovering the two rockets could prove crucial to the construction of China’s broadband internet megaconstellations. Like SpaceX’s Starlink, Chinese projects such as Guowang and Qianfan envisage eventually placing more than 10,000 satellites in orbit to provide global broadband coverage, creating both a potential global market and infrastructure of strategic military importance.

So far, Starlink has deployed more than 10,000 operational satellites and attracted over 12 million customers worldwide. Its extensive use by Ukrainian forces for battlefield communications has shown the military value of such a network.

By comparison, Beijing’s Guowang constellation and the Shanghai-backed Qianfan network have each deployed only around 200 satellites. Their expansion has been constrained partly by China’s lack of a reusable workhorse comparable to the Falcon 9.

Wednesday’s feat suggests China could translate its engineering talent and manufacturing abilities into cheaper, faster launches, positioning it to compete with the US as both nations accelerate the roll-out of internet satellites.

While US space agency Nasa has left reusable rocket development to commercial partners like SpaceX, China is playing on both fronts, with its state-run space programme building reusable boosters alongside the commercial sector.

The China National Space Administration said on Wednesday it helped coordinate the Zhuque-3 launch team, adding that it would continue to support the country’s reusable rocket technology.

The next test for China’s reusable rockets will be whether the recovered boosters can be refurbished and flown again, which is necessary to reduce launch costs and support more frequent launches.

LandSpace said the recovery of the Zhuque-3 laid a foundation for subsequent maintenance and reuse flights, and would help China improve launch capabilities to support commercial missions and the deployment of satellite constellations.

item.title: [SCMP] How China got caught in the crossfire of a US bacon fight
item.description:
Midwestern Americans watching television this summer may have been surprised to see China and bacon appearing together in political advertisements.

“The corrupt Save Our Bacon scam in the farm bill – it’s a giveaway to Chinese corporations,” one advertisement declared over images of the Chinese flag and Chinese President Xi Jinping. “Whose side is your senator on? America or China?”

Viewers might assume the advertisement was promoting yet another Republican-led effort to counter Beijing.
item.content:encoded:
Midwestern Americans watching television this summer may have been surprised to see China and bacon appearing together in political advertisements.

“The corrupt Save Our Bacon scam in the farm bill – it’s a giveaway to Chinese corporations,” one advertisement declared over images of the Chinese flag and Chinese President Xi Jinping. “Whose side is your senator on? America or China?”

Viewers might assume the advertisement was promoting yet another Republican-led effort to counter Beijing.

The reality is far more complicated.

Behind the aggressive campaign against the Save Our Bacon Act lies a fight over how pigs are housed – and perhaps the latest example of China being weaponised in US domestic politics.

The bill has created an unexpected collision of animal welfare, agricultural regulation and America’s growing political anxiety over China, with opponents accusing a Republican-backed farm measure of putting a Chinese-owned pork giant ahead of American farmers.

What is the Save Our Bacon Act?

The controversy traces back to California’s Proposition 12, which voters approved in 2018. The measure established minimum space requirements for breeding pigs and prohibited the sale of pork from animals raised below those standards, forcing producers nationwide either to modify their operations or risk losing access to one of the country’s largest markets.

The US Supreme Court upheld the measure in 2023 after legal challenges.

The economic impact of California’s law has become a key point of contention. A recent North Dakota State University study found that Proposition 12 was associated with a roughly 73-cent-per-pound increase in California’s retail pork price premium after full enforcement. Researchers estimated that consumers in California and Massachusetts, both of which have similar animal-confinement laws, spent an additional US$403 million on pork from 2024 to 2026.

Pork producers have argued that constructing Proposition 12-compliant housing could cost as much as US$4,000 per sow, a burden that could weigh particularly heavily on smaller family farms.

Enter the Save Our Bacon Act. Introduced by congresswoman Ashley Hinson of Iowa, the legislation would overturn Proposition 12’s requirements for pork sold in California.

Hinson, who is running for Senate and has secured the Republican nomination, has argued that the measure would protect interstate commerce for Iowa livestock producers by preventing one state from imposing production standards on farmers in another while preserving states’ authority to regulate their own producers.

Opponents, led by the American Meat Producers Association (AMPA), have launched a national campaign against the new bill in Congress.

“Farmers have built their lives and communities on fair, responsible farming,” AMPA said in a statement on its website. “If Congress eliminates these laws, those livelihoods will vanish, supply chains will shatter, and rural towns will lose the people who fuel their economy.”

AMPA was formed in late 2025 and led by Holly Bice, a government relations professional with experience lobbying on agriculture and animal welfare. The group has launched a US$30 million campaign targeting lawmakers in the Midwest over the Save Our Bacon Act.

Hinson has accused the group of being backed by meat companies that have already spent millions of dollars transitioning to Proposition 12-compliant facilities, giving them a financial stake in preserving and expanding such mandates across state lines and limiting competitors’ ability to operate under conventional production standards.

It is unclear who is funding the US$30 million campaign. Federal Election Commission filings show that the American Meat Producers PAC, an affiliated political committee, had raised about US$55,000 and spent about US$8,000 by the end of June. The filings list individual donors from across the country, including a US$5,000 contribution from Bice herself.

The campaign’s advertisements, targeting Midwestern states, have also attracted over a million views on YouTube.

Hinson, AMPA and Bice did not respond to requests for comment.

Why is China involved?

AMPA has transformed the debate into something much larger, arguing that the legislation would ultimately benefit Chinese corporations – an apparent reference to Smithfield Foods, America’s largest pork producer.

Smithfield, based in Virginia, was acquired in 2013 by WH Group, formerly known as Shuanghui International, a Chinese company listed in Hong Kong.

That acquisition, completed more than a decade ago, sits at the centre of the current political battle, as AMPA’s ads portray the legislation as a handout to Chinese-owned corporations rather than a measure intended to help American farmers.

Ray Atkinson, a spokesperson for Smithfield, said the company believes animal-welfare standards should be based on science and veterinary expertise, rather than voter initiatives.

“The reason we oppose Prop 12 is that it has raised pork prices for consumers and doesn’t objectively improve animal welfare,” Atkinson said. “The Save Our Bacon Act would prevent individual states from creating a patchwork of livestock production practices that make it difficult to keep food affordable for all Americans.”

Atkinson did not directly address how much of Smithfield’s production complies with Proposition 12. He said the company has established supply agreements for Proposition 12-compliant pork and is willing to work with retail and food service customers to expand the availability of compliant products.

The National Pork Producers Council (NPPC), one of the Save Our Bacon Act’s strongest supporters, told the South China Morning Post that AMPA’s campaign is an activist-driven effort, and pointed to a June statement describing the group’s claims as “baseless”.

In a video interview with Farm Journal in June, NPPC president Rob Brenneman said that AMPA’s campaign “is a lie”.

“It’s not about China. It’s not about any foreign-owned company,” Brenneman said. “It’s about livestock production in general and the consumption of meat in the United States, and they want to eliminate that, plain and simple.”

Smithfield, which raised about 550,000 sows in 2025, is a major player in the NPPC, with two company representatives currently serving on its board. NPPC says it represents more than 60,000 US pork producers. AMPA has not disclosed its membership, but its website features a handful of individual farmers supporting Proposition 12.

Hinson has similarly slammed AMPA as a radical animal rights activists, arguing that misinformation campaigns have falsely suggested the legislation would benefit foreign-owned corporations or harm American producers. Hinson’s Senate campaign is also being scrutinised over donations it received from organisations linked to Smithfield.

The Chinese embassy in Washington said that investment by Chinese companies in the United States had contributed to employment and economic growth while criticising the politicisation of mutually beneficial economic and trade relations.

“Actions and rhetoric that overstretch the concept of national security and politicise economic, trade and investment issues run counter to market economy principles and international trade rules,” the spokesperson said. “They undermine confidence in the US market environment and harm the interests of the American people themselves.”

China as an easy political target

The fight over the Save Our Bacon Act reflects a broader reality in American politics: invoking China has become one of the most effective ways to frame a political argument.

According to the Chicago Council on Global Affairs’ latest survey, 50 per cent of Americans view China’s rise as a critical threat to the United States, a figure that rises to 66 per cent among Republicans, making China a politically convenient target in domestic campaigns.

Democrats have embraced the same line of attack. The Iowa Democratic Party published a blog post titled: “Ashley Hinson Is ‘Holding Up the Farm Bill’ With Her Pro-China Save Our Bacon Act.”

The controversy also mirrors a political battle over Chinese ownership of American agricultural assets.

Filers whose primary investor was China reported owning 247,659 acres of US agricultural land as of December 31, 2024, according to the US Department of Agriculture. That represents roughly 0.5 per cent of the 46.3 million acres of farmland held by foreign investors nationwide.

Two of the five largest Chinese-linked landholders in the country are Smithfield entities, Murphy-Brown LLC and Murphy-Brown of Missouri, together accounting for roughly 40 per cent of all Chinese-held US farmland.

Congress has tried to address those concerns. The Protecting American Agriculture From Foreign Adversaries Act would expand federal oversight of farmland purchases by entities linked to countries such as China. But the legislation remains stalled in Congress.

The fate of the Save Our Bacon Act remains uncertain.

The House passed the measure as part of its farm bill in April, but the Senate version does not include it, and the Senate Agriculture Committee failed to advance its legislation before the August recess. Any final version would have to be negotiated if lawmakers eventually reconcile the two bills.

But the political lesson may already be clear: in today’s America, even a fight over how pigs are housed can quickly become a debate over China.

item.title: [SCMP] Will Washington’s tech crackdown test fragile US-China truce?
item.description:
Ahead of next month’s expected summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, a low profile US regulatory agency has opened a new front in the technology battle between the world’s two superpowers, even as it attempts to avoid sabotaging the vital high-stakes meeting.

The latest action by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in July saw it advance stringent bans on new Chinese robots and power inverters.

The move came after months of FCC measures that did not prompt a direct retaliatory response from Beijing, even as the agency continued to expand its restrictions.
item.content:encoded:
Ahead of next month’s expected summit between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington, a low profile US regulatory agency has opened a new front in the technology battle between the world’s two superpowers, even as it attempts to avoid sabotaging the vital high-stakes meeting.

The latest action by the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in July saw it advance stringent bans on new Chinese robots and power inverters.

The move came after months of FCC measures that did not prompt a direct retaliatory response from Beijing, even as the agency continued to expand its restrictions.

Although China held its fire ahead of the last Trump-Xi summit in May, that restraint appears to have ended following the FCC’s latest steps.

Beijing’s retaliation last week – imposing drone export controls and sanctioning US testing firms – signalled the expansion of an already crowded field of tit-for-tat actions involving tariffs, export controls and the blacklisting of each other’s companies.

Former senior FCC officials defended the agency’s national security mandate to protect US technology sectors and communication networks from Chinese influence.

But analysts said these aggressive regulatory moves highlighted a delicate balancing act for the Trump administration, which is seeking to curb Chinese presence without shattering the fragile trade truce brokered last October.

Experts argued the FCC offers the administration a relatively low profile tool to advance its technology agenda, targeting specific sectors, equipment categories and approval processes rather than relying on broad tariffs or export controls. Its existing regulatory authority also allows it to act through national-security and communications rules.

However, they cautioned that the approach could increase the chances of missteps.

“Securing the nation’s networks has always been a priority,” Tom Wheeler, the FCC chairman from 2013-2017, said in an email to the South China Morning Post.

“The Trump administration may be trying to restrict Chinese tech products without upsetting the Busan trade truce,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Centre at the Brookings Institution.

“There is certainly a risk of miscalculation here,” he added.

FCC spearheads China crackdown

The FCC has quietly emerged as one of the Trump administration’s most aggressive agencies targeting Chinese technology companies on national security grounds, even as other departments, including Commerce and Treasury, have taken a back seat.

Under Chairman Brendan Carr, the agency has pursued a two-pronged strategy: combining targeted measures against individual Chinese companies with sweeping, category-wide bans and supply-chain restrictions.

In April, it advanced a proposal to ban Chinese telecoms operators – China Mobile, China Telecom and China Unicom – from operating data centres in the US.

It also moved to bar Hong Kong telecoms carrier HKT International from operating in America, with Carr asserting that “CCP-controlled entities that pose national security risks to our country cannot connect to our telecom networks.”

That salvo followed a move in December last year, when the agency implemented a series of sector-wide crackdowns, including a stringent ban on imports of new Chinese drones, followed by restrictions on new models of consumer routers in May and robotics and power inverters in July.

The products were among those targeted by the FCC’s Covered List, which identifies communications equipment and services deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to US national security.

“Advanced robotic devices collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots,” the FCC said after announcing the robotics ban in July.

Additionally, it advanced a proposal to ban what it calls Chinese “bad labs” from testing electronic devices headed to the US. According to the agency, around 75 per cent of all US electronics are tested in China.

“Some of those labs themselves were linked or controlled by or tied to the PLA [People’s Liberation Army], so not necessarily the most trustworthy,” Carr told TBPN, a technology-focused online network, earlier this month.

“We’re now inserting national security checks in that lab process.”

The agency has increasingly invoked national security to justify measures targeting Chinese companies and technology across the US communications and technology ecosystem.

In March last year, Carr launched the FCC’s Council on National Security to “promote America’s national security and counter foreign adversaries.”

“Today, the country faces a persistent and constant threat from foreign adversaries, particularly the CCP,” Carr said at the time.

In response to a query from the SCMP, an FCC spokesperson said that “Covered List actions are country-neutral and apply to all foreign-produced devices that meet the criteria.”

“The FCC will continue to be in lockstep with the entire administration to protect Americans from foreign threats and make sure that the United States is in the best position to deliver on President Trump’s vision to lead the world on the next generation of technologies,” the spokesperson added.

The Chinese embassy in Washington did not respond to a request for comment.

Trump has repeatedly used the national security rationale to justify policies ranging from border fencing and mass deportations to tariffs, domestic energy policy and timber harvesting on federal land.

Analysts and legal scholars argue that “crying wolf” – using “national security” as a pretext for political expediency – risks undermining faith in institutions and eroding trust if a genuine catastrophe strikes.

However, Wheeler asserted that protecting national security is a core mandate of the FCC, noting: “National security is a Section One responsibility of the FCC, meaning the first section of the Communications Act.”

The FCC was established in 1934 under the Communications Act, which states that the commission was created “for the purpose of the national defence” and “for the purpose of promoting safety of life and property through the use of wire and radio communications”.

Rachelle Chong, a former FCC commissioner, argued that the agency’s council on national security “centralises the effort across multiple bureaus” and “expressly treats strategic competition with China as an organising agency priority”.

“The FCC’s national-security role is both older and broader than many people realise,” she said.

She described the first Trump administration as an “important turning point”, pointing to the FCC’s denial of China Mobile’s application, restrictions on the use of federal universal-service funds for Chinese tech companies Huawei and ZTE equipment, and the establishment of the Covered List and removal-and-replacement programme.

“Over the last decade, the FCC’s role has evolved from reviewing individual foreign entrants to protecting the communications supply chain as a whole,” Chong said.

Chan, of the Brookings Institution, noted that the FCC has emerged “as an increasingly popular tool for restricting Chinese tech products”.

“It can act relatively swiftly compared with other government restrictions,” he said, adding that the administration “appears to be making moves designed to operate below the threshold of upsetting the Busan truce”.

“The FCC is further away from trade negotiations with China compared with Commerce and Treasury.”

After months of escalation marked by high tariffs and China’s restrictions on rare earths, the two sides reached a one-year arrangement in Busan, South Korea, last year under which Washington agreed to suspend additional export controls in exchange for continued flows of critical minerals from Beijing.

Under the arrangement, the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) suspended its Affiliates Rule, which had expanded export restrictions to companies owned 50 per cent or more by entities on the Entity List, and has not added new Chinese entities to the list since last October.

While the Busan understanding was reaffirmed during the Trump-Xi summit in May, both sides have kept the pot simmering with tit-for-tat actions without allowing tensions to spiral, particularly ahead of Xi’s expected visit to the US next month.

After more than a year of refraining from directly retaliating against FCC actions, China’s response last week went beyond the tighter drone export controls to include sanctions against seven US companies and Beijing’s first foreign trade-related national security investigation.

“I assess it as a shot across the bow, especially as the FCC actions began to add up,” said Sourabh Gupta, the head of the Trade and Technology programme at the Institute for China-America Studies.

“You could call it a case of the ‘new normal’ in ties taking shape, one uncoupling at a time.”

Chan argued that there is a “risk of miscalculation” where a “relatively minor action by Washington may be interpreted as a major escalation by Beijing”.

However, according to Gupta, the FCC’s “nicks and cuts” are just “a small sting each time”.

“The very fact that the administration took recourse to the FCC in the first place rather than have Commerce’s BIS issue the order – say, by dumping the Chinese vendor on the Entity List – itself suggests that the administration is attentive to avoiding miscalculation.”

item.title: [SCMP] South Korea accelerates military self-reliance over Trump’s ‘unpredictability’
item.description:
US President Donald Trump’s abrupt move to scale back annual military drills with South Korea has handed President Lee Jae Myung a fresh impetus for greater defence self-reliance even as he seeks to maintain the long-standing alliance.

Lee on Tuesday called for accelerated efforts to regain wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces from the United States and build nuclear-powered submarines, casting both as part of a broader push to boost South Korea’s ability to defend itself.

His comments reflect Seoul’s growing concern over uncertainty in its alliance with the US under an “unpredictable” president, according to analysts.
item.content:encoded:
US President Donald Trump’s abrupt move to scale back annual military drills with South Korea has handed President Lee Jae Myung a fresh impetus for greater defence self-reliance even as he seeks to maintain the long-standing alliance.

Lee on Tuesday called for accelerated efforts to regain wartime operational control (OPCON) of South Korean forces from the United States and build nuclear-powered submarines, casting both as part of a broader push to boost South Korea’s ability to defend itself.

His comments reflect Seoul’s growing concern over uncertainty in its alliance with the US under an “unpredictable” president, according to analysts.

“Ironically, President Trump’s unpredictability allows President Lee to move with greater strategic flexibility,” said Chang Yong-seok, a senior researcher at the Institute for Peace and Unification Studies at Seoul National University.

“South Korea, like many other friends, has been whipsawed by President Trump, and this is another example of his capriciousness. But this gives President Lee all the more justification to push a greater self-reliance agenda,” Chang said.

At a government cabinet meeting on Tuesday, Lee highlighted South Korea’s growing defence capabilities.

“South Korea is ranked among the world’s top five military powers and is considered one of the world’s top four defence industry powers,” Lee said.

South Korea’s defence spending was equivalent to 1.4 times North Korea’s gross domestic product, he noted.

“Considering our weapons systems and the scale of our military capabilities, our ability to defend ourselves ranks among the world’s leading countries,” Lee said. “It would not be an exaggeration to say that our capabilities are more than sufficient.”

He added that “comprehensively upgrading our operational capabilities is essential to further strengthen our defence capabilities”.

Lee urged officials to step up efforts to regain wartime OPCON within his five-year term, which ends in June 2030, in line with the government’s initial plan.

At the same time, he stressed the importance of maintaining the alliance with the US while strengthening South Korea’s defence capabilities.

“A strong alliance will further solidify the foundation of our security, while strengthening our own capabilities will increase our value and necessity as an ally,” he said.

Lee also called for accelerated progress on a nuclear-powered submarine project, describing it as a symbol of a “more constructive and stronger future for the South Korea-US alliance”.

Washington has agreed to cooperate with Seoul on acquiring the necessary reactor fuel and addressing civil-military nuclear coordination to enable South Korea to build its first nuclear-powered attack submarines in the mid-2030s.

Lee’s remarks came after Trump ordered a major reduction in the scale of the Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS), the annual South Korea-US military exercise that kicked off on Monday.

Trump said in a social media post on Sunday that the exercises were not only “costly” but also sent a “totally inappropriate and hostile” signal to North Korea. He also emphasised his “very good relationship” with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

At a press briefing on Monday, Trump claimed that Kim had responded to his requests for talks. Trump met Kim three times during his first term: in Singapore in June 2018, in Hanoi in February 2019 and at the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom in June 2019.

Asked whether he was prioritising North Korea’s interests over those of long-time US ally South Korea by scaling back the joint drills, Trump argued that he was making the security situation “much safer”.

Noting that he had recently spoken by phone with Lee, Trump said the South Korean president had declined his request for Seoul’s help regarding the war in Iran. Trump nevertheless described Lee as “very nice actually”.

Chang said he was concerned that the inconsistencies in US policy could undermine South Korea’s key projects, including the OPCON transfer, nuclear-powered submarines and the reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel, all of which required US cooperation.

“President Trump is apparently dissatisfied with Seoul’s unresponsiveness to his request for help in his war against Iran and the slow implementation of its commitment to invest US$350 billion in the United States,” he said.

“Trump has some strong cards in his hand to put pressure on South Korea,” Chang said, citing Trump’s demand for greater burden-sharing by Seoul regarding the presence of 28,000 US troops and joint military exercises in South Korea.

Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies, said Trump’s remarks were aimed not only at luring North Korea back to dialogue but also at pressuring South Korea to contribute more to US efforts to address global security challenges.

Trump’s comments came ahead of Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi’s visit to Seoul from Wednesday to Thursday. Wang is scheduled to meet Lee on Thursday.

A South Korean Foreign Ministry spokesman said Wang and his South Korean counterpart Cho Hyun would discuss “bilateral ties, the situation on the Korean peninsula, and regional and international matters”.

Wang’s visit will be his first to South Korea since 2021. His previous meeting with Cho took place in Beijing in September last year.

“Ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, this will serve as an opportunity to review the results of the full restoration of Korea-China relations and to begin in earnest preparations for the next phase and high-level exchanges,” the spokesman said.

South Korea is expected to brief Wang on Lee’s latest proposal to formally end the Korean war, which ended with an armistice rather than a peace treaty.

Lee on Saturday proposed that the two Koreas begin talks on formally ending the war and discuss ways to halt the advancement of Pyongyang’s nuclear programme, pledging to seek a peace regime on the Korean peninsula.

Pyongyang, however, has yet to respond.

“Trump appears to be emphasising that any political gains achieved through a direct deal with Kim Jong-un should belong to him. The United States is likely to object if Seoul discusses an end-of-war declaration with Wang Yi,” Yang said.

He suggested that the US should hold talks with North Korea first, followed by inter-Korean talks and eventually four-party talks involving the two Koreas, the US and China.

“With Wang Yi’s visit and China’s growing interest in Korean peninsula affairs, Seoul should also make clear to Beijing that it intends to play a role as a facilitator of US-North Korea and inter-Korean dialogue,” he said.

“It is important to establish this position clearly so that China does not seek to constrain or undermine Seoul’s diplomatic efforts.”

Doo Jin-ho, director of the Eurasia Research Centre at the Korea Research Institute for National Strategy, said given Trump’s criticism of South Korea’s insufficient contributions to the alliance as well as his tendency to link trade and security, Seoul should accede to US demands to some degree.

“President Lee wants to complete key projects such as the OPCON transfer, nuclear-powered submarines and the reprocessing of spent nuclear fuel within his official term,” Doo said.

“However, South Korea can’t proceed with these agendas without consent from Washington. That’s the stark reality.”

item.title: [SCMP] Wang Yi heads to Seoul as Trump cuts South Korea drills, opening door for China
item.description:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi is set to visit Seoul days after Donald Trump called for the US to scale back military exercises with South Korea, sending ripples of unease through American allies in Asia.

The US president posted his decision to social media on Sunday, raising questions about the durability of Washington’s security commitments in a region increasingly defined by competition with Beijing.

He offered several rationales, including cost-saving considerations, a goodwill gesture towards North Korea, and dissatisfaction with Seoul’s refusal to join the US in the war against Iran.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi is set to visit Seoul days after Donald Trump called for the US to scale back military exercises with South Korea, sending ripples of unease through American allies in Asia.

The US president posted his decision to social media on Sunday, raising questions about the durability of Washington’s security commitments in a region increasingly defined by competition with Beijing.

He offered several rationales, including cost-saving considerations, a goodwill gesture towards North Korea, and dissatisfaction with Seoul’s refusal to join the US in the war against Iran.

Observers said such moves threatened to damage alliance coordination, causing disquiet among regional partners and handing China a strategic opening to dilute America’s network of regional partnerships.

Trump posted on Sunday that he had instructed the Pentagon to scale back what he termed “inappropriate and hostile” military drills with South Korea – exercises traditionally aimed at deterring North Korea, a country he described as “unthreatening and respectful” during his time in office.

He added that he had ordered the US defence secretary to “substantially reduce” the drills, citing Seoul’s reluctance to support America’s efforts towards the “denuclearisation of the Islamic Republic of Iran”.

As Seoul and other US partners navigate the latest shocks, Wang will begin a two-day trip to Seoul on Wednesday, his first bilateral exchange trip in five years.

Trump’s call for reduced commitment came just hours before Washington and Seoul launched the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield drills, one of the two major annual exercises.

Lee Dong-gyu, a senior research fellow at The Asan Institute for Policy Studies, said Trump’s statements revealed his willingness to trade alliance security for political gains, such as re-engagement with North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, a calculation Lee said would increase Seoul’s trust deficit in its alliance with Washington.

William Yang, senior analyst for Northeast Asia at the International Crisis Group, said the statement matched Trump’s usual playbook of signalling frustration towards allies he viewed as failing to respond to US demands for support.

“While the order may be a tactical move from the US, it could undermine long-standing trust between the two countries and prompt Seoul to put more resources into hedging between Beijing and Washington,” he said.

Leif-Eric Easley, professor of international studies at Ewha Womans University in Seoul, said that curtailing joint manoeuvres risked undermining operational coordination and weakening deterrence against possible conflicts in Asia.

Experts noted that the latest remarks would unnerve regional partners such as the Philippines and Japan, saying their frictions with China left them particularly exposed.

Trump has regularly criticised US allies during his second term, intensifying concerns over the reliability of Washington’s commitments and pushing partners towards self-reliance and strategic hedging.

However, in a sign of reassurance, the US undersecretary of defence for policy, Elbridge Colby, used his first Southeast Asia tour last week to stress that Washington was not disengaging from Asia but “digging in” to maintain a favourable balance of power in the Indo-Pacific.

But he added that Washington was prioritising burden-sharing as it realised its allies “can and are prepared to do more”.

According to Yang, Washington’s allies will bear in mind the more transactional foreign policy outlook that Trump subscribes to and try to respond to demands from Washington.

Meanwhile, Lee noted that Beijing was likely to exploit the scaled-back exercises as a tool, seeking to constrain Seoul’s participation in the US alliance network and diminish America’s military footprint in the region.

“At the same time, leveraging its friendly ties with Pyongyang, China is likely to intensify both its appeasement and pressure on South Korea under the pretext of fostering a favourable environment for US-North Korea dialogue,” Lee said.

Trump’s directive has sparked anticipation of his renewed engagement with Kim, although it remains uncertain whether the North Korean leader will reciprocate – particularly as Pyongyang appears to hold more cards than at the last summits with Trump in 2018 and 2019.

Following his summit with Kim in Singapore in June 2018, Trump abruptly suspended major joint military exercises with South Korea, calling them provocative, inappropriate and too expensive.

But since the collapse of high-level diplomacy in 2019, Pyongyang has aggressively expanded its missile tests and gained more battlefield experience by sending its soldiers to take part in the Russia-Ukraine war.

Lee Choong-koo, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defence Analyses, said Trump’s directive was part of a broader US diplomatic charm offensive towards North Korea – one that might require China’s cooperation.

Seoul has long expected Beijing to play a role in bringing Pyongyang back to the negotiation table, as Pyongyang neglects Seoul’s repeated calls to improve inter-Korean relations.

“His move may encourage greater diplomatic engagement between the US and China on North Korea,” Lee Choong-koo said, adding that Beijing might welcome Trump’s announcement.

“With Foreign Minister Wang Yi expected to visit Seoul this week, China may emphasise that its support is essential to advancing South Korea’s diplomatic initiative to launch multilateral peace talks.”

On Monday, Trump told reporters that Kim had responded to his recent overtures and described the current state of communication as “very positive”. Kim has not yet commented publicly.

Easley, however, offered a more sceptical assessment. He argued that Pyongyang was not interested in talking because it was profiting from Russia’s war on Ukraine while modernising its own military.

“The Trump administration’s ongoing difficulties negotiating with Iran do not enhance its credibility with the Kim regime.”

Meanwhile, some observers pointed out that Trump’s announcement could further weaken US-led deterrence against China – a development that might work in Beijing’s favour.

The mismatch between US strategic documents on defending the first island chain and Trump’s decision on joint drills with South Korea would strengthen regional countries’ belief that they needed to adopt risk-reduction measures against the US, Yang said.

“This trend will benefit China, as it creates an opportunity for Beijing to drive a wedge between the US and its regional allies.”

The first island chain consists of several strategic arcs – stretching from Japan and Taiwan through the Philippines to Borneo – that underpin a US-aligned security architecture to check Beijing.

Although traditionally not viewed as part of the chain, South Korea, now hosting some 28,500 US troops under a decades-old alliance, is increasingly seen as the northern anchor of the chain’s defence network.

item.title: [SCMP] Philippines’ Marcos slammed over US$3b family estate tax, says ‘very busy’ with government
item.description:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has put his anti-corruption drive at the centre of his presidency, but questions over his late father’s estate taxes and the family’s past ill-gotten wealth have prompted critics to question his commitment.

Last month, Marcos pledged in his address to Congress to continue fighting alleged irregularities in flood-control projects, stressing that the campaign would be a test of whether his administration could hold even powerful allies to account.

The Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) told This Week in Asia on Tuesday that it had recovered 309.84 billion pesos (US$5.05 billion) as of June 30, describing it as ill-gotten wealth linked to the Marcos family.
item.content:encoded:
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr has put his anti-corruption drive at the centre of his presidency, but questions over his late father’s estate taxes and the family’s past ill-gotten wealth have prompted critics to question his commitment.

Last month, Marcos pledged in his address to Congress to continue fighting alleged irregularities in flood-control projects, stressing that the campaign would be a test of whether his administration could hold even powerful allies to account.
