The Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG) told This Week in Asia on Tuesday that it had recovered 309.84 billion pesos (US$5.05 billion) as of June 30, describing it as ill-gotten wealth linked to the Marcos family.

The PCGG was created in 1986 as a special agency under the Office of the President and tasked by different administrations over the decades with recovering assets that it said were stolen by the late president Ferdinand Marcos Snr, his wife Imelda Marcos and their associates.

Asked by This Week in Asia on Friday whether he had paid more than 203 billion pesos (US$3.28 billion) in estate taxes on the estate his father left after the latter died in 1989, Marcos pushed back against any suggestion that the family assets should be treated as ill-gotten.

Speaking at a forum with the Foreign Correspondents Association of the Philippines (FOCAP), Marcos said: “To characterise them as ill-gotten wealth immediately, I have to respond and say, the reason why we won [those civil forfeiture cases] we were able to prove that these were not ill-gotten.”

The estate tax issue stems from assessments made after Marcos Snr’s death, which the Supreme Court later held had become final and enforceable, leaving the estate’s executors responsible for settling them.

“I have to admit that I have neglected some of my duties as co-executor because I’ve been very busy with all the things that a president is busy with,” Marcos said. Calling it “a family matter”, he said that “matters of state and governance are a thousand times more important than any family matter”.

He added: “And that is why I leave it, I’ve left it to the lawyers.”

Marcos promised to provide his lawyers’ contact numbers, but This Week in Asia has not received a response as of Tuesday.

The Bureau of Internal Revenue, which was also contacted for comment, sent an automated reply promising to respond “as soon as possible” but has not done so to date.

Jean Franco, a political science professor at the University of the Philippines, said Marcos’ replies “are consistent with his administration’s intention to revise history and change the narrative surrounding his father’s regime”.

“Talking about the [estate tax] issue is not a ‘family’ matter. It is something that is of great public interest. Not to talk about it is to depoliticise an important issue that has haunted the country for decades.”

She said Marcos’ anti-corruption drive “would be difficult to carry out” because “the flood control scandal has not been thoroughly resolved, aside of course from the Marcoses’ historical connection to corruption”.

The August 21 Movement (Atom), a pro-democracy group formed after the 1983 assassination of opposition leader Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jnr, has also accused Marcos of trying to distort history.

“Getting to Malacanang does not entitle him to distort Philippine history. Getting to Malacanang should not give anyone, for that matter, the audacity to violate the truth,” it said in a statement.

Atom’s vice-president Bien Gonzales told This Week in Asia that the group decided to speak out because it noticed the president’s “moves to change the narrative … [and] it’s the responsibility of Atom to become the vanguards of the true essence of history”.

Marcos’ long-pending estate tax case

Ruben Carranza, a former PCGG commissioner, said that as co-executor of his father’s estate, Marcos was duty-bound to pay the more than 203 billion pesos because the Supreme Court’s decision on the matter was final and binding in 1997.

Carranza called Marcos’ assertion that none of the wealth his father left behind was ill-gotten “a lie”.

“As you reminded him, the 2003 Philippine Supreme Court decision unequivocally said that any assets of Ferdinand and Imelda Marcos beyond the US$304,000 they earned as public officials is [in the Supreme Court’s words] ‘money stolen by the Marcos spouses from the Republic of the Philippines’.”

Carranza characterised Marcos’ remarks as an admission that he had failed to meet his tax obligations while in office.

Marcos’ explanation that he had not paid because “he has been busy” with matters of state as president was also “a lie” because the tax liability had existed for decades before he took office.

“If Marcos Jnr is aware of other civil cases he claimed they ‘won,’ then he can’t claim he doesn’t know that they lost that case in 2003 and that they then lost a cascade of cases based on that 2003 decision,” Carranza said.

Another unresolved case involves Arelma, an offshore entity tied to a US case to recover the Marcos assets, which the Philippine Supreme Court also awarded to the government.

US court records describe Arelma as a Panamanian entity linked to a New York Merrill Lynch account into which Marcos deposited about US$2 million in 1972.

Carranza said Marcos was wrong to suggest the issue was long dormant, saying “he lied about [Arelma] at the forum when he said he had not heard the word ‘Arelma’ in decades”.

In a separate interview with This Week in Asia, lawyer Robert Swift, who represents victims of human rights abuses during the late dictator’s rule, said that while the Arelma case remained pending, the current president’s lawyers were no longer involved in it.

The battle over the assets is now between about 10,000 human rights victims who are seeking to enforce a US$2 billion damage suit they won in 1995 against the Marcos estate before a federal court in Hawaii, and the Philippine government, which is also seeking to enforce the 2003 Philippine Supreme Court decision forfeiting the assets in favour of the state.

Swift said the victims’ motion against Manila’s claim remained pending before a federal court in New York.

In an August 2025 ruling, John M Walker Jnr, a judge of the US Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, described Marcos Snr as “a dictator and kleptocrat...[who] stole billions of dollars from the republic and its people and used networks of foreign financial accounts and shell corporations to hide stolen funds.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore’s universities race to embrace AI as job demands transform
item.description:
After years of concern over students using artificial intelligence to cut corners, Singapore’s universities are embracing the technology, driven not just by changes in the classroom but by pressure to prepare graduates for an economy that increasingly prizes AI literacy.

But analysts say educators still face the challenge of ensuring students use AI to sharpen their critical thinking rather than relying on it for quick answers and guidance.

On August 11, the National University of Singapore (NUS) announced that its students and faculty members would have access to ChatGPT Edu, an enterprise-grade platform by OpenAI, from August 31.
item.content:encoded:
After years of concern over students using artificial intelligence to cut corners, Singapore’s universities are embracing the technology, driven not just by changes in the classroom but by pressure to prepare graduates for an economy that increasingly prizes AI literacy.

But analysts say educators still face the challenge of ensuring students use AI to sharpen their critical thinking rather than relying on it for quick answers and guidance.

On August 11, the National University of Singapore (NUS) announced that its students and faculty members would have access to ChatGPT Edu, an enterprise-grade platform by OpenAI, from August 31.

The platform would be piloted in selected courses during the initial phase and be progressively made available for other courses where AI “adds educational value and augments learning objectives”, the university said in a statement.

Other universities are also expanding the use of the technology, with many mandating AI literacy courses.

Starting this month, students at the Nanyang Technological University (NTU) were given full access to a suite of Google AI tools, including Gemini Enterprise, as part of what the institution coined an “ambitious effort to transform its undergraduate education with AI”.

The university aimed to embed AI into 40 per cent of its courses by 2030, to reach its goal of producing students who could create and work with AI agents, it said.

“So much is happening so quickly with AI, and universities are playing catch up,” said Reuben Ng, an associate professor at the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy.

There was a huge skills gap in the employment market, with many job notices requiring AI skills left unfilled, he said. “One of the key purposes of Singapore’s universities is to funnel people towards the job market, so they need to create students that have these skill sets.”

Vijayakumar Tangarasan, International Workplace Group’s country head for Malaysia, Singapore and Brunei, said most local employers were willing to “pay a premium” for AI literacy, and academic qualifications alone were no longer the focus.

“Singapore’s modern workforce demands a symbiotic combination of technological literacy and irreplaceable human qualities,” he said, highlighting the importance of technological and human skills.

“As AI becomes increasingly embedded in our daily workflows, the traditional checklist for talent is being rewritten.”

AI paradox

While critics in the education field have long worried that generative technology is eroding critical thinking, Singapore’s universities seem to have a change of heart on AI.

Aaron Thean, NUS’s deputy president of academic affairs and provost, said the institution aimed to use the tools not as replacements, but as “powerful amplifiers of human intellect, creativity and judgement”.

While the goals set out are achievable, whether AI proves a boon or bane largely depends on how it is used, according to educational experts.

If a student were to accept the first output from the prompt, the tool would become a substitute for thinking, said Ina Conradi Chavez, an associate professor at NTU’s School of Art, Design and Media. But if students were to reject, re-prompt and critique, the technology would help refine thinking, she added.

Still, Conradi highlighted several risks, such as the inability to discern AI-generated content from authorship and the acceptance of visually plausible but incorrect output.

Mutlu Cukurova, the 18th CJ Koh professor at NTU’s National Institute of Education, acknowledged that current evidence showed the technology posed more harm, potentially leading to stagnant and declining competency levels. Recent research also found that it reduced persistence, with students instinctively turning to AI to solve difficult problems, he added.

But Cukurova said AI could have a positive impact if the system were built to ask, rather than answer or solve. “Intellect, creativity and critical thinking are not by-products of access to capable tools, but outcomes of deliberate design.”

Conradi urged institutions to teach students to use AI to examine bias and train data, rather than primarily for generative or interpretive purposes. “Students who only use AI generatively will be replaced by the next generation of tools and those who learn to interrogate AI critically will not.”

She highlighted that not all AI-assisted works should be put in the same box, noting the difference in user effort between continuously refining prompts and accepting the first output.

“Public conversation collapses everything into a single category called ‘AI art’ or ‘AI use’. That framing does real damage,” she said. “The paradox is real, but often framed the wrong way.”

Evolving assessments

With chatbots producing polished essays and high-definition visuals within seconds, concerns about plagiarism and integrity have also surged.

Last year, three NTU students were penalised for academic misconduct and given zero marks for an assignment after they were found to have used generative AI tools. Their assignments had contained non-existent academic references and statistics or broken web links.

Surveillance and detection were a “losing battle”, said Curukova, who is also a professor of learning and AI at University College London.

He urged institutions to design tasks that would require students to interact with and evaluate AI and its output. “A graduate who can prompt well but cannot judge when the output is wrong, or when the task should not have been delegated at all, is not AI-competent,” he said.

NTU will be moving away from automated surveillance to assessment designs that evaluate student learning, according to local media, citing an email from the institution to its faculty last Thursday.

Recognising that the detection tools used currently were “fundamentally unreliable”, the university said it would stop using them next year.

Conradi has already shifted her assessment focus. She now evaluates her students based on documentation and oral explanations, rather than the final product alone. Her students are asked to present their works on screens or at exhibitions, and she studies how they adapt conversations about their submissions to different audiences.

She also requires students to detail their use of AI, including exact prompts, rejections and reasoning behind each input.

“Assessment built around the finished artefact alone is increasingly meaningless,” she said. “The principle is now to assess the practice, not just the product.”

Ng noted that AI had sparked a return to the pen-and-paper format in physical settings, a method which he had adopted with his students.

“There needs to be a space where people do deep thinking and work, such as journaling with a pen and paper, debating or reflecting,” he said. “We need protected time for these things which cannot be replaced by technology.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s wealthy used grey zones to avoid taxes. Have new rules painted them into a corner?
item.description:
For Sarah Wang, a Shanghai-based tax lawyer who specialises in structuring offshore trusts, most of her high-net-worth (HNW) and ultra-high-net-worth clients have hit pause on their arrangements.

“Some clients were midway through establishing offshore trusts, but now they have put their plans on hold following the new regulatory developments,” she said. “Others weighing up similar structures are also shelving their plans for the time being.”

The “new developments” in question were rules unveiled by the Ministry of Finance on July 24, which for the first time set out clear provisions governing individual income tax levies on offshore trusts.
item.content:encoded:
For Sarah Wang, a Shanghai-based tax lawyer who specialises in structuring offshore trusts, most of her high-net-worth (HNW) and ultra-high-net-worth clients have hit pause on their arrangements.

“Some clients were midway through establishing offshore trusts, but now they have put their plans on hold following the new regulatory developments,” she said. “Others weighing up similar structures are also shelving their plans for the time being.”

The “new developments” in question were rules unveiled by the Ministry of Finance on July 24, which for the first time set out clear provisions governing individual income tax levies on offshore trusts.

With China’s wealthiest individuals increasingly targeted in the country’s tax enforcement drive, tightening scrutiny of offshore trusts comes as another sign of Beijing’s long-term institutional resolve rather than a means of generating short-term liquidity.

“Mounting fiscal pressure makes it necessary for the central government to broaden the tax base,” said Ge Yuyu, a professor at the Shanghai National Accounting Institute. “Targeting HNW individuals also aligns with the country’s goal of common prosperity.”

The enactment of the new rules follows months of intensified tax enforcement actions, mainly targeting tax avoidance among the ultra-rich – including undeclared offshore revenue – as well as top online influencers.

For the wealthy, the new policy means that there is even less room for grey-zone tax avoidance. It imposes a uniform 20 per cent rate across every stage of a trust’s life cycle: the transfer of assets into the trust, annual gains stemming from asset appreciation and its eventual wind-up.

And as long as most of their income is generated within the mainland, even those who have changed their nationality remain subject to the regulations.

“Previously, the law merely required that anyone who has offshore trusts should pay tax, but it lacked detailed implementing provisions. This update fills the regulatory void,” Ge said.

I don’t expect to see any new offshore trust formations over the coming months

Sarah Wang, Shanghai tax lawyer

Are offshore trusts still trustworthy?

The three primary offshore hubs traditionally favoured by Chinese investors are the British Virgin Islands, the Cayman Islands and Bermuda, according to an article written in 2023 by He Yingxin, an official at the Sichuan branch of the State Administration of Foreign Exchange (Safe).

“That’s because those jurisdictions enjoy strong international recognition, boast a well-established legal framework and offer innovative iterations of traditional trust structures – all of which greatly facilitate offshore trust formation,” He said.

There are no official statistics tracking the total volume of offshore trusts set up by Chinese investors. However, multiple lawyers and financial industry practitioners said that setting up offshore trusts has remained popular among wealthy individuals over the past two years for three reasons: asset protection, wealth succession and – last but not least – tax planning.

An inheritance dispute within the family of the late Zong Qinghou, the billionaire founder of Chinese soft-drink giant Wahaha Group who died in 2024, shed light on the amount of wealth tycoons were able to transfer to overseas accounts. In the court case, Zong’s three children born out of wedlock sought to freeze an offshore trust worth US$1.8 billion set up in Hong Kong.

According to Hong Kong court filings, Zong Qinghou signed a letter of entrustment dated February 2, 2024, appointing his daughter Kelly Zong Fuli to act as settlor to establish three offshore family trusts for the children.

If a court ultimately validates the existence of the trusts, the finance ministry’s new rules stipulate individual income tax liabilities when transferring assets into them – with the potential bill reaching US$360 million, according to estimates from Wang, the tax lawyer. Where the trust holds financial assets, annual gains generated by such assets will also carry a 20 per cent levy.

“The regulations are stringent, perhaps too stringent,” Wang said, adding the ministry’s announcement has delivered a heavy blow to the industry, with offshore trusts losing their appeal as a vehicle for tax planning. Many of the overseas trustees she has spoken with are now taking a wait-and-see stance, she said.

“Some trustees are now considering rolling out stricter Know-Your-Client procedures for Chinese clients, especially on source of funds. It is expected that establishing offshore trusts will become more complicated for mainland individuals, with substantially more paperwork required,” Wang said. “I don’t expect to see any new offshore trust formations over the coming months.”

The central government also appears to be encouraging affluent individuals to settle their tax liabilities voluntarily.

Under the new rules, individuals who transferred assets into offshore trusts between 2023 and 2025 will receive a 90-day window to make the relevant declarations to the tax authorities and settle any outstanding liabilities without incurring late-payment penalties.

Why personal income tax?

The finance ministry’s announcement came as a jolt to players in the trust sector. But to those versed in China’s tax system, the move was widely anticipated. A common sentiment among analysts: First tighter rules for cross-border stock trading, and now this.

Since last year, authorities have called on mainland citizens to self-declare their overseas capital income dating back to 2022. Offshore earnings from stocks are subject to a 20 per cent tax on capital gains and dividends, alongside potential late fees. Official data shows taxpayers reporting overseas income settled roughly 13 billion yuan (US$1.93 billion) in additional taxes during the first five months of 2026.

The Common Reporting Standard (CRS) – an information-sharing agreement among countries’ tax authorities designed to prevent tax evasion – also facilitated the exchange of data not only on stock trading but also offshore trusts, Ge said. China committed to adopting the CRS in 2014 and began its first round of CRS exchanges in September 2018.

“In recent years, a growing number of affluent individuals have set up offshore trusts, with tax reduction being one of the prime drivers. Considering the strained fiscal situation, the policy moves by the government were inevitable,” he added.

In fact, targeting the wealthy may long have been on Beijing’s radar. He Yingxin of Safe wrote that “domestic entrepreneurs accumulate wealth with the backing of national resources – including banking loans, preferential policies from local authorities and domestic market demand. If they ‘cash out’ on the mainland and then move their wealth offshore to avoid tax obligations, it will trigger severe losses of domestic capital.”

He also singled out the Haidilao hotpot brand. Though the globally popular chain restaurant was founded in southwest China’s Sichuan province in 1994, it has essentially become Singaporean on paper.

“Even though 87.6 per cent of Haidilao’s revenue [in 2022] came from the mainland, the company’s owner and his wife are already Singaporean nationals and their assets have already been moved offshore … The company’s owner has evaded substantial personal income tax liabilities.”

Oversight has continued to intensify and expand over the past year. Jason Zhao, an insurance agent at Shanghai-based Manulife-Sinochem Life Insurance, said that several of his clients have received calls from tax authorities asking them to declare dividends from overseas insurance policies.

“Tax officials didn’t ask my clients to pay back taxes – it was just a declaration requirement for now,” Zhao added.

One professor with close ties to the State Taxation Administration (STA), who requested anonymity due to the sensitivity of the matter, said that prioritising individual income tax was a natural policy choice for the central government.

“There are essentially no other levers left for Beijing to raise additional tax revenue,” the professor said.

“The sluggish economy has ruled out bigger increases in the value-added tax (VAT), while soft auto demand is weighing on consumption tax receipts. And amid the prolonged property market slump, expanding property tax pilot programmes to more cities is off the table – that leaves only individual income tax.”

Compared with developed economies, Chinese authorities are heavily reliant on indirect methods of taxation – such as VAT – for revenue rather than direct ones such as income taxes. The country’s personal income tax, meanwhile, has a narrower taxpayer base and a lower collection compliance rate, while also imposing a heavy tax burden on income from labour and a much lighter one on capital.

But thanks to Beijing’s recent policy push, individual income tax has reclaimed its position as China’s third-largest tax category out of a total of 18 after four years, overtaking consumption tax. In the first half of 2026, personal income tax revenues topped 898 billion yuan, marking an increase of 13.1 per cent year on year.

At a press briefing on July 28, Wang Shiyu, an official at the STA, attributed this shift to three factors: a buyout capital market, fast-growing sectors such as technology, and stepped-up tax oversight targeting high-income individuals.

“We have continued to strengthen tax compliance and set up supervision,” Wang said. “For taxpayers who need to settle outstanding tax liabilities, we provide full-cycle follow-up and guidance. At the same time, we are also standardising the tax oversight of offshore gains.”

Tax administration data shows that since 2024, the top 10 per cent of earners by annual income contributed just over 90 per cent of all personal income tax declared and paid.

If your wealth fails to contribute to the domestic economy, then the government expects you to pay tax

Jason Zhao, Shanghai

How stringent is too stringent?

Nevertheless, questions remain about whether policymakers can refine the rules and make them more equitable.

For instance, suppose an individual transfers stocks worth 100 million yuan into an offshore trust. One year later, the value of those stocks doubles. But even if no action is taken with respect to the shares, the trust owner would still be liable for personal income tax on gains that exist only on paper.

“Under China’s Individual Income Tax Law, taxation on income from asset transfers hinges on two conditions: transfer of asset ownership and realisation of proceeds,” Li Xin, a lawyer at Shenzhen-based DeHeng Law Offices, wrote in a report released in late July. “Yet the new finance ministry regulations mandate levying tax on paper gains … This clearly exceeds the scope of its legal mandate.”

Currently on the mainland, both on-paper and actual capital gains from freely tradeable shares are exempt from taxation. Only the profits from selling lock-up shares and dividend income are subject to tax. For cross-border trading, however, investment gains are subject to annual tax levies.

“Onshore and offshore investments are subject to differential tax treatment. I don’t think that’s fair,” said Wang, the Shanghai-based tax lawyer.

“It appears clear that the central government aims to keep capital within the country, either to shore up the capital market or bolster consumption,” said Zhao, the insurance agent. “If your wealth fails to contribute to the domestic economy, then the government expects you to pay tax. I believe that is the underlying logic at play here.”

Lawyers and finance practitioners said HNW individuals have yet to settle on alternatives to offshore trusts and are employing a cautious approach for now.

Meanwhile, their stance on tax avoidance appears to have shifted amid the widening crackdown that has closed an increasing number of regulatory loopholes.

Wang Shiyu of the STA revealed that 99.95 per cent of taxpayers ordered to settle outstanding tax liabilities have filed their declarations, adding that “taxpayers have shown markedly stronger awareness of tax compliance.”

“There is no legitimate tax avoidance. Any tax avoidance constitutes tax evasion,” said Ge of the Shanghai National Accounting Institute.

His views were shared by a domestic entrepreneur who wished not to be identified, and whose firm is awaiting its listing on the tech-focused ChiNext board.

“There appears to be little room for tax avoidance. Any attempt may lead to retroactive tax collection later. I want to stay out of the headlines, so law-abiding tax payment makes the most sense for me,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] US transshipment ‘scam’ claims put Asean exporters in a bind
item.description:
Southeast Asian exporters may soon face a heavier burden of proof to show they are not helping Chinese goods dodge US tariffs after the White House named nine countries in the region as part of what it called a global “Shadow Transshipment Network”.

The warning came in a White House report titled “The Great Transshipment Scam”, which alleged that Chinese-origin goods were being routed through lower-tariff jurisdictions and re-entering the US market under new national identities.

Analysts said the report could create fresh uncertainty for Southeast Asian economies that had benefited from “China plus one” manufacturing, in which companies shift parts of their supply chains from China to countries such as Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.
item.content:encoded:
Southeast Asian exporters may soon face a heavier burden of proof to show they are not helping Chinese goods dodge US tariffs after the White House named nine countries in the region as part of what it called a global “Shadow Transshipment Network”.

The warning came in a White House report titled “The Great Transshipment Scam”, which alleged that Chinese-origin goods were being routed through lower-tariff jurisdictions and re-entering the US market under new national identities.

Analysts said the report could create fresh uncertainty for Southeast Asian economies that had benefited from “China plus one” manufacturing, in which companies shift parts of their supply chains from China to countries such as Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia.

But they also warned that Washington risked blurring the line between deliberate tariff evasion and legitimate supply-chain diversification.

A supply chain touching China is different from illegal transshipment

Barrett Bingley, trade specialist

“A supply chain touching China is different from illegal transshipment, and we cannot let [Peter] Navarro gaslight the region on this,” said international trade specialist Barrett Bingley, Asia regional director at the Asia-Pacific Foundation of Canada, referring to the White House trade adviser who led the report.

“A multinational corporation moving production to Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand or Indonesia can be doing real diversification, not just slapping a new label on Chinese goods.”

The 25-page report claims the United States loses “tens of billions of dollars” a year to the illegal transshipment of goods from higher-tariff countries routed through more than 40 lower-tariff jurisdictions, with much of this activity involving “Chinese-origin goods”.

It said Chinese exporters increasingly routed goods through third countries, where limited assembly, finishing, repackaging, relabelling or documentation changes “could create the appearance of a different national origin”.

Among the countries named were many of Washington’s major allies and trade partners, including nine Southeast Asian economies.

Vietnam, Malaysia, Thailand and Indonesia were flagged as among the countries with the industrial scale, logistics capacity and integration into China-linked supply chains to move large amounts of China-linked goods into US-bound trade flows.

Other regional nations – namely Singapore, Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and the Philippines – were grouped in a lower category of risk due to lower absolute transshipment volumes, but the report identified them as “attractive opportunistic targets”, citing factors such as free zones, preferential US access and limited customs enforcement capacity.

Several members of this latter group – alongside Bangladesh and Sri Lanka – were labelled “micro-hubs” for allegedly facilitating the relabelling and re-export of China-linked goods, as well as providing light assembly and export-processing services.

Singapore was separately described as a “developed logistics platform” offering advanced customs, ports, trading houses, bonded warehouses and global re-export systems to the “network”.

Burden of proof

Illegal transshipment refers to the re-routing of goods through third countries with little or no processing, typically to hide their true origin and gain better market access.

This differs from legal transshipment, which allows for the necessary loading, unloading and transfer of cargo within custom-controlled zones, as well as activities to preserve the goods’ condition.

But there is “insufficient appreciation” of a third category, according to trade specialist Julia Tijaja, a non-resident fellow at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Indonesia: goods that had gone through “substantial transformation to claim a new country of origin”.

International trade law provided little clarity on this distinction, she said, currently offering “only a general rule of thumb with no agreed non-preferential rules of origin in detail”.

For countries that had “attracted substantial Chinese investment in recent years and rely heavily on imported industrial input”, the new US report created “significant uncertainty”, said economist Ahmed Albayrak, a research associate at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre.

Nor is Washington’s proposed roll-out of AI-powered enforcement likely to resolve the ambiguity, according to Tijaja.

“The administrative burden of meeting the origin verification requirements will likely be high, both for the US and the exporting countries, and especially so for small and medium enterprises,” she said.

“While the potential of technology significantly reducing the verification cost is high, the core issue remains unaddressed, which is [defining] what the US means by transshipment.”

Bingley said Washington needed to be “much more responsible” in making a clearer distinction between deliberate attempts to flout the rules and “companies genuinely restructuring supply chains because of tariffs, costs or geopolitical risk”.

“If Washington treats every diversified supply chain as circumvention by default, it ends up penalising the economies it wants as alternatives to China,” he added.

Forced to choose?

Observers said the report represented another effort by the Trump administration to justify steep tariffs against members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations and other trade partners while attempting to reduce dependence on China – though they pushed back against the idea of a full decoupling.

Kevin Chen, an associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies who tracks US-Asean trade relations, pointed to reports of a draft US State Department letter demanding that countries choose between membership in the US-led Pax Silica coalition and the Chinese-led World AI Cooperation Organisation.

“This is part of a broader push by Washington to force Asean governments to choose between them and Beijing,” he said, referring to the recent White House report.

Given China’s cost-competitiveness and the entrenched nature of its investments in regional supply chains, Chen said serious doubts remained about the feasibility of this drive – though he predicted it “will not stop Washington from trying, and it also gives US trade officials issues to pressure their trade partners on”.

Bingley called the report “less a serious decoupling effort” than an attempt by Washington to rebuild its “tariff revenue wall against the whole world and checking harder for holes in it, albeit with a special focus on China”.

It also appeared designed to build leverage ahead of Chinese President Xi Jinping’s planned visit to Washington in September, he added.

Albayrak said trade diversion had enabled some decoupling, as reflected in rising investment in Asean, but “full separation remains extremely difficult”.

“China’s earlier rare earth export restrictions underscored how deeply the two economies remain connected,” he said. “Supply chains take years to build and any meaningful decoupling will take just as long.”

For Southeast Asian governments, Bingley said the best response to the US report would be to close “genuine customs and logistics enforcement” gaps by introducing stronger customs systems, credible rules of origin and the ability to show where value was actually being added.

Tijaja urged Asean member states to speak with one voice in the face of US pressure, despite Washington’s preference for bilateral deals rather than negotiating with the bloc as a collective.

“This is a shared concern for the region that is not going away any time soon,” she said. “But it should not stop Asean countries from coordinating with each other to arrive at a consistent shared position, including also with other partners many of whom are also implicated by the report.”

She said Asean needed to demonstrate its commitment to policing illegal transshipment while at the same time clearly communicating “that just because the exports contained China-linked goods, it does not automatically mean there are illegal transshipments”.

“It is important for Asean to work together on this so as not to end up with fragmented or variable rules of origin that would defeat Asean’s own regional economic integration agenda,” Tijaja said.

item.title: [SCMP] Trump’s decision to scale back South Korea drills unsettles Asian allies: ‘makes no sense’
item.description:
President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea does not just slight a long-time ally but raises broader concerns about the security interests of the United States in Asia and elsewhere.

Trump explained his decision by citing South Korea’s refusal to join his war against Iran and pointing to what he said was his good relationship with North Korea’s reclusive dictator Kim Jong-un, a transactional and personal approach to foreign policy that has defined the Republican’s presidency.

“There is no American interest that I can see in this,” said Dan Fried, an assistant secretary of state for European affairs in the George W. Bush administration. “On all levels it makes no sense. It undermines the South Koreans, undermines the Japanese, frightens the Taiwanese, unnerves Nato and emboldens the Chinese, not to mention the North Koreans.”
item.content:encoded:
President Donald Trump’s decision to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea does not just slight a long-time ally but raises broader concerns about the security interests of the United States in Asia and elsewhere.

Trump explained his decision by citing South Korea’s refusal to join his war against Iran and pointing to what he said was his good relationship with North Korea’s reclusive dictator Kim Jong-un, a transactional and personal approach to foreign policy that has defined the Republican’s presidency.

“There is no American interest that I can see in this,” said Dan Fried, an assistant secretary of state for European affairs in the George W. Bush administration. “On all levels it makes no sense. It undermines the South Koreans, undermines the Japanese, frightens the Taiwanese, unnerves Nato and emboldens the Chinese, not to mention the North Koreans.”

Trump’s decision to side with North Korea, which strongly objects to the annual joint military exercises, was “firmly in the ‘hard-to see-how-it-could-be-worse’ category”, said Danny Russel, former assistant secretary of state for East Asia and the Pacific in Barack Obama’s administration.

Trump is punishing an ally while encouraging an adversary

Danny Russel, a scholar at the Asia Society Policy Institute

“It is tragically upside-down. Trump is punishing an ally while encouraging an adversary,” said Russel, now a scholar at the Asia Society Policy Institute in New York. “He is protecting Kim Jong-un’s sensitive feelings from an unfriendly signal at the expense of US-South Korean security.”

Trump on Sunday ordered the US military to downsize the 11-day Ulchi Freedom Shield exercises, which began on Monday as scheduled. It is not known which parts of the training are being scaled back.

His announcement baffled many in South Korea, which has been closely allied with the US for decades and where national security is a top priority due to threats from nuclear-armed North Korea.

It also drew instant criticism from many Democrats in Congress. “Treating one of America’s closest allies like an adversary weakens our alliances and benefits China and North Korea,” Representative Greg Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said in a statement.

Japanese Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said Tuesday Tokyo strongly supported joint security cooperation with key defence backer Washington and neighbour Seoul.

“As Japan faces the most severe and complicated security environment in the post-war era, the cooperation among Japan, the United States and South Korea is critical to the peace and stability of the region,” Koizumi said during a visit to Australia.

His Australian counterpart, Richard Marles, said Canberra was “very concerned about North Korea’s nuclear programme as well as its missile programme, and we have consistently made that point”.

South Korean officials have said the exercises had begun as planned and that they hoped the personal chemistry between Trump and Kim would bring them back to talks. Seoul’s presidential office said on Tuesday the drills did not reflect “any intention to attack North Korea or escalate tensions on the Korean peninsula”.

Its unification ministry – responsible for relations with the North – said it could not confirm whether communications between Kim and Trump had taken place. “While communication channels between the two sides exist, we cannot verify the specific content of the exchanges,” it said.

‘Great respect’

Trump on Monday doubled down, posting a photo of North Korea’s leader speaking on a phone. The caption read: “Hey Donald … We cool, right?”

Asked by a reporter in the Oval Office on Monday if Kim had replied to entreaties for talks, Trump said “he has”, without elaborating. The president called the development “very positive”. The White House declined to provide further details.

“Kim Jong-un has always treated me with great respect,” Trump said. “I understand him; he understands me.”

Retired US Ambassador Robert Wood, who served under Republican and Democratic presidents, said the joint military exercises were critical to deterring North Korea, which has shunned any talks with the US over its nuclear programme and has accelerated weapons testing.

“We also don’t want South Korea to draw the conclusion that a nuclear weapons capability is the only guarantee it has to ensure its security,” Wood said.

Matthew Kroenig, who previously served in defence and intelligence positions in Republican and Democratic administrations, said polls show that South Koreans had increasingly supported the idea of pursuing their own nuclear weapons.

“The United States has been working really hard to try to persuade South Korea that they are protected,” said Kroenig, who is now with the Atlantic Council, a Washington think tank. Scaling back the exercises “potentially undermines that message”.

Trump’s turnabout came even after the South Koreans worked to flatter the American president, eager to gain favour on critical issues such as trade and defence.

As soon as he sat down for his meeting with Trump last year, new President Lee Jae Myung praised the Oval Office’s elaborate decor. Laying it on thick, Lee affirmed Trump’s assertion that Kim would not have pursued his nuclear ambitions had Trump won a second consecutive term in 2020, while dangling the prospect of an eventual Trump Tower in North Korea.

Trump just hours earlier had appeared to show sympathy for Lee’s predecessor, Yoon Suk-yeol, who had been ousted from office after imposing martial law in December 2024.

On Tuesday, Lee’s office said the Ulchi exercise was defensive and not intended to attack the North or raise tensions.

Removing umbrella

Charles Kupchan, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, said Trump’s scaling back of the exercises might prompt long-time allies to think more about their own security without US help.

“They are hoping that the American umbrella is there for the future,” said Kupchan, who worked on the National Security Council under Democratic presidents Bill Clinton and Obama, “but they have to at least contemplate the idea that Uncle Sam won’t be there for them”.

Kupchan said Trump was not mistaken in wanting to have South Korea, as well as the Europeans, contribute more to their defence. But, he said, the president’s unpredictable approach cut through the solidarity that undergirded those alliances “because he ends up insulting allies”.

Fried said Trump seemed unwilling to “take a win” after browbeating Nato members and Asian allies into increasing their defence spending.

“Nato is building up, South Korea is building up, Japan is building up. Trump has a problem with taking the win,” said Fried, who is currently at the Atlantic Council. “It’s like he wants to burn it all down.”

John Herbst, a former ambassador to Ukraine under president George W. Bush, said the Korea decision showed how inconsistent the Trump administration could be in its policy pronouncements. But in general, he said, the US had maintained long-term alliances.

“If these things grow in frequency and in importance, obviously we will be in the process of taking apart the alliance system, which has served us so well since the end of World War II,” said Herbst, who also is with the Atlantic Council. “But despite some statements which seem to head in that direction, we have not headed there in a consistent, strong way.”

Kupchan agreed. While the president’s language could be taken as “we’re done with you”, he said, “the reality is that, at least as of today, Trump has left intact America’s forward bases and its core alliance relationships”.

Whether Trump’s message to South Korea will amount to a meaningful policy change or a fleeting social media post is up in the air.

“He’s an unpredictable president,” Kroenig said. “If we move on and the exercises go as planned and we never hear anything about this again, I wouldn’t be surprised.”

Additional reporting by Bloomberg, Reuters

item.title: [SCMP] Can Indonesia build on rising EV demand to become a production powerhouse?
item.description:
Indonesia’s next electric-vehicle push will test whether President Prabowo Subianto can turn rising demand, nickel wealth and consumer subsidies into an integrated domestic industry that captures more value at home, or merely make imported and locally assembled EVs cheaper to buy.

Analysts warn that without stricter local-content rules and stronger links between nickel processing, battery production and vehicle assembly, the incentives risk reinforcing Indonesia’s role as a large EV market rather than moving it up the supply chain.

Prabowo gave the agenda a public stage on August 13, when he marked the production of the 20,000th electric motorcycle at ALVA’s factory in Cikarang, West Java, and called on the manufacturer’s parent company, Indika Energy, to raise output to 200,000 units and eventually 2 million.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesia’s next electric-vehicle push will test whether President Prabowo Subianto can turn rising demand, nickel wealth and consumer subsidies into an integrated domestic industry that captures more value at home, or merely make imported and locally assembled EVs cheaper to buy.

Analysts warn that without stricter local-content rules and stronger links between nickel processing, battery production and vehicle assembly, the incentives risk reinforcing Indonesia’s role as a large EV market rather than moving it up the supply chain.

Prabowo gave the agenda a public stage on August 13, when he marked the production of the 20,000th electric motorcycle at ALVA’s factory in Cikarang, West Java, and called on the manufacturer’s parent company, Indika Energy, to raise output to 200,000 units and eventually 2 million.

The event launched what Prabowo and the government described as a “national electric-motorcycle ecosystem”, with a government release saying the initiative would include lower instalment rates and zero down payments.

Prabowo also said Indonesia aimed to begin mass production of home-grown electric cars no later than 2028.

The bigger test will come with a separate EV stimulus package, which officials have said will be announced shortly and is expected to set the rules for which vehicles, battery types and local producers receive support.

In his 2027 budget address on Friday, Prabowo linked those consumer incentives to industrial policy, promising support for domestic electric-motorcycle production and outlining plans for a wider supply chain covering batteries, components, software and after-sales services.

“Electric motorcycle subsidies and probably later electric cars will create markets for the national industry,” Prabowo said.

The key question is how far the eligibility rules will support local factories, component suppliers, battery production, technology transfer and jobs, rather than only reducing the cost of vehicles already on the market.

Earlier this month, officials said the stimulus would cover about 500,000 electric motorbikes and focus on products creating high value in Indonesia, but domestic-content (TKDN) requirements were still being finalised.

Purchasing incentives

The incentives being considered include a full exemption from the luxury goods sales tax and a government-borne value added tax incentive of 40 per cent for eligible models.

The relief would apply strictly to battery EVs, excluding hybrids and plug-in hybrid types. Battery composition was also confirmed as a criterion, with officials weighing whether to favour nickel-based batteries over other chemistries.

The Association of Indonesia Automotive Industries (Gaikindo) recorded sales of 69,739 battery EV units in the first half of 2026, an 80.8 per cent year-on-year increase for the category.

A July 15 report by Detikoto, an Indonesian car news portal, based on Gaikindo sales data, showed the top five brands dominating the national EV market were BYD at 30.73 per cent, followed by Jaecoo at 24.36 per cent, then Geely, Wuling and GAC Aion.

These figures indicate a rapidly expanding market where consumer incentives could play a decisive role.

In May, the Indonesian Business Council said electric motorcycle sales exceeded 100,000 units in 2024 for the first time but fell to 55,059 the next year after the previous subsidy programme – at 7 million rupiah (US$393) per unit – ended.

“This shows that public interest is growing, but affordability remains a key factor in consumer decisions,” the council said.

Missing segments

For analysts, the bigger question is whether fresh incentives can draw more production into Indonesia, rather than simply accelerate sales in a market still led by foreign brands.

Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Centre of Economic and Law Studies, said Indonesia had developed nickel processing at one end of the chain and vehicle assembly at the other without building enough of the stages between them.

“There is a hollow in the middle of the whole nickel supply chain,” Bhima said.

The entry of Chinese carmakers expanded the Indonesian market but had not yet been sufficiently connected to other parts of the country’s industrial ecosystem, he added. “We are just the market. We are not the producers that gain more value-added from this EV penetration.”

Bhima said much of the new vehicle investment concentrated in assembly, while EV and battery investment was capital-intensive and had a lower employment multiplier than Indonesia’s established automotive industry and its network of component makers and service businesses.

Indonesia does have vehicle and battery manufacturing projects in the works, including Hyundai and Wuling electric-car plants in Cikarang, HLI Green Power’s battery-cell facility in Karawang and planned ventures involving Indonesia Battery Corporation, CATL, Antam and a Chinese group led by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt.

But analysts said the existence of large projects did not show whether Indonesia was creating enough local suppliers, skilled jobs or technology transfer across the middle of the supply chain.

There is also a battery-chemistry question.

Bhima said many Chinese EVs entering Indonesia used lithium iron phosphate batteries and other chemistries, rather than nickel-based ones, meaning the technology did not match Indonesia’s nickel-based strategy.

Energy and Mineral Resources Minister Bahlil Lahadalia said earlier this month the government was considering differentiated incentives for nickel-based compositions, such as nickel-manganese-cobalt batteries.

Siwage Dharma Negara, a senior fellow and co-coordinator of the Indonesia Studies Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said the proposed stimulus should be understood in two stages.

“The short-term objective is basically to reduce fuel-subsidy consumption. To promote the industry, it is going to take some time,” Siwage said.

Large investment figures, he said, did not by themselves show how many jobs or domestic suppliers would be created because mineral-processing and battery projects were capital-intensive and did not need such a large workforce.

That puts more weight on TKDN regulations, which are meant to push carmakers towards local sourcing.

Currently, locally produced electric cars must reach a minimum of 40 per cent TKDN through 2026, 60 per cent from 2027 to 2029 and 80 per cent from 2030 onwards, according to a Gaikindo summary of the regulations.

Siwage said enforcement could end up being “more flexible” if companies failed to meet commitments and the government worried about losing investment, tax revenue or employment. “The goalposts keep moving. They try to make it more flexible, and of course that makes it less credible.”

Indonesia’s approach contrasts with Thailand’s EV3.5 plan, which uses escalating production obligations requiring manufacturers to build two domestic units for every imported EV in 2026 and three in 2027.

“Thailand has greater bargaining power because it offers an established supplier network, supporting infrastructure and a mature automotive cluster. Thailand has also become a production hub for hybrid vehicles,” Siwage said.

Bhima also pointed to Vietnam, which offered workforce capability, greater policy certainty and simpler bureaucracy.

“Without a more integrated industrial policy,” he said, “Indonesia risks remaining a large consumer market, or a supplier of raw or processed materials, rather than developing the middle of the EV supply chain.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why Siberia’s warming landscape could shatter Trump’s Arctic ambitions
item.description:
As the United States, Russia and China race to turn a melting Arctic into the world’s next major economic gateway, their strategic ambitions face a hidden threat: thawing permafrost.

Since returning to office last year, US President Donald Trump has pushed to expand America’s Arctic footprint. This includes investing in icebreakers to counter Russian and Chinese shipping ambitions, unlocking natural resources in Alaska and renewing efforts to buy or annex Greenland.

Yet, as the three powers vie for control of Arctic sea lanes and minerals, rapidly thawing permafrost in Russia’s Siberia could derail their plans. According to a new international study led by Chinese scientists, the massive cost of collapsing ground threatens to overshadow the region’s economic potential.
item.content:encoded:
As the United States, Russia and China race to turn a melting Arctic into the world’s next major economic gateway, their strategic ambitions face a hidden threat: thawing permafrost.

Since returning to office last year, US President Donald Trump has pushed to expand America’s Arctic footprint. This includes investing in icebreakers to counter Russian and Chinese shipping ambitions, unlocking natural resources in Alaska and renewing efforts to buy or annex Greenland.

Yet, as the three powers vie for control of Arctic sea lanes and minerals, rapidly thawing permafrost in Russia’s Siberia could derail their plans. According to a new international study led by Chinese scientists, the massive cost of collapsing ground threatens to overshadow the region’s economic potential.

Warming in the Arctic is occurring almost four times faster than the global average. This phenomenon, known as Arctic amplification, has triggered a rapid thaw of the permafrost that covers most of the region.

Permafrost refers to the ground in cold regions that has stayed at a temperature below 0 degrees Celsius (32 degrees Fahrenheit) for at least two consecutive years, and its melting could release a huge amount of greenhouse gas that pushes temperatures even higher.

Around 46 per cent of the northern hemisphere’s permafrost is in Siberia.

By 2050, higher methane emissions as a result of permafrost thaw and increasing wildfires in Siberia could offset 20 per cent of the global methane reduction required to meet our climate targets, according to the study led by the Chinese Academy of Sciences and published in the peer-reviewed journal Science on August 6.

Methane is the second most abundant human-made greenhouse gas after carbon dioxide, but it is more than 28 times more potent at trapping heat in the atmosphere, according to the US Environmental Protection Agency.

Increasing methane emissions from thawing permafrost could result in a “climate-carbon feedback” loop – a cycle where permafrost degradation releases greenhouse gases that in turn further amplify climate change.

“Global targets to keep global mean temperatures below even 2 degrees Celsius of preindustrial values will be compromised, even if only a fraction of the carbon presently stored in permafrost thaws and is released to the atmosphere,” the team said.

On the ground across the Arctic, the consequences of losing permafrost are already unfolding. This includes land subsidence, landslides, soil volume loss, coastal erosion, and shifting of land from terrestrial to aquatic, because much of the region’s land is bound together by ice.

Thawing permafrost not only alters the natural landscape, but also poses a major threat to human infrastructure, according to a study published in the peer-reviewed journal Polar Science in June last year. Buildings, roads, railways, airports, pipelines, oilfields, and mines are already being affected by the current state of thaw.

By the middle of the century, about 69 per cent of fundamental circumpolar infrastructure, including industrial facilities, is at risk of damage, according to the researchers from Paris-Saclay University, the Helmholtz Centre for Polar and Marine Research, and research centre Nordregio.

They found that thawing across the entire Arctic circumpolar permafrost region – across Russia, Canada, Alaska, Denmark, Greenland, Norway, Finland, Sweden and Iceland – could result in tens of billions of dollars in economic losses by mid-century.

Russia, which has both the largest permafrost area and the most infrastructure built on its permafrost, is the most at risk of economic loss. This includes its mining, oil and gas operations, a critical corner of the country’s economy.

Alaska is another region that could face major losses, with permafrost present on about 80 per cent of its land surface.

The Polar Science study said there were advantages to a de-iced Arctic, including reduced heating costs, diminishing sea ice allowing for more marine and coastal development, the expansion of agricultural land and the potential to exploit more local resources.

Russia highlighted some potential positive consequences in a 2020 national action plan for climate change adaptation, including “improved conditions for transporting cargo in the Arctic seas” and greater access to the country’s extended continental shelf.

The icy Northern Sea Route – the shortest passage between the Asia-Pacific and Western Eurasia – is becoming navigable for longer periods each year because of global warming.

As the world witnesses multiple shipping crises, from the Suez Canal to the Strait of Hormuz, the promise of an alternative Arctic sea lane emerging from under the ice has drawn intense interest from Russia, China and the US.

Trump says he wants to acquire Greenland, an autonomous territory of Denmark, for “national security” reasons.

However, some believe his interest in Greenland and the wider Arctic is driven by lucrative, untapped natural resources below the ice, which will become easier to exploit as the region warms.

According to the US National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), Greenland is not immune to permafrost thaw, which threatens infrastructure as the ground grows unstable and prone to collapse. Hotter conditions could also create more vegetation and peat fuel for wildfires.

For any mining ambitions in the Arctic, the Red Dog mine in Alaska – one of the largest zinc mines in the world and a major local employer – serves as a cautionary tale.

Thawing permafrost has increased particulate levels in the creek where the mine pumps its treated waste water. As a result, downstream levels have surged above regulatory limits despite no change in the mine’s actual discharge, according to a report by the Alaska Beacon in December.

To resolve the issue, operator Teck Resources may need to spend hundreds of millions of dollars and up to a decade to develop a solution, such as a waste-water pipeline to the ocean.

Last week, Trump withdrew federal support for the Arctic Report Card – an annual report on issues such as changing sea ice and thawing permafrost that NOAA has published for two decades, according to the Alaska Beacon on August 12.

In Russia, fossil fuel producers have spent years adapting to thawing permafrost – taking steps such as driving foundation piles deeper into the ground and investing in technology to keep the ground frozen to avoid disrupting operations.

Thawing permafrost also poses a risk to human health. It can mobilise environmental contaminants like the heavy metal mercury and pathogens such as emerging infectious diseases that would otherwise have remained trapped in ice, according to the Polar Science paper.

In 2016, an anthrax outbreak in northwestern Siberia’s Yamal district that killed more than 2,300 reindeer and resulted in the death of a young boy was linked to the thawing of the bacteria from permafrost, according to Russian news agency Tass.

Another Polar Science paper published in June last year noted that the Russian invasion of Ukraine had made permafrost thaw mitigation more challenging, with Russian-Western joint research suspended and Western scientists denied access to vital Russian monitoring stations.

Data collection is crucial for properly monitoring the permafrost carbon feedback mechanism and anticipating climate tipping points, but this break in collaboration is a “serious blind spot” for the Western scientific community, according to the researchers from UiT The Arctic University of Norway and France’s School for Advanced Studies in the Social Sciences.

Moscow’s most recent national action plan for climate adaptation, approved in June, targets key challenges including permafrost degradation and infrastructure resilience in thawing regions.

According to the Norway-France team, Russia is supporting the development of a state-run permafrost monitoring system and increasing monitoring infrastructure to measure emissions.

While localised measures such as rewilding and adaptive infrastructure can delay thawing, the consensus among scientists is that curbing global warming is the only viable long-term defence against widespread permafrost thaw.

item.title: [SCMP] Word on the StrEAT: 6 Hong Kong chefs share pre-service rituals that fuel their kitchens
item.description:
Before the first ticket lands, every restaurant team prepares for a night of service in its own way. In kitchens where the pace can shift from quiet to chaotic in minutes, those final moments are crucial for getting mentally and physically ready.

From espresso shots and sparkling water to staff karaoke, rotating playlists and meticulous station checks, rituals – both practical and personal – help chefs set the tone for the hours ahead. Here, chefs from across Hong Kong’s dining scene share the routines, superstitions and small acts of self-care that help them find focus before their doors open.

Chef Tony Mok, Path
item.content:encoded:
Before the first ticket lands, every restaurant team prepares for a night of service in its own way. In kitchens where the pace can shift from quiet to chaotic in minutes, those final moments are crucial for getting mentally and physically ready.

From espresso shots and sparkling water to staff karaoke, rotating playlists and meticulous station checks, rituals – both practical and personal – help chefs set the tone for the hours ahead. Here, chefs from across Hong Kong’s dining scene share the routines, superstitions and small acts of self-care that help them find focus before their doors open.

Chef Tony Mok, Path

“We have a fairly small team of four – including [a] dishwasher! We [start the night] by greeting everyone and checking on each other. Show a bit of love to everyone.

“The playlist changes from Cantopop to more casual lofi pop songs like Keshi. Andy Hui is one of Sean’s (our Texan GM’s) favourites. Our team ritual is to sing together. It opens up our voice more before the night starts. ⁠After service begins, we are definitely more locked in to serve our guests.

“We also always stash gummies inside our kitchen to sweeten our service – a bit of a sugar rush also helps!”

Chef Sean Yuen, Jija by Vicky Lau

“Five minutes before service is the ‘calm before the storm’. Everyone is running their final checks, and the air is noticeably tense. I review tonight’s cover count, find out when the peak hour hits, and check for any VIPs or special dietary requirements. Once I have those numbers in mind, the rhythm of the night becomes completely clear.

“Downing a shot of espresso right before service not only wakes me up, but also acts as a mental trigger to switch into battle mode. [We] turn on all the heat lamps at the pass and the moment those lights go on, it means all the prep work is done.

“One hour into service, everyone is fully in the zone – hyper-focused, with the entire kitchen running at a fast yet meticulously organised pace. During peak rush hours, taking a two-second break to grab a sip of water gives me a quick moment to pause, clear my mind, and jump straight back into position.”

Chef Tara Margarita, Bourke’s

“Music is essential for us. Kitchens get hot and high-stress, so the right tunes keep the energy light during prep before the inevitable service rush. Anyone in hospitality knows the absolute pain of listening to the exact same pre-service loop for years on end. We’re lucky to have a diverse team with different cultural backgrounds, so we like to rotate the prep-DJ duties.

“If I’m on the aux, my recent go-to tracks are ‘Summer Romance’ by Incubus, ‘Given Up’ by Linkin Park and ‘Killing in the Name’ by Rage Against the Machine.

“Work is intense, but work isn’t life – it’s important not to lose sight of that. So personally, I always make time to stretch and check in with my team on a human level.

“On fully staffed days, those last five minutes are pure ‘calm before the storm’ and your final chance to double-check line set-ups or fire off last-minute backups. I change into my shift shoes and jacket and pull my hair back in a way that’s guaranteed to hold up for the next 14 hours.

“During service, front of house has made a habit of buying me Kinder Buenos – especially if I’m looking a bit stressed on the pass. I keep a dedicated 1/9 pan in my lowboy [refrigerator] stocked with bite-sized Kinder Buenos to get through the push.”

Chef Ryo Matsui, Torikaze Hong Kong

“Before anything else, I want to see, touch and taste what has arrived that day. It tells me how we need to cook.

“We make sure every station is clean, organised and complete. It may sound simple, but this is important – the state of your station reflects the state of your mind. I need to see the charcoal glowing properly and have my fan beside the grill. The fire is alive, and it changes constantly, so the fan is not only a tool to control the heat; it is how I communicate with it. When the binchotan is ready, the whole station feels ready.

“There is a quiet tension. Everyone is focused on their own station, checking small details one more time. [Then] the kitchen becomes more fluid – less thinking, more instinct. Communication is shorter, movements become more precise, and the team finds its rhythm together.

“When it becomes busy, I return to the next plate. Not the whole service, not the tickets waiting behind it, just the dish in front of me. You cannot control everything at once, but you can always control the quality of the next action.”

Chef Uwe Opocensky, Petrus

“As a junior cook, I was on a station, and being ‘ready’ meant my mise en place was perfect and I was set for whatever came at me during service. These days I run the pass, so readiness looks different. It’s less about my own station and more about checking that everyone else is ready and everything is exactly where it should be.

“The first thing I always do is greet everyone; that sets the tone for the whole day. Then I do a walk-through to see what’s going on: checking the bookings, events and anything that may have changed since the night before. After that, I sit down with my senior chefs and go through notes I’ve written the night before – ideas, things we could do better, things I think we can improve on. It’s important to me that the day starts with the team, not just with the food.

“Consistency is the ritual. I go over the booking sheet one more time. I check that everything is set up and ready – down to the tasting spoons and seat numbers. Then I get a large glass of sparkling water for myself before service starts. By the time I step through the doors of Petrus, I’m focused.

“The one constant through all of it has been a small espresso. It’s less about the caffeine and more about the signal; it’s my way of telling myself I’m ready to go.”

Chef Alex Fargas, La Paloma

“I believe every dish matters, and every person we work with and serve matters. Every day at 5pm we hold a team meeting. We dedicate the first 20 minutes to discussing the previous day’s situations and focusing on customer satisfaction. The next 20 minutes are dedicated to staff training, motivation and development. Finally, the last 10 minutes are spent discussing personal healthy habits, life goals or any important matters anyone has on their mind.

“We take that time to connect, share how we’re feeling, and discuss what we are aiming to achieve on that particular day.

“We set clear objectives for every day and week, assigning both individual and team goals. This keeps everyone connected, aligned with our targets, and fully engaged during our daily meetings.

“We take it one dish and one person at a time, ensuring we give everything the attention it needs to achieve excellence. One step at a time – that’s how we operate at La Paloma.”

item.title: [SCMP] Making tracks through China’s past and present
item.description:
“Peking wore the green lace of spring, its thousands of willows and imperial cypresses making the Forbidden City a place of wonder and enchantment,” American journalist Edgar Snow wrote of Beijing in 1936.

Ninety years later, strolling before the vermillion ramparts of the Forbidden City, it’s clear that Beijing’s mass conversion to electric vehicles has rendered the city not only cleaner than it has been of late, but also quieter – allowing Zhongshan Park to bloom much as Snow described.

Snow’s description was included in his wartime account of a journey to Yanan, Red Star Over China (first published in 1937), his destination then being the base of the Chinese Communist Party. But the city has made headlines much more recently, with the December opening of the Xian-Yanan high-speed railway taking the length of China Railway’s operational network past the 50,000km (31,070 miles) mark.
item.content:encoded:
“Peking wore the green lace of spring, its thousands of willows and imperial cypresses making the Forbidden City a place of wonder and enchantment,” American journalist Edgar Snow wrote of Beijing in 1936.

Ninety years later, strolling before the vermillion ramparts of the Forbidden City, it’s clear that Beijing’s mass conversion to electric vehicles has rendered the city not only cleaner than it has been of late, but also quieter – allowing Zhongshan Park to bloom much as Snow described.

Snow’s description was included in his wartime account of a journey to Yanan, Red Star Over China (first published in 1937), his destination then being the base of the Chinese Communist Party. But the city has made headlines much more recently, with the December opening of the Xian-Yanan high-speed railway taking the length of China Railway’s operational network past the 50,000km (31,070 miles) mark.

It took Snow more than two days to cover the 1,000km (621 miles) from Beijing to Xian by rail, but China’s 21st century public transport will make my own pilgrimage to Yanan, with some history-imbued detours along the way, far smoother.

With tickets bought online, I set my sights first on Jinan, the capital of Shandong province, located on the upper reaches of the Yellow River and 400km (249 miles) to the south of Beijing.

At the massive, oval-domed Beijing South station, I board a G-class train that makes light work of the Central Plain, rocketing across an area the size of Paraguay characterised by undulating wheat and rapeseed-flower fields. It takes just over two hours to reach the far side of the mighty Yellow River, a reminder that Beijing was one of the few ancient Chinese cities that were not fed by the “mother river”.

Jinan’s urban district stands to the south of the river. First impressions upon arrival at dusk are of a typical second-tier city composed chiefly of modern high-rises strung together by flyovers. My mood isn’t much improved by the hotel I pre-booked, which is located down a gloomy Shizhong district alley, past street-side barbecue joints populated by drunks, with electrical wires dangling overhead and between adverts for spas and KTV (karaoke television) lounges. The labyrinth of hotel corridors has tobacco-stained carpets and room service comes courtesy of R2-D2-like robots.

Morning illuminates Jinan in a better light.

A short walk leads to Wulongtan (“Five Dragon Pond”), a classical garden comprising several natural springs. It was mentioned in the Spring and Autumn Annals, the official chronicle of the state of Lu (1042BC-249BC), which existed here before the unification of China under Qin Shi Huang.

Bamboo-lined pathways lead between concave-roofed pavilions and goldfish ponds sprinkled with water lilies. Some park-goers are writing classical verses in calligraphic characters on the ground with giant brushes dipped in water, while a group of aunties practises a traditional sword dance beside a man who, unfazed by their music, drifts through the elegant postures of tai chi.

Wulongtan is one of several public gardens fed by spring water that dominate Jinan and help explain its motto, splashed on numerous billboards: “City of springs, no worries for people”.

To the north, the Jinan Baili Huanghe Scenic Area flanks the south bank of the Yellow River, which, in truth, is more of a coffee colour. Here, elders stretch while courting couples watch the sunset from viewing points along the river’s edges. Farmers still cultivate the muddy riverbanks, using nutrient-rich loess soil that has flowed down from Shaanxi province to feed rows of green vegetables, as they and their ancestors have done since the dawn of Chinese civilisation.

Following the riverfront path eastwards leads to the Luokou Yellow River Railway Bridge. Conventional rolling stock still uses this century-old, German-built viaduct, which was completed in 1912.

Also of German vintage in Jinan are a few villas, a colonial-era post office and the former station house on the Jiaoji Railway – Shandong’s first railway, which connected with the port of Qingdao.

Jiaoji Railway Station, which now houses a museum, was completed in 1915 and built in early European Renaissance Revival style. It is distinguished by a prominent central colonnade beneath a large clock. The line itself has been modernised and no longer leaves from the station-turned-museum, but from Daminghu station, near Daming Lake Park.

Unfortunately, the art nouveau Jinan Railway Station depicted in the museum, and which stood 500 metres (1,640 feet) from Jiaoji station, came to be regarded as “a symbol of colonialism” and was replaced by an unexceptional building in 1992. It’s from here that I depart for Taian, just a 20-minute hop away by high-speed rail.

Taian would be an unremarkable provincial city were it not for a mountain considered so sacred for so many centuries, it has assumed the status of a god.

Mount Tai is the easternmost of China’s nine Daoist peaks, attracting up to a million pilgrims a year, who attempt to follow the emperors’ journey 8km (five miles) up the mountainside, paying homage to Heaven and Earth, at the summit and foot of the mountain, respectively.

I set out early to beat the crowds, but my 6am hotel alarm call is not early enough; everyone else has made the same calculation. It’s not so much a hike, then, as a communal walk along stone steps carved out of the mountainside as far back as Qin times, some two millennia ago.

Amid cypress trees and gushing streams, every rock we pass has been inscribed with poetic verse and it becomes apparent that the passage from the First Heavenly Gate to Jade Emperor Peak owes its glories – the temples and pavilions – to the patronage of the imperial court.

Past the Immortal Bridge, a natural formation of three huge boulders, the ascent to the Nantian Gate, some 1,500 metres (4,920 feet) above sea level, funnels hundreds of walkers between two walls of rock. Almost everyone is grasping the handrails as they haul themselves upwards at this point, cries of “jia you” (“add oil”) ringing out as pilgrims encourage one another to keep going.

There’s more than a sense of achievement to reward those who make it to the top of the mountain, where Tianjie (“Heaven Street”), a tourist strip with plenty of restaurants, awaits hungry hikers.

Unashamedly, I take the cable car back down to Earth, and the following day, I take the morning train to Kaifeng, in Henan province. There’s no fast service between the two cities, so I’m relegated to a second-class bunk in a half-full carriage, a sign that conventional rail might be dying out in the age of high-speed.

My fellow passengers are all tall northerners, their skin cracked by the sun of the high latitudes. Men in leather jackets and tightly fitting shirts walk back and forth along the gangway at 20-minute intervals, to find somewhere to smoke; women fondle their Xiaomi phones. Over seven hours of rail travel, there’s little to do but meditate on China’s heartland passing gently by while sipping tea and dipping into Red Star Over China.

Kaifeng is depicted in one of China’s great masterworks, Along the River During the Qingming Festival, a 12th century scroll painting that hangs in Beijing’s Palace Museum, as the Forbidden City is officially known, and reveals the bustling street markets and classical architecture of the capital of the Northern Song dynasty (960-1127) in its imperial heyday. The view from my taxi suggests the contemporary prefecture-level city is a few centuries past its prime: Soviet-style tenements jockey for space with modern towers, all of which appear to have adopted a colour code inspired by the muddy waters of the Yellow River.

The roads are the domain of e-bikes and e-trikes, which buzz like hornets around a nest within the refurbished city walls that frame the former capital.

In the middle of an anarchic roundabout stands the Drum Tower – three layers of green-tiled roofs atop a grey-brick foundation, the result of a complete 2013 rebuild – looking regal amid the shabby storefronts and chain hotels of downtown Kaifeng. At night, the eaves of the tower are illuminated with LED lights as it becomes the focus of a market.
