Hundreds of carts are pushed from side streets, to congregate around the tower, and from them issue the hissing and sizzling of cooking oil, with notes of garlic, ginger and pork fat, as diners feast on crispy wheat cakes and mutton noodle soup.

Kaifeng might not ooze the kind of laid-back prosperity I experienced in Jinan, but what it lacks in polish, it makes up for with heritage.

From the Old Town’s central access, Shudianjie (“Bookshop Street”), where some time-honoured book vendors are still in business, it’s easy to walk to some of the chief attractions, including the Shanshangan Guild Hall, a social hub established by northern merchants in the late 18th century.

Flanked by its own mini drum and bell towers, the hall has traditional roofing, the eaves of which have been decorated with lively scenes from the lives of travelling merchants and other wood carvings. One, in the Eastern Hall, depicts a man being dragged along the ground by his horse; others show golden bats, a symbol of luck, beneath animals and birds frolicking among bunches of grapes.

A 10-minute walk away, the Buddhist Daxiangguo Temple is still populated by robed monks 1,500 years after its founding. Watching the faithful prostrate themselves before Arhat statues at the back of the Main Hall, I’m reminded that train travel in China can be as much about time as it is space.

Kaifeng’s principal reminder of its Northern Song heyday is the 1,000-year-old Iron Pagoda, which towers 56 metres (184 feet) over the northeastern corner of the walled city. It is not made of iron but earned its name from the patterned glazed Buddhist tiles on its exterior, which give the tower the russet tones of rusted iron.

Despite Kaifeng’s plethora of historical marvels, it’s the tumble-down backstreets, where the rhythms of life remain unchanged by China’s high-speed dash towards a neon-hued future, that are hardest to bid farewell to when I depart from Kaifeng North station, bound for Xian.

Snow was received by the Kuomintang governor of the city when he visited Xian. I’m met with crowds pushing onto Metro Line 2, eager to get to the walled city centre. Yet, on emerging from Zhonglou station, which lies beneath the Bell Tower, it is impossible not to be impressed with what was, after all, the capital of 13 dynasties. Xian has the panache of somewhere that mattered, and mattered for a very long time – a self-confidence evident in the swagger of its denizens as well as the power architecture: the enormous Soviet-style Bell Tower Hotel, facing the Bell Tower; the “twin Tang towers” to the south of the city – the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda and Small Wild Goose Pagoda; the enormous walls and the broad boulevards that stitch it all together. Everything is on a scale that is only really rivalled by Beijing.

Having scarcely encountered another foreigner since leaving the capital, it’s something of a culture shock to witness legions of Western tourists, most of whom are taking advantage of the 30-day visa exemption policy to strike Qin Shi Huang’s Terracotta Army off their bucket list.

There again, Xian was the capital of the cosmopolitan Tang dynasty (618-907) and long served as the eastern gate to the Silk Road. This multicultural history is reflected in the Tang-era Great Mosque, which stands off a narrow, covered alley filled with vendors of tourist tat. One of the largest mosques in China, it was established in 742, although heavily restored during the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), and integrates Arabic features into a familiar Chinese design. Attracting mostly religious tourists from Central and Southeast Asia, the mosque’s tranquillity stands in contrast to the adjoining Muslim Quarter, which gets my vote for the finest street food in East Asia.

After braving the throngs several times for bowls of biang biang noodles, barbecued naan bread and persimmon doughnuts, I feel sufficiently energised to complete my railway quest.

Snow travelled north through fields of opium poppies that “nodded their swollen heads, ready for harvest, along the newly completed motor road” before sleeping “in a filthy hut […] with pigs and donkeys quartered in the next room”. I, on the other hand, cruise across the Loess Plateau at 250km/h (155mph) in an air-conditioned carriage.

The Yan River, a major tributary of the Yellow, bisects Yanan. The waterway and city are best viewed from Pagoda Hill, atop which stands the 44-metre (144 feet) Baota Pagoda, an octagonal brick tower that dates back to Tang times. Most of Yanan’s other tourist sites recall events that took place 90 years ago.

I taxi to the Date Garden, which was the site of the Communist Party Secretariat from October 1943 to March 1947. As well as various war bureaus, the former residences of officials, including Mao Zedong, Zhu De, Liu Shaoqi and Zhou Enlai, are located in the grounds of this erstwhile warlord’s manor, their humble furnishings still decorating their yaodong (“cave houses”), as earth-sheltered dwellings still common in Shaanxi province are called.

Concluding that to truly appreciate Yanan, I too should sleep in a cave, I consult a taxi driver parked outside the Date Garden, who takes me to Jingjiawan Village, where enterprising locals have converted family cave homes into guest houses.

A bright-eyed, middle-aged man, Xiao Zhang, greets me in the courtyard of the Old Yanan Cave Dwelling Hotel before showing me to my cavern for the night. Snow recounts sharing a kang, a traditional northern bed, with rats. But my kang has an electric blanket, while my cave is equipped with a widescreen television, an en suite bathroom and even voice-activated lights.

After a nap and a shower, I’m told to find an alfresco table on the edge of a cliff overlooking a large valley, a dramatic landscape of windblown yellow soil that has created steep ravines divided by deep gullies. The land here is rich in nutrients and has been cultivated for centuries, a history evident in crumbling terraces that were abandoned in the late 20th century as farmers emigrated to work in east-coast factories.

Lao Zhang, the family patriarch-turned-chef, takes my order and brings me a Wusu beer, with which I toast my journey back in time, from capital to cave.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s growing wealth inequality: will it be an M- or olive-shaped society?
item.description:
An ageing society and a widening income gap threaten Hong Kong’s social fabric. In the last of a five-part series on the city’s five-year plan, we look at what can be done to address these key issues. Read part one here, part two here, part three here and part four here.

At 71, Man Chi-ying is the sole carer for her husband, Fung Yu-hoi, a Parkinson’s disease patient.

Fung, who is also 71, has stiff limbs and, on some days, needs his wife’s help getting dressed. She has to hold his hand to keep him from falling. About two months ago, Fung fell and scratched his face while they were out for a walk.
item.content:encoded:
An ageing society and a widening income gap threaten Hong Kong’s social fabric. In the last of a five-part series on the city’s five-year plan, we look at what can be done to address these key issues. Read part one here, part two here, part three here and part four here.

At 71, Man Chi-ying is the sole carer for her husband, Fung Yu-hoi, a Parkinson’s disease patient.

Fung, who is also 71, has stiff limbs and, on some days, needs his wife’s help getting dressed. She has to hold his hand to keep him from falling. About two months ago, Fung fell and scratched his face while they were out for a walk.

The couple live in a public housing flat in Tsing Yi. They rely on government allowances for the elderly, amounting to a combined HK$8,690 (US$1,108) a month. Their daughter, son-in-law and nine-year-old granddaughter live in Canada.

Man herself is battling multiple health conditions, including high blood pressure, high cholesterol and heart disease, and takes eight types of medication a day.

“I used to believe that I would depend on his care, but it has turned out to be the opposite,” Man said.

“What will happen if something happens to me? Who will look after him?”

Their plight is all too familiar for social workers tending to Hong Kong’s growing low-income elderly community.

As the city draws up its first five-year plan, experts say that a double whammy of a rapidly ageing population and a potential widening of the wealth gap, accelerated by the advent of artificial intelligence (AI), ranks among the most pressing livelihood challenges.

To cope with social challenges presented by demographic changes and worsening disparities, the city needs a comprehensive population policy, they say.

Their calls align with the national 15th five-year plan, which has a chapter dedicated to population policy and identified addressing an ageing society and a dwindling fertility rate as key priorities.

“We need to look at the overall picture of Hong Kong’s demographic changes over the next five years, including both the quantity and quality of the population,” said Nelson Chow Wing-sun, an emeritus professor at the University of Hong Kong’s (HKU) department of social work and social administration.

“When planning for healthcare, education, social welfare and housing, it ultimately comes down to population shifts, and the resulting demand for these services.”

Ageing population, demographic shifts and declining birth rate

Significant demographic restructuring has shaped Hong Kong in the past decade.

In 2025, about 1.78 million residents were aged 65 or older, accounting for a quarter of the total population – a 60 per cent increase from around 1.11 million, or 16 per cent, in 2015.

“If any society has over 25 per cent [of the total population] aged 65 or above, it is not going to be sustainable,” said Paul Yip Siu-fai, chair professor of population health at HKU’s department of social work and social administration.

Over the same period, the labour force declined from 3.9 million to 3.81 million. The number of births also fell to a record low of 31,100 last year.

“Our working population is shrinking. But at the same time, our population is still growing,” Yip noted. “It will create a lot of challenges in terms of how we can maintain our population to be developed in a healthy and sustainable manner.”

The trend placed a heavy burden on public finances and healthcare services, while also risking a vacuum in the younger workforce that could slow the momentum of development, Yip said.

Even as residents have left Hong Kong for other places, the city has welcomed newcomers under various talent schemes.

Official statistics showed that authorities approved more than 450,000 applications under a slew of talent admission schemes since 2023, with about 330,000, or 73 per cent, from mainland China.

Among them, around 130,000 applications were approved under the Top Talent Pass Scheme alone. The programme is for high earners or graduates from top universities.

Chow said the continuing arrival of such talent would affect housing demand.

The educated newcomers, together with more mainland students, would also lift the city’s overall educational profile and impact the labour market, especially low-income jobs, he said.

He also highlighted changing family structures, including a rise in single-person households due to an ageing population and more people living alone.

All these shifts would determine the city’s housing, social welfare and healthcare needs, he said, and would require careful planning to address the resulting demands.

While at the upper end, newcomers and residents alike will compete for what they can afford, bidding and outbidding one another, at the lower end, the struggle is vastly different.

Housewife Zeng Meishi is among them. Living in a 200 sq ft flat, the 32-year-old mother of two said it was difficult to make ends meet, with the household relying on her husband’s monthly income of about HK$15,000 from construction work.

The family moved into a transitional housing flat in Cheung Sha Wan last month, paying about HK$5,000 in monthly rent. Before that, they had been crammed into an even smaller subdivided flat.

Apart from rent, utilities and other household expenses, Zeng sets aside about HK$2,000 every month to send to her parents on the mainland.

The family obtains supplies, such as rice and cooking oil, from a food bank, and receives second-hand items such as clothes from relatives.

Zeng travels to Shenzhen to see a doctor when she is ill, even though the journey can make her condition worse.

“As long as we do not go hungry, that is all that matters,” Zeng said.

The family cannot afford to enrol her 10-year-old daughter and six-year-old son in English tuition, which costs about HK$200 per session. They had fallen behind in school and felt disheartened, she said.

“I hope for a better life and that my children can receive a good education to have a more promising future,” she said, as she appealed for more financial subsidies.

Sze Lai-shan, deputy director of the Society for Community Organisation (SoCO), said low-income residents were desperately in need of more cash allowances, jobs and public housing flats, and cheaper medical services, as well as better education prospects for their children.

The NGO called for poverty alleviation efforts to be stepped up in the five-year plan, including identifying more targeted groups such as new arrivals from the mainland and carers.

These groups, SoCO said, should matter as much as the three vulnerable groups already recognised by the city’s welfare safety nets – elderly households, single-parent families and residents of subdivided flats.

It also suggested allocating more resources to families with young children through tailored support programmes to help break the cycle of intergenerational poverty.

AI and the wealth gap

As the national blueprint has tasked Hong Kong with becoming a global innovation and technology hub, the government expects the information and technology (I&T) sector to drive economic growth and create high-quality jobs, thereby improving people’s livelihoods.

However, the rise of AI could pose a deeper long-term challenge – widening income inequality.

Unemployment among younger residents has been climbing. According to the Census and Statistics Department, the jobless rate for people aged 20 to 24 rose from 8.8 per cent in 2023 to 11.2 per cent in 2025, and for those aged 25 to 29, from 4.5 per cent to 5.2 per cent.

The jobless rate in higher-paying sectors is also on the rise.

Unemployment in professional and business services climbed from 2.8 per cent in 2023 to 4 per cent in 2025, while the rate in the information and communications sector rose from 3.6 per cent to 4.2 per cent, both exceeding the overall rate.

Although still below the peak recorded during the Covid-19 pandemic, the figures are approaching levels seen during the 2008 global financial crisis.

While an uncertain economic outlook is partly to blame, academics warn that AI is beginning to displace middle-class, well-paid roles.

“AI can do the co-piloting, can be the research assistants, can do the secretarial job and a lot of the programming job,” Yip said, expressing the fear that AI would change Hong Kong’s income structure from an “olive-shaped” to an “M-shaped” society.

An M-shaped society is one in which the middle class is hollowed out, with two peaks in the high- and low-income distribution reflecting wealth polarisation, while an olive-shaped society has a large middle class and two narrow ends representing the rich and poor.

“If [the middle-class] can learn AI well and adopt well, they will move up. Not learning well, and then they will be pushed down … It is happening. It is just going to get worse, and I am not sure it will get any better,” Yip said.

Cleo Ng, an analyst at a business consultancy firm specialising in digital transformation, is among those hard hit by the rise of AI.

“People in our industry now rely on AI to prepare proposals, but clients themselves can also access AI, so they may no longer need consultants and can already get the same answers,” she said.

“AI has also made it easier for people to enter the profession, but at the same time it has made the job less sought-after than before.”

The 26-year-old observed that demand for manpower in the industry was declining. A project that typically required eight to 10 people in the past now needed only five, with fewer junior positions available.

As consultancy work itself risks being replaced by AI, Ng noted that some clients now preferred to deal directly with technology providers or reduce their budgets, making it harder to secure projects.

“People are frustrated regarding where they should be going,” said Hui Kai-lung, associate provost of academic development and Elman Family Professor of Business at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

“We do not know what options there are for us if we were to change right now. As a result, people want to cling to what they had.”

But he argued that whether AI would widen the wealth gap depended on how people adopted and capitalised on the technology.

While a static snapshot might show a shrinking middle class as some roles gradually disappeared, Hui preferred to look at the dynamic nature of the job market, predicting that new occupations could emerge and fill the gap as innovation advanced.

The national blueprint highlighted the need to address AI’s impact on employment and to create more job opportunities by developing AI and emerging industries.

Hui urged the government to set out a clear 10- to 15-year economic vision and map out how technology could empower key sectors such as finance, tourism, healthcare, and education, alongside a loosely regulated environment that would allow industries to innovate and transform.

HKU’s Yip stressed the need for the government to maintain a balanced approach during the transition, avoiding an excessive tilt towards the I&T sector and manpower misalignment.

He also called for a review of the city’s HK$100 billion annual welfare spending and stronger efforts to retrain residents, particularly underprivileged groups, in AI skills so “no one is left behind”.

Call for a long-term population policy

Beyond such measures, experts urged the authorities to move away from myopic piecemeal schemes and formulate a long-term population policy.

Chow said achieving a demographic composition that supported economic growth and ensuring sufficient services to meet demand were vital.

“The city needs enough manpower and population to support economic growth on one hand, while on the other, it also needs sufficient social services, housing and healthcare to support the demands brought on by these changes,” he said.

The government established the Steering Committee on Population Policy chaired by the chief secretary in 2007, later revamped and expanded it in 2012 to include professionals from various sectors.

The committee published a report in 2015 proposing an array of measures to attract talent, raise the birth rate, and improve care for the elderly, before it was disbanded in 2017.

Former labour and welfare minister Law Chi-kwong acknowledged that the last review of the population policy dated back to 2015. He noted that declining populations were a global trend, citing the mainland, South Korea, Japan and Taiwan.

“Why should Hong Kong be different?” he asked.

According to Law, the city’s strategy should focus on slowing the worsening birth rate, which he believed could not be reversed, and stepping up efforts to attract overseas students by improving housing options.

Population expert Yip, who served on the committee, called for the re-establishment of a high-level, interdepartmental platform to devise a clear population policy, citing the current lack of coordination among bureaus.

“Population policy is a continuous policy … Especially in the last few years, Hong Kong has undergone a lot of demographic changes,” he said. “You do need someone who is overseeing the situation and then monitoring carefully and doing the timely intervention.”

He proposed key indicators, including an annual population growth rate of 1 per cent to ensure sustainable socio-economic growth without exceeding the city’s capacity.

He also called for diversifying talent sources beyond the mainland.

“Once we become too monopolised by single sources, I think that will put ourselves in an unhealthy situation,” Yip said. “Because if there are any changes to these sources, that will affect us.”

He also suggested setting a target for the city’s working-age dependency ratio to avoid overburdening the economically active population.

Yip expected the city’s inaugural five-year blueprint would lay the foundation for a clear population policy.

“Once we know what role we are going to play, then we can plan our manpower provision, our educational system and our population policy, including the migration aspect, so that everything falls into the right place,” he said.

Such a comprehensive policy may help people like Man, if it does not come too late.

She wants to know how there can be support for her ailing husband if she were to fall ill. For now, she feels relief each day they can rely on each other.

“Sometimes when I’m not feeling well, he’ll bring me a glass of water,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Foreign capital is dipping its toes into China’s property sector. Is a rebound in store?
item.description:
From shopping malls to warehousing and logistics companies, a wave of deals by foreign funds in China is injecting liquidity into a property sector scarred by years of struggle.

Several Wanda Plazas – the sprawling mixed-use developments that were once the flagship assets of tycoon Wang Jianlin’s Dalian Wanda Group – received fresh capital injections from global asset manager PAG in June and July.

The cash-strapped developer has been forced to offload properties to repay debt. Such deals, alongside a pickup in property transactions in mainland China’s top cities this year, have drawn growing market attention.
item.content:encoded:
From shopping malls to warehousing and logistics companies, a wave of deals by foreign funds in China is injecting liquidity into a property sector scarred by years of struggle.

Several Wanda Plazas – the sprawling mixed-use developments that were once the flagship assets of tycoon Wang Jianlin’s Dalian Wanda Group – received fresh capital injections from global asset manager PAG in June and July.

The cash-strapped developer has been forced to offload properties to repay debt. Such deals, alongside a pickup in property transactions in mainland China’s top cities this year, have drawn growing market attention.

Five years after the Evergrande crisis triggered a prolonged slump in the property market, renewed activity by international investors – often thought of as “smart money” – has raised hopes over whether the sector has passed an inflection point.

“For global funds with a strategic allocation to China, the current market opens up opportunities to acquire high-quality assets at significantly more attractive pricing than in recent years,” said James Macdonald, head of research for China at property consultancy Savills.

“Investors are not necessarily calling the bottom. Rather, many believe valuations have adjusted sufficiently to offer a more favourable risk-adjusted return profile.”

The ‘bottom fishers’

Foreign commercial property investment in China peaked between 2018 and 2021.

In addition to foreign developers that benefited from the country’s decades-long residential property boom, global asset managers – including US private equity groups Blackstone and KKR, Singapore’s property group CapitaLand, and US real estate investment manager AEW – poured money into commercial property.

Sustained participation from foreign capital … has injected much-needed liquidity into the market … helping accelerate the bottom-finding process and supporting stabilisation and recovery

Yan Yuejin, E‑house China Research and Development Institute

This included grade A office buildings, urban renewal projects and long-term rental flats in first- and second-tier cities. These investors remained active even during the worst of the Evergrande crisis.

New York-headquartered Blackstone, co-founded by US billionaire Stephen Schwarzman, made headlines in June 2021 with its HK$23.66 billion (US$3 billion) offer for Hong Kong-listed Soho China, the largest office developer in Beijing and Shanghai. The deal collapsed three months later after parties failed to surmount regulatory hurdles.

In 2024, four Hong Kong-registered units under Blackstone spent 279 million yuan (US$41.3 million) to buy out the remaining 20 per cent stake in four mainland China-based warehousing and logistics companies, consolidating full ownership. The portfolio remains with Blackstone.

When meeting Vice-Premier He Lifeng in Beijing in March 2025, Schwarzman said Blackstone had full confidence in China’s economy and was willing to expand its investments in the country.

In its purchases over the summer, PAG acquired three Wanda Plaza properties: one in Shanghai; another in Quanzhou, southeastern China’s Fujian province; and another in Zhanjiang, Guangdong province. The deal, which expanded its footprint in the mainland’s commercial property sector, was closed by the PAG-led Suzhou Anyi Equity Investment Fund.

Unlike last year’s landmark transaction – in which 48 Wanda Plaza assets were sold to a consortium made up of PAG, Sunshine Insurance Group, JD.com and Tencent Holdings – the latest agreement stemmed from independent negotiations between PAG entities and Wanda Group.

Correction creates opportunity

China remains the world’s second-largest economy and one of the largest institutional real estate markets. Despite weaker household holdings, property – along with stocks, gold and other alternative investments – continues to be a key asset class for institutional investors.

National industrial and logistics transactions reached 58.5 billion yuan in the 12 months to March 15, up 19.3 per cent year on year, according to Savills.

Domestic buyer activity remained broadly stable, while foreign investment rose noticeably, with more capital deployed by overseas fund managers in the sector, the consultancy said.

“Established regional and community shopping centres with a strong mix of retail, food and beverage, and leisure tenants have generally proven more resilient, supported by stable consumer demand and uses that are less easily replicated online,” Savills’ Macdonald said.

“Combined with an experienced operating platform, this provides scope to enhance asset performance through active asset management while benefiting from long-term income generation.”

Yan Yuejin, vice-president of Shanghai‑based property consultancy E‑house China Research and Development Institute, said global capital had helped steady market expectations, particularly after years of adjustment drove a roughly 30 per cent correction in valuations across the country’s commercial property market.

“They are bullish on core cities with deep housing price corrections and robust consumer markets, with relevant policy support expected to gain further traction,” Yan said.

PAG, he added, was not just buying the assets but overseeing operations and value‑add improvements, laying the groundwork for future exit options, including through real estate investment trusts.

Asset price corrections have unlocked opportunities attracting interest from global long-term investors, who nonetheless remain selective.

“Sustained participation from foreign capital, especially inflows from opportunistic funds, has injected much-needed liquidity into the market and brought professional asset revitalisation expertise, helping accelerate the bottom-finding process and supporting stabilisation and recovery,” Yan said.

Domestic players step in

Chinese companies are also revitalising distressed assets. One Sunac Opus, a top luxury residential project near Beijing’s central business district, was scheduled to be delivered by the end of this year, China Citic Financial Asset Management said on July 30.

The state-owned asset management company (AMC) helped to complete the debt restructuring of Hong Kong-listed Sunac, founded by property magnate Sun Hongbin and once among China’s largest private developers.

A major project in downtown Beijing, the development faced numerous challenges, including construction delays and sluggish sales.

Through a full-cycle solution by the AMC – including debt acquisition, restructuring, closed-end fund management and supervision of project operations – the project’s legacy risks have been resolved, allowing the development to resume regular operations.

Hints at housing recovery

While global investors are showing interest in China’s commercial property assets, the residential housing market remains in a separate phase of the adjustment cycle, largely driven by domestic policy support and supply-demand rebalancing.

Foreign investments reflected confidence in the long-term fundamentals of specific assets rather than a broad-based recovery across China’s real estate market, Savills’ Macdonald said.

Over recent months, local governments have continued to roll out optimised home-purchase policies and inventory-destocking measures, supporting gradual stabilisation in the property market.

New home prices in China’s four first-tier cities – Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou and Shenzhen – rose by an average of 0.1 per cent in June, extending a four-month rebound and signalling a gradual recovery in sentiment, according to the National Bureau of Statistics.

Beijing’s local housing authorities jointly announced on August 7 that for households without the capital’s hukou – China’s residency registration system – the mandatory social security or personal income tax payment requirement for buying commercial housing inside the city’s Fifth Ring Road was lowered from two years to one year.

Beijing recorded 93,583 online-signed transactions for second-hand homes in the first six months, up 5.7 per cent year on year and hitting a new high since the same period in 2021, according to a report by China Index Academy this month.

While transaction volumes had rebounded notably, the sustainability of the recovery depended on whether trading momentum could hold and how price trends evolved, the report said.

Our positive sector view is backed by likely stabilising sales growth in July to September … and a stronger new launch pipeline from September

Griffin Chan, Citi Research

Signs of improving home sales have also emerged in other cities. A Citi Research report in late July forecast sales growth and a recovery in new housing launches starting in September.

July already saw improvements in transaction volumes for both new and pre-owned homes. Among 18 monitored cities, second-hand home sales rose 7 per cent year on year, with first-tier cities leading the recovery at a 14 per cent annual increase, the report said.

“Our positive sector view is backed by likely stabilising sales growth in July to September on resilient transaction volumes in core cities and a favourable low base, and a stronger new launch pipeline from September,” said Griffin Chan, an analyst at Citi Research.

Foreign capital helps steady the market

Beijing’s policymakers, who have mobilised a variety of measures to ensure home delivery in recent years, have continued rolling out supportive policies for the housing sector.

Largely driven by residential development, the property sector was once estimated by market players to contribute roughly a quarter of the country’s economy, but has turned into a drag over the past five years.

At a July 30 meeting, the Politburo – a major decision-making body of the ruling Communist Party – made fresh vows to stabilise the property market, part of its efforts to establish safeguards within broader economic risk-prevention measures.

Meanwhile, authorities have optimised institutional conditions for foreign individual investment in domestic property. Since 2025, China has refined its policy framework for stabilising foreign capital inflows, gradually rolling out a raft of supporting measures.

In September 2025, the State Administration of Foreign Exchange issued a guideline: non-resident individuals meeting home purchase conditions may settle foreign exchange funds for property purchases at banks upon presenting a sales contract, and then submit the filing documents to the bank.

The measure streamlined review procedures and expanded nationwide a scheme that was previously piloted with Hong Kong and Macau residents, allowing them to purchase homes in mainland cities that were part of the Greater Bay Area.

item.title: [SCMP] Wear now, pay later: the new rules of Southeast Asia’s indulgence economy
item.description:
With its padded leather and gold “CC” lock, Coco Chanel’s instantly recognisable bag is practically part of the uniform for any self-respecting Bangkok property agent – an apt accessory for a city that recently edged into the top 10 anywhere for luxury spending.

But in chastened economic times liquidity and luxury are no longer in lockstep, challenging many of those with expensive tastes to find new ways to keep up appearances while balancing their books.

Jirapun Ngam, 42, works in the fast-paced business of buying and selling the Thai capital’s skyline.
item.content:encoded:
With its padded leather and gold “CC” lock, Coco Chanel’s instantly recognisable bag is practically part of the uniform for any self-respecting Bangkok property agent – an apt accessory for a city that recently edged into the top 10 anywhere for luxury spending.

But in chastened economic times liquidity and luxury are no longer in lockstep, challenging many of those with expensive tastes to find new ways to keep up appearances while balancing their books.

Jirapun Ngam, 42, works in the fast-paced business of buying and selling the Thai capital’s skyline.

She pays for her designer goods on instalments, keeping cash to buy, renovate and flip homes as they hit the market.

“I need cash to invest in my business, but I also want luxury items,” she said. “With instalment plans, I get the product immediately and pay it off monthly with only a small amount of interest.”

Her calculation reflects a growing mindset among Southeast Asia’s aspirant middle class, a cohort unwilling to let their tastes decouple from the super-rich, despite the economic turbulence of the last few years.

Instead, an alternative luxury economy is evolving.

Live-streamed bargains, online resale markets and instalment purchases are bridging the gap between aspiration and affordability.

It is a market tier that is “resilient rather than immune” to economic headwinds, according to Mariella Merlino, a luxury commercial and merchandising executive.

“The higher end of the customer base remains strong, while more aspirational consumption is more exposed to macroeconomic pressure.”

But even in belt-tightening times, setting luxury aside can be hard to do.

Jirapun said the Chanel Classic bag and Rolex watches lent “a polished and distinguished image” to her and her husband.

“Could I afford to buy them without financing? Absolutely. But this makes more sense.”

Similar forces that are squeezing household spending have reshaped how governments plot their economic plans for the coming months as the jarring blows of tariffs, fuel costs and inflationary spikes rip up growth forecasts.

Throughout Southeast Asia, luxury has become a bellwether of confidence – holding firm from Jakarta to Ho Chi Minh City and growing in the region’s bling capital, Singapore.

In Bangkok, a city whose haves flit through a world of glamour and valet-parked supercars, top brands have clustered around the money.

Louis Vuitton and Dior opened concept stores over the last two years – the latter a garish “Gold House” in downtown Chidlom, where ultra-high net worth visitors arrive in Lamborghinis at malls stacked with high-end shops and restaurants.

Thailand’s luxury retail sector is estimated at around US$4.4 billion and expected to grow by 5 per cent each year for the next two to three years, despite the flattening out of demand from China where an economy in the teeth of Washington’s tariffs has lost some of its sheen over the last few years.

The big beasts of Thailand’s luxury property sector certainly have faith in the future.

They are backing the continued spending of the global uber-rich whose record stock gains, tech assets or energy holdings have soared in value while the real economy has been ground down by the US-induced Iran crisis.

On Tuesday, Asset World Corporation – majority-owned by Thai billionaire Charoen Sirivadhanabhakdi, one of the country’s richest people – announced a US$90 million investment in a new ultra-luxury hotel on the city’s Chao Phraya river.

Thailand’s leading mall operators Siam Piwat, Central Group and The Mall Group are also developing hundreds of thousands of square metres of prime Bangkok property for shopping experiences shaped by luxury brands.

“What makes Southeast Asia particularly interesting is that luxury brands are not looking at the region purely as a defensive market. They are investing for future growth,” said Merlino, former regional head of luxury for Singapore-based online fashion giant Zalora.

“The amount of investment going into malls, flagships, hospitality-led concepts and client experiences suggests that both brands and developers see Southeast Asia’s affluent consumer base becoming strategically more important within Asia.”

While those aim at the global super-rich who spend freely as they flit across Asia’s capitals, wealth experts say the thriving second-hand and resale market for luxury points to multiple layers of demand in Southeast Asia.

For Paphon Manaspakorn, CEO of Brandname Money, credit and collateral are proving a lucrative entry point to the luxury market.

He says his company’s balance sheet proves demand for luxury is here to stay, with around 200 million baht (US$6 million) in loans out so far for bags, watches and jewellery – on down payments of 30-50 per cent of the item’s value.

“People are completely open and accustomed to paying in instalments,” he told This Week in Asia, as the embarrassment of buying luxury on finance – or pawning it for quick cash – dissolved.

In fact, the taboo of today’s society may be not having the item, rather than how you got it.

“Your car is on instalments, your house is on instalments. You can see on TikTok that people even do TikTok instalments, or Shopee PayLater,” Paphon said.

Customers pay back at reasonable, legal rates of under 12 per cent a year, he says, insisting there is none of the strong-arming associated with the loan industry in Thailand if clients miss a payment.

“Should luxury only belong to the very wealthy? We wanted to make it accessible – so that you can achieve this kind of success sooner, as long as you are financially disciplined and pay in instalments.”

Instead of a contraction as the global economy bucks under energy price pressures, Paphon forecasts a doubling of the value of loans his firm seeks to provide in coming years.

And the “other side” of the business – pawning luxury items – is also doing a roaring trade.

“As the economy slows, many people come to pawn items to get cash,” he said. “I have a married couple who are customers who pawned two watches worth 11 million baht combined – one a Richard Mille and the other a Patek Philippe.”

Rich getting richer

The world’s super-rich are accumulating so much, so fast that they have in many ways cut ties with the “normal” economy experienced by the majority.

Last year, there were 556,850 ultra high net worth (UHNW) individuals across the world, according to Altrata which maps wealth – a nearly 15 per cent increase on the year, mainly powered by the technology boom.

Altrata’s most recent report, published in June, defines someone with US$30 million or more in assets as UHNW.

The US dominates with about 40 per cent of the world’s UHNW individuals.

But Asia is growing fast, with just over 141,000 people, a quarter of the global number, most of them clustered in China, India, Japan and South Korea.

The Asian super-rich also differ from their American peers, according to Julius Baer, a Swiss wealth management firm.

They are younger – and count many more women among them – and their businesses across manufacturing and tech supply chains have proved adaptive despite the US tariff onslaught on China.

“Luxury demand globally is increasingly concentrated among high net worth and top tier clients, whose spending tends to be less sensitive to short-term economic cycles,” Merlino said. “In Southeast Asia, this is reinforced by continued wealth creation and a growing concentration of affluent consumers across the region.”

In Julius Baer’s annual wealth and lifestyle report, published last month, five of the top 10 cities for spending by the global rich were in the Asia-Pacific.

Singapore retains top spot, with Hong Kong (fourth), Shanghai (sixth), Sydney (eighth) and Bangkok creeping in at 10th spot – elbowing out New York and Dubai.

The study, based on an index of prices for 20 goods and services from supercars to private education, showed being super-rich was around 10 per cent more expensive this year than last due to inflation.

Wealth experts say luxury goods have increased by an average of 12.3 per cent, with gold doubling in price, taking with it other precious metals to drive up the prices of jewellery and watches.

Still, Julius Baer said the Asia-Pacific “remains a powerhouse of global affluence”, with Singapore “the world’s most expensive city for HNWIs [high net worth individuals] for the fourth consecutive year”.

The report was compiled before the impact of the Iran crisis.

Taste and spending patterns are changing, with some experts saying Chinese consumers are warming up to domestic luxury brands, suggesting that Western fashion houses may not have it all their way going ahead as currency fluctuations and geopolitical ructions lead many to spend their money closer to home.

Rental vehicles

Yet in an economy whose gears are shifting, even high net worth Thais and holidaymakers are seeking to avoid onerous financial burdens without jettisoning their luxe experiences.

Twenty-four hours behind the wheel of a McLaren 720S will set you back around US$5,400 at Primes Automotive, a Bangkok-headquartered luxury car rental company.

While the lights have flashed red on growth, government debt and the household spending of many Thais, the cost of renting a supercar seems to be no barrier to those with money to spend.

Company marketing manager Anakin Rittimontree says hard times tend to sieve out those who want a luxury just for show.

“Some people used to want them [supercars] for events, others for multilevel marketing businesses or to project an image of success,” he told This Week in Asia.

“These days, far fewer people rent luxury cars simply to create an image. Most of our customers are genuine car enthusiasts.”

The company has seen 22 per cent growth over the last year in the rentals of the 50 or so Bentleys, McLarens, Ferraris and Lamborghinis at its Bangkok showroom.

It was a sign of a more discerning, mobile global elite who “view everything as an investment”, Anakin said.

“If they know they will drive a luxury car fewer than four days a week, they choose to rent rather than buy. Consumers are becoming smarter. They pay only for what they actually use, and financially it makes much more sense.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Vietnam’s ‘streamlining revolution’ may lead to uneven success
item.description:
Third plenums are ordinarily the quiet part of Vietnam’s political calendar. Between its five-yearly congresses, the Communist Party of Vietnam governs through numbered plenums of its Central Committee (CC): the first two settle personnel decisions, and the third, six months on, usually does no more than ratify the term’s work programme.

This time, the third plenum of the 14th CC, held from July 20 to 24, did more. It set out the next phase of the country’s most sweeping administrative overhaul in decades: the move from streamlining the apparatus to building the capacity to govern.

An unusually crowded agenda of 13 major items includes issues such as the development model, the land law and national security. These were organised around General Secretary To Lam’s “four strategic shifts”: improving the party’s leadership capacity and the state’s operating quality; unifying the governance of development space and national resources; shifting growth towards productivity, technology and human capital; and moving from reactive crisis management towards prevention and resilience.
item.content:encoded:
Third plenums are ordinarily the quiet part of Vietnam’s political calendar. Between its five-yearly congresses, the Communist Party of Vietnam governs through numbered plenums of its Central Committee (CC): the first two settle personnel decisions, and the third, six months on, usually does no more than ratify the term’s work programme.

This time, the third plenum of the 14th CC, held from July 20 to 24, did more. It set out the next phase of the country’s most sweeping administrative overhaul in decades: the move from streamlining the apparatus to building the capacity to govern.

An unusually crowded agenda of 13 major items includes issues such as the development model, the land law and national security. These were organised around General Secretary To Lam’s “four strategic shifts”: improving the party’s leadership capacity and the state’s operating quality; unifying the governance of development space and national resources; shifting growth towards productivity, technology and human capital; and moving from reactive crisis management towards prevention and resilience.

The four shifts together describe the developmental state To Lam wants to build: one that steers growth through deliberate coordination rather than leaving it to markets alone. But the first shift – improving the party’s leadership – is the hinge on which the others turn. The second, a unified development space, requires local institutions capable of executing plans drawn up in Hanoi. The third, productivity-led growth, requires predictable regulation and quick approvals. The fourth, prevention over reaction, depends on the ability to detect problems early and respond coherently.

This is what makes the plenum a turning point in the “streamlining revolution” to cut the size of the state bureaucracy. In the past 12 months, the reform concentrated on structure: for example, reducing the number of provinces and centrally governed cities from 63 to 34, abolishing the district tier of government and consolidating commune-level units. It also removed people: nearly 210,000 civil servants and public employees took early retirement or severance under the restructuring. That was the first test, and the leadership passed it. The plenum entailed a second, and perhaps harder test: whether the machinery emerging from upheaval would be effective.

Vietnam now has two tiers of local government, provinces and communes. The communes, the lower of the two, absorbed most of what the missing district tier used to do. This constitutes more than 1,000 tasks, including issuing land-use certificates, granting construction permits and administering welfare. But the communes inherited the workload of the districts without inheriting its specialists. When the district tier was abolished, its staff had various options: move up to the provincial level, shift down to the commune level or leave the service altogether. Only a third of the commune’s 150,000 staff arrived that way. The rest had always worked at the commune level and had little experience in handling land titling or construction permits.

Nor did staffing keep pace with size. The average commune now has more than twice as many staff as before but three times as many residents, on top of the district’s old caseload. That leaves one official for roughly 700 people, against 490 before the mergers. This is why communes are so easily overwhelmed by their new tasks. In one documented case, a commune has 49 staff serving more than 66,000 residents, a ratio of one official for 1,350 people.

The strain is measurable. The Ministry of Home Affairs admits that only 30 per cent of commune staff fully meet the requirements of their new duties. This is already visible in service delivery. A nationwide survey found that only 71.1 per cent of land-certificate applicants received results on time, more than a quarter of applicants had to deal with multiple offices, and 12 per cent resorted to informal intermediaries. The figures do not suggest universal failure, but they reveal functional overload and uneven competence at the tier on which the new system depends.

The Central Committee’s Conclusion 76, issued days after the plenum, recognised the problem. It identified factors such as incomplete institutions, unclear decentralisation, mismatched staffing, thin resources and weak digital integration as obstacles to effective government. The committee also sought to shift the reform’s emphasis from organisational streamlining to operating quality. The centre is to set the framework, the provinces will coordinate, and the communes implement.

The remedies match the diagnosis. Devolved responsibilities are to come with the resources to discharge them, staffing is to follow workload rather than adhere to a strict quota, and specialists are to be steered towards communes. Cadres will be judged by results and public satisfaction, and those who innovate in the public interest are promised greater protection. The Politburo’s Plan 06 turns this into a timetable, assigning institutions to revise laws and clarify authority this year, with integrated databases, commune-level digital systems and a new evaluation framework due in 2027. By naming the responsible bodies, it makes delays easier to track.

That improves the reform’s prospects. Success, though, is likely to be partial and uneven.

The first problem is sequencing. Communes have already carried expanded responsibilities for a year, while the legal, staffing and digital fixes run into 2027. Re-training commune staff will not be completed until 2031. The burden of transition, therefore, falls on communes before the tools needed to manage it are in place.

The second is that specialist capacity cannot be created by decree. The rotation of specialists from higher tiers and training can ease shortages, but land, planning, finance and technology require experience that many rural and remote communes cannot quickly acquire. Flexible staffing works only if local authorities have access to capital, recruitment powers and qualified personnel.

The third concerns discretion. Output-based evaluation and digitalisation improve accountability, but they also create new reporting burdens. Poor databases cannot produce reliable indicators, and artificial intelligence cannot reconcile unclear laws or contradictory instructions. Conclusion 76’s governing principle is that accountability and supervision extend as far as the authority granted. That is sound design. Yet the main constraint on officials is not too little supervision. Rather, it is uncertainty over which decisions are his to make, and whether he will be protected when a reasonable one goes wrong.

Vietnam’s streamlining revolution has produced a smaller state, and the plenum has correctly diagnosed why this is not enough to deliver the “strategic shifts” that To Lam wants. Whether the new state becomes more capable will depend less on what Hanoi can measure, but more on whether the appropriate resources, expertise and authority reach the communes.

Nguyen Khac Giang is Visiting Fellow at the Vietnam Studies Programme of ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute. He was previously Research Fellow at the Vietnam Centre for Economic and Strategic Studies. This article was first published by ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute’s commentary website fulcrum.sg.

item.title: [SCMP] Zhu Rongji’s death a reminder of what US-China relations have lost
item.description:
With the death of former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji, both China and the wider world have lost a great leader.

Zhu took personal risks for better US-China ties. He believed that productive Sino-American relations were good for China and for the world.

He was a global leader before China had achieved its current great power status. In mid-1990, when I was president of the National Committee on United States-China Relations, our organisation invited Zhu, then Shanghai mayor, to the United States. Several colleagues and I spent nearly three weeks travelling to several US cities with him.
item.content:encoded:
With the death of former Chinese premier Zhu Rongji, both China and the wider world have lost a great leader.

Zhu took personal risks for better US-China ties. He believed that productive Sino-American relations were good for China and for the world.

He was a global leader before China had achieved its current great power status. In mid-1990, when I was president of the National Committee on United States-China Relations, our organisation invited Zhu, then Shanghai mayor, to the United States. Several colleagues and I spent nearly three weeks travelling to several US cities with him.

This trip occurred about a year after June 4, 1989 – the first high-level visit to the US by a Chinese leader after the trauma and bloodshed of Tiananmen Square.

Making this journey at that time was a risk for him. He could have been publicly humiliated by the withering criticisms of Americans outraged by the June 1989 tumult. If he was too strident defending his government in America, he would fail in his mission to improve ties with US citizens and leaders. On the other hand, if he was perceived back home as a weak defender of China’s dignity, he would be vulnerable to nationalistic backlash.

American praise of him could be construed by his domestic detractors as criticism of China’s central leadership. He did not want to appear to be the darling of the West when his superiors in Beijing were prohibited from contact with US officials because of Washington’s post-Tiananmen sanctions. Zhu candidly hinted at his quandary, saying: “I wish they [the US press] would quit calling me ‘China’s Gorbachev’ – it’s killing me in China. I am not China’s Gorbachev, I am China’s Zhu Rongji.”

Leadership greatness is anchored in character. Our rides together during his extended 1990 US trip, subsequent opportunities to meet him one on one and with groups over subsequent years and my conversations with other world leaders about their interactions with Zhu left me several indelible impressions about his character and qualities of leadership. The trust that Chinese citizens and foreigners alike placed in Zhu rested upon his pragmatism and cosmopolitan vision, inquisitiveness, humour, capacity to communicate across cultural divides and ability to convey reality as he saw it.

‘In the end, we are all mixed systems’

On the evening of July 7, 1990, Zhu and his delegation of five other mayors from some of China’s largest cities, plus the venerable former mayor of Shanghai Wang Daohan, landed at John F. Kennedy Airport in New York. As we rode into New York City, the illuminated bridges spanning the East River suddenly popped into view, as did the twin towers. He asked me, “Tell me. You have something here called the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey. What is it? What does it do? Why was it established?”

I inadequately explained that the Port Authority was a multi-state/municipality special-purpose jurisdiction to plan, develop and operate infrastructure and promote region-wide economic and social development. Showing his cosmopolitanism and practical nature, he said: “That is important. Though you are capitalist, you need planning. And we, though socialist, need a lot more market. In the end, we are all mixed systems.” He was right.

Congress ‘reminds me of my barber shop’

Get a person laughing or seeing things from your angle of view in the first two minutes of speaking with them, and you are 99 per cent of the way to mutual understanding. Zhu was a master at that.

In my experience, Zhu never spoke with a group before first asking who was in the audience and what they cared about. He almost never read a speech. Also, unlike most Chinese leaders, he did not live in fear that someone in the audience would ask an embarrassing question.

One day, as we headed for Capitol Hill to meet with members of Congress, he was undaunted by the prospect of meeting Nancy Pelosi, a junior House member from California. She was calling for protecting the visa status of Chinese students then studying in the US and tying most-favoured-nation status for China to its human rights behaviour. Heading towards that meeting, I cautioned the mayor that he would get what he might see as hostile, unfriendly questions, which I don’t think he needed me to tell him. I explained that he should not take personal offence at the way Congress operated. It would all be very un-Chinese. Members of Congress would convey more moderate views privately to him, then go out and lambast China.

All this he understood, and more. As we left the last meeting of that day on the Hill, he said: “Well that wasn’t as bad as you warned. Reminds me of my barber shop. People come in, people go out, everyone talks over everyone else. Yeah, like my barber shop.”

The world’s Zhu Rongji

My experience seeing many members of Congress interact with Chinese leaders is that they generally identify a legitimate concern, then come up with a proposed remedy or to-do list for their Chinese interlocutor. Such was the case in April 2002 – about a year before the US invasion of Iraq – when he was urged to support the US invasion of Iraq to forestall what the George W. Bush administration argued was Baghdad’s drive to acquire nuclear and other weapons of mass destruction.

Zhu replied: “I cannot agree with you on the Iraq issue. You can’t produce solid evidence that Iraq has nuclear weapons. To destroy a country at will is very dangerous. The whole Arab world will fall out with you. We don’t hope to see this.” Nearly two decades later, the US still lives with the consequences of not heeding this advice, as well as repeating the error with respect to Iran today.

While Zhu Rongji was China’s Zhu Rongji, he also was the world’s Zhu Rongji. Reflecting on him and the current US-China relationship shows how much the world has lost in terms of a leader and a constructive global approach.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Chinese youth are turning to an 84-year-old Cambridge professor for support
item.description:
Wearing a black mariner’s cap and with a wall-to-wall bookshelf as a backdrop, Cambridge University professor Alan Macfarlane greets his social media audience with a soft ni hao – “Hello” in Chinese.

In his latest video, Macfarlane follows this signature opening by thoughtfully answering a question pulled from the comments: why has making genuine friends become so difficult?

Few would have expected an 84-year-old British anthropologist and historian from Cambridge University to become a social media heartthrob in China – yet Macfarlane has done exactly that.
item.content:encoded:
Wearing a black mariner’s cap and with a wall-to-wall bookshelf as a backdrop, Cambridge University professor Alan Macfarlane greets his social media audience with a soft ni hao – “Hello” in Chinese.

In his latest video, Macfarlane follows this signature opening by thoughtfully answering a question pulled from the comments: why has making genuine friends become so difficult?

Few would have expected an 84-year-old British anthropologist and historian from Cambridge University to become a social media heartthrob in China – yet Macfarlane has done exactly that.

Young Chinese affectionately call him “Grandpa Cute” or “Dumbledore”, after the beloved Harry Potter character, while his gentle, jargon-free reflections on education, purpose, anxiety, relationships, artificial intelligence (AI) and cultural understanding resonate deeply in a fast-paced, high-pressure society.

Through an intimate Q&A format, Macfarlane has amassed more than 2.4 million followers in roughly one year since launching on the Chinese social media platform RedNote in 2025, with videos often gaining millions of views.

His channels on Douyin – China’s version of TikTok – and Bilibili, another major video-sharing platform, have also attracted about 170,000 and 540,000 followers, respectively.

Beyond answering personal questions, Macfarlane addresses timely topics, ranging from discussions about football during the World Cup to rituals around China’s tomb-sweeping day.

Macfarlane, who originally started sharing his ideas on YouTube, expanded his online outreach to China, which he has visited 20 times and where he taught as a visiting professor, at the suggestion of his editor at Cam Rivers Publishing.

Driven by his long-standing vision to bridge academia and the public, Macfarlane launched his social media presence in China with the aim of communicating with the Chinese public and learning more about the country.

According to Macfarlane, his deep familiarity with China, built through these connections alongside his extensive research on the country, has been a cornerstone of his rapid social media growth, enabling him to relate his answers to his Chinese audience.

“I can speak to them as people whose culture and history I know something about, and I think that makes them feel that I’m not a stranger,” Macfarlane said in an interview.

For instance, when addressing questions about China’s national higher education entrance examination, or gaokao, he drew on his knowledge of Chinese educational history, Macfarlane said.

Understanding the exam’s role as a critical ladder for social advancement allowed him to empathise with the intense pressure students faced from parents and teachers, helping them to navigate their anxieties with genuine insights.

Macfarlane’s anthropological and historical perspectives offer comfort to China’s young generation by framing their personal struggles within a broader historical and spatial context.

Many of his audience said they found relief in realising that their private worries were shared by peers across different times and cultures, allowing them to learn from how others navigated similar challenges.

Yang Zhongcheng, a 20-year-old student at Beijing University of Technology, has rarely missed an update since he started following Macfarlane on RedNote in 2025. “This helped me jump out of the well and view myself from a broader, more compassionate perspective,” he said.

Surrounded by peers locked in fierce academic competition and facing the rapid advance of AI, Yang felt disoriented by the overwhelming pace of society but had learned to let go of his perfectionism and focus on the present through Macfarlane’s content.

Yang added that he particularly appreciated Macfarlane’s non-patronising approach. “[He] makes me feel we are totally equal, and that he’s keeping us company rather than lecturing us.”

Echoing this sentiment, Macfarlane observed that a lot of Chinese education and family life was hierarchical. While young people were accustomed to being told what was right or wrong, they often harboured a quiet resistance to top-down lecturing, he said.

Macfarlane also attributed his appeal to his Cambridge background and distinct delivery characterised by a refined accent, clear language and a measured pace.

According to Macfarlane, the questions he receives cover themes spanning jobs to relationships and technology changes, yet nearly all boil down to how to cope with a rapidly shifting world.

“Is there really no future for humanities majors?” one user wrote in the comments section of Macfarlane’s RedNote channel. “How can an ordinary person lead a fulfilling life?” another asked, while a third wondered, “Why do humans never seem to learn from historical lessons?”

Macfarlane said the questions were not surprising “because China has gone through the biggest economic, social, political and ideological change of any civilisation in history in the fastest time”.

He noted that such a swift and dramatic transformation had a profound impact on people’s psychology, attitudes and feelings, with the younger generation of Chinese bearing the brunt.

Unable to draw on the experiences of their elders, who grew up in an entirely different era, young Chinese were left to question almost everything. Into this void stepped Macfarlane, offering an empathetic listening ear and a broader perspective.

Beyond personal solace, the channel has also fostered cross-cultural understanding. Instead of traditional top-down lectures, these digital interactions encourage young viewers to ask questions and discuss ideas openly in the comments.

Li Lin, a 19-year-old student whose desire to explore Western culture was sparked by the videos, said Macfarlane’s content “inspires young people to grasp the differences between East and West, while actively exploring diverse cultures and the depth of civilisations”.

Driven by the professor’s insights, fellow viewer Yang was even inspired to spend a few weeks visiting Cambridge.

While Macfarlane clearly knows China well, some of his audience feel that his advice occasionally misses the mark because of the inherent limits of viewing the country through a Western lens.

For Li, Macfarlane’s different viewpoint is a benefit. “Eastern and Western thoughts are neither right nor wrong; they are simply distinct perspectives shaped by different historical and social backgrounds,” she said.

“And this very difference is precisely the bridge for us to learn from and understand one another.”

Cultural exchange is largely one-way

Macfarlane acknowledged that the cultural exchange generated by his videos remained largely one-way, with Chinese audiences making far more effort to understand the West than vice versa.

Yet he noted that the reach of his videos extended beyond China, drawing in “TikTok refugees” who migrated to RedNote when a ban of the platform in the United States seemed imminent last January.

Against this backdrop, Macfarlane said he hoped his channel would serve as a bridge to the wider world, sparking curiosity about China among non-Chinese audiences and gradually dispelling deeply rooted mistrust.

He also aimed to foster a deeper realisation of China as one of the world’s “greatest, most ancient, and most sophisticated civilisations” – one with immense wisdom to share, especially after having made such great efforts to absorb the best of the West, he added.

However, Macfarlane stressed that such mutual dialogue remained hindered by prejudice in the West, even as language barriers had gradually faded with AI translation technologies.

Western perceptions of China were often decades out of date and compounded by geopolitical anxiety, he argued. China’s rise challenged long-held assumptions in the West about its superiority in political governance, free-market capitalism, innovation and religious faith.

“Our economies have stalled and inequality is growing hugely in the West. And then we look at China – China is still growing reasonably and it has, to a considerable extent, made that wealth available across [society],” Macfarlane said.

He also pointed to a subconscious Western fear of retaliation stemming from a history of imperialist aggression against China, which has fuelled political and media distrust.

Despite these geopolitical headwinds, Macfarlane remains convinced that the solution lies in sustained, grass roots engagement.

“The deep answer is more exchange – more Chinese coming here, more of our Western people going to China, working with and becoming friends with Chinese,” he said. “And then we might have a chance of living in a more peaceful world.”

item.title: [SCMP] The 11 key achievements of China’s ‘iron premier’ Zhu Rongji – in his own words
item.description:
Known for his sharp intellect, no-nonsense demeanour and relentless drive for reform, China’s former premier Zhu Rongji was the primary architect of the country’s transition from an isolated, rigidly planned economy to a market-driven titan connected to the rest of the world. During his tenure from 1998 to 2003, he engineered an economic “soft landing”, steered the nation through the Asian Financial Crisis and secured entry into the WTO, laying the groundwork for the country’s historic transformation.

Here is a look back at his key contributions, remembered through his most memorable and hard-hitting quotes.

1. Spearheading Shanghai’s revival
item.content:encoded:
Known for his sharp intellect, no-nonsense demeanour and relentless drive for reform, China’s former premier Zhu Rongji was the primary architect of the country’s transition from an isolated, rigidly planned economy to a market-driven titan connected to the rest of the world. During his tenure from 1998 to 2003, he engineered an economic “soft landing”, steered the nation through the Asian Financial Crisis and secured entry into the WTO, laying the groundwork for the country’s historic transformation.

Here is a look back at his key contributions, remembered through his most memorable and hard-hitting quotes.

1. Spearheading Shanghai’s revival

During his time as Shanghai’s mayor from 1988 to 1991, Zhu restructured the city’s industrial base, focused on exports and kick-started the construction of the Pudong New Area, an economic development zone. Early on, he recognised that foreign direct investment was key to the city’s future growth.

“If there’s one thing about me, my guiding principle, it’s independent thought. I feel that whatever’s on my mind is what I should say out loud. … What Shanghai needs most right now is grounded, practical follow-through.” – Giving a speech as a candidate for Shanghai mayor in 1987.

2. Defusing “triangular debt”

When Zhu was appointed governor of the People’s Bank of China in 1993, the country’s financial and payments system faced immense challenges with banks and state-owned enterprises (SOEs) hopelessly enmeshed in “triangular debt”.

Put simply, the phrase describes a chain of debts – Company A owing money to Company B, Company B owing money to Company C and Company C owing money to Company A – which can paralyse the economy.

Zhu tackled this issue by injecting targeted funds, establishing the responsibility of borrowers and allowing those unable to pay their debts to go bankrupt.

“The main source of triangular debt is that government departments, localities and enterprises blindly carry out construction projects in pursuit of rapid growth, resulting in a large fixed asset investment gap.” – Speaking at a national conference on clearing up triangular debt on September 3, 1991.

3. Engineering a “soft landing” for the Chinese economy

In the early 1990s, China’s breakneck economic expansion led to surging inflation and speculation, prompting fears that the boom would spin completely out of control. As head of the central bank, Zhu imposed strict macroeconomic tightening, controlled the money supply and clamped down on loose credit and speculative fixed-asset investments. Such tough measures successfully steered China towards a “soft landing” without triggering a devastating crash.

“Having worked in economics for over 50 years, I’ve felt the brunt of our country’s recurrent syndrome: the moment life gets even slightly better, then comes the grandstanding, the blind complacency, the pointless thrashing about and the totally ignorant decision-making.” – Giving a speech at the Ninth Plenary Meeting of the State Council, January 27, 2003.

4. Weathering the Asian Financial Crisis

As premier, Zhu had to face down the 1997-1998 Asian Financial Crisis, standing firm against pressure to devalue the Chinese currency, which helped stabilise regional markets and prevent a cascading competitive devaluation across Asia.

He also provided steadfast economic backing to Hong Kong as speculative attacks hit the local currency and stock market, leaving a legacy as a resolute crisis manager.

He also launched massive domestic infrastructure spending, aggressive restructuring of state-owned enterprises and financial sector reforms.

“No matter whether there is a minefield ahead of me or a deep abyss, I will charge forward, never looking back and dedicate myself wholeheartedly to the country until my last breath.” – Speaking at a press conference soon after his appointment as premier on March 19, 1998.

“The past year was extraordinarily tough for me – far tougher than I had anticipated. First, I did not expect the Asian financial crisis to hit with such severity. Second, the historic, devastating floods that struck our country also caught me off guard.” – Speaking at a 1999 press conference.

5. Backing Hong Kong’s future

Throughout his tenure as premier, Zhu was the face of Beijing’s support for Hong Kong in the wake of the 1997 handover, frequently reminding mainland and local officials alike of their historic duty to ensure the city’s success under the framework of “one country, two systems”.

“I just do not believe Hong Kong cannot be run well. If Hong Kong goes down the drain, it’s not just your responsibility – it’s ours, too. If Hong Kong, after returning to the motherland, gets ruined on our watch, wouldn’t that make us ‘sinners of the nation’? That will not happen.” – Remarks in Hong Kong on November 19, 2002.

6. Overhauling the tax system

Zhu presided over a landmark overhaul of China’s fiscal structure, introducing a tax-sharing system that divided powers and revenues between the central and local governments, cementing Beijing’s macroeconomic control.

By the early 1990s, China faced a severe fiscal crisis that threatened Beijing’s ability to govern effectively and could have undermined the country’s economic transition. Under the then fiscal contracting system, local governments collected revenues and negotiated fixed remittances to the central government, which often led to provinces hiding funds in off-budget channels to avoid sharing funds with Beijing. Deprived of money, the central government struggled to maintain macroeconomic control, manage regional disparities and fund national infrastructure projects.

Zhu Rongji spearheaded the landmark 1994 tax-sharing reform by intensively negotiating with reluctant provincial leaders to secure their compliance. The reform abolished discretionary negotiations in favour of a clear, rule-based tripartite tax scheme, with the newly created State Administration of Taxation collecting both central and shared taxes.

The results of the 1994 overhaul were immediate and transformative. In the first year, the central government’s share of total national tax revenues surged from 22 per cent to over 55 per cent, instantly revitalising Beijing’s fiscal capacity and cementing its authority over monetary and economic policy.

However, the reform left behind a persistent structural imbalance: while Beijing centralised revenue collection, local governments still had to pay for most public services. This mismatch eventually forced local authorities to rely heavily on off-budget financing, land sales and local government financing vehicles – creating fiscal challenges that China continues to navigate today.

“At present, the central government’s finances are in dire shape, nearly unsustainable. If the central government’s revenue is not properly concentrated and its financial resources are not strengthened, we will not be able to make our ends meet, and ultimately the whole country will suffer and everything will be stalled.” – Speaking to Guangdong province cadres during his tax reform research trip in September 1993.

7. Modernising the financial sector

Under Zhu’s watch, China launched sweeping reforms of its financial sector. He clarified the functions of the central bank, deepened reforms of commercial banks, foreign exchange systems and the securities and futures markets to create a unified and strictly managed financial system.

“If you are not diligent in your duties, nor honest in your work, indulging in wining and dining, issuing arbitrary approvals, practising nepotism, cultivating relationships everywhere, and treating state property as if it were yours, and you still sit on the podium giving a report, how can the people sitting down there not criticise you?” – Criticising financial officials’ misconduct at the 1993 National Financial Work Conference.

8. Persisting with painful SOE restructuring

Zhu placed SOE reform at the heart of China’s economic transition. Championing a modern enterprise system defined by “clear property rights and separated government and enterprise functions,” he drove a massive restructuring that controversially resulted in millions of lay-offs, while simultaneously pushing for a new social security net.

“State-owned enterprises only need a third of their current workforce … I refuse to believe that SOEs cannot perform just as well as foreign and private companies.” – Remarks made in 1999 during an interview with German newspaper Die Zeit.

9. Reshaping urban housing

In 1998, Zhu unveiled China’s housing blueprint, which aimed at replacing a system in which housing was mostly provided by the state with one in which private firms did the heavy lifting, laying the foundation for the urban housing market which later became a major driver of the Chinese economy.

“Right now, some cities are recklessly selling off land and carrying out mass demolitions without thinking through the consequences, completely ignoring the displaced residents. If this continues, it’s going to threaten social stability. The proceeds from land sales must first go towards rehousing evicted residents – the central government simply cannot afford to shoulder this burden.” – His handwritten comments on June 4, 1994, regarding the Ministry of Construction.

10. Championing WTO entry and Sino-US diplomacy

Zhu was perhaps the most important official behind China’s gruelling 13-year marathon to join the World Trade Organization (WTO), securing the country’s integration into the global economy. During his historic US visits, he deployed charm, wit and firmness to manage the nations’ complex ties.

“There will be differences of opinion between us. Yet only friends who hold differing views can be the best of friends; only honest critics make true friends.” – Speaking in the United States in April 1999

“When President Lincoln fought to preserve America and opposed secession, he did not hesitate to use force. We ought to learn from President Lincoln.” – Responding to a question from the press on Taiwan in Washington on April 8, 1999.

11. Crusading against corruption

Perhaps what endeared him most to the public was his fiery disdain for corrupt officials. He demanded integrity and famously staked his own life on the fight against corruption, during both his time in Shanghai and Beijing. He was also a strong advocate for simplified protocols, clean government and high efficiency.

“I have prepared 100 coffins here; 99 are for corrupt officials, and one is for myself. It’s a matter of mutual destruction, but it will bring long-term stability and development to the country and restore the people’s confidence in our cause.” – Giving a speech at a central anti-corruption conference in 1998.
