In June, Prime Minister Anwar said the federal government continued to recognise Tuanku Muhriz, after Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar was proclaimed as the new ruler at a hotel in neighbouring Melaka.

The dispute remained entangled in litigation and arguments over the authority of the undang and the state’s royal council.

Wan Ahmad Fauzi said the controversy exposed a widespread misunderstanding of Negeri Sembilan’s royal structure.

“The ruler of Negeri Sembilan is not the Yang di-Pertuan Besar alone,” he said, arguing that the constitutional duties of the ruling chieftains should not be dismissed as merely customary positions.

The episode differed sharply from the 2022 federal deadlock, but both forced Malaysians to confront the architecture beneath their monarchy, including powers and traditions that usually remain distant from everyday political debate.

Historian Milner said the central question was whether the monarchy could continue supplying stability when elected institutions faltered.

“Monarchy, on the face of it, is an outdated institution,” he said. “In recent times, however, it may be gaining new support, especially as people look at other types of constitution.”

Constitutionally, Malaysia’s political upheavals stemming from its democratic process have shown that the monarch has played a decisive role, exercising some level of discretion on who leads the nation based on parliamentary majority and support.

Lim, the constitutional lawyer, said decisions made by the palace had gone beyond what was widely deemed as a ceremonial role previously.

“So when political parties are not as strong as they used to be, the monarchs invariably fill that power vacuum and play a much more influential role in governance, at least compared to pre-2018,” he told This Week in Asia.

According to Lim, rulers’ constitutional powers are enumerated in the federal constitution and have the force of law which is not open to question while the constitutional convention acts as a long-standing practice derived from the UK which Malaysia’s system is largely based on.

From legal observations, Lim said monarchs were not overstepping their constitutional powers. “I think the constitution is working as intended for now.”

However, he said constitutional convention might evolve, stemming from any instability of political coalitions.

“For example, it may now be a constitutional convention for the king to be consulted on the annual budget or on major public policies before they are rolled out, which I definitely see happening unlike before,” Lim said. “The monarchs will no doubt be playing a larger role in governance due to the instability of political coalitions.”

New normal

Awang Azman Awang Pawi, a political analyst at the University of Malaya, said Malaysia appeared to be entering a form of conditional new normal as long as politics remained fragmented.

He said the monarchy was likely to remain more visible in matters involving government formation, legislation dissolution and determination of majority support.

“The healthiest constitutional model is one in which the monarchy remains influential but firmly bound by the constitution; respected but not politicised; and committed to safeguarding the democratic process rather than competing with the elected government.”

That prominence carries advantages and risks. Royal intervention can help break a deadlock when no political leader commands a majority, but sustained dependence on the palace may allow political parties to avoid the harder task of rebuilding durable coalitions and settling disputes through parliament.

The institution’s legitimacy also rests partly on remaining above partisan combat, even as political actors increasingly appeal to rulers, invoke palace relationships or portray royal approval as a source of authority.

For Darwisy, those arguments remain beyond the purpose of his portraits. His focus is the cultural language surrounding the institution and how it can reach a generation more familiar with short videos than royal archives.

“Not everyone reads history books, but today many people connect with art on social media,” he said. “My hope is that people don’t just see a royal portrait, but also discover and appreciate the beauty of Malaysian culture through the artwork.”

item.title: [SCMP] Vintage charm is blended with modern elegance in a timeless Hong Kong flat
item.description:
Needing a designer to renovate his newly purchased, 38-year-old apartment in Central, businessman Harry Sun found the perfect fit in an unexpected place. He and interior designer Dominic Cheung, co-founder of Crimson Company, were both regulars at the same tailor’s shop – and when their paths crossed, the introduction sparked an instant connection. The two shared sensibilities that extended beyond sartorial savoir faire to a mutual appreciation for classicism with a youthful touch.

Thus began a harmonious collaboration to make over the 620 sq ft mid-rise apartment in quintessentially “old” Hong Kong, with its views of historic St Paul’s Church ringed by mature trees.

Sating his penchant for vintage and antique European designs, Sun already had an assemblage of finds he’d been collecting from markets since his university days in Britain. These would inform the interiors, as Cheung revised the floor plan from two bedrooms to one, enabling a bigger dining room and a slightly enlarged bathroom.
item.content:encoded:
Needing a designer to renovate his newly purchased, 38-year-old apartment in Central, businessman Harry Sun found the perfect fit in an unexpected place. He and interior designer Dominic Cheung, co-founder of Crimson Company, were both regulars at the same tailor’s shop – and when their paths crossed, the introduction sparked an instant connection. The two shared sensibilities that extended beyond sartorial savoir faire to a mutual appreciation for classicism with a youthful touch.

Thus began a harmonious collaboration to make over the 620 sq ft mid-rise apartment in quintessentially “old” Hong Kong, with its views of historic St Paul’s Church ringed by mature trees.

Sating his penchant for vintage and antique European designs, Sun already had an assemblage of finds he’d been collecting from markets since his university days in Britain. These would inform the interiors, as Cheung revised the floor plan from two bedrooms to one, enabling a bigger dining room and a slightly enlarged bathroom.

“Our goal was to create a space with a strong, yet quiet, architectural identity that feels both intentional and deeply personal,” says Cheung. “By integrating classic European details within a modern, clean envelope, we created a backdrop designed not to dominate, but to age gracefully over the years.”

His client’s brief for “cosiness” – a space that could tastefully house his furniture and objets d’art – excited Cheung, himself a lover of things vintage.

“Vintage pieces big and small can introduce a storytelling element, adding more depth to the space. Our shared vision was to juxtapose old and new, without making it look like an antique shop.”

An 18th century Louis XVI commode and a 19th century Louis Philippe gilded mirror set the tone for the dining room, where, additionally, mid-century modern Wishbone chairs are paired with a custom-made Calacatta marble table. Resisting the temptation to install ornate chandeliers, lighting designer and Crimson Company co-founder Rosana Asencios opted instead for two simple brass pendants. “Their patina will change with age,” she says, “responding very well to the antique pieces and the history in the room. It’s about having a sleek accent, without being too overwhelming.”

French-inspired wall mouldings and herringbone oak flooring lend subtle sophistication.

In the separate living room, twin bay windows frame neighbourhood views, and a mahogany library wall houses Sun’s collections of books – history and literature among his favourites – and vinyl records.

A green velvet sofa adds a youthful, mid-century modernist touch beside a vintage handmade rug. Sun’s prized analogue turntable sits atop a minimalist, Scandinavian-inspired coffee table; all other audiovisual equipment is concealed behind slatted joinery inlaid within the wall panelling.

With his client needing to work from home only occasionally, Cheng tucked a study nook into a walkway, behind two pocket doors inlaid with antique glass panels.

Cheung’s intent to “frame different moments in the home” is evident in the simply furnished bedroom, where two elegant oak and glass pendants, a custom bed and an oak-finish wardrobe take centre stage. The only hung artwork is a small framed print picked up on a trip to Italy during his school days.

Proving that even a compact kitchen can have style as well as substance, handmade Moroccan splashback tiles pair gracefully with natural stone benchtops, brass knobs and pulls punctuating the light-grey, powder-finished cabinetry.

The same quiet refinement carries through to the bathroom. Neither space is merely entered – one arrives from the dining room via a dramatic Nero Marquina marble arched portal and floor threshold.

Every corner and every wall holds a focal point, yet nothing feels forced or crowded.

“In this not-so-big apartment, a lot is happening, but you don’t feel like a lot is happening. The flow is easy,” Cheung says.

The result is a harmonious dialogue between modernism and classicism, where all details are intentional but never laboured.

A delighted Sun says the refurbishment, completed in December 2024, never ceases to amaze him. “It’s one of those places that’s well built, well designed and feels very comfortable when you live there.”

Living room

Mahogany bookcase, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Sofa, from B&B Italia. Coffee table, from Norr11. Record turntable, from Cambridge Audio. Side table, from Mater. Wall lamp, from Santa & Cole. Vintage handmade rug, from Blanc Marine Boutique. Artwork is a Liu Peng landscape, from Asian Art Platform Singapore

Dining room

Calacatta Viola dining marble, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Wishbone chairs, from Carl Hansen & Søn. Candela di Vals pendant lamps in natural brass, from Viabizzuno. Sun found the small oil painting of a fig years ago. In the alcove, a Louis XVI mahogany commode with Carrara marble top, from Inessa Stewart’s Antiques. Above it, a Louis Philippe gilt mirror with crown, from 1stDibs. Behind the mirror, Ianthe Mono wallpaper in Lapis from Liberty Fabrics

Dining room detail

Nero Marquina marble arched portal defines the threshold leading to the bathroom and kitchen. Wall mouldings and wall finish, in St Leo plaster paint (stleointeriors.com). Polished brass dimmer switches and sockets, from Varilight (varilight.co.uk). Wall-hung printed abstract, from The Poster Club (theposterclub.com)

Study nook

Pocket doors in the study nook feature antique glass inlay panels. Vintage brass handles from Etsy. Desk joinery in burl wood veneer, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life, who also installed the herringbone-pattern engineered timber floor

Bathroom

Brass-framed mirror and cabinetry with custom Calacatta Viola marble vanity top, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Basin and French gold-finish tapware, from Kohler. Small lamp, from Audo Copenhagen. Overhead light, from Visual Comfort

Bedroom

Bed with upholstered headboard, custom-designed by Crimson Company and built by Sankon Interiors. Pair of hanging lamps, from Santa & Cole. Bedside tables, from Ikea. Wardrobe in oak timber finish, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life

Kitchen

Kitchen cabinetry with natural quartz stone tops, by Crimson Company and Design for Life. Handmade Zellige tiles, from Zia Tile. Brass knobs and pulls, from Willow & Stone. Artwork on benchtop, by Molly Supplee

item.title: [SCMP] Wok with Yan’s return: Hong Kong-Canadian TV chef Stephen Yan resurfaces decades after disappearing
item.description:
“When Marco Polo went to China, you know what he did? We showed him how to make chow mein noodles, we showed him how to make wontons.”

An energetic Chinese man with a high forehead and gregarious smile is standing in a studio kitchen, dishing out as many puns as he is plates of wok-fried rice for a studio audience at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), in Vancouver.

From 1978 to 1995, Stephen Yan garnered legions of fans in Canada, the United States and beyond, largely thanks to half-hour episodes of Wok with Yan, each seeing a dish prepared from start to finish in real time. The chef would cook up Cantonese classics such as beef and broccoli, garlic spare ribs and stir-fried prawns while dressed in aprons emblazoned with witticisms such as “Wok’s New, Pussycat?”, “Wok up a Storm” or, in this early episode, “Wok-a-Doodle-Doo”.
item.content:encoded:
“When Marco Polo went to China, you know what he did? We showed him how to make chow mein noodles, we showed him how to make wontons.”

An energetic Chinese man with a high forehead and gregarious smile is standing in a studio kitchen, dishing out as many puns as he is plates of wok-fried rice for a studio audience at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), in Vancouver.

From 1978 to 1995, Stephen Yan garnered legions of fans in Canada, the United States and beyond, largely thanks to half-hour episodes of Wok with Yan, each seeing a dish prepared from start to finish in real time. The chef would cook up Cantonese classics such as beef and broccoli, garlic spare ribs and stir-fried prawns while dressed in aprons emblazoned with witticisms such as “Wok’s New, Pussycat?”, “Wok up a Storm” or, in this early episode, “Wok-a-Doodle-Doo”.

“When [Polo] went back to Italy, he learned how to make it all right,” says Yan to the camera, in his Cantonese-inflected English, “but he changed the name chow mein to spaghetti and changed wonton to ravioli. Wok the heck, I’m going to make one thing perfectly clear: I want to make this thing right and correct. I don’t want to make it the wrong way. I want to make it the Yan way.”

Once Yan had plated a dish, he’d invite someone from the audience to dine with him, and, this being Canada in the 1980s, they would not all be proficient with chopsticks. Yan would open a fortune cookie, translate the Chinese message inside and then, as the credits rolled, the rest of the studio audience would make sure no food went to waste.

With the coast-to-coast-to-coast reach of the CBC, Yan became a national figure and arguably the first Asian celebrity television chef in the West.

“I watched [Yan] with my grandparents because, back then, your house had one TV,” says Karon Liu, who was only a few months old when his family moved to Toronto in 1987, one of more than 355,600 Hongkongers who moved to Canada in the late 80s, according to the Canadian International Council. “So, what they watched, you had to watch,” says Liu, who is now a food reporter with the Toronto Star newspaper. He remembers his grandmother hollowing out a cucumber and filling it with stir-fried beef, making it look like a boat, because that’s what Stephen Yan did in one episode.

“He was the Chinese Julia Child. He wasn’t some snooty Michelin French chef; he cooked the way my grandmother would cook at home,” says Liu. “He explained a lot of ingredients that weren’t as well known outside of a Chinese audience at that time.”

While Chinese-Canadians delighted in Yan’s familiarity, other Canadians were learning that Chinese food was not just egg foo yung or sweet and sour chicken balls, a step towards the multiculturalism the country would more fully embrace. But then one day in 1995, after more than 500 episodes, Wok with Yan ended, and the chef was not seen on television or in other media again – well, until he briefly surfaced the year before last.

Born and raised in the Toronto, Ontario suburb of Scarborough in the 80s, one of Yan’s biggest fans was Steve Gaskin. Before he was old enough to go to school, Gaskin’s Guyanese father and Chinese mother would drop him off at his grandparents’ home at 7am before going to work, and pick him up 12 hours later.

“I found it very hard to connect with my gung-gung [maternal grandfather] because my parents never spoke Cantonese, and he didn’t speak much English. I took Cantonese lessons, but I didn’t retain any of it,” says Gaskin. His grandfather, who ran a laundromat business in his adopted home, brought his family from Hong Kong to Canada via Guyana more than 50 years ago.

“My gung-gung only communicated in Chinese,” says Gaskin, “but just from grunts and facial cues, I knew what he was saying.”

The pair managed to bond over Wok with Yan. “I would sit next to him on the La-Z-Boy and just without even talking, we would laugh at the jokes and he would just kind of nudge me when something funny came on, or he wanted me to watch the technique.

“In the 80s, Stephen Yan was probably the only Chinese-Canadian celebrity. I was probably six years old, and the only Asian person on the big screen was Bruce Lee or Jackie Chan, so to see somebody like Stephen Yan, who’s in Canada, who was so approachable, was really important.”

In 2018, Gaskin and a friend launched Retrokid, a company that, through T-shirts and accessories, recalls childhood memories for Gen Xers who grew up watching Canadian television shows such as Mr Dressup, Polka Dot Door and Degrassi. Gaskin was determined to track down his hero.

After years of dead ends, in 2022, he finally got a response. But it wasn’t until a year later that Yan agreed to meet him.

Gaskin is coy about how he finally got in contact with Yan, divulging only that the former chef wanted “to work with a company that understands everything he’s done”. And with the success of Retrokid and the wider appetites for online nostalgia spun into products, Yan the savvy businessman must have seen that the time was ripe for a revival.

“Stephen Yan always said that he appreciated that there was this personal connection I had with my gung-gung as to why he wanted to do this with us.”

Together, they turned out “Wok with Yan” T-shirts, hoodies, tote bags, badges and fridge magnets, bearing the chef’s likeness from his television days. And, of course, a range of aprons with witty Yan-isms has proved to be the bestseller.

To help launch the collection, Yan agreed to fly from Vancouver to Toronto in August 2024 for a meet-and-greet with fans.

“It was pretty shocking to see him just come out of the arrivals gate,” says Gaskin, who picked Yan up at the airport. “Like, oh my God, it’s Stephen Yan. I didn’t know if he was going to come off a plane in a wheelchair or on crutches, right? But no, he’s super strong and mentally healthy for 85.”

While Yan was in Toronto, Retrokid gave Liu a chance to interview the chef for the Star, and, like Gaskin, the reporter was transported back to his childhood.

“It was really surreal,” says Liu. “He was still making jokes, he was just like a grandpa, where you ask one question and then his answer is, like, 10 minutes long because he’s lived such a full life.”

According to what he said in the interview, it was Yan who decided to pull the plug on his show in 1995.

“One day, I asked my accountant how much money I needed to survive,” Yan told Liu. “He said I already had a house and I didn’t need a dollar more. I wanted to contribute my time to those less fortunate, so I helped out with orphanages and schools in places like Thailand and China. I had enough earthly belongings.

“Back then, I had three restaurants [in Vancouver] and I had three disciples, including Martin Yan [no relation; a Hong Kong-American who worked with Yan in the 70s],” he explained. His protégé’s own television show, Yan Can Cook, also first aired on Canadian television in 1978 (initially as Yan Can), before having a highly successful run in the US, on PBS.

Stephen Yan also told Liu that, after quitting the show, he spent more time with his family and became much more active. “I ran 11 marathons, four times at the Boston Marathon and won the masters division. I also climbed Mount Everest.”

For someone so beloved, there isn’t a lot of biographical information available online about Yan, and he guards his private life closely. His birth date, for example, is not widely known, only that he was born in Hong Kong in 1939.

Not long after, in December 1941, the Japanese occupation of the city began and basic ingredients such as rice, flour and oil were rationed.

“[As a child,] I was poor and went to people’s stores where they would give me leftover food,” Yan told Liu.

“I was spending my time on the streets next to a theatre that was starring a Chinese actor, who was Bruce Lee’s father. Bruce and I became friends, and we used to play in a nearby warehouse, but I needed a job.”

When Yan was nine years old, a restaurant cook gave him work in exchange for food. One of his most laborious tasks was to take thousands of lotus seeds from a pot of boiling water, without gloves, and use a toothpick to push out their bitter cores. After three months, Yan was allowed into the kitchen, to learn from the cook, who taught him how to kill and pluck chickens, and use every part of the bird, as well as shop for the best ingredients.

Yan claimed to have been the fastest dishwasher at the restaurant. “Humans are adaptable and can do anything if they have the opportunity,” he told Liu.

He became a fully-fledged cook, and when he was around 15 years old, the chief cook of the restaurant arranged for him to go to school. Later, Yan said, he was one of two students chosen by an American senator to study business administration in the US, to which he sailed on an 18-day voyage to San Francisco.

Fearing being called up to the military as the US fought in Vietnam, Yan crossed the border to Canada in the late 50s or early 60s, he told Liu, one of 20,000 to 30,000 draft dodgers to have done so, according to Canadian immigration statistics.

By the late 70s, Yan was already managing his own restaurants when he was noticed by a television talent scout while leading cooking demonstrations in a shopping mall in the run-up to Chinese New Year.

The weekly Yan’s Woking debuted on Vancouver station BCTV in 1978. Two years later, national broadcaster CBC bought the show, rebranded it as Wok with Yan and shifted formats to present a daily afternoon cooking series.

Gaskin says some 230 people showed up at Toronto’s storied Royal Theatre for 2024’s meet-and-greet.

“It was great to give [Yan] a platform where he could just say thank you to all of his fans and the fans showed up,” says Gaskin. “Obviously, we could have packed that theatre to 500 people, but we also wanted to give the fans a chance to meet him, to actually go up and take a photo, and they loved it.”

Since then, Yan has remained elusive. All attempts to contact him by this author have been fruitless. The Retrokid team has been sworn to secrecy; Liu says he never got direct contact. And even now, almost two years after Yan’s rarest of public appearances, he shows no signs of emerging into the spotlight again, even to contribute to this article, to connect with his hometown, Hong Kong.

Vancouverite Billy Snaychuk wasn’t at the meet-up but considers himself a fan. “My most favourite part about Stephen Yan would have to be his aprons, and the way he always made the audience laugh,” he says. “He just captured the audience right away from the get-go. He definitely caught me as a kid, because I just loved watching him.”

Snaychuk’s father, a fisherman and entrepreneur, got to know Yan through Chinese friends who caught fish for the chef, delivering them to his restaurant, Yan’s Garden. From the age of six, Snaychuk watched Wok with Yan with his mother every day after school.

“My parents had the largest collection of Stephen Yan books, and I remember sneaking out of my room in the middle of the night and grabbing his books on the bookshelf and bringing them back. And I would just look at all the pictures and read the recipes,” he recalls, with a chuckle.

Once a month, his parents invited friends over and cooked dishes from Yan’s cookbooks, including Snaychuk’s favourite, gold coin beef.

“The flavour profile in it is just next level. And the texture of the beef, you can almost chew it with the roof of your mouth and your tongue, it’s just that tender,” says Snaychuk, who would follow in his hero’s footsteps and become a chef himself. He was promoted to executive chef at the age of 28 and went into restaurant consulting and even competed in the Food Network Canada cooking reality TV show Wall of Chefs.

As he got older, Snaychuk paid attention to Yan’s technique, particularly how he created flavour profiles by adding ingredients to the wok at different times.

“A lot of people, when they cook, they just kind of throw everything in there. If you do that, the whole dish is basically going to taste the same. But if you add things at different times and take them out and put them back in, you layer the flavours. And that’s something I really noticed – he layered his flavours with his cooking.”

While watching Yan was a joy for so many, working for him was not always so pleasurable, says former assistant Brenda Gonneville, who also has no idea where Yan lives now. “He’s not the face you see on TV.”

In 1981, Yan hired a 26-year-old Gonneville to help him in his office, which was above Yan’s Chinese restaurant, in Port Coquitlam, British Columbia. She had worked as an assistant to high-powered executives in the steel industry, says Gonneville, so was “well versed in dealing with high-powered, difficult people”.

Her job, as a native English speaker, was to look after Yan’s public relations, devise witty lines for the aprons and procure props and have them shipped to Ottawa, where his show was taped for two seasons before moving back to Vancouver. She recalls being the only Caucasian in an office full of Cantonese-speaking people but says she got on well with all the other staff. Gonneville was aiming to forge a career in entertainment, so worked for a low wage. After paying rent, she says, she was left with enough money only for a diet of white rice and boiled eggs.

“After three months, I’d had enough,” she says, “because he is a perfectionist, and nothing pleases him. He’s a hard worker. He expects more than 100 per cent from his employees.”

One day, she says, he was dictating content for a show and Gonneville was struggling to write it all down in shorthand, because he was speaking quickly.

“He had me read it back and I said, ‘I’m sorry, I didn’t get most of that.’ I decided then and there, and so did he, that we’d come to the end of the road.”

Fortunately, her brief stint with Yan led to a 20-year career in film and television.

When she returned to pack up her things, the office manager “took my hand and said, ‘Don’t you worry, you lasted longer than anybody’”, she recalls with a laugh.

“[Yan’s] an A-type personality, he’s driven. He expected everybody to put in the same effort as him, and if you failed, he wouldn’t put up with it.”

Difficult he may have been for those he employed, but, given the delight he’s brought to television viewers, one cannot begrudge his telling the hosts of Toronto daytime talk show The Social, in August 2024, that, “I was hiding; I want a simple life.

“I […] cannot believe that people remember me after 30 years,” he said on The Social. “And they want to know, am I alive? I am! I’m alive!”

And maybe that’s enough, to know that he’s alive. With Yan now well into his 80s, a quiet, simple life is perhaps just wok he needs.

item.title: [SCMP] Ready player 3: India offers Asean a US-China alternative
item.description:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.
item.content:encoded:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.

“That’s the main reason why we decided to sign up on short notice,” she said of the Indusfood expo, held in Greater Noida at the start of this year.

“With India having a bigger population than China … and a lot of them are vegetarian, we thought they’d be more open to those types of food ingredients.”

Sheentaro’s products were previously showcased at the China-Asean Expo in Nanning and Cordero said the reception was so positive that “when this opportunity in India came about, we said ‘let’s try it again’”.

Southeast Asian nations are increasingly looking to India as an alternative market, arms supplier and technology partner as China and the US vie for regional influence.

India is more than happy to oblige, observers say – though it also knows its limits. It cannot out-trade China, nor can it supplant America’s security umbrella. What is offers instead is room to manoeuvre, free of the demand to choose sides.

That message travelled to Manila last month, where India’s foreign minister, S. Jaishankar, used Asean-led meetings to press the case for deeper cooperation, calling it the only way to “de-risk and diversify”.

He spoke of energy security and food security, and how precarious both had become. Neither these nor public health could be taken for granted in this new “era of volatility and disruption”, Jaishankar said, identifying maritime trade as a further source of anxiety.

A more stable and secure future was in reach, he said, but only by working together: an animating theme of India’s Act East Policy, launched 12 years ago to forge stronger economic, strategic, and cultural ties with Southeast Asia and the broader region.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi were also in the Philippine capital last month for talks with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on the South China Sea, supply chains and security – a reminder of how much great-power rivalry still shapes regional diplomacy.

The economic dimension of India’s engagement push was on full display earlier in July, when Delhi hosted talks on upgrading the Asean-India Trade in Goods Agreement, a decade-old free-trade pact that officials say no longer reflects current realities.

Two-way trade came in at US$128 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, according to India’s Commerce and Industry Ministry – respectable, but only a fraction of the US$1 trillion and change that China did with the bloc.

Analysts say India’s strategy appears to be centred around pairing diplomacy with trade, defence exports and maritime cooperation, offering Southeast Asia a third option beyond the US-China binary.

It is best described as “a search for mutual wins”, according to Arvind Raj, a geopolitical analyst and associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ Centre for Multilateralism Studies in Singapore.

A more multipolar neighbourhood would give Southeast Asian nations more choices and more room to hedge, he said – as India, in turn, secured a larger foothold in a region that it had long courted from the margins.

Summitry to substance

For years, India’s Asean diplomacy has been heavy on the ceremony, but light on the delivery.

“Asean sits at the centre of India’s Act East Policy on paper, but for most of the past decade the relationship ran on summitry rather than substance,” said Oorja Tapan, a doctoral researcher of international politics at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi.

Analysts say the clearest evidence of how that dynamic is beginning to change can be seen in the region’s expanding arsenals.

During a three-day state visit last month, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi sealed a deal for Jakarta to buy BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles – jointly developed by India and Russia – making Indonesia the third Southeast Asian buyer after Vietnam and the Philippines.

A separate deal for Jakarta to acquire India’s Astra air-to-air missiles was also signed.

Pooja Bhatt, an associate professor of international relations at India’s O.P. Jindal Global University, calls such defence cooperation “not only part of increasing trade with Asean but also a form of strategic signalling” – proof that Delhi can deliver hardware, not just handshakes.

India wanted to become Southeast Asia’s “resident partner”, Tapan said, offering “capability without a formal alliance demand attached” and without asking the region to choose sides.

Pairing defence exports with renewed free-trade negotiations showed that Delhi wanted to be seen as “a dependable partner offering security cooperation, technology-sharing and balanced regional influence”, said Shristi Pukhrem, a visiting fellow at the India Foundation think tank and director of its Act East Centre.

Foreign policy researcher Joanne Lin concurred that weapons sales alone would not be enough to anchor the relationship.

India’s relevance depended on it delivering across “trade, maritime security, connectivity, tech and supply chains”, said Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and visiting scholar at the MIT Centre for International Studies.

“This is why India is trying to address concerns over trade imbalance, rules of origin and possible re-routing of Chinese goods through Asean, while Asean looks forward to market access with fewer barriers.”

Beyond US-China?

Ultimately, India’s pitch boils down to optionality.

Delhi is not seeking “supremacy in Asean”, according to Abhishek Sharma of the Observer Research Foundation think tank in the Indian capital, but rather is trying to advance its own trade interests while pushing for a stronger, more secure – and more multipolar – Indo-Pacific region.

This framing allowed the South Asian nation to cast itself as an independent pole, distinct from both Beijing and Washington and without the associated baggage, said Sharma, a junior fellow with the foundation’s strategic studies programme.

Lin agreed that India functioned as an additional option for Asean rather than a direct replacement for either the US or China.

India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner

Joanne Lin, foreign policy researcher

“They are looking for partners that can widen their strategic space without forcing them into rigid alignments,” she said of Southeast Asian nations. “India’s strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and Global South positioning resonate with Asean’s own instinct to diversify partnerships and preserve room for manoeuvre.”

In Tapan’s telling, India “lowers the cost of hedging” for the region, due to it being “aligned enough with the West to be useful, [but] non-aligned enough that buying Indian missiles doesn’t read in Beijing as joining a containment bloc”.

Still, Lin was careful not to overstate Delhi’s diplomatic standing within the region.

India “is not yet in the same league as China or the US” in terms of Southeast Asia’s “perceptions of influence”, she said.

“China remains deeply embedded economically, while the US remains central to security calculations. India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner, useful, non-coercive and increasingly visible, but still needing stronger economic delivery.”

‘Some way to go’

India still had “some way to go” to match the scale of Chinese capital, trade volume and state-driven speed, said Bhatt, the international-relations professor.

China’s trade with Asean was about eight times higher than India’s last year – a gulf that does not look likely to close any time soon.

But Delhi’s diplomacy need not be based on countering China alone.

India and Asean spoke “a common language of non-alignment” and shared “a common belief in the Global South”, Bhatt said.

Soft-power advantages bolster India’s appeal, according to Pukhrem, pointing to Delhi-funded restoration work at heritage sites such as Cambodia’s Angkor Wat and Vietnam’s My Son temples as evidence of outreach that “builds soft power rooted in shared civilisational ties rather than transactional influence”.

Tapan agreed that it was not a case of “India vs China’s clout, but India raising the price of Chinese dominance”.

The recent BrahMos sales had demonstrated regional appetite for Indian weapons systems, she said, further pointing to demand for naval hardware, generic pharmaceuticals and digital public infrastructure “that no Chinese product can substitute”.

Tapan also identified India’s growing appeal as a “China plus one” destination for companies looking to diversify supply chains.

“None of this beats a trillion dollars of trade. But Asean’s operating logic is hedging,” she said. “The realistic question is whether India can be indispensable in the places where China is either unwelcome or absent.”

Lin cautioned against India defining its Asean engagement purely in oppositional terms.

“Asean does not want to be treated as a theatre for India-China rivalry,” she said, adding that Delhi could make the most impact by helping the bloc diversify supply chains, build maritime capacity and strengthen digital and health cooperation.

“India’s broader influence will depend on whether it can also deliver in areas that matter to Asean’s economic and development priorities,” Lin added.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s 1,000-year-old tea heritage is being rediscovered and rehabilitated
item.description:
Ask a Hongkonger where the city’s tea story begins, and they will probably point to the British – the colonial traders who funnelled Chinese leaves through Victoria Harbour to the world.

Only, they would be off by about eight centuries.

Most Hongkongers today don’t know the city ever had its own tea plantations, let alone that tea had been growing here long before the British arrived in the mid-19th century. Li In, a co-founder of the Hong Kong Tea Production Institute (HKTPI) who has practised the art of tea-making for more than a decade, found out in 2017 – in a London classroom, at the UK Tea Academy.
item.content:encoded:
Ask a Hongkonger where the city’s tea story begins, and they will probably point to the British – the colonial traders who funnelled Chinese leaves through Victoria Harbour to the world.

Only, they would be off by about eight centuries.

Most Hongkongers today don’t know the city ever had its own tea plantations, let alone that tea had been growing here long before the British arrived in the mid-19th century. Li In, a co-founder of the Hong Kong Tea Production Institute (HKTPI) who has practised the art of tea-making for more than a decade, found out in 2017 – in a London classroom, at the UK Tea Academy.

“I was born and raised in Hong Kong and it took a British instructor, Jane Pettigrew, mentioning tea gardens in Lantau for me to first hear about [Hong Kong’s tea heritage],” she says.

Ngong Ping Tea Garden, the plantation in question, on Lantau Island, was founded in 1948 by Brook Bernacchi, a British lawyer and politician who arrived in Hong Kong as a marine with the World War II liberation forces in 1945. He built a life on the plateau near the Po Lin Monastery. His Lotus Brand was marketed as “the only Hong Kong tea”.

By the early 1980s, unable to compete with mass production, the tea plantation area was downsized. After cycling through different hands and functions – a recreational space, a restaurant – the site was eventually abandoned in 2014, its remnants still sitting beneath a pine tree, on a trail south of the Big Buddha – a colonial relic.

Li went looking for it anyway. In March 2023, she and a small group of enthusiasts harvested what they could from the site’s overgrown tea bushes and processed them into a small batch of red and green teas. It didn’t amount to much, but it proved one thing: tea was still growing in Hong Kong, decades after Lotus Brand had folded and the city had moved on.

Li was determined to take local tea cultivation seriously, but she needed more than a ruin. Four months later, her search took her to the upper slopes of Tai Mo Shan, to Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden.

Established in 1956 by the Kadoorie brothers as an agricultural aid station for struggling farmers, the 148-hectare sanctuary is widely recognised for its “nature as a classroom” model, welcoming visitors to see its resident animals, wander the terraced gardens and breathe air that doesn’t taste like exhaust fumes. Less known is the fact that Kadoorie has been quietly growing tea on its property since the early 2000s.

Kadoorie’s plantation wasn’t always hidden in plain sight: the farm first brought tea plants over from Ngong Ping in the 70s and 80s, strictly for exhibition. In 2004, the decision to actually grow tea was made, born of a pragmatic desire to fully use the available land. At 400 metres above sea level, the mountainside terrace is a difficult site, plagued by strong winds, thin soil and no reliable water source. Vegetables would struggle in these conditions, the team at Kadoorie assessed. But the same terrain was ideal for tea.

“It was about picking the right plant for the right place,” says Yip Tsz-lam, Kadoorie’s regenerative agriculture manager, who has worked at the farm since 2003. “Of course, we also wanted to continue Hong Kong’s centuries-old tea culture.”

Single-lane and steep, the road up to the terraces is a series of hairpin turns. It takes about 10 minutes by car, before the incline levels out. On our visit, Tai Mo Shan lives up to its colloquial name – “Big Mist Mountain” – its slopes wrapped in clouds so dense the tea bushes in the distance vanish into white.

It’s the kind of climate tea plants dream about. China’s great tea-growing regions, such as Fujian and Yunnan provinces, thrive in similar environments. Mist diffuses the sunlight, slowing photosynthesis to give the leaves time to accumulate amino acids, the compounds that become sweetness and complexity in the cup.

On these terraces are three cultivars, all sourced from Fujian: Ming-fa, Wong-chi-heung and Purple Bud Buddha’s Hand. Many people assume green and red teas come from different plants, when, in fact, they all belong to the same species; the difference is in the processing. Likewise, herbal teas are not tea at all. Only leaves from Camellia sinensis qualify; the rest are tisanes (herbal infusions). What Kadoorie is growing is the real thing.

Of the 2,000 bushes planted in 2004, about half died in the first few years. “We lacked experience with the terrain,” says Yip. But the survivors spread into the gaps and the yield held steady.

Growing the tea, however, was just the start. Kadoorie’s first harvest, in 2008, caught the team off guard. “Our initial amateur attempts resulted in terrible-tasting tea,” Yip recalls.

Kadoorie needed help, and found it closer than they expected. A colleague at the farm’s apiary introduced his mentor, Wong Tung-pui. Si Gung (“Grandmaster”), as he was known, was a Hakka man from Huizhou, in Guangdong province, who came to Hong Kong in the 70s. In his youth, he managed a tea plantation on the mainland and had learned the Hakka tradition of pan-frying leaves by hand.

When Kadoorie approached him, Si Gung was no longer working in agriculture – he kept bees and grew plants for pleasure in the countryside – but he still had the knowledge. “We were lucky to find him,” Yip says. “At that time, finding anyone in Hong Kong who still knew how to manually fry and process tea was incredibly difficult; the broader tea industry, including in mainland China, had already shifted almost entirely to machine-processing.”

Si Gung passed on the pan-frying tradition of his people, a rare skill that has faded even within Hakka communities. Kadoorie adopted it by default. “It wasn’t a planned cultural preservation effort,” Yip says. “It was born out of sheer necessity.”

For the next 15 years, Kadoorie’s tea operation ticked along quietly, following the rhythm of the 24 terms in the solar calendar. Between the winter solstice and Ching Ming in early April, the plants were pruned and fertilised, then the leaves were harvested until the end of the rainy season, usually around the autumn equinox. A limited amount was sold at the farm shop. Kadoorie never thought to promote the tea; they saw no reason to draw attention to something that still felt unfinished.

Connecting with Li and her HKTPI co-founders, Chan Tsz-ting and Season Li Tin-on, gave Kadoorie the downstream partner it needed. Kadoorie would manage the tea-growing and HKTPI would take the leaves further than ever before, experimenting with oxidation levels, producing multiple styles from a single cultivar and bringing the results to the public through workshops. Without them, “a lot of the tea’s potential would be wasted”, Yip says.

Li developed a method she calls “guerrilla tea-making” to process the leaves. On harvest days, the initial withering took place on the farm, in the sunlight. By dusk, the leaves were packed and taken home. In her living room, with no climate-control equipment, she relied entirely on her senses: watching the leaves, feeling the humidity, adjusting each step. “My job is not to decide what the tea tastes like,” she says. “It’s to show what the land, the weather and the leaves are giving us.”

With just the Ming-fa cultivar, Li produced several teas with different characters, evoking Hong Kong’s history as a crossroads of tea cultures, where the toasted-rice notes of Hakka pan-fried green, the floral sweetness of British-style black tea, the intense fragrance of Chaozhou Phoenix Dancong and the roasted oolongs of Fujian had come together and been absorbed.

When Li gave a finished red-tea variant to Ip Wing-chi, founder of Lok Cha Tea House and a doyen of Hong Kong’s tea world, he likened it to Taiwan’s Oriental Beauty. Also known as Dongfang Meiren, Oriental Beauty is one of the most expensive oolong teas in the world – harvests can sell for thousands of dollars per kilogram – so this was no small compliment. But why would a red tea from Tai Mo Shan carry that same oolong note at all?

Plot 107, where the leaves were plucked, held the answer: the buds there were stunted, fibrous and difficult to process. “We investigated and found tea green leafhoppers,” says Li.

Barely visible, the leafhopper’s bite causes the plant to release a chemical defence with a honeyed fragrance: the signature of Oriental Beauty. In Taiwan’s Miaoli and Hsinchu regions, farmers deliberately cultivate these insects. A pest, under the right conditions, became a gift for the tea-makers.

Li had not expected to find leafhoppers thriving on Tai Mo Shan. Warmer temperatures, driven by climate change, scrambled harvest seasons, but it also made the insects more prolific.

“It’s a double-edged sword,” Li says. Leafhoppers trigger the sweet aroma, but they reduce yields to one-fifth of a standard harvest. For a farm already operating at micro scale, the numbers were punishing.

But the trade-off posed an important question: “Do we want volume or quality? Hong Kong has the means and should pursue quality. If we could only produce a plain, characterless tea, producing it here would be meaningless.”

Li does not claim perfection for the “Hong Kong Oriental Beauty”, but the experts have given their verdict. Dr Chen You-ren, former director of the Taiwan Tea Research and Extension Station, and Dr Kim Young-suk, a Korean tea studies professor, were satisfied with the quality. It matters to Li that the validation comes from Asia’s tea-making heartlands: “It gave us confidence that Hong Kong tea can reach the international artisan stage.”

But Li had more in mind than just making good tea – she wanted to know its origins. HKTPI co-founder Chan, a tea historian, had dug through academic papers and Qing dynasty gazetteers in an attempt to map out where Hong Kong’s earliest tea gardens used to be.

His findings rewound the clock by centuries. Hong Kong Society Before the Colonial Era, a 1990 textbook by historian Siu Kwok-kin, described tea cultivation in the New Territories during the Ming dynasty (1368-1644). By 2019, Siu had revised his position, arguing for Song dynasty origins, and Chan found further evidence: Southern Song (1127-1279) records of tea-growing clans migrating to the New Territories and Northern Song (960-1127) tea-ware excavated at Sung Wong Toi, in Kowloon. Compare that to the start of British colonial rule, in 1841 – tea was never just a footnote in Hong Kong’s history.

During the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), the written record started to catch up. An account in the 17th century Guangdong Xinyu encyclopaedia described tea-growing on the cliffs of Bui Dou Saan – present-day Castle Peak – with “the scent of orchid and jasmine, sweet and fragrant”.

By the Jiaqing period (1796-1820), the Xin’an County Gazetteer, a pre-colonial record of the region, had listed four famous teas grown locally: Phoenix Tea, from Lantau’s Phoenix Mountain, harvested by indigenous villagers and prized for its cooling properties; Mung Saan Tea, from Castle Peak, steeped in cloud mist and said to rival its famous Sichuan province namesake; Daam Gon Tea, from Tsing Yi, known for aiding digestion; and Ching Ming Tea, from Tai Lam, a fermented, medicinal tea preserved with salt.

Chan’s research included a 1986 paper by Dr Patrick Hase, a historian specialising in the New Territories. It described Hakka families in Mau Tso Ngam, a village in the foothills of Fei Ngo Shan, who still grew tea, sustaining two centuries of continuous cultivation.

In December 2024, the co-founders went on a “treasure hunt” to Mau Tso Ngam, along the MacLehose Trail, timed to the flowering season of Camellia sinensis so its white blossoms would make surviving tea trees visible. What they found was not a ruin.

A handful of elders remained in Mau Tso Ngam, along with mature tea trees planted decades and centuries ago, by mothers, grandmothers and ancestors. Cheng Kwun-ming, the village head, walked the visitors through the trees, pointing: this one, his mother planted 50 years ago; that one, a woman in her 80s told them, had been there since her father-in-law was alive. He used to carry the leaves across Fei Ngo Shan to Hong Kong Island to sell. Stories unspooled, rooted in the soil, still growing.

One of the villagers still harvesting and processing the leaves is Cheng Hung-ying. Now in her 70s, “Sister Hung” has picked and pan-fried tea since her teens. In her 30s, she cleared a patch of bamboo forest on the slope behind Mau Tso Ngam and planted tea trees. “Her mother could only drink the village’s own tea,” Li says. “So, that’s why she started. It was an act of care.”

“Cheng [the village head] always asks me the same question,” Li recalls. “‘What do you taste?’ And I tell him about the aroma, the sweetness, the body. And he says, ‘No. It’s yan ching mei [the taste of connection and community].’”

Somewhere along the way, Li’s search for Hong Kong’s forgotten tea had become a search for herself. Last year, while consulting with Lam Man-ying, director of the Hong Kong Hakka Association, to gather context on Mau Tso Ngam, the conversation turned to her family background. As they mapped out her grandfather’s village, the pieces clicked: Li is of Hakka descent. She has, unknowingly, spent years chasing her own heritage.

Li keeps returning to Mau Tso Ngam. On another visit, Sister Hung shows her the Hakka pan-frying process from start to finish.

Moving through her tea trees with ease and familiarity, Sister Hung demonstrates how to pick the bud and the two youngest leaves, pinched clean with a flick of the wrist.

Back in the village, at an outdoor wok set-up weathered by years of use, she gets the fire going in just a few minutes, using wood she chopped herself, from behind the small row of houses, most of them now uninhabited. In the three hours it takes to pan-fry the leaves, one person tends the fire, the other keeps the leaves moving to stop them from burning. She uses no thermometer, no timer – only her hands and decades of instinct.

With the wok at around 300 degrees Celsius, Sister Hung works fast to saat ching (“kill the green”), using a Y-shaped wooden tool passed down from her father. Next, she rolls the leaves back and forth on a bamboo withering tray with her gloved palms – the same motion as kneading dough – until the cell walls break down and the juices coat the surface, so the flavour can build.

Finally, the leaves return to the wok at a lower heat. With her bare hands, she turns them, lifting and dropping, pressing and spreading, for the better part of two hours. If she loses the rhythm, the batch is ruined.

Sister Hung no longer lives in Mau Tso Ngam year-round, but she comes back to pan-fry tea and make alkaline rice dumplings, another Hakka tradition recognised as part of Hong Kong’s intangible cultural heritage. She is the last person in her family who knows how to do it.

“My children didn’t want to learn; they don’t even want to try the tea I pan-fry any more,” she says. “I come back every year anyway. It has become a ritual for me.”

Li, who trained in Taiwan, Japan and Britain, understands the science of oxidation, amino acids and catechins. But what Sister Hung knows is held in the body, passed down through years of watching and copying until the skill becomes instinct.

“My job is to understand her, to turn what she knows into something we can replicate, to carry forward the culture,” says Li.

When the village head learned that Li and her team worked with Kadoorie, he welcomed them without hesitation. In the 50s and 60s, the Kadoorie Agricultural Aid Association supported Hakka farmers across the New Territories; the trust already existed.

HKTPI is reviving that decades-old partnership for a new purpose. Mau Tso Ngam’s tea trees represent a living gene bank of cultivars that have adapted to Hong Kong’s terroir. If the ageing tea-makers can’t tend to them, the genetic knowledge will be lost.

Last November, HKTPI invited the villagers to Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden to plant saplings from Mau Tso Ngam’s heritage trees, bringing their cultivars into Kadoorie’s conservation infrastructure.

“We’re not reviving a lost craft,” Li says. “We’re a bridge. One end connects to the tea traditions Hakka ancestors cultivated; the other end connects to the present, the land, what’s still here.”

HKTPI and Kadoorie now co-host workshops where the public can harvest leaves from the terraces and try their hand at traditional pan-frying. At the Hong Kong International Tea Fair 2024, they poured cups of Tai Mo Shan tea for visitors who did not believe the city could produce anything worth drinking.

Some visitors asked what the point was. Even if the tea were good, what did a few kilograms from a mountainside matter? It’s true that Kadoorie’s harvests are too limited to sustain widespread commercial production. But Chan has greater ambitions than just retail growth: “Our dream is that one day, when foreign dignitaries visit the city, the tea they are served is ours.”

Inspired by her findings, Li is building another stage: the Hakka Tea Theatre, a clear expression of her role as a “translator”. Here, the tea served is Hakka pan-fried green, the food is Hakka yellow-wine chicken, the stories are from Mau Tso Ngam and the crafts are local. But the format is British afternoon tea.

The project mirrors her own trajectory, from running a British-style tearoom in Mong Kok, training overseas in various tea cultures, to serving tea at a consulate in London. She understands both lexicons – the formal precision of a Western tea service and the embodied knowledge of a Hakka village. At the Tea Theatre, the two meet. “I’m not asking people to choose between Chinese and Western,” she says. “I’m showing them that the tea doesn’t belong to either. It belongs to the land it came from.”

Chan thinks about the future in two timelines. In five years, HKTPI will have the resources to sustain the partnership with Kadoorie, safeguard tea-making traditions in Mau Tso Ngam, explore other forgotten tea plantations and stage more Hakka Tea Theatre experiments. In 10 years, a younger generation will join them, “to inherit the culture, the technique and the vision of this land”.

Li had learned, through a serendipitous journey, that this land belongs to her, too. She had started in a London classroom, followed the trail through an abandoned colonial plantation, up a misty mountain and into a tiny village that had never stopped making tea, and found herself inside the story she was chasing.

“Letting the next generation know that Hong Kong has this history is not just about tea,” Li says. “It’s the confidence of knowing that we are not rootless; we carry something we can be proud of.”

[Correction: An earlier version identified Cheng Sui-wing as the village head who welcomed the visitors to Mau Tso Ngam. It has been amended to Cheng Kwun-ming, who also serves as the village head for Mau Tso Ngam, alongside Cheng Sui-wing.]

item.title: [SCMP] Investment with Chinese characteristics: how Beijing’s money is reshaping tech ventures
item.description:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.
item.content:encoded:
On the surface, China’s cutting-edge tech sector – from the algorithmic breakthroughs of DeepSeek and Zhipu AI to the hardware of Unitree Robotics and ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) – mirrors Silicon Valley’s venture capital-backed ecosystem.

But a closer look at their financing histories reveals a common investor: the Chinese state.

Beijing’s strong presence underscores a more profound structural shift in how China’s frontier technology is being funded. As Western venture capital and domestic private wealth retreat, the government has been steadily expanding its role in the market, constructing a state-capitalist apparatus which blurs the line between public policy and private equity.

Rather than operating via a single entity, this public capital flows through a layered matrix of national funds, local investment vehicles, state-owned enterprises (SOEs) and privately managed funds. It is a system that converts top-down policy priorities into private-market bets, with an alternative perspective on what can be considered a return on investment.

Last year, state-affiliated investors supplied more than 90 per cent of the committed capital tracked in China’s private-equity market, a surge from just under 79 per cent in 2021, according to domestic data provider Zerone.

This mandate comes directly from the top. At a high-level national science and technology gathering in Beijing on July 8, President Xi Jinping urged financial capital firms to “invest early, invest small, invest for the long term and invest in hard technology”.

How this capital is deployed could determine whether China will succeed in its ambitions to become a self-reliant tech superpower – or suffocate its economy under the weight of state-engineered overcapacity.

How the money moves

“2018 was roughly the turning point for us,” said Shen Qinhua, founding partner of Puhua Capital, a Hangzhou-based investment firm with about 40 billion yuan (US$5.91 billion) under management. Puhua aimed to raise between 7 billion and 8 billion yuan in 2026, with state-affiliated investors expected to account for about 90 per cent of the total, he said.

According to Shen, it was around eight years ago that traditional private-business owners in eastern Zhejiang province started to pull back their investments in Puhua, as they realised that venture funds’ long holding periods had failed to match their liquidity expectations.

China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage

– Zhou Kaibing, Hangzhou Venture Capital Association

Around the same time, dollar funds began retreating amid escalating US-China tensions. More recently, restrictions on investment in sensitive technologies from both sides have deepened the financial divide, while Beijing’s aggressive push into strategic technologies has drawn a diverse array of state investors.

This state support arrives in vastly different forms and at distinct stages of a company’s life cycle.

For CXMT, which is headed for a blockbuster public market debut in Shanghai next week, a combination of national, provincial and municipal investors supplied the massive capital, credit support and project construction resources required to build a capital-intensive memory chipmaker from scratch. Industrial and private investors came later.

It is one of the clearest examples of the “Hefei model”, under which the provincial capital of central China’s Anhui uses state investment vehicles to back strategic industries, absorb early risk and anchor companies locally before bringing in market capital.

By contrast, state funds entered Unitree Robotics much later in the game. That financing came after the robot maker had already proven its technological and commercial viability, timing that aligned with Beijing’s elevation of robotics to a strategic priority.

Unicorn artificial intelligence firm DeepSeek, initially funded entirely by private wealth, only recently drew backing from the national AI fund after emerging as a powerful symbol of China’s challenge to US tech supremacy.

Hong Kong-listed Zhipu, whose market cap at the market close on Friday was HK$585.95 billion (US$74.72 billion), attracted a cluster of local government funds when it neared its initial public offering in January, as cities vied for a stake to secure a share in the booming AI sector – or remain economically relevant.

One main delivery mechanism for state capital is the fund-of-funds model.

Puhua Capital, for instance, has twice been selected to manage sub-funds backed by the National SME Development Fund, which is financed by central and local fiscal capital alongside smaller state and institutional investors.

In this set-up, the national fund typically provides a 30 per cent anchor commitment. Puhua would raise another 30 per cent to 40 per cent from provincial, municipal or district-level state vehicles, before securing the remaining balance and deciding where to base the fund.

Puhua would retain its day-to-day investment autonomy, but operate under strict oversight. An appointed observer, separate from the investment committee, could join deal discussions from an early stage and veto proposed investments.

Furthermore, at least 70 per cent of the capital must be deployed into “522” companies – businesses with no more than 200 million yuan in annual sales, 200 million yuan in assets and 500 employees. Performance metrics and related-party transactions would be regularly audited.

“The requirements are higher,” Shen said, “but so is the support for policy direction and industrial coordination.”

In this way, a fund-of-funds brings in broader outside capital while steering it to policy priorities. Meanwhile, the National Venture Capital Guidance Fund, launched late last year, operates further upstream, channelling central fiscal money through regional funds into hundreds of professionally managed sub-funds focused strictly on early-stage technologies.

Some point towards specific industries. For example, the “Big Fund” – China’s flagship semiconductor investor – concentrates capital into this fiercely competitive arena, taking equity stakes directly and backing specialist funds across the chip supply chain.

Others can be deployed through local platforms that take stakes or finance construction, as in Hefei, as well as via investments and acquisitions by state-owned companies.

Who bears the risk?

Capital is pouring into strategic industries through funds with longer lifespans as exit routes expand. Platforms like Shanghai’s Nasdaq-like Star Market and the Hong Kong stock exchange now allow these companies to go public sooner, enabling broader retail investors to share in the potential gains.

“A loop is gradually taking shape, directing more capital towards hard tech companies,” said Mi Lei, founder of CAS Star, a venture-capital firm spun out of an institute under the state-run Chinese Academy of Sciences. The firm’s early bets on China’s photonics sector have begun to see tangible returns amid the AI boom.

However, state investors and private funds do not always share the same scorecard. While a market fund is judged mostly on financial returns, local governments must also account for the number of factories built, jobs created and taxes generated – competing goals that can weaken financial discipline and fuel intercity rivalries.

This local tournament has made China’s industrial policy unusually entrepreneurial – and competitive. Beijing signals the strategic direction, while cities fiercely contest fund structures, industrial estates, credit support and real-world applications.

In the nascent stages of an industry, this rivalry can foster healthy development, or what Shen described as “a hundred flowers blooming”. But it can also lead to severe overcrowding, driven by local governments’ fear of missing out on the next big macroeconomic wave.

The solar panel and electric vehicle (EV) sectors offer stark cautionary tales for today’s policy darlings, such as AI, semiconductors and embodied intelligence.

Expanding production capacity can benefit a single city seeking to boost its local economy, but when dozens of cities replicate the strategy simultaneously, the result is crippling overcapacity and collapsing profit margins on a nationwide basis.

“China’s enormous industrial advantage has not yet translated into a profit advantage,” said Zhou Kaibing, chairman of the Hangzhou Venture Capital Association. He noted that some companies with little initial appetite for scaling up began to aggressively add capacity after winning government support.

The structural risks of this approach were highlighted by state broadcaster CCTV in April through the downfall of Neta, a once-prominent EV brand owned by Hozon Auto.

Local governments in Tongxiang in Zhejiang province, Yichun in central Jiangxi province, and Nanning in Guangxi Zhuang autonomous region all took equity stakes in Hozon, providing factories, land, subsidies and financing to secure production bases within their regions – even as the carmaker remained deeply unprofitable.

As its products lost ground in a brutally competitive domestic market, the company fell into court-supervised restructuring in 2025. The failure has put billions of yuan in state-backed equity, subsidies and fixed industrial assets at risk.

This raises an uncomfortable question for policy architects: are these losses an acceptable cost of doing business in a nascent industry, or do they represent a fundamental failure of discipline in public investment?

Zhou argued that to mitigate these risks, governments should avoid trying to act as talent scouts themselves. Instead, they should delegate capital management to professional fund managers, who are better equipped to pick market winners and diversify risk.

The state investment system excels at moving money, but it is still learning how – and where – to take risks, he said.

Course correction

Beijing, however, is very much aware of these structural vulnerabilities.

At the same science and technology gathering in Beijing, Xi issued a pointed warning, saying that regions must adapt policy to local conditions rather than blindly chase hot sectors or engage in wasteful, copycat development and “involution-style” competition.

The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure. You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return

– Mi Lei, CAS Star

Policymakers are now attempting a delicate balancing act: mobilising unprecedented capital for technology while imposing rigorous discipline on how it is deployed.

In recent years, this policy response has been rolled out in stages. The State Council’s 2024 policy document, which introduced 17 guidelines on promoting high-quality venture capital, served as the sector’s broadest overhaul since 2016.

It encouraged “patient capital” with a more long-term outlook, shifting the evaluation metrics from a deal-by-deal basis to that of a fund’s full life cycle, while protecting managers from liability for honest failures and broadening exit strategies beyond initial public offerings.

By 2025, new rules shifted the focus directly onto government fund management. This guidance curbed overlapping funds and duplicate local investments, demanded more professional management and called for a greater tolerance for legitimate, due-diligence-backed investment losses.

This year, the State Council’s guidance for investment approval extended the course correction to the factories, industrial estates and public liabilities that often accompany state-backed investments. It also tightened its oversight of fixed-asset projects, enabling it to halt disorderly capacity expansion while introducing lifetime responsibility for officials whose unlawful investment decisions cause serious economic consequences.

“The nature of venture capital is to take risks and tolerate failure,” said CAS Star’s Mi. “You only need one winner to deliver an outsize return.”

The ultimate test for the equity investment model with Chinese characteristics is whether its bureaucracy can not only learn to accept the inevitable losers that are inherent to venture capital, but also retain the discipline required to cut their losses after failed bets.

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesia’s Bali financial hub ‘a matter of survival’: economic tsar
item.description:
Bali has “aura” and political titan Luhut Pandjaitan wants to channel it to transform Indonesia’s famed resort island into an international financial centre.

But President Prabowo Subianto’s special adviser and economic tsar is not relying on subtle nods to Gen Z slang to sell paradise. Instead, he conjures up a striking image to make his case.

A friend recently sent him a photograph of kamikaze drones lighting up the skies over Abu Dhabi, accompanied by a plea: help us get out.
item.content:encoded:
Bali has “aura” and political titan Luhut Pandjaitan wants to channel it to transform Indonesia’s famed resort island into an international financial centre.

But President Prabowo Subianto’s special adviser and economic tsar is not relying on subtle nods to Gen Z slang to sell paradise. Instead, he conjures up a striking image to make his case.

A friend recently sent him a photograph of kamikaze drones lighting up the skies over Abu Dhabi, accompanied by a plea: help us get out.

Indonesia, safely removed from the Iran war’s turmoil, was the obvious choice, he said.

“They said ‘We’d like to move our assets, we’d love very much to stay away from here and live in Bali, because it’s so peaceful in Bali’,” he recalled. “The Middle East conflict is not going to end next month or next year, I don’t believe that.”

Speaking to This Week in Asia on the sidelines of the Nusa Dua Forum in Bali on July 17, the 78-year-old chairman of Indonesia’s National Economic Council was a study in moustachioed calm – a far cry from the crisis of confidence that has roiled Southeast Asia’s largest economy this year.

For us … it’s a matter of survival

Luhut Pandjaitan, National Economic Council chairman

Investors, spooked by scepticism over Prabowo’s populist policies and rattled further by a global energy crisis that sent fuel prices soaring, have pulled billions out of Indonesia in recent months.

Acknowledging the market rout and concerns over money laundering, Luhut pledged greater transparency and to stamp out corruption.

“Without this, it’s very hard to gain trust and credibility,” he said, going on to describe the financial hub in existential terms. “For us … it’s a matter of survival.”

On Tuesday, Indonesia’s parliament passed legislation paving the way for the new financial centre just 20 days after talks on it had first begun.

Its precise location and the full range of associated incentives are still under wraps, but Luhut says the legislative speed should come as no surprise – he first floated the idea two years ago.

The centre could be up and running as soon as next month, he said, hinting that Prabowo might time an official announcement to coincide with the country’s independence day on August 17.

Instead of Indonesia’s civil code, the centre will operate under international commercial law, according to Luhut, who drew a parallel with Hong Kong.

“It’s like one country, two systems,” he said. “Which is not the ideal … But the purpose is to improve the credibility and trust of Indonesia.”

Sceptical of the notion that only Singapore, Hong Kong or the United Arab Emirates could host such hubs, Luhut said he had consulted a range of investors – from American hedge fund manager Ray Dalio to the Porsche family – and found them in agreement.

“They said they love the aura of Bali,” he quipped.

Separately, at the forum – co-organised by the South China Morning Post and Indonesian sovereign wealth fund Danantara – Indonesia’s former coordinating minister of maritime and investment repeated his pitch to a room filled with officials, investors and family office principals.

“We’re going to be very transparent. We’re going to be more efficient, there’s going to be less corruption,” he declared. “I’m pretty confident about that.”

Unshaken optimism

Luhut’s optimism does not end at the new international financial centre. He is convinced Indonesia’s digitalisation push and its young, skilled workforce can deliver Prabowo’s target of lifting economic growth from 5 to 8 per cent by 2029.

“I think 8 per cent – with digital infrastructure support, artificial intelligence and also with the family offices – I don’t think it’s a big deal,” he said, brushing off economists’ scepticism.

Technological progress over the past few years had been nothing short of “beautiful”, Luhut said, outlining how data collected from eight government ministries and major institutions now fed into an AI-supported system to drive efficiency gains.

“Indonesia will be different within two years,” he vowed, referring to a local “brain and talent factory” he founded where students are selected based on IQ scores and put through a curated curriculum.

Addressing the prevailing gloom surrounding coverage of Indonesia’s economy and policies, Luhut blamed a failure of messaging and argued that there was an information disconnect between the government and the public.

Earlier this year, global index provider MSCI warned it could downgrade Indonesia from emerging to frontier market status amid concerns over transparency and stock market manipulation. A May deadline it set to see signs of progress has since been pushed back to November.

A brighter spot came earlier this month, when S&P reaffirmed Jakarta’s sovereign credit rating, forecasting that recent financial strains would ease thanks to higher commodity prices and spending cuts.

The government projects its budget shortfall to widen to 2.85 per cent of gross domestic product this year, just shy of the 3 per cent statutory ceiling. Prabowo’s flagship free meals programme – a cornerstone of his populist economic agenda – has drawn much of the flak for exacting a heavy toll on state finances since its launch in January 2025.

On Tuesday, the programme’s budget was slashed again – now reduced by more than 100 trillion rupiah (US$5.6 billion) from its original allocation – and the agency chief charged with overseeing it resigned a day later, citing health reasons.

Luhut defended the scheme as essential to inclusive growth and insisted the administration had committed to making it more “targeted” by focusing on remote areas.

“You have to adjust, because every province faces a different situation,” he said.

Indonesia’s troubleshooter

Luhut’s current role is just the latest chapter in a political and business career spanning four decades.

A former four-star army general, he first entered politics as Indonesia started its transition to democracy in the late 1990s, before stepping away several years later to build a business empire in energy, minerals and coal.

He returned in 2014 after helping finance Joko Widodo’s successful presidential campaign that year, becoming his chief of staff – a newly created position – and trusted troubleshooter, later spearheading both Indonesia’s downstreaming strategy and its pandemic response.

Also Widodo’s point man on China, Luhut called Jakarta-Beijing relations “very good”, revealing plans for an impending meeting between Prabowo and around 20 Chinese firms invested in Indonesia.

In May, Chinese businesses had raised concerns about Jakarta’s rising levies and stricter enforcement, with several Indonesian ministers pushing back, insisting the country must prioritise sovereignty over its natural resources.

To avoid misunderstandings, Luhut said Prabowo’s relationship with Chinese leader Xi Jinping had to become “much closer”.

“I said to the president, the biggest investor in this country is still China, whether you like it or not,” he said, noting that Beijing was “very willing” to share its technology and research capabilities.

Prabowo’s stricter demands of tycoons – including a plan to funnel proceeds from palm oil exports and other key resources through sovereign wealth fund Danantara to curb under-invoicing – has further unnerved investors, but Luhut shrugs off the unease.

“This country, with a 300 million population, it’s not easy to govern,” he said. “But we explain to them that the best time to invest in Indonesia is today.”

During the 2024 presidential election, when Luhut backed Prabowo’s campaign, he declined any ministerial post, opting instead to remain an adviser, according to state news agency Antara.

Asked about Widodo’s surprise return to the political stage this year – touring the country to support his son Kaesang Pangarep’s Solidarity Party – Luhut was philosophical,

“Jokowi is still active because, of course, he has to survive,” he said, referring to the former president by his popular nickname. “Otherwise, if you retire fully, it’s easy to get very old.”
