President Xi Jinping led commemorations for the birth centenary of late state leader Jiang Zemin at a grand ceremony in Beijing on Monday, in a show of political continuity and party unity ahead of next year’s major power reshuffle.

Addressing thousands of officials and delegates at the Great Hall of the People, Xi delivered a 40-minute speech that highlighted Jiang’s contributions to the Communist Party and the country.

A large portrait of Jiang was displayed above the rostrum – a practice reserved for deceased former top leaders like Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping.

All seven members of the Politburo Standing Committee, along with a long list of retired state leaders, attended the ceremony in a show of solidarity within the party.

They included former premier Wen Jiabao, who served between 2003 and 2013, and former vice-presidents Wang Qishan and Zeng Qinghong. Former president Hu Jintao was absent.

The ceremony was also attended by members of the Jiang family as well as people who worked around him, according to Premier Li Qiang, who moderated the event.

Xi, Li and other top leaders met Jiang’s family before the ceremony, according to state broadcaster CCTV.

The commemorative event comes a year ahead of next autumn’s 21st national party congress, where a new leadership line-up will be unveiled and Xi is expected to secure another five-year term as party leader.

Xi praised a long list of Jiang’s achievements, from political loyalty to the party and economic development to foreign and defence policy, while drawing clear parallels to his own governance priorities, including fighting corruption, a firm stance on the party’s unchallenged right to rule and decisive leadership in times of crisis.

“During the 13 years [of his leadership], the international situation was complex and volatile, and Jiang led the party leadership in unswervingly upholding the party line,” Xi said.

Xi called on the entire party to learn from Jiang’s “rock-solid political conviction”, praising him for his unwavering commitment to the party’s line and policies.

Xi has repeatedly declared that the party and the country should have confidence in the path, system, theory and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

In his speech on Monday, Xi also noted that Jiang had voluntarily stepped down from his party leadership positions in 2002.

The event was the latest in a series of commemorations marking the 100th anniversary of Jiang’s birth, following a high-profile, 12-episode documentary that aired on CCTV from last Tuesday to Sunday.

In his tribute speech, Xi placed particular emphasis on Jiang’s courage and sense of responsibility in confronting crises – qualities he has also long urged party cadres to cultivate.

Xi highlighted the critical situation facing the party in the late 1980s and early 1990s – the period after the Tiananmen crackdown and collapse of the Soviet Union.

Jiang “unswervingly upheld economic development as the central task” while sticking to “the Four Cardinal Principles”, which translate into upholding the party’s unchallenged rule, Xi said.

“Jiang upheld reform and opening up, carried out rectification, engaged in diplomatic struggles, and resolutely safeguarded the country’s independence, dignity, security and stability,” he added.

Xi has long stressed the need to prevent the infiltration of Western ideology into China and has highlighted what he sees as the threat it poses to national security and stability.

Xi also praised Jiang for never making concessions on issues of sovereignty, listing achievements including the handover of Hong Kong in 1997 and Macau in 1999.

Next year marks the 30th anniversary of Hong Kong’s return to Chinese rule.

Xi also praised Jiang for his tough stance against “Taiwan independence”.

“Jiang promoted the reaching of the 1992 consensus between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait embodying the one-China principle, and vigorously carried out the struggle against separatism and Taiwan independence,” he said.

Under the oral understanding, reached in 1992 during Jiang’s tenure between Beijing and Taiwan’s then-ruling party Kuomintang, both sides agreed there was “one China”, but differed over how that “one China” should be interpreted.

Xi also praised the former leader for recognising the “strategic opportunity period” faced by China, as announced in 2002 following the country’s accession to the World Trade Organization.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not see Taiwan as a state but are opposed to a change of the status quo by force.

Xi further praised Jiang for managing major political and economic risks, as well as natural disasters, highlighting his management response to the 1997 Asian financial crisis and the devastating floods of 1998.

Xi hailed Jiang for “calmly responding to a series of international emergencies concerning China’s sovereignty and security” – in an apparent reference to the 1999 Nato bombing of the Chinese embassy in Yugoslavia as well as the 2001 collision between a Chinese fighter jet and a US surveillance aircraft over the South China Sea.

He further held up Jiang’s continued support for successive leaders after his retirement in 2004, particularly in the “fight against corruption”. Anti-corruption has been one of Xi’s central priorities since he came to power in 2012.

The event concluded with the audience standing for The Internationale – the traditional communist anthem.

Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Strategic Studies, Tsinghua University, said Xi’s address served as “a retrospective on Jiang’s life while highlighting the points of continuity and alignment with the party’s priorities today”.

Xi’s praise of Jiang’s mandate – specifically that “governing the country requires governing the party first, and governing the party must be strict” – echoed the theme of the 20th Central Committee’s coming fifth plenum in October, Xie noted.

The Politburo announced in July that the conclave would focus on “consistently exercising full and rigorous governance over the party”.

Under the same slogan, the anti-corruption campaign has brought down senior officials of ever-higher ranks and at a faster speed than many thought possible, with few signs of slowing down as it nears its 15th year under Xi.

According to Xie, the president’s speech also signalled continuity on economic reform from the Jiang era.

“Adapting to the requirements of time-honoured development and practical needs, [Jiang] continuously advanced theoretical innovation, institutional innovation, technological innovation, cultural innovation and innovations in all other areas,” Xi said in his address.

The reference reaffirmed Beijing’s current focus on high-quality development and innovation-driven growth, Xie noted.

By recalling how Jiang navigated severe domestic and external turbulence without wavering on party authority or core sovereignty, the intention was to demand that today’s leadership display a tenacious “fighting spirit” and superior fighting skills, Xie said.

These would be needed to navigate the tests of “high winds, rushing waves, and even perilous, stormy seas” when “confronting unprecedented global changes in a century and complex geopolitical dynamics such as US-China relations”, he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Chinamaxxing: is the trend really about China or Gen Z fleeing Western fatigue?
item.description:
The iconic wrapper of White Rabbit, a six-decade-old Chinese milk confectionery, has recently gone viral in the West.

Shared this month in a post on social media he retro packaging was hailed as an “absolute masterstroke of graphic design”.

Its distinctive waxy paper – featuring a white rabbit against a red circle, with blue-and-white rabbit motifs lining both edges – has since racked up more than 6 million views and 260,000 likes.
item.content:encoded:
The iconic wrapper of White Rabbit, a six-decade-old Chinese milk confectionery, has recently gone viral in the West.

Shared this month in a post on social media he retro packaging was hailed as an “absolute masterstroke of graphic design”.

Its distinctive waxy paper – featuring a white rabbit against a red circle, with blue-and-white rabbit motifs lining both edges – has since racked up more than 6 million views and 260,000 likes.

In the comments section, online users from around the world have shared custom creations such as tattoos, phone cases and T-shirts inspired by the wrapper.

The aesthetic frenzy surrounding this piece of candy wrapper is part of a wider trend that has swept Western social media: Chinamaxxing.

Young foreigners – especially Gen Z Americans and Europeans – are “maxing out” on Chinese lifestyle elements, posting videos of themselves sipping hot water, drinking goji berry tea, eating congee, practising tai chi and wearing viral Adidas “Tang” jackets with traditional pankou toggles and mandarin collars.

Some Western youths have even translated their cultural curiosity into real-world journeys by travelling to China – experiencing its dramatic landscapes, from the stunning sandstone pillars of Zhangjiajie National Forest Park to the sprawling skylines of metropolises such as Shanghai and the “cyberpunk city” of Chongqing.

As Chinamaxxing took off, content creators on TikTok and Instagram joked about entering a “very Chinese time” in their lives.

Experts say this trend reflects growing dissatisfaction among Westerners with life at home, alongside a growing fascination with Chinese culture and aesthetics, while some caution that it is unlikely to translate into greater political goodwill in the short term.

China on TikTok remains largely a projection screen for Western youth contrarianism and lifestyle aspirations

Jessica Imbach, academic

The buzzword “Chinamaxxing” peaked early this year, with related social media hashtags such as “#becomingchinese” and “#verychinese” accumulating billions of views so far.

Chinese-American TikTok influencer Sherry Zhu played a central role in popularising the meme.

In a viral video posted last December with over 350,000 likes, Zhu joked: “If you love hotpot, dim sum, Sichuan cuisine and biang biang noodles, then you are Chinese. Your body is simply yearning for that wonton.”

TikTok users reacted rather enthusiastically, with many commenting: “First day being a Chinese, kinda nervous”.

Zhu also posted content on Chinese wellness and household customs, which sparked widespread imitation. Western social media users began sharing their newly adopted Chinese daily habits, such as making digestion-aiding apple tea and wearing house slippers to avoid cold floors.

Samuel Corseaux, a former pilot from France, also took inspiration from this online trend, as seen in his new habit of drinking hot water now and then. Corseaux views Chinamaxxing as a fun way to celebrate Chinese culture, heritage and daily habits.

“Overall, I think this trend is also a way to push back against the negative narratives and propaganda that the West has spread about China for years,” he said.

Young Westerners have also extended their everyday engagement with Chinese culture to travelling to the country for a first-hand experience.

Driven by expanded visa-free policies to revive the domestic economy, China recorded 23 million inbound foreign trips in the first half of the year, up by more than a fifth from the same time in 2025, and with nearly 80 per cent using visa-free entry, according to official immigration figures.

Among this growing wave of overseas visitors was Matteo Rikabi, an architect from Italy, who said his trip to the city of Chongqing far exceeded his expectations.

“It feels like a real-life cyberpunk city, with skyscrapers, neon lights, roads built on multiple levels, and trains passing through buildings. It has such a unique atmosphere that I’ve never experienced anywhere else,” he said.

Rikabi also visited other iconic Chinese destinations, including Shanghai, Beijing and Zhangjiajie in Hunan province.

Photos posted to his social media show him posing in a viral Adidas jacket – designed in the style of a traditional Chinese Tang suit – against a backdrop of misty skies and dense primeval forests.

The journey, he noted, somewhat shifted his assumption that Chinese-made products lacked quality.

Corseaux similarly explored multiple regions, including the provinces of Yunnan and Guangdong.

As an influencer with 26,000 followers, Corseaux regularly documents his global travels. His social media posts about China quickly garnered widespread attention and likes, as viewers were intrigued by the country’s modern infrastructure, advanced technology and striking landscapes.

Corseaux said his content had even inspired some viewers to travel to China and experience it for themselves.

In response to growing follower requests, Corseaux began organising small group tours to China. His followers asked for a mix of modern urban experiences – like those in Chongqing – alongside immersive lifestyle activities, including 24-hour Chinese spas, traditional Chinese medicine and acupuncture.

“It’s funny because China really embodies these ‘two worlds’: extreme modernity and deep tradition,” Corseaux said.

Few had expected this trend, given the long-standing Sinophobia surrounding the Covid-19 pandemic, alongside recurring “China threat” rhetoric in Western media.

However, overall Western attitudes towards China appear to be undergoing a subtle yet profound shift.

A new Pew Research Centre survey across 20 countries reveals a clear shift in global public opinion: favourable views of China rose from 32 per cent to 46 per cent between 2023 and 2026, while those for the United States fell from 58 per cent to 36 per cent.

Wang Wen, dean of the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University, noted that “Chinamaxxing” reflected how the Western Gen Z was actively exploring and embracing Chinese lifestyles and development models within a specific social context.

“Many young people in the West feel disillusioned by political polarisation and social fragmentation in their home countries and are searching for a lifestyle paradigm that offers greater continuity and certainty,” Wang said.

Beyond domestic frustration in the West, the trend was equally driven by the practical appeal of everyday Chinese living, he argued.

From drinking hot water and practising baduanjin qigong to using mobile payments and riding high-speed rail, these viral trends reflect a distinctly Chinese emphasis on a pragmatic, human-centric approach, according to Wang.

For young Westerners seeking a sense of control in an unpredictable world, this practical efficiency offered a reassuring sense of order, he said.

Furthermore, Beijing’s expanding visa-free travel policies had allowed young foreigners to see a real, vibrant China, gradually pushing past long-standing stereotypes reinforced by traditional mainstream media.

This fascination carries striking historical parallels.

Jessica Imbach, assistant professor in Chinese studies at the University of Freiburg in Germany, echoed Wang’s view on Western political fatigue.

She noted that the trend resembled the 1980s cyberpunk wave and its projection of futuristic visions onto a rising Asian power – first Japan, and now China.

For Wang, Chinamaxxing is reshaping China’s global image, marking a new phase in the country’s soft power development.

He said the trend had effectively dismantled the long-standing “China threat” narrative in Western discourse, reframing the country’s image from an abstract geopolitical concept into something tangible, relatable and humanised through everyday life.

“This organic shift in public perception, originating from the grass roots, carries far more persuasiveness and resonance than top-down official messaging,” Wang said.

Imbach also said China’s image in the West was gradually shifting, citing positive coverage of other Chinese cultural exports, such as the TV drama The Untamed or the video game Black Myth: Wukong.

“It thus speaks to a larger and quite noticeable pivot away from China’s predominantly politics- and economy-centric portrayal in Western media,” she said.

Still, Imbach remained sceptical about whether China’s aesthetic momentum in Western media would translate into greater political goodwill.

“China on TikTok remains largely a projection screen for Western youth contrarianism and lifestyle aspirations,” she noted.

In line with its ongoing efforts to enhance soft power, Beijing has embraced the trend, with state media highlighting it as a sign of China’s growing cultural clout.

However, Wang cautioned against heavy-handed intervention by official agencies or overly polished marketing.

item.title: [SCMP] South Korean shipbuilders first to benefit from Trump’s plan to keep US Navy afloat
item.description:
South Korean shipbuilders could be among the first US partners to benefit from President Donald Trump’s push to rebuild America’s naval industrial base, analysts have said.

Trump last week signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum allowing foreign shipbuilders with US investments to build up to two vessels at their parent shipyards – a move aimed at quickly addressing gaps in US Navy capacity while restoring the country’s own shipbuilding sector.

The directive comes as Washington seeks to strengthen its naval position against China in the Indo-Pacific, where US officials have warned that America’s shipbuilding capacity has fallen behind strategic demand.
item.content:encoded:
South Korean shipbuilders could be among the first US partners to benefit from President Donald Trump’s push to rebuild America’s naval industrial base, analysts have said.

Trump last week signed a National Security Presidential Memorandum allowing foreign shipbuilders with US investments to build up to two vessels at their parent shipyards – a move aimed at quickly addressing gaps in US Navy capacity while restoring the country’s own shipbuilding sector.

The directive comes as Washington seeks to strengthen its naval position against China in the Indo-Pacific, where US officials have warned that America’s shipbuilding capacity has fallen behind strategic demand.

Under the memorandum, foreign companies must either build a new US shipyard or acquire a controlling stake in an existing one – a requirement that South Korea’s Hanwha already meets after taking over Philadelphia’s Philly Shipyard, one of the few large commercial yards on the US east coast, in 2024.

Foreign shipbuilders must also train American workers and transfer proprietary techniques to their US operations. Additional vessels will have to be built in the US.

“We’re now studying this announcement,” a Hanwha Ocean spokesman said, declining to give further details.

Trump signed the memorandum to “fix critical long-term issues in navy shipbuilding and ship repair programmes and restore capacity and competition to the maritime industrial base”, the White House said last week.

The interim measure was designed to “bridge gaps on a quick turnaround, while additional ships will be built in revitalised American shipyards”, it said.

The opportunity for South Korean shipbuilders comes as Trump is sending mixed signals to Seoul on security cooperation, saying in a social media post on Sunday that he had instructed Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth to “substantially reduce” joint military exercises with South Korea because of their cost and the signal they sent to North Korean leader Kim Jong-un.

South Korea on his mind

The US move provides a strategic opening for allied shipbuilders from South Korea, Japan and Australia to integrate more deeply into the US defence market, according to analysts.

“Which country is on top of President Trump’s mind? It’s an easy guess. It’s South Korea, of course,” said Moon Keun-sik, a maritime expert and professor at Hanyang University.

Moon said Trump asked him whether South Korea could help build 10 US military vessels quickly when they met at June’s G7 summit in Evian-les-Bains, France. Moon’s reply: “Of course it is possible, and we will do our best.”

Both sides held follow-up discussions at Trump’s request during the Nato summit in Turkey last month. Officials from both countries agreed to establish a working-level group to further discuss shipbuilding cooperation.

South Korea has committed to putting in US$150 billion in the US shipbuilding sector as part of a US$350 billion investment pledge under last year’s bilateral trade and investment deal.

The large-scale cooperation project, dubbed “Make American Shipbuilding Great Again”, is part of the Trump administration’s aim to rebuild the industry in the US in response to China’s capacity.

“The security memorandum is an administrative order. For long-term cooperation with allies, legislative steps should be taken to amend existing laws”, Moon said. This includes the Byrnes-Tollefson Amendment, which requires navy vessels to be constructed in US shipyards.

Jang Won-joon, a professor at Jeonbuk National University’s Department of Advanced Defence Industry Studies, said the US was under pressure to seek help from allies to bolster its naval power against China in the Indo-Pacific.

“Cooperation between South Korea and the United States in this sector is highly likely to expand further beyond the existing MRO [maintenance, repair and overhaul] services to the construction of US military vessels, technology transfer and worker training,” he said.

Biggest beneficiaries

Hanwha Group is widely seen as the best-placed South Korean company to benefit from the new opening, not only because of its US foothold but also because it has already begun expanding production capacity there.

Since acquiring Philly Shipyard, Hanwha has invested more than US$200 million to upgrade its workforce, capabilities and production capacity. It plans to finance an additional US$5 billion, with the goal of increasing its annual shipbuilding capacity from the current 1 to 1.5 vessels to 20.

This could support a strategy in which initial US warships are rapidly constructed at Hanwha Ocean’s Geoje facility in South Korea, while subsequent vessels are produced at the Philly Shipyard.

The company is also pursuing additional shipbuilding facilities in the US.

Hanwha Ocean, the South Korean parent company of Hanwha Philly Shipyard, is already providing MRO services to the US Navy.

In March, the company said its US subsidiaries – Defence USA and Philly Shipyard – had been selected as subcontractors partnering Vard Marine US on the navy’s next generation logistics ship programme. Financial terms of the contract, a major step towards gaining access to the US defence market, were not disclosed.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and White House Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought last month announced a US$2 billion investment to build two specialised missile-tracking and range instrumentation ships for the US military at Hanwha Philly Shipyard.

Hanwha has also submitted an acquisition offer of between US$1.05 billion and US$1.2 billion for Austal USA, which builds vessels for the US Navy and Coast Guard. If successful, this will give it a second US naval vessel production base – in Mobile, Alabama.

The company has already increased its stake in the global defence shipbuilder to 19.9 per cent after receiving approval from the Australian government.

“Hanwha has made it a priority to significantly contribute to revitalising American shipbuilding and is exploring a range of options to expand our footprint in the US,” the company said.

Jang said the acquisition, if successful, “would mark a decisive step forward in advancing into the US maritime defence market”.

South Korea’s HD Hyundai Heavy Industries and Samsung Heavy Industries are also eyeing a wider role.

HD Hyundai is collaborating with Huntington Ingalls Industries, the largest US defence shipbuilder, on ship construction and shipyard modernisation.

Samsung Heavy Industries is also expanding cooperation with US shipbuilders in areas including unmanned surface vessels and maintenance, repair and overhaul services.

If these efforts lead to greater local investment in the US, competition among South Korean shipbuilders to win US Navy vessel orders could intensify, according to Jang.

“Hanwha Ocean and Hyundai are expected to be front runners in the competition for this order.”

item.title: [SCMP] Nirupama Rao and Lin Minwang on the great India-China face-off
item.description:
Welcome to Open Dialogue, a series from the South China Morning Post where we bring together leading voices to discuss the stories and subjects occupying international headlines.

In this edition, we invited a leading Chinese scholar of South Asian affairs and a former Indian foreign secretary and ambassador to China to reflect on the deep fault lines in India-China relations. They debate whether the biggest barrier is history or politics, clash over the border, Pakistan and India’s ties with the United States, and examine whether Beijing and New Delhi can move beyond suspicion in an increasingly multipolar world.

Lin Minwang is a professor and vice-dean at the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University, and deputy director of the university’s Centre for South Asian Studies. His research focuses on international relations in South Asia, with particular emphasis on China-India relations and China’s foreign policy. He is the author of Choosing War and The Belt and Road Initiative and Geopolitics in South Asia.
item.content:encoded:
Welcome to Open Dialogue, a series from the South China Morning Post where we bring together leading voices to discuss the stories and subjects occupying international headlines.

In this edition, we invited a leading Chinese scholar of South Asian affairs and a former Indian foreign secretary and ambassador to China to reflect on the deep fault lines in India-China relations. They debate whether the biggest barrier is history or politics, clash over the border, Pakistan and India’s ties with the United States, and examine whether Beijing and New Delhi can move beyond suspicion in an increasingly multipolar world.

Lin Minwang is a professor and vice-dean at the Institute of International Studies at Fudan University, and deputy director of the university’s Centre for South Asian Studies. His research focuses on international relations in South Asia, with particular emphasis on China-India relations and China’s foreign policy. He is the author of Choosing War and The Belt and Road Initiative and Geopolitics in South Asia.

Nirupama Rao is a former Indian foreign secretary (2009-11) and the first woman to serve as India’s ambassador to China (2006-09). She also served as ambassador to the United States and high commissioner to Sri Lanka. A career diplomat with more than four decades of experience, she is the author of The Fractured Himalaya: India, Tibet, China 1949-1962.

A large section of Indian opinion still regards China as an expansionist power shaped by conflicts in 1962 and Galwan in 2020. How do you respond to that view, and what can China realistically do to change it?

Lin: Part of the reason is that the history of 1962 has become an important part of India’s national identity. Indian leaders, when explaining India’s history – or even discussing the mistakes made by Indian decision-makers at that time – have often had to describe China as an expansionist power. That is why I think it is very difficult to change this perception. Because if you want to change, you have to change all your narratives, which have been deep-rooted in the national identity narratives.

Now, we are also seeing more and more Chinese people develop negative perceptions of India. One reason is that it has become much easier for Chinese people to understand how the outside world views China. Especially after Covid-19, many Chinese internet users have found it easier to access information about how Indians perceive China.

This is part of the challenge for both countries. From the Chinese side, we have made many efforts, and personally, I have also been involved in these kinds of initiatives. But ultimately, I find that what we have done over the past 10 years has not made much progress in changing the views of the Indian elite.

Rao, do you agree that the negative perception of China is part of the national identity of India and it’s opportunism on the part of politicians trying to make China look bad? As we speak, there is also a significant part of Chinese opinion that continues to see India as chaotic and unreliable.

Rao: I believe that, as Professor Lin just now said, both countries have to change the narratives about each other. That’s a fundamental requirement but a complicated issue. It is overladen with historical memory, with perhaps prejudice from both sides, ignorance and a lack of knowledge. To my mind, what is most fundamental, is a lack of curiosity about each other, a lack of curiosity about our cultures, civilisations, histories, the nature of each country. It’s very important that knowledge becomes the fundamental basis with which both countries understand each other better. That is one point I’d like to make.

You mentioned that the Chinese opinion often sees India as chaotic and unreliable and essentially anti-China. I would answer that question by saying that mutual misperceptions have become one of the greatest obstacles to our relationship. Many Chinese observers look at India’s democracy as disorderly. They look at diversity as weakness. And from the Indian perspective, these qualities are the very source of our resilience. Ask any Indian, and he or she will very proudly proclaim that the fact that we are united in our diversity is, in fact, our greatest strength. Has India’s policy towards China been one of hostility? I really wouldn’t put it that way. But I believe that there is a fundamental lack of trust between the two countries – political trust.

We engaged with each other over the years realistically after the conflict of 1962 till the clash in the Galwan Valley happened in 2020. We had some violence on the border in 1975, but by and large that border had remained quiet, and the conflict in Galwan brought it all collapsing down literally like a house of cards because since 1988 our engagement with each other had been tempered by realism. We had sought to build confidence, even as the boundary remained unsettled. But trust obviously cannot exist independently, because experience always intervenes.

For many Indians, the events of 1962 and all the histories that have been written about it have left deep scars. In fact, my book, The Fractured Himalaya, sought to address this and put it in perspective, and to say that both countries need to understand the history of what went into the tragedy of 1962 much more deeply and much better, and then you had Galwan in 2020, which again profoundly altered Indian opinion. So the change, I don’t think, was manufactured by politicians or the media. It arose because Indians at large, by and large, felt that the understandings that had painstakingly been built over 3½ decades had been disrupted.

So, how are we to rebuild confidence? Both our sides, two of the largest countries in Asia, are next-door neighbours. There is an asymmetry of power between the two countries, and China has leapfrogged ahead, literally, of India in the last few decades. But both sides must first acknowledge that perceptions matter, and strategic stability between the two countries should begin, should be founded, should be established on strategic empathy.

Question to Lin: as Rao just mentioned, we had built that understanding over the years, and Galwan kind of made it collapse in a matter of one incident. What role do you think the border issue plays in these misconceptions and mutual suspicion of each other?

Lin: I think you have mentioned the Chinese side always likes to talk about properly handling the border issues. When I was a junior diplomat and when I read in the Indian news, most of the Indian comments said China refuses to negotiate with India on the border issues. China is willing to settle the border issues, but we have a really clear understanding of the position of both sides. If the Indian position is not going to change, China will have actually no negotiation room. There is no way to find a way we can talk about resolving the boundary issue.

Rao: When they say we should properly handle the boundary question, it’s essentially what it translates into is that we should compartmentalise it. We should set it aside. Deal with other questions which can be more easily handled and keep the boundary question to be worked upon as time goes by. But it cannot simply be set aside while other aspects of the relationship flourish as far as India is concerned, because this is not merely a territorial dispute; the boundary issue has become a measure of political trust between the two countries.

For India, as a democracy that values public opinion, we just cannot shut the door on the boundary issue and say that we have decided to build common ground in other areas, and we’ll take up the boundary issue once it’s ripe for discussion. It just doesn’t work that way, and we saw that the agreements that we had painstakingly negotiated since 1993 – the various border peace and tranquillity agreements along the Line of Actual Control – had collapsed after Galwan. India had taken into account the understanding that peace along the Line of Actual Control would enable cooperation elsewhere, and we tried, we did that for three decades. But then, what happened with Galwan? It just showed that we don’t have a completely and accurately, and in a detailed way, delineated Line of Actual Control between the two countries. And there are gaps in understanding. There are conflicts in interpretation, and that’s exactly what happened with Galwan.

So the entire premise about properly handling the boundary question has been weakened in the process. The challenge is not simply just technical disengagement between the two sides, but it has to be a restoration of confidence on several political commitments. And I come back to the question of political trust.

Question to Rao: we have had several rounds of border talks. We are expecting President Xi Jinping to visit New Delhi for the Brics summit before he goes to Washington to meet President [Donald] Trump. We saw all the Chinese journalists had to leave but now are hearing that India is thinking about issuing new visas to Chinese journalists, while China has given a few visas to Indian journalists. Where do you see these efforts going? How do you see the nature of the India-China rivalry and also the recent efforts to kind of work towards a balancing of the relationship? Do you think it is primarily a regional power competition, or a deeper contest that can direct the future of the Global South itself?

Rao: I wouldn’t overread these moves. We are trying to revert to a pattern that existed for some years, for some decades, and so you have some Indian journalists now who have returned to Beijing, and there is talk of the Xinhua correspondent being posted in Delhi, and we don’t know what follows after that. The two-way passage of information, especially for the benefit of the public, for the benefit of those who access social media and the media at large, is essential. But it has to be based on information that contributes to a better understanding. There is too much bias, too much prejudice, too much misinformation and ill-informed opinions that keep circulating. So, if there is a way to clear the air on these issues, I think that is a good step.

How do you see the nature of the India-China rivalry, especially competing for the Global South leadership position? Do you think it is primarily a regional power competition, or a deeper contest that can direct the future of the Global South itself?

Rao: There is enough space for India and China to do good within the Global South. We should have an open perspective on the question of how we deal with each other as far as the Global South is concerned, and how we deal with the Global South in a world that is becoming increasingly multipolar. And I think India and China have a lot to do to contribute to stability in a multipolar world. Their bilateral differences apart.

Lin: I think actually there is a big misunderstanding here on both sides. Regarding the Global South, China and India are not in competition. China is the largest trading partner for over 114 countries worldwide. In the economic aspect, I do think China and India have some competition, but there is not really a competitive dynamic between us. And why do we have this kind of narrative? I think it’s a basic narrative which was constructed by Western media, and unfortunately, some of the Indian friends and also some of the Chinese scholars accept these narratives. Part of the reason is the [Narendra] Modi government has not invited China to join the Global South dialogue. So for some, they see India was actually trying to push China out of the Global South agendas. I think this is not true. China was part of the Global South, and India will not be able to push China out. So that’s why I say both sides actually have a really big misunderstanding on these issues.

Question to Rao: do you agree with what Lin said?

Rao: I believe India is a presence in itself. India is a country that counts as far as the world community is concerned. It is a country that is recognised in the Global South for what it stands for: its democracy, its skilled manpower, its economic potential, and the history of the contributions that it has made to progress in many countries of the Global South. So, in that sense, I don’t believe India is punching above its weight, and I don’t believe we are essentially in competition with China when it comes to the Global South. I said before that there is enough space within the Global South for both India and China. We are both countries that belong there. We intrinsically belong. Our identities and histories are so intertwined. Our interests are so intertwined with those of the Global South. So where is the need for rivalry when it comes to this? I think the rivalry comes in within the bilateral context, within the regional context.

I would like to mention the Pakistan issue, for instance. Now, China’s relationship with Pakistan causes a lot of misunderstanding within India. There’s a long-standing strategic partnership from Beijing’s perspective with Pakistan, but why should it define China-India relations? Yet it has come to define the China-India relationship. It shapes the strategic environment for us because Pakistan is not simply any other neighbour. It remains our principal security challenge, and in the 2025 conflict, we saw the extent of Chinese support and Chinese backup for Pakistan.

We’re not expecting China to abandon Pakistan. That is not what I seek to emphasise here. But I do hope China will recognise this, and this is where mutual sensitivity is added on to mutual trust – the trust factor that I referred to.

We need sensitivity for each other’s concerns. China has to recognise that military transfers, strategic coordination and diplomatic positions taken during times of crises inevitably influence Indian perceptions. So we can’t compartmentalise these things. If you understand me, you know these are all so tangled together. It’s a very tangled web.

In recent Chinese studies, there is a suggestion that scholarship in China is moving beyond a purely geopolitical lens towards examining India’s development capacity and its state power. Lin, do you think this shift is meaningful among Chinese elite? Is China gradually starting to read India differently?

Lin: Historically, the Chinese approach to India has been heavily focused on geopolitics. So when you just focus on the geopolitics lens, then you will always tend to overstate India’s strategic importance, and on the other side, be frustrated over India’s daily policy towards China, especially now the Modi government is pro-United States. After more than 10 years’ change, the recent shift is they are trying to re-evaluate India based on actual national capacity and India’s state power. It is a much more rational lens, and would make people understand India without so much emotion. It’s a good sign and I am happy to see this trend.

Rao, do you agree with Lin’s assessment that the Modi government for a long time was very pro-United States? What are some of the things that you think make India at par with China in a lot of ways when it comes to state power and development capacity?

Rao: I think Chinese take a very narrow, prismatic view about India’s relations with the US. I don’t think they understood India’s position of strategic autonomy. It’s a very fiercely independent position. We have never hitched our wagon to the Americans, in the sense that the Chinese think we did. Of course, relations between India and the US did improve significantly. But it is every country’s sovereign right to develop these relations if they are contributing to the national interest of the country, whether it’s in science, technology, defence or nuclear technology. Did China ever come forward to help or to offer to assist India in these fields? So China should not take a one-sided view of these issues.

I think China, as a big, mature civilisation, can afford to be much more inclusive and much more broad-minded in its assessment of India’s relationships with friends, with partners, with neighbours. That is where the problem lies, and I think China has to look inside itself, do a little self-correction on its own part to understand the nature of Indian foreign policy, the nature of India’s sovereign decisions to promote its national interest and to protect its national security.

But I do welcome recent Chinese scholarship that examines India beyond familiar stereotypes. That’s very important, and that there is greater recognition today that India possesses significant state capacity, technological ambition, economic potential. I think that represents progress on the part of Chinese understanding of India. I know that all the assumptions still persist, and that India is sometimes viewed through the lens of political fragmentation rather than institutional resilience and democracy. Chinese have a fundamental misunderstanding of how democracy functions. To them, democracy appears untidy.

Everything doesn’t fall into place in democracy, the way they look at it. But that should not be mistaken for weakness. Democracy should not be mistaken for weakness. The same openness that defines India generates debate. It generates adaptability. It generates resilience. Look at India. We are now approaching the 80th year of our independence.

Look at the way we have grown. Progress has reached many sections of the population. It is a very different approach from what China has taken. But China cannot claim that its approach is the only right anointed approach as far as progress is concerned. I think a little more accommodation on the part of China would be very much welcomed. I would recommend that to my Chinese friends because I’ve been working on China for 42 years from 1984. China must understand India’s capacity to adapt. That it is one of India’s enduring strategic strengths, and that is where strategic empathy comes in.

Lin, as Rao said that strategic autonomy is the reason India is growing closer to the US, do you think China can make the same argument when it comes to its relationship with Pakistan? How do you see the argument that Rao just made that China does not understand India’s democracy and views democracy as weakness?

Lin: I would first like to talk about why the mainstream opinion in China is that the Modi government is on US lines. There is no strategic autonomy now in Delhi because the Modi government actually has signed military agreements with the United States, which are cooperation between a military alliance. Also over the past several years, India took all the US positions towards China. As the United States pursues a full range of policies to contain China, the Modi administration in India has, in essence, aligned itself with US initiatives, mirroring Washington’s positions across economic, technological, and defence policies. So that’s why we say India and the United States actually were in the same position, and why India actually has no strategic autonomy, especially in the military aspect.

On China-Pakistan relations, most Chinese will say during the Cold War or after, the US was the primary military partner for Pakistan, and America has provided the most advanced weapons to Pakistan, but over the last 10 years the situation has changed. Pakistan now tries to seek more military cooperation with China. The reason is also very clear. It’s because the Modi government signs a lot of the military treaties with the US while the Joe Biden administration did not allow Pakistan to buy some weapons from the US, then Pakistan shifted towards China. So this is the background why China and Pakistan now have more military cooperation. It is part of the change of the dynamic in South Asia.

On democracy, we have different understanding about democracy and the political system. I would say China does not have any ideological bias towards democracy. But when someone says Indians have a much better political system, I think for most of the Chinese young generation, they will see it as a joke. Every time when I lead a delegation to Delhi, there are many young faces in Chinese delegations, which are good opportunities for young generations to gain more experience and exposure. But it is not the case on the Indian side, there is no young face.

So that’s why we don’t think India’s political system is better, not just because you have the general election. China and the Communist Party also have elections. We have competition within the party, but we don’t have a general election which is nationwide, so we actually have a different political system. We also have a different assessment about political systems. This is a different perception of both sides.

Rao: I may say very frankly and candidly, it is certainly not within Professor Lin’s remit to be judgmental about the state of the youth in India and the opportunities provided to them. Given the fact that we are a democratic country with an open environment, we lay out our emotions for everybody to see whether we are happy or unhappy. We are a free country in every sense of the word. That’s the first point I’d like to say. Professor Lin referred to several military treaties that we have signed with the US. I must say this is news to me because I’m not aware of any military treaties that we have signed with the US. We have a strategic partnership. It is fully within our sovereign right to transact such a partnership with the US. It’s a relationship that has had its ups and downs. That is not a perfect relationship, but it is a relationship that has delivered for India. India is not a handmaiden of the United States.

I want to make that clear to Professor Lin. We are nobody’s handmaiden. We march to the sound of our own drum. We don’t march to the sound of anybody else’s drum. We are completely sovereign in that respect. And let us look at the history of China-Pakistan relations. Professor Lin has completely compartmentalised it and said in the last 10 years they never got any assistance from the United States. But think of the last 60 years where China and Pakistan became ironclad brothers and that iron brotherhood has lasted through thick and thin. It has extended into nuclear technology. It has extended into missile technology. It has extended to all sorts of cooperation. That is the history of China-Pakistan relations.

I remember hearing 30, 35 years ago, prime minister Li Peng of China telling one of our leaders that China can never forget the good that Pakistan has done for China through the last few years – I’m talking of the early 90s – and that is that Pakistan was responsible for the opening for China to the United States. Let’s not forget history. And as far as our young people are concerned, yes, we have agitations, we have demonstrations, people are speaking their minds. I believe the government is listening to what they have to say, and I hope these matters will be resolved to the satisfaction of our young people, because our dreams, our future really rest with the young people of India. Let’s understand India. I think the Chinese do not understand complexity. Although China is such a complex civilisation, when it comes to India’s complexity, there seems to be a mental block. I hope that block is lifted because that is the key to understanding and having better relations.

Lin: It’s actually really difficult to promote the good dialogue. I supervise two Indians, PhD candidates, in the university that I am working with. Last year, the Chinese embassy in New Delhi issued visas for more than 300,000 Indian people to China, but how many Chinese have been issued Indian visas? It’s only 2,000. So that is why the Chinese public was so angry about it. It’s really difficult for them to visit Indian or open some business in India. So that’s why I partly agree with the former ambassador Rao that we have a different understanding about the political system. It’s only a political system that is good for India, but not for China.

item.title: [SCMP] Zhu Rongji’s legacy: how the late premier reshaped state firms, Pudong and China’s economy
item.description:
Turn-of-the-century images of Zhu Rongji alongside former US president Bill Clinton have largely accompanied coverage following the former Chinese premier’s death on Wednesday.

The moment in April 1999 was more than a diplomatic milestone. It underpinned some of China’s most consequential reforms that defined Zhu’s tenure, from its drive to join the World Trade Organization to an overhaul of the state sector and opening its markets to the world.

And in recent years, Zhu’s historic trip to Washington has also become a subject of reflection among American lawmakers, think tanks and officials, as a strategic rivalry with China has emerged across nearly every economic and business front.
item.content:encoded:
Turn-of-the-century images of Zhu Rongji alongside former US president Bill Clinton have largely accompanied coverage following the former Chinese premier’s death on Wednesday.

The moment in April 1999 was more than a diplomatic milestone. It underpinned some of China’s most consequential reforms that defined Zhu’s tenure, from its drive to join the World Trade Organization to an overhaul of the state sector and opening its markets to the world.

And in recent years, Zhu’s historic trip to Washington has also become a subject of reflection among American lawmakers, think tanks and officials, as a strategic rivalry with China has emerged across nearly every economic and business front.

Zhu, who died on Wednesday at the age of 97, was also remembered for promoting entrepreneurship, introducing foreign management expertise, and reviving Chinese enterprises, according to four people who knew him for decades.

“Intelligent, insightful, outspoken and decisive,” said Zhang Chongqing, honorary president of China Group Companies Association, recalling his first impression of Zhu and their early work together on economic reform, dating back to 1980 when they were both at China’s top economic planner.

Zhang, who pioneered enterprise reform as deputy director general of the government-backed China Enterprise Management Association – now known as the China Enterprise Confederation – in the 1980s and ’90s, recalled the eagerness of the late premier to learn foreign management expertise and find a way forward for state-owned enterprises, which were a core part of China’s centrally managed economy for decades.

When Beijing was forging ties with the Switzerland-based European Management Forum in the 1980s, before it became known as the World Economic Forum in 1987, Zhu was an active participant in their joint meetings.

Zhang recalled how Zhu did not simply give a prepared speech at these meetings; he also dared to speak candidly and engage directly with participants.

“On one occasion in Beijing, he shared his office phone number” with foreign guests, Zhang said. “He was a bold, free-spirited sort of person – daring, open, and uninhibited in his speech.”

Domestically, Zhu placed great value on home-grown entrepreneurs.

Zhang recalled a particular moment in 1996, about two years before the retirement of Zhao Zhongyu from Pangang Group – the southwestern Chinese steelmaker that Zhao had spent decades building into a leading producer.

Zhao had asked Zhu, who was then vice-premier, to conduct a field inspection of Pangang. Zhu was said to have replied quickly, and he went on to help advance the company’s technological innovation and preparations for a stock market listing.

When it came to supporting entrepreneurs, “he was very generous”, Zhang recalled.

After all, what would have happened if state-owned enterprises hadn’t been reformed?

Zhang Chongqing, China Group Companies Association

As premier, Zhu launched China’s biggest reform campaign involving state-owned enterprises (SOEs), bankrupting tens of thousands of inefficient “zombies” and laying off millions of workers. The controversial measures helped revitalise the economy and create room for more efficient private and foreign-owned firms.

Despite the lay-offs becoming a source of generational pain in regions heavily reliant on SOEs, Zhang said it was a price that had to be paid.

“He was surely a leader who made outstanding contributions to driving China’s economic revitalisation,” Zhang said of the late premier. “That deserves full recognition.

“After all, what would have happened if state-owned enterprises hadn’t been reformed?”

Zhu Tian, a chair professor and co-dean of the Shanghai-based China Europe International Business School (CEIBS), said he had long been impressed by the “immense personal charisma” of Zhu Rongji, dating back to the early days of Tsinghua University’s School of Economics and Management, which the former leader helped establish in 1984.

Although trained as an engineer – a common background among leaders of his generation – Zhu Rongji recognised the importance of economic management. In addition to helping set up the business school, he advocated for the broad adoption of advanced foreign management textbooks to align teaching and research with international standards.

The CEIBS professor, who graduated with a degree in management information systems from the business school in 1986, recalled how the founding dean would write personal yearbook messages to graduates, and had made a point of noting to him the importance of “combining economics, management and technology”.

“[Zhu Rongji] was the premier with the deepest understanding of the economy; he possessed exceptional leadership and execution capabilities,” professor Zhu Tian added. “Pragmatic, witty and wise, he eschewed empty rhetoric in favour of plain speaking.”

[Zhu Rongji] was always curious and investigative, and had the urgency to bring change to China

Joerg Wuttke, former president of EU Chamber of Commerce in China

The late leader also introduced a powerful advisory board of world-class entrepreneurs and scholars in 2000. The current cohort includes SpaceX founder Elon Musk, Meta Platforms founder Mark Zuckerberg, Apple CEO Tim Cook, Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, Blackstone chairman Stephen Schwarzman and former United States Treasury secretary Henry Paulson.

Up until about 2018, the former premier was still regularly meeting with visiting foreign entrepreneurs. He remained the board’s “honorary chairman” until 2024, when the title was passed to former vice-president Wang Qishan. Zhu Rongji was then designated the “founding honorary chairman”.

For Joerg Wuttke, who worked in China for decades, Zhu Rongji was always keen to sit down with foreign investors, listen to their concerns and present a friendly face – in sharp contrast with his impatience towards Chinese officials who delivered long, unproductive reports.

When the late leader was tackling economic work as vice-premier in the early 1990s, Beijing faced deep scepticism overseas and was making extensive efforts to attract foreign investment.

“[He has been] my hero since … he was still vice-premier,” said Wuttke, former president of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, who had frequent contact with Zhu Rongji.

On one occasion, Wuttke recalled, when the former leader was asked what kind of economic data he valued the most, he answered simply: “Tax.” During his tenure as vice-premier, Zhu coordinated the overhaul of China’s central-local tax-sharing and fiscal reform.

“He was never shy of pointing out problems,” Wuttke recalled from their meetings. “He was always curious and investigative, and had the urgency to bring change to China.”

For many people from Shanghai, the late premier, who was once the city’s mayor, is remembered as one of the most important architects of the Pudong New Area, now a booming district in one of the mainland’s most developed metropolises, and home to the Shanghai Stock Exchange and a Disney resort.

Zhou Hanmin, now a standing committee member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, and once a prominent think tank researcher who advised in the 1980s and ’90s on Pudong’s development, said Zhu Rongji’s resolve and reformist outlook helped drive the district’s rise.

At the end of April 1990, the Shanghai government unveiled 10 preferential policies to encourage foreign investment and participation in the region’s business activities. Months later, Zhou accompanied Zhu Rongji on an official visit to the US. Their first stop was New York, where they were confronted with a pointed question from an American reporter on how to persuade foreigners to invest capital in the city.

Zhou recalled how Zhu Rongji quickly replied off the cuff, vowing: “We will enforce relevant legislation to ensure the success of the development and opening-up, as well as safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of foreign investors.”

Zhou recalled being impressed with the rapid answer.

“Upon our return to China, we plunged straight into research work,” Zhou told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday. “Within two months … nine sets of regulations governing Pudong’s development and opening-up were released to the world simultaneously in Chinese, English and Japanese.”

Turning an ambitious vision into action, Zhu Rongji helped “draw people and enterprises from near and far”, added Zhou, who was a deputy governor of Pudong from 2000 to 2008.

And today, despite 36 years passing since the former leader helped set Pudong’s transformation in motion, “images of that time remain vividly etched in my memory”, Zhou said.

Additional reporting by Emma Ma

item.title: [SCMP] Newcastle University Medicine Malaysia graduates in limbo after UK rule change
item.description:
When S* enrolled at Newcastle University Medicine Malaysia (NUMed Malaysia) in the Southeast Asian nation, the British-born Pakistani student believed the five-year medical degree would give him a realistic route into Britain’s National Health Service (NHS).

The pathway was never formally guaranteed, but S said NUMed had highlighted a decade-long record in which students who applied for the UK Foundation Programme (UKFP) – the supervised training route for medical graduates – had secured posts.

For international students such as S, who spent about US$134,500 on a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree, the UK route was crucial because alternatives were limited.
item.content:encoded:
When S* enrolled at Newcastle University Medicine Malaysia (NUMed Malaysia) in the Southeast Asian nation, the British-born Pakistani student believed the five-year medical degree would give him a realistic route into Britain’s National Health Service (NHS).

The pathway was never formally guaranteed, but S said NUMed had highlighted a decade-long record in which students who applied for the UK Foundation Programme (UKFP) – the supervised training route for medical graduates – had secured posts.

For international students such as S, who spent about US$134,500 on a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree, the UK route was crucial because alternatives were limited.

Malaysian NUMed graduates could opt for housemanship locally, while NUMed says international graduates are not eligible for the pre-registration internship required to practise medicine in Malaysia.

Then, during S’s final year, the UK parliament changed the rules.

The Medical Training (Prioritisation) Act, which became law in March, gave priority for UKFP places to medical graduates who had completed most of their training in Britain.

The British government has said the policy aims to protect taxpayer investment in medical training, give domestically trained doctors a clearer route into the NHS and reduce reliance on overseas recruitment.

The law does not bar other applicants from applying, but changes the order in which posts are allocated.

Although S holds an MBBS awarded by Newcastle University and recognised by the General Medical Council (GMC) as a UK primary medical qualification, his five years of training in Malaysia mean he is allocated after priority applicants trained in Britain.

For students who had built their futures around the NUMed degree’s British status, the rule change has upended expectations about where it could take them after graduation.

As of July 30, Newcastle University told This Week in Asia that 68 of NUMed’s 102 eligible graduates had secured UKFP posts, leaving 34 without confirmed placements.

S remains among those without a post.

Across Britain, the UK Foundation Programme Office initially placed 738 non-priority applicants on a reserve list after allocating 10,810 priority-group individuals in March.

Reserve-list applicants are offered posts only as vacancies emerge after the priority group has been allocated, using a computer-generated rank and applicants’ preferences.

By the end of July, 204 remained on the reserve list, and a fifth and final allocation round from the reserve applicant list is slated for Wednesday.

Not guaranteed

“It [the UK pathway] was not something that was guaranteed, but this was one of the selling points which the university used. Everyone who applied from Newcastle University to UK foundation training got a UKFP position,” S said.

He acknowledged that prospective students had been told placement ultimately rested with British authorities, but said the experience of previous NUMed cohorts shaped how he and his classmates planned their careers.

“We saw four batches of our seniors, they all got it [training posts].”

Newcastle University said access to postgraduate training was never guaranteed and its published information always stated that routes including UKFP were subject to change.

The university added that the UKFP became a mainstream route for NUMed graduates from 2017, with over 600 graduates entering its training pipeline. Previously, most had undergone housemanship training in Malaysia or used overseas routes.

“The trend since 2017 has moved sharply towards UKFP: 31 per cent in 2019, 64 per cent in 2020, 75 per cent in 2021, and 83 per cent by 2025, with the rest going into Malaysian housemanship or other pathways each year,” the university said.

“That rise tracked NHS workforce pressure and a relaxing of UK immigration rules for overseas medical graduates from 2020. This is also the first cohort to graduate under the new prioritisation rules.”

The university said it wrote to students within two days of the bill’s introduction to parliament in January, tracked its progress and held briefings and town halls.

After the bill became law in March, the university confirmed to students that their eligibility to apply for the UKFP had not changed and individual support was available.

S said the change nevertheless came too late for final-year students to seek alternatives.

“They changed it mid-cycle, leaving us completely stranded,” S said.

Few alternatives

For international graduates, the alternatives are limited.

S’s family lives in a third country where he spent most of his life before medical school, but practising there would require accreditation and a medical licensing examination in a language in which he did not study medicine.

He estimated that the Australian Medical Council pathway would cost another US$7,000 to US$8,000.

Instead, he is pursuing the United States Medical Licensing Examination after completing a two-month elective at a US university while also considering research and a PhD.

“Whatever I had planned for five years has been pretty much down the drain because of whatever changes have taken place,” he said.

In a written reply to This Week in Asia, the GMC said NUMed’s MBBS remained recognised as a UK primary medical qualification despite the policy change.

“Newcastle University’s Medicine Malaysia campus is an overseas campus of a UK medical school. Its medical degree is recognised by the GMC as a UK primary medical qualification, and there have been no changes to that recognition,” it said.

The regulator has stressed, however, that deciding who receives a UKFP post is the remit of the programme office.

The UK Foundation Programme Office and Department of Health and Social Care did not respond to This Week In Asia’s requests for comment.

The change has forced current students to rethink their future plans.

Unaizah Ahmed, a fourth-year NUMed student from Pakistan living in the United Arab Emirates, said that earlier cohorts had reinforced students’ expectations that NUMed graduates could progress to UK training. Since the rule change, she and her classmates have been looking more seriously at alternatives including Australia and the US.

“I’d be lying if I said I am not concerned about my future with all these changes,” she said. “So far, my main goal is to complete my studies first, and I shall look at my options during or after I’m almost done with my final year.”

Newcastle University said it recognised that “this is a particularly stressful time” for students who could not secure UKFP posts, and was determined to support them.

Professor Geoffrey Williams, a higher education analyst and visiting fellow at Universiti Malaya, said the rule change exposed a distinction between the regulatory status of a degree awarded by an overseas British campus and its practical value for graduates seeking UK training.

NUMed’s qualification had not lost regulatory recognition, he said, but the difference lay in its practical value for graduates seeking priority access to the NHS training system.

“The loss of value is the difference between immediate priority access versus stand-in-line certificates,” he said.

“A Malaysian student who studied in the UK has immediate priority access to the UK training programme. A British student who studied in the Malaysian franchise campus as a foreign student here would stand in line too when she went home.”

*Name changed to protect interviewee’s identity

item.title: [SCMP] Too high, too fast? China’s rocket failure prompts questions about intense launch schedule
item.description:
The rare failure of China’s Long March-7A rocket on Monday – which resulted in the loss of a communications satellite – has prompted questions over whether it was an isolated operational setback or a systemic problem.

While space experts caution against immediately linking the incident to China’s rapidly increasing launch cadence, the ongoing investigation will determine if the event was caused by a localised technical anomaly or deeper systemic vulnerabilities within the Long March rocket family.

With attention turning to coming missions – particularly for the lunar-bound Chang’e-7, which shares engine technology with the failed booster – China’s ability to balance its ambitious launch schedule with the rigorous scrutiny required to secure its track record will be under the spotlight.
item.content:encoded:
The rare failure of China’s Long March-7A rocket on Monday – which resulted in the loss of a communications satellite – has prompted questions over whether it was an isolated operational setback or a systemic problem.

While space experts caution against immediately linking the incident to China’s rapidly increasing launch cadence, the ongoing investigation will determine if the event was caused by a localised technical anomaly or deeper systemic vulnerabilities within the Long March rocket family.

With attention turning to coming missions – particularly for the lunar-bound Chang’e-7, which shares engine technology with the failed booster – China’s ability to balance its ambitious launch schedule with the rigorous scrutiny required to secure its track record will be under the spotlight.

Around 8pm on Monday, the 60-metre (197-foot) Long March-7A blasted off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on the southern island of Hainan, piercing the night sky as it carried the ChinaSat-4B satellite towards high-Earth orbit.

But less than 90 seconds into the flight, the rocket erupted into a fireball engulfed in thick black smoke, according to videos posted on social media by spectators near the launch site.

Space observers suggested a major anomaly might have triggered the rocket’s flight termination system, destroying the vehicle. Both the rocket and satellite were lost over the South China Sea.

State news agency Xinhua confirmed the failure and said the cause was being investigated.

Reacting to the incident on social media, American space flight company SpaceX founder Elon Musk said: “Rockets are insanely hard. There is a reason for the idiomatic expression. I hope they have a speedy recovery.”

Images circulating online, apparently taken from long-wave infrared tracking footage of the launch, appeared to show the rocket snapping near its upper section moments before it was destroyed.

The apparent snap happened around Max-Q, the point in a launch when a rocket comes under the greatest aerodynamic pressure as it accelerates through the atmosphere, according to space observers.

Some speculated that the rocket experienced a structural failure, likely triggered by a sudden surge in wind force at high altitudes shortly after launch, leading it to bend and break.

One military blogger wrote on social media: “A single setback does not mean a retreat. The key is whether the cause can be found and eliminated. For China’s space programme, what deserves real vigilance may not be any one failure, but rather how to maintain uncompromised quality control across every flight within an intensive launch schedule.”

This launch marks the fourth launch failure in China this year, following the state-owned Long March-3B and private company Galactic Energy’s Ceres-2 launches in January, as well as Beijing-based start-up Space Pioneer’s Tianlong-3 attempt in April.

China has conducted 56 launches this year, before Monday’s failure, which would have been the 18th launch of a Long March-7A vehicle.

Astrophysicist Richard de Grijs, the immediate former executive director of the International Space Science Institute-Beijing, said while the incident was a significant failure, it was not evidence of a systemic problem in China’s space programme.

“Rocket failures do occur, even in mature programmes, and the more frequently you launch, the more often you will eventually encounter one,” said de Grijs, who is a professor at the school of mathematical and physical sciences at Macquarie University in Australia.

He cautioned against connecting the incident with China’s rapidly increasing launch cadence, noting that while a high operational tempo put pressure on manufacturing, quality control and operations, one failure did not prove there was a systemic link.

“What matters now is whether investigators identify an isolated component failure or something with implications across a wider family of launch vehicles.”

The ChinaSat-4B satellite was expected to provide radio, television and other communications services to users around the world. Low-numbered ChinaSat satellites are also believed to be used for military communications.

No official details have been released about the satellite, but it is reportedly one of the most expensive of its kind China has built, with a price tag exceeding 1 billion yuan (US$148.20 million).

Its sister satellite ChinaSat-4A, launched in 2024 and now operating about 36,000km above Earth, had an estimated launch mass of about 5 tonnes at launch, according to space-flight tracker Jonathan McDowell.

The Long March-7A is one of China’s new-generation rockets and has become a workhorse for sending large satellites to high orbits. It burns mainly kerosene and liquid oxygen.

The rocket failed on its maiden flight in March 2020 but successfully returned to flight a year later. It has since completed a string of successful missions, most recently sending the Tianlian-3 (01) satellite towards geostationary orbit on July 29.

Those consecutive successful flights carried a wide range of communications, remote-sensing and data-relay satellites, mostly to high orbits, giving the Long March-7A a well-established track record for high-orbit missions.

Monday’s launch had been expected to set a speed record of a different kind. Chinese media reported before lift-off that the roughly 12-day gap since the previous Long March-7A mission would be the shortest turnaround yet for the rocket – and for any of China’s new-generation Long March launchers.

The loss of ChinaSat-4B means the communications capacity it was intended to provide will now be delayed. Geostationary communications satellites can play important roles in both civilian and military communications, and the broader impact will depend in part on how quickly China can launch a replacement.

The failure could have knock-on effects for coming launches. LandSpace’s Zhuque-3, which had been due to launch from Jiuquan early on Tuesday, has been postponed ahead of what would be the company’s second attempt to achieve China’s first orbital-class rocket recovery.

It is not clear if the incident will affect Chang’e-7, China’s robotic mission to the lunar south pole, which is scheduled to lift off from Wenchang on August 24 aboard a Long March-5.

The Long March-5’s boosters use engines from the same YF-100 family as the Long March-7A, meaning an engine-related problem could potentially have implications for its schedule. If the failure proves to be structural and specific to the Long March-7A, however, the impact may be more limited.

De Grijs said that given they shared some technologies, “because Monday’s accident occurred early in flight, before we know its cause I would not say categorically that Chang’e-7 is unaffected”.

He said that because Chang’e-7 was a critical scientific and strategic lunar mission, Chinese authorities remained highly motivated not to take unnecessary risks. Delaying the launch by several days or weeks was considered far less damaging than launching before the underlying cause of this failure was properly understood.

“If the investigation quickly identifies an issue specific to the Long March-7A, I would expect the broader programme, including Chang’e-7, to proceed largely as planned,” he said.

“If it points to a shared engine, component or quality-control issue, the consequences could be considerably wider.”

Meanwhile, de Grijs said the Zhuque-3, whose launch planned for Tuesday was postponed, was a commercial rocket that was developed independently and used distinct technology, meaning that a Long March-7A failure was unlikely to have a direct technical impact on it.

“At this stage I would interpret that primarily as sensible caution rather than evidence of a shared problem,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Historian Wang Gungwu on US credibility and why Xi thinks ‘only the party can save China’
item.description:
Professor Wang Gungwu is regarded internationally as an authority on Chinese history. The 95-year-old is best known for his explorations of Chinese history in the long view, and for his writings on the Chinese diaspora. He has been a professor at the National University of Singapore since 2007 and emeritus professor at the Australian National University since 1988. He was vice-chancellor of the University of Hong Kong from 1986 to 1995.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The US-China rivalry is now quite prominent on the world stage. Do you think these two countries are facing the Thucydides Trap? How do you see their rivalry unfolding?
item.content:encoded:
Professor Wang Gungwu is regarded internationally as an authority on Chinese history. The 95-year-old is best known for his explorations of Chinese history in the long view, and for his writings on the Chinese diaspora. He has been a professor at the National University of Singapore since 2007 and emeritus professor at the Australian National University since 1988. He was vice-chancellor of the University of Hong Kong from 1986 to 1995.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The US-China rivalry is now quite prominent on the world stage. Do you think these two countries are facing the Thucydides Trap? How do you see their rivalry unfolding?

At one level, it is really similar to the United States and Soviet Union Cold War because both have nuclear weapons.

The question of having to fight one another and the possibility of using nuclear weapons makes it unlikely that they will fight each other. Fighting through proxies would be the same as during the Cold War.

I think military strategists would think that the way to deal with the situation when there’s US and China rivalry is to have another Cold War, and for the US to use the same methods that they used to destroy the Soviet Union.

They would destroy the China threat in the sense of undermining its power. If they can do that without fighting, that would be ideal because fighting is dangerous.

I think the strategists ever since the fall of the Soviet Union have decided that there’s no power out there that can threaten the United States. The only possible one was China in the long run.

They have been preparing for this for quite some time and have had arguments within the United States as to how to deal with China.

There are those who say that if you give China the chance to join the World Trade Organization, the Chinese economy will develop more like a capitalist economy. Then one day China will have a large middle class, no ideology to divide us. We can coexist and there’s no need to fight.

That view took precedence, and China was allowed to join the World Trade Organization. And the Chinese developed economically at a fantastic rate.

Some US analysts said that was the wrong decision because China is now strong enough to challenge the United States. How do you see the future US-China relationship?

What they discovered was that China was not like the Soviet Union. The Soviet Union had military power but was economically weak. One key reason was that they had no access to the oceans.
