The Baltic was blocked. So was the Black Sea. They never managed to develop an economy like that of western Europe.

The Chinese people were not only entrepreneurial but also had easy access to maritime trade. That has given them the capacity to fund military expansion. When the Russians tried to match the United States in their arms race, their economy collapsed. China can manage an arms race to defend itself if its economy continues to do well.

But I think the Chinese believe that they will never benefit from fighting the Americans. They just want to be secure from any aggression from the oceans.

In the past, China’s enemies had come only from the continent. But in the 19th century, the British and the French attacked from Southeast Asia where they had their naval bases.

The Americans joined in when they took the Philippines. When the whole of Southeast Asia was in the hands of foreign powers, the Chinese coasts were vulnerable.

That forced China to accept all those unequal treaties. But it taught the Chinese a lesson. They will never neglect maritime power again. They are now prepared for any threats by land, sea or air.

They are very concerned about attacks by sea. You can see how, in the South China Sea, their focus is on missiles that can deter powerful naval forces like aircraft carriers from getting near China. You can make a long list of what the Chinese have done. It is basically defensive to make sure that the Americans can never attack China from nearby.

As the US marks the 250th anniversary of its independence, some are asking if America’s golden days are over, especially after what has happened in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. What’s your take on this?

They have certainly lost their credibility. In other words, in the past when they said they would do something, they succeeded because they had the power to do so.

In the Iraq-Afghanistan conflicts after 20 years of fighting, spending billions of dollars and achieving absolutely nothing, they lost credibility. The Iran thing looks a bit like that. They want to control and destroy the regime in Iran, but they find they can’t do so.

The only way they can do so is to invade Iran, but the Iraq-Afghanistan affair taught them a lesson. Don’t attack on land.

They are trying to destroy everything that Iran has, hoping Iranians will give up and just surrender. That has turned out to be much more difficult than they expected. The only way they can win is to land troops.

I think [Donald] Trump knows that he has made a mistake to have gone this far and is trying to end the war by persuading the Iranians to do a deal. But the Iranians are making it difficult for him to say that he has won.

Their main weapon is to control the Strait of Hormuz. It’s not a legal problem any more. It’s a question of whether they have the capacity to control the strait. In the meantime, the allies of the United States are also having a hard time, shipping is almost completely blocked, and the whole world is being badly affected.

So we cannot conclude that the US is in decline yet – we can only say it lost the Iranian war?

The word “decline” is not the right word because it is still the most powerful military force in the world. The US spends far more on their military than most of the major powers added together.

I have lost count of how many military bases they have in all continents. They have aircraft carriers in every ocean, and they have tremendous air power. And nuclear weapons which only a few other countries have.

I would say that in military terms and in terms of the economy, the Americans are not doing badly despite all these problems. They are still in charge of so many economic levers, imposing tariffs on everybody.

They’re probably not doing as well as they want, but there is no doubt that the military and the arms industry are doing extremely well. It is obvious that the richest people in America are getting richer every day.

Also, the capacity to be inventive and make technological advances is still very great. I think that the Chinese know that they’re catching up but they’re still behind. The Chinese are still learning from the people they sent to America to learn.

Furthermore, the US has one advantage that China and others don’t have. It is totally safe in its hemisphere. No country in the Americas can threaten the United States. Therefore, they are free to send their aircraft carriers anywhere around the world to exercise their hegemonic power.

In comparison, China has problems in its neighbourhood. On land, China tries hard to keep good relations with Russia and North Korea. At sea, they have to make friends with the countries in Southeast Asia and are trying very hard to make sure that their borders are safe.

China is working closely with Russia to promote a multipolar world order, which the US probably doesn’t like. Do you think this multipolar world order will happen and the US will have to face it?

The Chinese say that they want a multipolar order and believe that that’s safer for them.

The Americans believe that a multipolar order would be a very difficult one to control and the disorder would be distracting. If they can’t have universal hegemony, they would prefer a bipolar order.

With bipolarity, they could concentrate on China. They have learned lessons from the way they destroyed the Soviet Union and would focus on undermining China’s economic growth.

They can limit China’s rich markets in North America and western Europe. They could allow the Belt and Road Initiative to help China reach the markets and resources of the underdeveloped world, but those countries cannot buy much from China.

The Chinese could go on producing manufactured goods cheaper and faster, but if the West can limit the Chinese sales, China’s economy would slow down significantly.

In one interview you talked about continuity in Chinese history – how the rulers highlighted the importance of a centralised bureaucracy and the people believed it and this was the case for hundreds of years. Do you think the way modern China is governed continues this pattern, and is there anything unique about the governance of modern China?

I think China is unique in its sense of continuity from the Shang-Zhou dynasty down to the present. And although it had dynastic changes, many foreign invaders, and was even under total foreign rule, it has always been China. Even the Mongols and the Manchus had to rule China primarily in the Chinese way – what the Chinese literati believed was the best way to rule China.

In historical records, they kept a picture of China as having had one history as a centralised bureaucratic state.

It was the Qin-Han empires that produced the mix of Legalist and Confucian ideas by which everything had to be decided from the centre. Officials were appointed to ensure total control.

The Qin dynasty did not last long. The people couldn’t stand its harsh Legalist system and revolted against it after Qin Shi Huang’s death.

The Han dynasty was wiser. Its founder led the rebellion against the Qin. He and his successors developed a softer regime. They retained the Legalist central bureaucratic state but brought in Confucian officials to reform the structure.

The new officials placed emphasis upon the emperor being a good man, being moral and caring, serving and looking after the people, making sure there is social harmony, and so on. That way, you have security within the country and the people won’t rebel.

Confucius advised that rulers must be good. They must make their people feel that they care for their livelihood. For example, they should worry about them and make sure, for example, that their taxes are very low. They should on the whole leave people alone to live their lives with minimum government interference.

They appointed officials from the centre, but these officials were not asked to do much. Don’t do much more than just collect the taxes and make sure that there were no rebellions. Those were the two main jobs they had to do well so the people were left very much alone to do whatever they wanted for their families.

Every part of the country could develop in its own way. The idea was that in this way everyone looked to the centre for a caring ruler who would always have the mandate of heaven. Although the mandate of heaven was normally won on the battlefield, heaven was on the side of the people, and the mandate was given to the person whom the people believed would be a good ruler.

If you were a good ruler, you would have the mandate. If you were a bad one, the people had the right to rebel against you. That was the mechanism of dynastic change whereby the people could determine who should head the new dynasty.

Another test was whether the ruler could defend the country against the enemy. Rulers who could always do so would retain the people’s respect. Their dynasties would then survive for longer with the people’s loyal support.

The Confucians described the various ways the rulers could best care for their people. That was the most important contribution to the good governance that was so valued throughout all Chinese history. In short, performance record was the key.

In modern times, the 1911 revolution threw out the emperors of the dynastic system and became a republican state modelled on France and the United States. Sun Yat-sen’s Republic of China became a nation state – that is, the state of all the citizens of China.

It didn’t work because the Chinese simply didn’t understand what a republic was, what was a citizen, what were his/her constitutional rights, freedom, liberty, democracy because all these ideas were new. It took a couple of decades to teach people about modern politics.

In the meantime, the country was pressured by the Japanese and there were unequal treaties that hampered economic development. Also, the country was falling apart because of the civil war among the warlords and the ideological struggles between the Nationalists and the Communists. In the end, the Nationalist Party were ousted in 1949 by Mao Zedong’s Communist Party.

Now the Communists brought in something new. They brought in the idea of a very disciplined party dedicated to revolution to make sure that you don’t depend on the past. They set out on a new path to progress. As you know, the Marxist idea of historical progress was a European idea.

Karl Marx showed that in history, stages of change meant that there was progress. His example of progress was to prove that socialism was the stage after capitalism. Before that, there had been slavery and feudalism followed by capitalism.

By the 19th century, capitalism was all-powerful. But capitalism will eventually become socialist. This was what Marx predicted. The progress to socialism meant there would then be a state that was more caring.

In China, this was taken up by the Communists who set out to revolutionise society so that there would be no poverty, better distribution of wealth, with nobody too rich, nobody too poor and where social harmony prevailed.

In recent years, some leaders in the People’s Republic have revived the idea of a caring state organised to produce a fairer distribution of wealth. There are thinkers who have compared that to some Confucian references to rulers being committed to the well-being of their people.

The terminology used by the Communists is quite different but the sentiments behind the words can be compared favourably with some moral goals that would find favour with Confucian philosophers.

The caring is not by one man as a good and moral emperor, but a political party consisting of highly disciplined members. In the Chinese tradition, the emperor was above the law because he made the law. The Communist Party, like the emperor, is not subject to the law courts because it made the law.

When the Communist Party discovers that somebody in the party has done something wrong and party discipline has found him guilty, the person is sacked from the party. He would then be charged in a court of law because, as a party member, he is above the law. That would be very strange in most countries, but it is more like the way Chinese emperors were above the law.

As a result, serious problems can be created. With the country ruled in that way, it is understandable that people have little confidence that the legal system can be just.

When the economy was doing very well under Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, corruption was pervasive throughout the country. Xi Jinping saw it when he was in Fujian and Zhejiang. He didn’t have the power to do much, but he must have observed it with deep concern.

When he was given the power to act as secretary general of the party, the first thing he did was to tell the Communist Party to study what happened to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

The CCP was modelled on that, so look how quickly that party collapsed. There was corruption and factionalism and the leaders could not agree as to what they could do. They had lost their revolutionary ideals and the party did not have the sense of purpose to discipline its members.

Xi Jinping talked to the party about every member being subject to the law of corruptibility. In that sense, his legalistic intervention was to try and save the party. I think he genuinely believes that only the party can save China and make China strong so that it can recover its position in the world today.

He believes that, to save the party, the party must be clean and disciplined. Only then will the people love the party and believe that only the party can save China.

I think this is what he is determined to do and why he wants better control of everything in the country. It’s not easy because corruption is so pervasive.

He has been in power for about 14 years now and he is still finding corrupt people in high office. He is still catching thousands of party leaders every year, sending them to the law courts and putting them in jail, including having some of his most senior PLA generals sentenced to death.

That’s how serious it is after 14 years. This shows that fighting corruption is not enough. There are important institutions that need to be totally reviewed and restructured.

In the meantime, the system could be locked up so that few dare to take initiative with original projects. Officials would feel safer by continuing with projects that have worked in the past.

Everyone is wary of being caught in the anti-corruption campaign. If you were a bureaucrat or a party secretary, you would have to be brave to start a new project. If you start a project with other officials, how can you be sure that none of them are corrupt?

The net result is that less is being done and only safe decisions are being made.

Of course, not everything depends on the centre. It is in the Chinese tradition that the centre did not expect every part of the country to wait for the centre to tell them what to do.

There had always been decentralisation of power to provinces, cities, counties where officials were encouraged to familiarise themselves with local conditions and find the best way to make their respective areas successful.

Today, when GDP rises, everybody is happy, and if protests occur, they are resolved effectively and not allowed to spread. If the official manages these well, he can expect to be promoted.

If an official initiates something new, there are always risks. To be ever careful, it is probably wiser to do as little as possible.

In general, the industrial economy looks as if it is stagnating. Unemployment has become serious. The number of graduates looking for jobs is huge. As a result, the sense of security is not as good as the party leaders had hoped for.

And because of this lack of social security, there has been the trend to extend control over anything foreign – for example, restrictions on reading materials published outside. Professors refrain from teaching from textbooks that are not published and approved by the party. A picture emerges that such controls are actually making people less confident in their daily lives.

There are tensions in China, especially among the young generation, that the party has not been able to lighten.

My view is that China’s problems are more domestic. Outside, its leaders know how to handle the United States, like the way they managed the visits of Presidents Trump, [Vladimir] Putin and Kim [Jong-un].

In external affairs, the Chinese are managing alright. The domestic problems look much more serious. It is not a matter of having enough fresh talent. The people are very talented, but they need to be given more freedom and opportunity to be creative and make things even better.

What’s your view on Taiwan? How can it be resolved? Or do you think the tension will only worsen?

Taiwan reminds me of the “one country, two systems” issue that Hong Kong is familiar with. Taiwan was always part of China. After the war ended in 1945, everything taken by Japan had to be returned to China. That was internationally recognised.

When Chiang Kai-shek went to Taiwan in 1949, the issue was still clear and open.

A few months afterwards, however, North Korea invaded the South and United Nations forces were sent to war. China’s volunteers supported North Korea and drove the UN troops back to the 38th Parallel.

With China fighting the UN armies, conditions rapidly changed for the PRC’s [People’s Republic of China’s] chances to replace the ROC [Republic of China, Taiwan’s official name] in the UN.

As a result, the Republic of China in Taiwan was recognised as China for another 22 years.

The PRC was the enemy of the US in the Cold War and any question of the United States and China talking about diplomatic relations and admission into the UN was completely lost. The US could use its veto power to stop the PRC from taking over the ROC’s position in the Security Council.

It was not until the United Nations General Assembly voted with a two-thirds majority in favour that China was admitted.

At that point, America was prepared to recognise the ROC in Taiwan as an independent state and support its membership in the United Nations.

I believe that Chiang Kai-shek refused on the grounds that there was only one China and it was wrong to allow the PRC to take over from the ROC.

Once the PRC was in the UN Security Council, it would have used its veto against the ROC’s admission anyway.

What was significant at the time was that Mao Zedong would have agreed with Chiang that there was only one China.

Later, the local Taiwanese people found that the constitution of the Republic of China allowed for democracy. After Chiang Ching-kuo passed the presidency to Lee Teng-hui, the elections that followed could for the first time vote in a pro-independence party to form the government.

The new Taiwanese leaders were then able to claim that the Taiwan people had voted to say that they wanted to be independent. They now had a government that was of the people, by the people and for the people.

The PRC leaders did not accept that and made it quite clear that if the new leaders declared independence, they would have to take the island by force.

This led the Americans to intervene to tell the Taiwanese not to count on their support if they declared independence. They recognised that a declaration of independence would have crossed China’s red line.

For now, it is a balanced situation with the status quo acceptable for both sides. It allows the Taiwanese to say that they don’t need to declare independence as the Republic of China has been there since 1912. And the US Congress continues to vote for military equipment to be sold for Taiwan’s defence as long as it does not declare independence.

Taiwan continues to make friends with other countries that are anti-communist. Japan for one seems ready to help. This angers the Chinese.

But I believe that the Chinese do not want to fight over Taiwan because that would mean killing other Chinese and it would involve interventions by countries coming to Taiwan’s defence. No one would gain out of that war.

I think both Americans and the PRC would agree not to fight a war over Taiwan.

What Beijing wants to be sure of is that Taiwan is not used by its enemies in any attack on China.

If Taiwan remains friendly to Beijing or at least stays neutral or in sympathy with Beijing and recognise themselves as Chinese people with the same culture and civilisation, I think the status quo could remain for quite a while.

In any case, the Chinese can take a long view. There’s no immediate hurry.

With the long view, such divisions within China have happened many times in Chinese history. During those periods of division, the view was that China would always become one again.

How do you see your own legacy?

I don’t know that I have any legacy. I would like to believe that I have convinced some people that history is very important.

Everybody has history and everybody’s history is useful to know so that you have some idea of what it was like in the past. What mistakes were made, what would be the right things to do. What made for good governance, for example, would be very important in modern affairs in any kind of world order.

Good governance is extremely important and history tells us about that in the way that is part of the Chinese tradition.

History is not about the truth. Finding out what exactly happened is important. But it is not why knowing the past is often crucial.

History is what is known about the past that could help you understand the present and give you a clearer idea of what is likely and what can and cannot happen.

To make history meaningful to your own thinking about anything in the world could be very interesting and valuable anyway.

It would be very satisfying if I could convince people that everything has a past and every past has some usefulness. If they learn to use the past to get a better understanding of what is happening, they would find that enlightening.

I believe that knowing the past also helps good governance. History changes all the time and is often rewritten. Therefore, governments who pay no attention to history are likely to make mistakes.

Think of the number of times history has been rewritten in the last few decades. How many are written by the Europeans, by the Americans, by the Chinese Nationalists, by the Japanese, by the Communists? Every one of their histories can be changed over time.

During the early decades of the PRC, people wrote history using Marxist arguments about everything, but today nobody writes like that any more.

People don’t write Chinese history following Marx’s stages of change. What Marx did teach them was about the idea of progress. He showed that human beings have been progressing; they produced more and better goods, became better than slaves and feudal peasants.

In today’s terms, he could be interpreted to argue that capitalist wealth could lead to a better socialist redistribution of that wealth.

The idea of progress shows that the past helps you to understand where we came from and might be going to. This can be seen in the way the Chinese say, look at China today. Can you imagine the kind of science and technology that is happening in China today a hundred years ago? Unimaginable. Therefore, progress is possible and progress will continue to be possible.

I think this is what the Chinese learned by looking at their past. The past has taught them not only that China can survive but can also fall and rise yet again.

But whatever they did, if they put their heart into it, worked hard at it, learned from the past and provided good governance, there would be more progress. And to believe in that idea of progress would depend on their understanding of the past.

item.title: [SCMP] Beijing and Manila should avoid South China Sea ‘miscalculation’: top diplomats
item.description:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Philippine counterpart in Manila on Wednesday, with both sides highlighting the need for “reducing the risk of miscalculation” and maintaining stability in the South China Sea.

The meeting on the sidelines of the Asean foreign ministers’ gathering marked the first formal talks between the top diplomats since Maria Theresa Lazaro assumed office in July last year.

It also came days after fresh tensions in the disputed waters, with Chinese coastguard and Philippine Navy vessels clashing on Monday near the Second Thomas Shoal, the first serious maritime encounter in months between the rival claimants.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Philippine counterpart in Manila on Wednesday, with both sides highlighting the need for “reducing the risk of miscalculation” and maintaining stability in the South China Sea.

The meeting on the sidelines of the Asean foreign ministers’ gathering marked the first formal talks between the top diplomats since Maria Theresa Lazaro assumed office in July last year.

It also came days after fresh tensions in the disputed waters, with Chinese coastguard and Philippine Navy vessels clashing on Monday near the Second Thomas Shoal, the first serious maritime encounter in months between the rival claimants.

The Philippine foreign ministry described Wednesday’s meeting between Wang and Lazaro as “candid, comprehensive and constructive”.

“The two sides underscored the importance of maintaining peace, security, and stability in the region, reducing the risk of miscalculation, and sustaining dialogue on matters of mutual concern,” it said in a read-out.

The talks covered a wide range of topics, including maritime disputes, security, law enforcement, trade and investment cooperation as well as tourism and regional issues, according to the ministry.

It said Lazaro reiterated Manila’s protest against “violent actions” by China Coast Guard personnel near the Second Thomas Shoal, known as Renai Jiao in China and Ayungin Shoal in the Philippines.

She also reaffirmed the Philippines’ position on the maritime dispute and raised concerns over Chinese actions that “have infringed on the maritime rights and entitlements, including incidents affecting the safety of Filipino personnel and fishermen”.

Beijing has accused the Philippines of instigating Monday’s incident by sending small rubber boats to approach its coastguard vessel, while Manila says one of its navy personnel was struck on the head with a wooden baton.

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr summoned the Chinese ambassador on Tuesday, condemning the incident as a matter of national security.

Hours earlier, the Philippine envoy in Beijing had been summoned by the Chinese foreign ministry, which accused Manila of provocation.

The Wang-Lazaro meeting also came days after a diplomatic row over a Chinese state media video mocking the 10th anniversary of a South China Sea arbitral ruling favouring Manila.

The video, published by China Daily on July 10, showed a monkey dressed in traditional Philippine attire being manipulated by figures representing the United States and Japan before being blasted by water cannon, something China has been alleged to have deployed against Philippine vessels in contested waters.

Manila strongly condemned the depiction as racist propaganda and lodged a formal diplomatic protest.

Beijing distanced itself from the video, saying it did not represent an official position, while asserting its territorial claims.

Lazaro raised the issue with Wang, according to her ministry.

“Disagreements over legal and political issues do not justify resorting to disturbing imagery,” she was quoted as saying.

She also described the video as “deeply offensive, distressing, and unacceptable”.

“The Philippines emphasised the need to exercise restraint, avoid actions that increase tensions, and resolve disputes peacefully in accordance with international law, particularly the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the 2016 South China Sea Arbitral Award,” the read-out said.

Lazaro also reiterated Manila’s one-China policy, it added.

Additionally, both sides underscored the importance of “maintaining open channels of communication, enhancing mutual understanding, and strengthening confidence-building measures”.

According to the read-out, both foreign ministers highlighted progress on the South China Sea Code of Conduct and reaffirmed their commitment to wrapping up related negotiations this year.

The Philippines is this year’s rotating chair of the 11-member Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Manila is hosting regional ministers this week for discussions on regional flashpoints ranging from the South China Sea to Myanmar and the economic impact of the Middle East conflict.

In separate meetings on Monday with Asean Secretary General Kao Kim Hourn of Cambodia and Malaysian Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan, Wang emphasised that maritime disputes should not derail ties and called for joint efforts to exclude perceived external meddling.

During his talks with Kao, Wang described the South China Sea as a shared home for regional countries while hailing Beijing as “the most important anchor of stability in the region”.

“Certain forces within the Philippine military and maritime law enforcement ranks have deliberately provoked incidents in the South China Sea to serve the interests of external forces, undermining the process of improving China-Philippines relations as well as peace and stability in the South China Sea,” Wang told Kao.

On July 12, the Philippines marked the anniversary of the 2016 arbitral ruling with a joint statement alongside the US, Japan and 11 other nations. Beijing denounced the declaration as “a distortion of facts and an act of vilification against China”.

The Wang-Lazaro meeting would be significant, Asean spokesman Dominic Xavier Imperial of the Philippine foreign ministry had said on Monday, noting it would cover not only bilateral relations but also regional issues.

“We believe that this engagement is very important because not only will it address … the bilateral relations between the Philippines and China, but it will also have something to do with … the impact of what’s happening globally to the region, to Asean,” he said, according to the Manila Bulletin.

Imperial added that negotiations on the South China Sea code of conduct, ongoing for nearly 17 years, would “always be part of the discussions” during both bilateral and Asean meetings.

In 2023, Asean and China agreed to speed up talks with the goal of concluding the agreement within three years, but progress has been slow as both sides still dispute the legal basis of Beijing’s claims in the strategic waterway.

Despite expanding trade and Chinese investment in the Philippines, the South China Sea dispute remains central to their relations, which have fluctuated between tension and engagement since Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jnr took office four years ago.

Encounters between Chinese coastguard vessels and Philippine ships have become more frequent, particularly around Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal, over which Beijing asserts “indisputable sovereignty” alongside much of the South China Sea.

While China sees Asean as a critical arena to push back against what it considers “external interference” led by the US and Japan, the Philippines has hardened its stance in recent months, accusing the Chinese of aggressive manoeuvres.

Defence Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jnr, sanctioned by Beijing last month over “erroneous remarks”, has asserted that the Philippines is justified in avoiding defence engagements with China.

Manila has strengthened military ties with the US, Japan and their allies over the years, while maintaining bilateral channels with Beijing to manage disputes and avoid escalation.

Both sides have also kept communication channels open, despite frequent clashes and maritime incidents.

During a working-level dialogue in Manila on June 30, Liu Jinsong, director general of the Chinese foreign ministry’s Asian affairs department, urged the Philippines to “honour its commitments and match words with deeds”, while expressing “serious concerns” over what Beijing saw as negative moves.

Philippine officials at the meeting, led by Marshall Louis Alferez of the foreign ministry, reaffirmed a commitment to dialogue and the one-China principle, while expressing a readiness to manage disputes constructively and avoid unintended incidents.

Philippine read-outs described the talks as building on earlier bilateral sessions this year in Cebu, Beijing and Quanzhou, where officials discussed South China Sea issues, provisional arrangements to reduce incidents during resupply missions and potential practical cooperation.

item.title: [SCMP] Wang Yi and Marco Rubio at Asean discuss Xi’s planned US visit, South China Sea clash
item.description:
The Chinese president’s planned trip to the US and the Beijing-Manila South China Sea dispute led the agenda when the top Chinese and American diplomats met in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in the Philippine capital, Manila, for 90 minutes of talks on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ meeting, which ends on Thursday.

According to a readout published by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, Wang described the meeting as “pragmatic, positive and constructive”, and urged both sides to pursue “strategic stability” and “peaceful coexistence”.
item.content:encoded:
The Chinese president’s planned trip to the US and the Beijing-Manila South China Sea dispute led the agenda when the top Chinese and American diplomats met in the Philippines on Wednesday.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met in the Philippine capital, Manila, for 90 minutes of talks on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations foreign ministers’ meeting, which ends on Thursday.

According to a readout published by Chinese state broadcaster CCTV, Wang described the meeting as “pragmatic, positive and constructive”, and urged both sides to pursue “strategic stability” and “peaceful coexistence”.

Without explicitly mentioning the issue, Wang said he had conveyed China’s position on the “recent series of negative words and actions by the US” and called on Washington to respect China’s core interests.

“Our responsibility now is to follow the path set by the two heads of state, eliminate interference and overcome obstacles, and ensure that the consensus reached by the leaders is translated into consensus and action across the entire government and all sectors,” Wang was quoted as saying.

Rubio also said there were still differences between the two countries but that their job was to manage them.

He added that there were areas of potential cooperation, and they discussed President Xi Jinping’s planned trip to the US, according to Reuters.

“The work we need to do now [for] September is to identify what those areas are, so that we can lay the groundwork for a very positive visit … we talked a lot about that,” Rubio said.

He described Monday’s clash between Beijing and Manila over Second Thomas Shoal as very negative and benefiting no one.

When asked about the progress of arms sales to Taiwan – a sensitive subject at the China-US summit in May – Rubio said they were still under internal review because Washington had to take its own stockpile and availability into consideration.

“There is a huge effort on our part to restart a definite defence industrial base and restart its ability to produce,” he said.

Washington is reviewing a US$14 billion weapons package to the island and has not yet formally submitted the proposed sale to Congress, with the delay attributed to production capacity and ammunition reserves.

After his trip to Beijing in May, US President Donald Trump said that holding off on the package could be a “negotiating chip”.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary.

Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

On the subject of America’s conflict with Iran, Rubio described China as in some ways cooperative with the US.

“One thing in particular is that they have been pretty clear that they don’t support any tolling or restrictions on global shipping through international waterways,” he said of China.

Before Rubio’s trip to Manila, the US State Department said the visit was meant to advance “a clear US priority: a free and open Indo-Pacific that delivers safety, security and prosperity for the region and for the American people”.

The diplomatic engagement comes as a rekindled US-Iran war puts Southeast Asian economies under intense economic and energy strain, and follows Washington’s allegations of Chinese electoral interference in the 2020 presidential election.

In a prime-time speech last week, Trump accused China of meddling in US elections, alleging it obtained 220 million American voter records beginning in the 2020 election cycle for “the largest compromise of election data in history”.

Beijing firmly rejected the accusation on Friday.

On Wednesday, Rubio said the allegations of election interference were not discussed in his meeting with Wang.

He also said the state of China-Japan ties was “troubling”, and that deep cooperation between Washington and Tokyo would continue.

Wang and Rubio last spoke in early July in what both sides described as a “positive and constructive” phone call. It was the first reported cabinet-level communication since Trump’s state visit in May.

The dialogue is a critical follow-up to the summit in which both countries pledged to establish a “new vision of building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability”, with Beijing committed to buying more planes, agricultural produce and energy products.

The rival powers are in a fragile trade truce reached by Xi and Trump in October last year and are trying to manage risks and stabilise ties to avert a total decoupling.

But their underlying tensions and rivalry – such as on critical supply chains and advanced technology – remain unchanged.

China has increasingly said it calls for managed competition rather than confrontation, while avoiding major concessions on issues over trade or Taiwan.

Meanwhile, on Friday, the US did not renew a national emergency declaration over Hong Kong and lifted sanctions on nine government officials from Hong Kong and mainland China.

The move was welcomed in Beijing, which described Washington’s decision as “an important step in fulfilling the consensus reached in bilateral talks”.

On Tuesday, Trump signalled that Washington would confront Beijing over the alleged interference but played down the prospect of retaliation.

“We’re going to talk to them about it,” Trump said, adding that the alleged interference “took place a long time ago” and that China might be “a little bit different today than it was then”.

“They do things to us and we do things to them,” he said. “I’ll be honest, we do things to them too. It’s not a one-way street, but we’ll be talking to them.”

Both sides have indicated that Xi’s planned visit remains on track.

On Sunday, before heading to Manila, Rubio said Xi’s trip was still expected to happen in September.

And on Monday, China’s foreign ministry said that both sides had kept in contact on the arrangements for the heads of states’ interactions later this year.

“We anticipate that the trip is happening in September. They’ve continued to send over their teams to prepare for it, and I’ve heard nothing otherwise,” Rubio said.

item.title: [SCMP] Norman Foster’s hi-tech HSBC masterpiece turns 40
item.description:
Forty years ago, a building rose above Central district that would rewrite the rules of architecture. The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (HSBC) Main Building – a tower so radical in its conception that it made every high‑rise built before it look timid – remains as startling today as the day it opened. To mark the anniversary, we tell its story in two voices: those of architect Norman Foster, who, as he returns to the city, reflects on the inspiration behind the building that defined his career; and Ian Lambot, the photographer who was there as it rose from the ground.

When Norman Foster explains the thinking behind the HSBC Main Building, he uses a word you don’t usually find in architectural manifestos: “stuff”. He means everything typically crammed into a high-rise core – circulation, structure, bathrooms and mechanical equipment. By pushing all that to the edges he clears the way for something seminal: flexible, light-filled floors with uninterrupted views. The result is what Spanish architecture critic Luis Fernández-Galiano would categorise as a building of fully exposed “bones”.

Constructed as the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation’s fourth-generation global headquarters, which it remained until 1993, the building was the avant-garde of what commentators called “hi-tech architecture”. It is still the building with which Foster is perhaps most closely associated in the public consciousness and helped bestow on him the lofty titles he would later receive: Sir, then Lord. But honorifics – and the 1999 Pritzker Prize – were hardly on the agenda when the bank was just a set of competition sketches and his company had never built beyond three storeys.
item.content:encoded:
Forty years ago, a building rose above Central district that would rewrite the rules of architecture. The Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation (HSBC) Main Building – a tower so radical in its conception that it made every high‑rise built before it look timid – remains as startling today as the day it opened. To mark the anniversary, we tell its story in two voices: those of architect Norman Foster, who, as he returns to the city, reflects on the inspiration behind the building that defined his career; and Ian Lambot, the photographer who was there as it rose from the ground.

When Norman Foster explains the thinking behind the HSBC Main Building, he uses a word you don’t usually find in architectural manifestos: “stuff”. He means everything typically crammed into a high-rise core – circulation, structure, bathrooms and mechanical equipment. By pushing all that to the edges he clears the way for something seminal: flexible, light-filled floors with uninterrupted views. The result is what Spanish architecture critic Luis Fernández-Galiano would categorise as a building of fully exposed “bones”.

Constructed as the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation’s fourth-generation global headquarters, which it remained until 1993, the building was the avant-garde of what commentators called “hi-tech architecture”. It is still the building with which Foster is perhaps most closely associated in the public consciousness and helped bestow on him the lofty titles he would later receive: Sir, then Lord. But honorifics – and the 1999 Pritzker Prize – were hardly on the agenda when the bank was just a set of competition sketches and his company had never built beyond three storeys.

“In 1979, I came to do what would be the tallest tower in the city,” he tells PostMag. “During the competition, I wrote, ‘It’s not about being the tallest’ and arguably that remains the case – although the city’s vertical scale has changed.”

Unlike other competition entrants, Foster and his team remained, to familiarise themselves with Hong Kong, its banking practices and the people for whom they would be building. The impressions garnered then have stayed with him. “I am always impressed by Hong Kong’s incredible energy, which captured our imagination during that first visit,” he says. “Its essence is unchanged – the streets, buildings, movement, signs and shopfronts, the everyday life of the working population, the city’s smells and flavours, its climate, density, escapes, shrines, landscapes, spirit – all the things you can measure and everything that cannot be quantified. These are the characteristics – the DNA – that make Hong Kong so special and draw me back each time.”

The HSBC brief – “the best bank building in the world” – pushed Foster Associates, as the firm was then called, to overturn the “central core concept” that had governed high-rise office-building design for a century, shifting the steel suspension structure to the perimeter and liberating the interior.

“This radical elimination […] created a space at the base of the tower, which we opened up as a public thoroughfare that forms a natural extension of Statue Square. It also enabled a banking hall to be arranged around a lofty atrium accessed by escalators from the plaza below,” he writes in Norman Foster. Networks, a collection of his essays on architecture recently republished by Taschen.

Foster’s strategy of raising the banking hall in the air also allowed him to develop the site at a better-than 18:1 plot ratio – for every square metre of land, the building has 18 square metres of floor space – when others were achieving 14:1, representing a substantial bonus for the bank.

But the building’s greatest dividend may prove harder to assess. “As China moves towards becoming a cashless society,” he writes, “I can imagine the banking hall itself becoming obsolete, but the structure is flexible enough for the voids to be filled and the hall to be reborn as conventional workspaces.”

And as he points out to PostMag: “If you design to accommodate change, to anticipate a future which is largely unknown, then the fact that [the bank’s] interior has changed several times is surely a validation of that value judgment.”

Foster’s latest return, for the 40th anniversary celebrations, is “perhaps the best expression of how HSBC and the people of Hong Kong view the building – that is, both rewarding and moving”, he adds. He approaches the visit not with nostalgia but with “joyful anticipation” and the same curiosity that drove his original plans. “As a designer you are constantly reappraising every decision you have made or have been party to,” he reflects. “When asked my advice for the future by a graduating class, I replied, ‘Stay a student’.”

The camera doesn’t lie – but it doesn’t always reveal everything either. Ian Lambot has spent years pointing his lens at the HSBC Main Building, and publishing volumes on its construction, yet still it catches him off guard. “It is amazing. It comes as a surprise even to me,” he says, agreeing that it just doesn’t look like anything else.

Does it have another 40 years in it?

“Oh yeah.”

Officially opened on April 7, 1986 as the world’s most expensive building, at a cost of HK$5.2 billion, the tower is still arguably Hong Kong’s defining landmark. HSBC has occupied its chief Central site since 1865, and the Main Building is the fourth headquarters the bank has raised on the same plot – each eventually superseded. Until now.

“He’s a great architect, Norman, no doubt about that,” says Lambot, almost wistfully. At his home in rural Wiltshire, England, he is taking PostMag through his collection of photographs of the Main Building and recalling his time on site, watching it rise from foundations to rooftop. Foster’s other instantly recognisable landmarks include the City of London’s “Gherkin”, the glass dome crowning Berlin’s renovated Reichstag and Chek Lap Kok Airport in Hong Kong.

How Lambot became the visual biographer of HSBC’s Main Building is, he says, “a convoluted story” in which he was simultaneously a Foster company insider and a trusted bank outsider – while working for neither. But it was another “starchitect” who opened the first door.

“I started with Richard Rogers, just by chance, through a friend,” says Lambot. “They needed a model made and I was an architectural model-maker much of the time, because I did it as a summer job while going through university, studying architecture.” But Rogers’ work on another celebrated “inside-out” building, Lloyd’s of London, later stalled, leaving Lambot at a loose end.

“My brother, a civil engineer, was working on the MTR, so I said, blithely, ‘Well, I’ll go and visit Andrew then!’” he recalls. In Hong Kong, his model-making skills soon had him in demand.

After Foster Associates won the design competition, Lambot came to their attention: “They introduced me to HSBC and I got to know people there.” Working independently, he prospered as Hong Kong’s construction boom took hold. Then came a curveball.

With the bank taking shape, a job offer from the architecture firm took him back to London for what would be 18 intense months. “When I arrived, the team working on the building had settled on the eventual design. But I’m fascinated by how things work, so they got me doing the drawings, which is why I ended up doing the floor plans. I was also good at coordinating all the material for the different teams and doing their big master drawings.”

However, the workload was “mad”, he recalls. “You got a day off and you had a splitting headache. Suddenly, working with Norman was just insane and he was a real taskmaster: tough, tough, tough. But I was only 27, 28; you put up with it in those days.”

The lure of Asia proved stronger than any job description. Lambot left London and headed back to Hong Kong, where he soon found himself supervising the making of models of the bank, again as an independent, and doing “a bit of photography”. “It was all happenstance,” he says.

Later, no longer tied to Foster Associates, Central-based Lambot and his medium-format Zenza Bronica camera were free to come and go on site – or onto the roofs of surrounding buildings, and occasionally up in a helicopter for aerial shots – for the following three years. “I had easy access,” he says. “The photographs became more and more important, but it was very ad hoc.”

From his vantage points above and around the site, Lambot watched a building assembled in a way that was as revolutionary in its construction as its conception. “Norman wanted a completely open floor plan. It’s all suspended from the trusses, including the floors beneath,” he says.

“Nothing gets in the way – which worked enormously to the bank’s advantage. One of the reasons the building was so expensive was that it was designed to be redesigned constantly: when it was built, they were just beginning to have computers, but they were all run out of a central server in one of the modules and the whole of the underfloor was a web of cables, which have all now gone.

“That’s the thing,” he adds. “There were huge costs upfront, but they’ve saved vast amounts of money since in being able to reconfigure those floors. In a weekend they could shift everything around.”

Bamboo scaffolding, lashed together in dense lattices, features prominently in many of Lambot’s photographs. While its use may have been de rigueur all the way up the building’s 47 storeys and 180 metres, Foster’s ambitions for the bank as an integral component of life in the city went further – beyond the site boundary. In unrealised, pedestrian friendly Foster plans, the bank would have been linked to Statue Square, then the Queen’s Pier Star Ferry Terminal, farther on, by “an elevated plaza that floated above the traffic like a magic carpet”, he writes in his Taschen essays. “Beneath the plaza we envisaged a network of shopping arcades and markets, tied into the life of the surrounding streets.”

One innovation that was realised continues to have environmental benefits. “They knew they were going to use seawater for lavatory flushing and air conditioning, so all the AC units are down in the basement,” says Lambot, citing the construction of the tunnel that runs from below the bank to Victoria Harbour. “There would be a four level basement for the services and the main bank vault. The tunnel was coming in from the harbourfront, while they were putting floors in, then digging out underneath those floors until the two ends met.”

The building is also perhaps surprisingly international. Its structural steelwork was made in Britain and its aluminium cladding in the United States; riser frames with vertical pipes and ductwork came prefabricated from Japan and service system items were produced in West Germany.

The prefabricated washrooms, also manufactured in Japan, were designed as fully equipped modules. They were shipped to the site with all fixtures installed, then plugged into the structure – much like machine parts. The rapid installation of these and other modular components significantly shortened the building’s construction schedule.

And if you have ever wondered why the escalators from and to ground level are offset, Foster has the answer. “In the run-up to the international competition for this project I commissioned a geomancer [Koo Pak Ling] to advise our team on the feng shui aspects of the site,” he writes. “He talked about dragons and hidden forces, suggesting an oblique entrance to the new building.”

Later, he adds, he came across a forgotten sketch by the geomancer, showing a “diagonal entrance direction which anticipated the angle of the escalators, finalised a year later”.

For Lambot, years of accumulated shots, all on colour film (Fuji for the exteriors and Agfa for the interiors), would steer him into a publishing career. His first two books, under his own Watermark Publications imprint, featured the project from start to finish; the foreword to the second was written by Foster, on whose oeuvre Lambot would later publish a four-volume monograph.

Four decades on – and on the cusp of the completion of another Foster project in Hong Kong, Central Crossing – the bank building at 1 Queen’s Road Central continues to inspire architects everywhere, including its maker.

Last October, JPMorganChase opened its Foster + Partners designed headquarters in New York. “Here the exposed structure is the architecture, and the architecture is the structure,” Foster explains. “In the universal striving for elevation, this is a longstanding tradition perhaps best exemplified by the cathedrals of the Medieval Age.”

More than twice as tall as the original, at 423 metres, the edifice revels in a now-familiar structural expressionism – such that Foster has described it as a direct descendant of the HSBC Main Building.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s Xi praises former president Jiang’s contribution in show of party unity
item.description:
President Xi Jinping led commemorations of the 100th anniversary of the birth of former state leader Jiang Zemin at a grand ceremony in Beijing, in a show of political continuity and party unity ahead of next year’s major power reshuffle.

In a 40-minute speech, Xi addressed thousands of officials and delegates from various sectors at the ceremony, held in the Great Hall of the People, delivering a speech that highlighted Jiang’s contribution to the party and the country.

A large portrait of Jiang was displayed above the rostrum – a practice reserved for deceased former top leaders like Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping – and all seven members of the Standing Committee of the Politburo, as well as a long list of retired state leaders, were present, in a show of solidarity within the party.
item.content:encoded:
President Xi Jinping led commemorations of the 100th anniversary of the birth of former state leader Jiang Zemin at a grand ceremony in Beijing, in a show of political continuity and party unity ahead of next year’s major power reshuffle.

In a 40-minute speech, Xi addressed thousands of officials and delegates from various sectors at the ceremony, held in the Great Hall of the People, delivering a speech that highlighted Jiang’s contribution to the party and the country.

A large portrait of Jiang was displayed above the rostrum – a practice reserved for deceased former top leaders like Mao Zedong and Deng Xiaoping – and all seven members of the Standing Committee of the Politburo, as well as a long list of retired state leaders, were present, in a show of solidarity within the party.

They included former premier Wen Jiabao, who served between 2003 to 2013, former vice-presidents Wang Qishan and Zeng Qinghong. Former president Hu Jintao was absent.

The ceremony was also attended by members of the Jiang family as well as people who worked around him, according to Premier Li Qiang, who moderated the event.

The commemorative event was hosted a year before the 21st Party Congress, scheduled for next autumn, when a new leadership line will be formed and Xi is set to renew another five-year term as the party’s leader.

Xi praised a long list of Jiang’s achievements, from political loyalty to the party to economic development, foreign policy and defence policy, with clear reference to his own governance style, including fighting corruption, a firm stance on the party’s unchallenged status to rule and decisive leadership when facing crisis.

“During the 13 years [of his leadership], the international situation was complex and volatile, and Jiang led the party leadership in unswervingly upholding the party’s line,” Xi said.

Xi called on the entire party to learn from Jiang’s “rock-solid political conviction”, praising him for his unwavering commitment to the Communist Party’s line and policies.

Xi has repeatedly articulated that the party and the country should have confidence in the path, system, theory and culture of socialism with Chinese characteristics.

Xi also mentioned that Jiang voluntarily stepped down from his party leadership positions in 2002.

The event was the latest to commemorate the 100th anniversary of Jiang’s birth, following a high profile 12-episode documentary that aired on state broadcaster CCTV from last week.

In Monday’s speech, Xi placed particular emphasis on Jiang’s courage and sense of responsibility in confronting crises – qualities he has also long urged party cadres to cultivate.

Xi highlighted the critical situation facing the party in the late 1980s and early 1990s – the period after the Tiananmen crackdown and collapse of the Soviet Union – saying Jiang “unswervingly upheld economic development as the central task” while sticking to “the Four Cardinal Principles”, which translate into upholding the party’s unchallenged rule.

“Jiang upheld reform and opening up, carried out rectification, engaged in diplomatic struggles, and resolutely safeguarded the country’s independence, dignity, security and stability,” Xi said.

Xi has long stressed the need to prevent the infiltration of Western ideology into China and has highlighted what he sees as the threat it poses to national security and stability.

Xi also praised Jiang for never making concessions on issues of sovereignty, listing achievements under Jiang including the handover of Hong Kong in 1997 and Macau in 1999. Next year will mark the 30th anniversary of Hong Kong’s return to Chinese rule.

Xi also praised Jiang for his tough stance against “Taiwan independence”.

“Jiang promoted the reaching of the 1992 consensus between the two sides of the Taiwan Strait, embodying the one-China principle, and vigorously carried out the struggle against separatism and Taiwan independence,” he said.

Under the oral understanding, reached in 1992 during Jiang’s tenure between Beijing and Taiwan’s then-ruling Kuomintang, both sides agreed there was “one China”, but differed over how that “one China” should be interpreted.

He also praised the former leader for recognising the “strategic opportunity period” faced by China, announced in 2002 following the country’s acession to the World Trade Organization.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not see Taiwan as a state but are opposed to change of status quo by force.

In the speech, Xi praised Jiang for managing major risks facing the country, including political and economic risks as well as natural disasters.

He singled out Jiang’s management of the 1997 Asian financial crisis, as well as the massive flooding event of 1998.

Xi also praised Jiang for “calmly responding to a series of international emergencies concerning China’s sovereignty and security” – an apparent reference to the 1999 Nato bombing of the Chinese embassy in Yugoslavia as well as the 2001 collision between a Chinese fighter jet and a US surveillance aircraft over the South China Sea.

Xi further highlighted Jiang’s continued support for successive leaders after his retirement in 2004, particularly in the “fight against corruption”. Anti-corruption has been one of Xi’s central priorities since he came to power in 2012.

The event concluded with a standing salute to the Internationale.

Xie Maosong, a senior researcher at the National Institute of Strategic Studies, Tsinghua University, said Xi’s address served as “a retrospective on Jiang’s life while highlighting the points of continuity and alignment with the party’s priorities today”.

Xi’s praise of Jiang’s mandate – specifically that “governing the country requires governing the party first, and governing the party must be strict” – echoes the theme of the coming 20th Central Committee’s fifth plenum in October, Xie noted.

The Politburo announced in July that the conclave would focus on “consistently exercising full and rigorous governance over the party”.

Under the same slogan, the anti-corruption campaign has disgraced senior officials of higher ranks and at a faster speed than many thought possible, with few signs of slowing down as it enters its 15th year under Xi.

According to Xie, Xi’s speech also signalled continuity on economic reform from Jiang’s era.

“Adapting to the requirements of time-honoured development and practical needs, [Jiang] continuously advanced theoretical innovation, institutional innovation, technological innovation, cultural innovation and innovations in all other areas,” Xi said in the speech.

The reference reaffirmed Beijing’s current focus on high-quality development and innovation-driven growth, Xie noted.

By recalling how Jiang navigated severe domestic and external turbulence without wavering on party authority or core sovereignty, the intention was to demand that today’s leadership possess a tenacious “fighting spirit” and superior fighting skills, Xie said.

These would be needed to navigate the tests of “high winds, rushing waves, and even perilous, stormy seas” when “confronting unprecedented global changes in a century and complex geopolitical dynamics such as US-China relations”, he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Does K-pop need the Grammys? BTS’ boycott reignites debate
item.description:
For Asian musicians, the Grammy Awards represent the ultimate dream and recognition of success in the global music industry long dominated by their Western counterparts.

When BTS, widely regarded as the world’s most famous Asian pop act, decided not to submit their music for consideration at next year’s Grammys in an apparent protest against the creation of a new best Asian pop music performance category, it created a dilemma for their K-pop and regional peers.

Should K-pop and Asian pop artists embrace the category or should they follow BTS’ lead, thus giving up a chance to win the world’s biggest music award?
item.content:encoded:
For Asian musicians, the Grammy Awards represent the ultimate dream and recognition of success in the global music industry long dominated by their Western counterparts.

When BTS, widely regarded as the world’s most famous Asian pop act, decided not to submit their music for consideration at next year’s Grammys in an apparent protest against the creation of a new best Asian pop music performance category, it created a dilemma for their K-pop and regional peers.

Should K-pop and Asian pop artists embrace the category or should they follow BTS’ lead, thus giving up a chance to win the world’s biggest music award?

In a social media message announcing their decision last month, the seven-member supergroup wrote: “We hope music can be heard and loved for what it is, rather than being divided by region or language.”

BTS have received six Grammy nominations to date – thrice in the best pop duo/group performance category and one each in the album of the year, best music video and best recording package categories – and lost all of them.

The best Asian pop music performance category covers various genres of Asian music including K-pop, J-pop and C-pop.

Its introduction ahead of the award show in Los Angeles in February has drawn criticism from Asian music fans and industry figures who argue that non-Western artists should not be placed in a separate Grammy category.

The controversy has raised questions of whether the category represents genuine recognition by The Recording Academy, the organisation behind the awards, of the rise of Asian artists or a consolation prize to shunt them away from winning the most prestigious categories.

The academy’s CEO Harvey Mason Jnr responded by saying the category was created to celebrate the “depth, diversity and extraordinary growth” of pop music coming out of Asia.

“More categories mean more artists’ work is recognised,” he wrote, adding that submitting music in a genre category would not prevent an Asian artist from also being considered for the record of the year, album of the year or song of the year categories.

As a genre, K-pop secured its first-ever Grammy win in February when “Golden”, from the Netflix hit film KPop Demon Hunters, won best song written for visual media. It failed to win in the song of the year, best pop duo/group performance and best remixed recording categories.

In the same event, Rose from K-pop girl group Blackpink made history by becoming the first female K-pop artist to receive a Grammy nomination. She was nominated for record of the year, song of the year, and best pop duo/group performance alongside American singer-songwriter Bruno Mars for their smash hit “APT”, but they did not win in any of the categories.

Decision time for K-pop

Following the BTS boycott, attention turns to whether other K-pop artists will submit their names and works for consideration by the academy before the deadline on Friday.

Hybe, which represents BTS, said the band’s decision did not apply at the agency-wide level.

“If other artists under our agency wish to submit entries, we plan to proceed with the submissions as scheduled,” Hybe said.

Stray Kids, one of the biggest K-pop boy bands in recent years, were asked about the Grammys at a press conference earlier this month. Rather than reveal whether they planned to submit their names to the academy, the members emphasised that their music was independent of any awards.

“We’ve never once set out to make an album chasing a particular award or record,” said Seungmin, singer of the eight-member band. “It’s less about outside expectations around awards and more about capturing the sound and story we want to tell.”

An executive at a major entertainment label in Seoul, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told This Week in Asia that BTS’ decision “shocked everyone” in the industry.

“BTS have such influence that it is making other groups and agencies think twice about the Grammys’ latest decision,” the source said.

“There are business interests that may eventually persuade agencies to pursue the award, but it’s clear that BTS’ decision has given the industry something to think about.”

Controversy lingers on

Supporters of the new category have expressed unhappiness about the extensive attention given to the controversy.

Zeena Koda, a co-founder of Asian American Collective and a member of the Recording Academy’s Gold Music Alliance core committee, said in a social media post that she was among the Asian representatives who pushed for the creation of the category.

The aim was “to bring visibility for Asians in the Grammys, none of which has existed before”, Koda said. The category was never intended by those who proposed it to be a contentious issue, she added.

Critics, however, argue that the category smacks of tokenism by grouping artists by region.

“I often count the number of person of colour/Asian nominees in a book prize longlist, and when I see just one, I can tell immediately it was the token pick,” said Anton Hur, one of the co-translators of the Beyond the Story: 10-Year Record of BTS best-selling book, in a separate social media post.

“BTS was always being used to shore up viewer numbers for the Grammys.”

Korean pop critic Kim Do-heon, a member of the Korean Music Awards’ selection committee, described BTS’ announcement in a social media post as “a highly effective strategy” that had “stirred up public opinion and exploited the weaknesses of the [Grammy] awards ceremony”.

Kim also said the BTS debate should become “a starting point for a discussion about what Asian pop actually means”.

A question of validation

BTS are not the only artists to have boycotted the Grammys.

American singer-songwriter Frank Ocean, Canadian rapper and singer Drake and Canadian singer-songwriter and record producer the Weeknd have previously refused to submit their music for consideration due to concerns about the awards’ voting process and what they considered to be discrimination against artists of colour.

The question now is whether BTS’ decision will have any lasting effect on the K-pop industry.

Kim Sung-hwan, another member of the Korean Music Awards’ selection committee, said the main problem was that the academy did not explain clearly what “Asian pop” meant before introducing the category.

“If the academy intends to boost the profile of K-pop acts, it would have been better to explicitly recognise K-pop as a genre and create its own category,” he said.

Other major US music awards, including the Billboard Music Awards, American Music Awards and MTV Video Music Awards, have K-pop categories.

Kim said he doubted other K-pop artists would push through with a similar boycott. Whether this happens is a moot point, as the global success of K-pop – particularly BTS – shows that there is no need for top artists of the genre to win a major international music award for validation, according to Kim.

“There is a certain level of pride with BTS now. Even if BTS doesn’t win, BTS is still BTS to people around the world. The group itself has become a source of national pride.”

item.title: [SCMP] Australia urged to lead Indo-Pacific cable shield as hybrid war risks rise
item.description:
The cables that link Australia with the rest of the world lie mostly unseen, stretched across the seabed and threaded through some of the Indo-Pacific’s busiest and most contested waters.

This vulnerability could also become a strategic advantage, a new report says, urging Australia to position itself as an “Indo-Pacific preferred cable hub” as threats to submarine cables raise economic and national security risks across the region.

That view is echoed by regional analysts, who say Canberra would need to treat cable resilience not only as a domestic security issue but also as a shared regional project.
item.content:encoded:
The cables that link Australia with the rest of the world lie mostly unseen, stretched across the seabed and threaded through some of the Indo-Pacific’s busiest and most contested waters.

This vulnerability could also become a strategic advantage, a new report says, urging Australia to position itself as an “Indo-Pacific preferred cable hub” as threats to submarine cables raise economic and national security risks across the region.

That view is echoed by regional analysts, who say Canberra would need to treat cable resilience not only as a domestic security issue but also as a shared regional project.

Geopolitical concerns and rising investment from “hyperscaler” technology firms such as Google and Meta Platforms are reshaping the Indo-Pacific cable network and could bring new investment into Australia’s undersea infrastructure, according to a paper published this month by the Australian National University’s National Security College.

The report, partly funded by the Department of Defence, said these developments were creating a “significant opportunity for Australia”. Its geography, political stability and “status as a trusted network partner” could attract cable investments that had previously transited “now increasingly geopolitically sensitive chokepoints”.

“Australia lacks a comprehensive strategy to properly protect and govern its submarine cable networks, to respond to a range of threats, or to take full advantage of economic opportunities,” the report said, adding that policies that enhanced security “are also the settings that attract investment”.

Around 99 per cent of Australia’s international data traffic flows through submarine cables – “the backbone of the nation’s digital connectivity”.

They carried critical data including “financial transactions worth trillions of dollars annually, government communications, cloud computing services, and the vast majority of internet traffic”, the report said.

“Major disruptions to submarine cables can have immediate and severe economic impacts, disrupting financial markets, halting international trade, and severing cloud-based services.”

Cutting edge

Recent incidents have sharpened concern over the vulnerability of submarine cables.

Cables connecting Taiwan with the Matsu Islands, which it administers near mainland China, were severed 27 times between 2018 and 2022, with several other incidents recorded around Taiwan in 2025. Taiwan has previously said there was no evidence Beijing had deliberately tampered with the cables.

In Europe, the Norwegian Ocean Observatory in the Norwegian Sea lost communication in April 2021 after a 12-tonne section of underwater communications was cut, while in November 2024, a Chinese-flagged vessel reportedly cut two submarine cable networks. Swedish prosecutors later said they had found no evidence of deliberate damage.

While attribution and intent remain contested in those cases, the report said the pattern suggested state actors were “actively probing and testing cable infrastructure in peacetime” as part of broader hybrid warfare strategies.

“The loss of international connectivity has the potential to send a country into a digital dark age,” said David Brewster, a senior research fellow at the college and one of the report’s authors.

“Over the last several years we have seen numerous incidents relating to cables in Europe and around Taiwan, many of which are likely to be intentional. Australia has mostly been lucky so far.”

International cables were likely to be among the first targets of an adversary in a hybrid war or wider conflict, he said.

Troy Lee-Brown, a research fellow at the University of Western Australia Defence and Security Institute, said while the threats predominantly came from accidental damage by anchors and fishing vessels, there was a “growing risk for intentional sabotage as evidenced elsewhere in the world”.

This was concerning as “Australia relies heavily on subsea cables for its data, and many of those cables come ashore in the same areas, such as in Perth”, he said.

According to the report, submarine cables are difficult to protect from physical attacks because of their offshore and underwater locations. Defending them from deliberate state-based attacks requires a mix of military and civil capabilities – which Australia has gaps in.

Asean interconnected

As cables tend to cross international waters, the report urged Australia to improve international cooperation and enhance the resilience of cable networks across the Indo-Pacific.

Southeast Asia remains central to Australia’s connectivity plans, with several of its cables linked to the region and many routes passing through strategic maritime chokepoints.

“Australia and Asean share the same maritime chokepoints. Cables linking Australia to Asean and onwards to India, Europe and the US, all pass through the Malacca and Singapore straits, as well as the Indonesian archipelago,” said Sarah Soh, an associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ regional security architecture programme.

There are also direct cable routes connecting Australia and some members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, including the Australia-Singapore Cable, the INDIGO cable system linking Singapore to Perth through Jakarta and the Matrix Cable System, which connects Singapore and Indonesia, with an extension to Perth.

“Australia should work with partners to enhance the resilience of cable networks in Southeast Asia,” the report said.

It suggested joint exercises to improve monitoring and response, as well as an Indo-Pacific conference bringing together partner states and regional cable operators to “clarify legal responsibilities, develop common standards, and develop shared responses to threats and incidents”.

Soh said Asean members “are key nodes in Australia’s undersea cable network”, adding that Canberra “could potentially tap into the region’s modest repair fleet” owned by Asean Cableship.

Australia could also offer capacity-building support through its Cable Connectivity and Resilience Centre while investing in infrastructure that diversified routes and reduced reliance on the Singapore and Malacca straits corridor, she noted.

Mark Manantan, a research fellow and lead of the Southeast Asia-Australia Resilient Cable Connectivity Initiative at the La Trobe Centre for Global Security, saw the relationship between Australia and Asean over undersea cables as one of mutual dependence, not donor-recipient.

Australia’s digital resilience increasingly runs through Southeast Asia, according to Manantan. Canberra needed to build resilient regulatory and political relationships “with the countries its cables depend on”.

“Resilience is not just about laying more cables. It depends on landing rights, permits, seabed access and how quickly repairs can be authorised. That means decisions in Jakarta, Singapore, Manila or Dili can directly affect Australia’s connectivity,” he said.

Southeast Asian states provided geography, landing locations, seabed access and regulatory authority, while Australia brought financing capacity, technical expertise, regulatory experience and training, Manantan said.

“Each side therefore holds something the other needs.”

item.title: [SCMP] Russia’s role in Middle East politics endures, shifts to being ‘secondary power’
item.description:
Russia is confounding expectations that its influence in the Middle East would drastically decline after the downfall of Syria’s Assad regime in 2024.

At the time, Moscow operated about 100 military facilities in the war-torn country, following its intervention in the Syrian civil conflict from 2015 to prop up then president Bashar al-Assad in alliance with Iran and its regional proxies.

When Assad was forced to flee to Moscow, and control of most of Syria was seized by Islamist rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa, Russia looked set to lose the air and naval bases that enabled it to project power in the Middle East and North Africa.
item.content:encoded:
Russia is confounding expectations that its influence in the Middle East would drastically decline after the downfall of Syria’s Assad regime in 2024.

At the time, Moscow operated about 100 military facilities in the war-torn country, following its intervention in the Syrian civil conflict from 2015 to prop up then president Bashar al-Assad in alliance with Iran and its regional proxies.
