When Assad was forced to flee to Moscow, and control of most of Syria was seized by Islamist rebels led by current President Ahmed al-Sharaa, Russia looked set to lose the air and naval bases that enabled it to project power in the Middle East and North Africa.

Instead, President Vladimir Putin’s government has managed to hold on to its two most precious assets in Syria: Hmeimim airbase and a portion of the port in Tartus, Russia’s only warm-water naval base in the Mediterranean.

According to a deal announced by the Syrian foreign ministry on Sunday, Russia’s only two official military bases outside the former Soviet Union would be turned into “joint training and capacity-building centres, within new arrangements that preserve mutual interests”.

No further details were given, but Russian military contingents would reportedly remain at both facilities under the new arrangement.

Administrative control of both bases, however, will be returned to the Syrian government, along with the civilian airport at Hmeimim and a dedicated berth at Tartus port, dealing a hand that “reflects Russia’s disempowered status”, according to Caroline Rose, senior director of the Soufan Centre, a New York-based think tank.

Russia’s current goal was to hold tightly to its footprint, prioritising its presence along the Syrian coast to retain access to warm-water ports, Rose said.

Emil Avdaliani, professor of international relations at the European University in Tbilisi, said maintaining and repurposing the Syrian bases showed Moscow’s ability to preserve its strategic assets even after Assad’s fall.

This means Russia is now an “important secondary power” in the Middle East, “rather than a major power broker”, although the Ukraine war has reduced Moscow’s capacity for power projection, according to Avdaliani.

Rose said Russia was “playing a long game” as it was unable to substantially expand its presence in the Middle East at a time when the war with Ukraine had put enormous pressure on its personnel and resources.

Putin is seeking to exploit the loss of US credibility in the region since launching its war against Iran alongside Israel on February 28.

Analysts say Washington’s subsequent failures to ensure the security of the Gulf Arab states against Iranian retaliation and prevent the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz have created more political space for China and Russia, although neither has the capacity nor desire to replace the US as the region’s security guarantor.

Instead, Russia is seeking to maintain its presence and partnerships with Middle East countries as the US recedes from the region, according to Rose.

As the world’s second largest oil exporter and a member of the Opec+ alliance with Gulf producers, Russia could “shape energy prices and output levels, ultimately counteracting the effects of Western sanctions” against Moscow, Rose said.

Due to the Russian Black Sea ports’ proximity to the eastern Mediterranean, Moscow is a major supplier of crude oil and refined petroleum products to Turkey and the Levant.

Russia is also the Middle East’s largest supplier and operator of civilian nuclear power reactors, demand for which is growing as countries in the region shift to renewable energy sources.

State-owned Rosatom has operated a reactor near the Iranian city of Bushehr since 2013. It has signed multibillion-dollar agreements with Tehran to build eight more by 2040.

Rosatom is also constructing two gigawatt-scale nuclear power complexes in Egypt and Turkey under deals valued at US$20 billion each, and has signed memorandums of understanding with its counterparts in Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Jordan for similar projects.

According to Avdaliani, Rosatom is a way for Middle Eastern governments to diversify their nuclear partnerships beyond Western and Chinese suppliers.

Several key attractions for Rosatom’s partners were that its deals did not come with “political conditionality” often seen in Western contracts, covering areas ranging from construction and fuel supply to training, and that the company was flexible about reactor sizes and financing arrangements, he added.

Rosatom’s expanding regional presence was part of Russia’s wider pivot towards the Global South following its near-total rupture in ties with the West over its invasion of Ukraine, Avdaliani said.

Nuclear power projects would fit in well with this approach as signatory nations would be locked into “multi-decade dependencies” on Russian technology, fuel and expertise, while also shaping local opinions in Moscow’s favour.

Russia is also a leading supplier of grain and other agricultural commodities to Middle Eastern markets, and plays an important role in the region’s food security.

As a leading producer of urea and sulphur fertilisers, Russian suppliers have helped plug supply shortfalls in the region caused by the closure of petrochemical plants in the Middle East due to the Iran war.

This represents a reversal of roles from when Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, with disruptions to Russian production and the imposition of Western sanctions at the time prompting Gulf fertiliser manufacturers to make up for the shortfall.

The stage is set for a gradual resurgence of Russian influence in the Middle East, once the Iran and Ukraine wars wind down, according to analysts.

Moscow will have to navigate a region divided into three centres of geopolitical gravity by nearly three years of war: Israel and the Abraham Accords signatories, in particular the United Arab Emirates; Iran and the Axis of Resistance; and Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan through the recently signed Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.

The Putin administration has reportedly supplied Iran with upgraded drones and intelligence during its ongoing conflict with the US.

Avdaliani expects Russia to avoid exclusive alignment with any regional bloc, seeking to preserve its partnership with Iran while maintaining strong relationships with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and the UAE and “pragmatic engagement” with Israel and Pakistan.

Rose said Russia would aim to protect its access to warm-water ports, while using its levers of economic and political influence in the region. To achieve its objectives, Russia would rely on economic tools like grain exports, which have made it a pivotal player in regional food supply chains.

Investment in nuclear and logistical infrastructure in the Middle East, along with energy market coordination with oil producers in the region, would be Moscow’s way to expand its influence, “maximising on many Middle Eastern countries’ imperative to diversify relationships beyond the US”, according to Rose.

item.title: [SCMP] China waits in wings as Mecca pact signals Gulf shift away from US security umbrella
item.description:
The grand security bargain between the United States and Gulf countries is widely perceived to be fraying, creating what analysts see as an opening for Beijing to expand its presence in the region.

For decades, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states relied on Washington’s defensive shield, while it in turn relied on them for access, energy and influence.

Riyadh’s decision to sign a mutual defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan is the clearest sign yet of that shift.
item.content:encoded:
The grand security bargain between the United States and Gulf countries is widely perceived to be fraying, creating what analysts see as an opening for Beijing to expand its presence in the region.

For decades, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states relied on Washington’s defensive shield, while it in turn relied on them for access, energy and influence.

Riyadh’s decision to sign a mutual defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan is the clearest sign yet of that shift.

Signed this week in Mecca, the pact declares that an armed attack on one will be treated as an attack on all three, in an echo of Nato’s Article 5.

But the significance of the Mecca pact goes beyond a new regional security arrangement. Three middle powers – a Gulf energy giant, a Nato member and nuclear-armed South Asian state – are taking steps to reduce their reliance on US-dominated security architecture and build their own collective defence framework.

Such independent alliances among middle powers have been rare since the early Cold War, making the pact a potential model for other countries.

It could also complicate matters for countries such as India and prompt them to reassess their own security partnerships.

“For Riyadh, this agreement bolsters the country’s leverage as it both copes with an emboldened Iran and confronts the limits of US deterrence in the region,” Allison Minor from the Atlantic Council think tank wrote in a recent analysis.

She described the pact as “further evidence that Riyadh is abandoning its quest for an Article 5-like security guarantee from Washington.”

Rich Outzen, a former military and civilian adviser at the US State Department who is now with the Atlantic Council, argued that the agreement marked “an inflection point in the emerging multipolar order in the Middle East and South Asia.”

The pact also brings together countries with very different strategic relationships with China.

John Spencer from the Madison Policy Forum, a New York think tank, said Pakistan was “dependent on China with a military heavily equipped by Beijing”.

Highlighting Pakistan’s fragile economy and reliance on international bailouts, he added: “This is the last country a Nato member should be entering into an Article 5-style mutual defence commitment with.”

For China, however, the new arrangement could create an opening.

As Imran Khurshid from the US-based Middle East Forum wrote in an analysis published last month: “China is using Pakistan for weapons promotion as a gateway to enter the region’s defence landscape.

“Moreover, if the potential ‘Islamic Nato’ that many of these countries, including Pakistan and Turkey, discuss takes shape, China might believe it has an augmented market.”

Khurshid added that China had “aggressively advertised its weapon platforms and builds narratives around its defence systems in the region”, including claims about the success of the JF-17 fighter jet and other Chinese weapons during last year’s India-Pakistan conflict.

That military relationship could become more significant as Saudi Arabia deepens its ties with Pakistan.

According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, more than 80 per cent of Pakistan’s arms imports between 2021 and 2024 came from China.

Under the Saudi-Pakistan mutual defence pact signed last year, Pakistan sent JF-17 fighter jets and other Chinese-made systems to Saudi Arabia, giving them greater visibility and operational experience.

Khurshid said such deals created lasting partnerships because they “typically involve long-term commitments related to maintenance, spare parts, training and logistical support,” embedding Chinese systems more deeply into the recipient’s military structure.

Ali Chishti, from the New Pakistan Foundation, an Islamabad-based think tank, wrote recently that China was “ecstatic” about the Mecca pact and pointed to Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan’s recent visit to Beijing as evidence of Riyadh “deepening ties beyond the West”.

However, Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council, pointed out that the three signatories “have gone to great lengths not to cast this as a Nato-style alliance”, adding that it suggested they would want to “avoid the optics of enthusiastically pooling their resources to purchase Chinese arms”.

“Such transactions would therefore be done quietly and also not at great volume ... Turkey may be able to provide to Pakistan and Saudi Arabia what China could, and at a better price,” he said.

The combination of China’s close relationship with Pakistan and its broader strategic ambitions in the Middle East could therefore give Beijing an indirect route into the Gulf’s defence architecture.

The three-way pact also complicates India’s strategic calculus. New Delhi has moved closer to Washington in recent years, but ties have soured sharply during Donald Trump’s second term.

Meanwhile, the US has moved closer to Pakistan, which is trying to help mediate a deal to end the war with Iran.

Any future Indian military conflict with Pakistan could be framed by Islamabad as an attack that triggers the pact’s collective defence clause – a possibility that may push India and Israel closer together.

India’s former foreign secretary Kanwal Sibal described the situation as “on the face of it, a very negative development for Indian interests”.

The country needed to “explore more options with the United Arab Emirates, Israel, Greece and Cyprus. And Afghanistan”, he added. “We should consult Iran. All this is a fallout from the disastrous US aggression against Iran.”

The Mecca pact followed by months of Iranian missile and drone strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure and sustained Houthi attacks.

Despite the extensive US military presence in the region, American forces were unable to intercept every attack.

The US-Israel war against Iran has also led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas supplies, further reinforcing concerns in Gulf capitals about relying exclusively on Washington for security.

Those concerns have been compounded by reports the war has used up significant stocks of key US weapons.

Around 65 per cent of Patriot air defence interceptors and a substantial share of Terminal High Altitude Area Defence interceptors have reportedly been used up, according to multiple reports citing senior officials, as well as assessments by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

Stocks of long-range precision weapons have also been heavily depleted, including virtually all available ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, while Tomahawk cruise missile inventories have fallen by nearly half.

Restocking will take years, partly because of global supply chain constraints, and the Pentagon has already been forced to delay weapons deliveries to allies and partners.

For Gulf states, the lesson may be less about abandoning the US than about reducing their dependence on it.

Rebeccah Heinrichs of the Hudson Institute pointed to the close ties between Islamabad and Beijing, saying: “It is not in US interests for the Pakistanis to be aligning closer with Saudi and Turkey and our approach towards Iran should keep that in mind.”

But Kugelman said that the new pact, with its “emphasis on burden sharing and implied objective of deterring Iran, should go down well in Trump’s Washington”.

item.title: [SCMP] Vietnam pays the price at home for sending workers abroad
item.description:
Vietnam’s seafood and garment sectors are facing a labour shortfall even with raised wages, as Hanoi expands a drive to send more workers overseas for higher-paying jobs.

The contradiction reflects a broader challenge for the Southeast Asian country as it pushes to move up the value chain while banking on labour migration to generate remittance revenue, analysts say.

According to the home ministry, between 130,000 and 150,000 Vietnamese go abroad to work annually. The overseas labour market totalled nearly 900,000 by the end of last year.
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam’s seafood and garment sectors are facing a labour shortfall even with raised wages, as Hanoi expands a drive to send more workers overseas for higher-paying jobs.

The contradiction reflects a broader challenge for the Southeast Asian country as it pushes to move up the value chain while banking on labour migration to generate remittance revenue, analysts say.

According to the home ministry, between 130,000 and 150,000 Vietnamese go abroad to work annually. The overseas labour market totalled nearly 900,000 by the end of last year.

This May alone, 1,948 Vietnamese went abroad to work in places such as China, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Europe, according to a Department of Overseas Labour report on June 3.

Vietnamese abroad remit between US$6 billion and US$7 billion a year, contributing significantly to the national economy.

This exodus has led to a labour shortage at home.

A report submitted in late June by the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers to the Ministry of Finance highlighted worker shortages as a major shortcoming the industry is facing in key hubs such as the Mekong Delta and Ho Chi Minh City. Even salary increases of 25 to 30 per cent did not help with recruitment and retaining labour.

Similarly, the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association issued a report after a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc in May saying that competition for labour was “increasingly fierce”.

The industry was contending not just with overseas rivals but also higher-paying electronics and machinery producers, said Hoang Lan Anh, a labour migration researcher at the University of Melbourne.

Association chairman Do Ngoc Tai said in an industrial conference on July 30 that many garment factories lacked “sufficient manpower to ensure order deadlines or secure new contracts” and had to compete for workers with “electronics and many other manufacturing sectors”.

Forced migration

However, the picture is more complicated than factory workers simply leaving for overseas jobs.

For many people from poorer central provinces, the choice was between overseas or domestic migration, and low-paid work in industrial hubs – rather than a local job versus emigration, Anh said.

“Labour exports have been treated by the government primarily as a poverty-reduction strategy because migrant workers mainly come from the disaster-prone and resource-poor central Vietnam, where food processing and manufacturing roles offer very low wages,” she said. Salaries in the area usually range from US$200 to US$250.

Hoang said most central Vietnamese she interviewed told her they would need to migrate to earn a living, as there were no viable local opportunities. So it was more worthwhile to go overseas and earn more money than what would be offered in north or south Vietnam.

“If someone migrates from Nghe An province [in central Vietnam] to Binh Duong [a major industrial hub just north of Ho Chi Minh City] to work, their capacity to visit the family and perform care duties is not much different from that of someone in Japan or South Korea,” Anh said.

Moreover, central Vietnam migrants were “socially disadvantaged when competing for the higher-paying electronics or industrial manufacturing jobs in the north and south, where social networking was important for entry and mobility in the labour market”, she added.

Though there were plenty of vacancies in the seafood export and garment sectors, workers usually earn between US$250 and US$350 a month – barely sufficient for household expenses.

“By comparison, Vietnamese workers in destinations such as Japan and South Korea can earn three to five times more. Overseas employment offers rural migrant workers the only avenue for ensuring the family’s economic security,” Anh said.

Workers’ protection

This is a familiar calculation for Jiho Yoshimizu, the representative director of the Japan-Vietnam Tomoiki/Mutual Support Association.

The association has provided consultation and support to about 50,000 Vietnamese – from students and technical trainees to skilled workers – in Japan since it was registered as a non-profit organisation in 2014.

“Many Vietnamese workers hoped to earn and save more than they can at home, send money to family, pay their recruitment debts, build a house and support their families, or start a business when they return,” Yoshimizu said.

However, the high earnings expected do not always reflect the final savings, with deductions such as tax, social insurance, housing, utilities and other costs taking a chunk out of the worker’s salaries.

Recruitment and training debts could also leave some Vietnamese workers vulnerable to exploitation and unable to leave workplaces, even when they encountered harassment, unpaid wages, overworking or a totally different job than what had been promised.

“The main issue is not simply whether wages in Japan are higher than those in Vietnam,” Yoshimizu said. “It is whether workers receive accurate information before departure, whether recruitment costs are reasonable, and whether they can work in a safe environment where their rights are protected.”

Nguyen Thi Bich Ngoc, from the central Ha Tinh province, moved to Japan first as an international student, then found a full-time job through an online recruitment platform and obtained a work visa.

“In Vietnam, I worked as a customer support agent for an international online learning platform. Here, I work for a company that provides support services for foreign residents, helping them set up essential utility services,” Ngoc said.

She would return to Vietnam, she said, if she could find a job that would pay her a competitive salary and give her the opportunity to use her English and Japanese skills. “Being close to my family and friends is something I value very much,” Ngoc added.

Ngoc has the luxury of being able to wait for the right opportunity. Most of her fellow Vietnamese in Japan tended to be rural residents with limited formal education or recognised skills – who would likely have ended up in similarly low-skilled or manual jobs had they remained in Vietnam.

“Most migrant workers aim only to earn a fair wage and save enough money to provide for their families. They may pick up new skills along the way but there is a high chance those skills are irrelevant to their future livelihoods back home,” Anh said.

Rather than assuming overseas work would automatically provide a route into higher-skilled employment on return, Anh said the more immediate task was to protect workers’ rights abroad.

“What seems to be more realistic is to make sure that workers’ rights are protected, they receive the same wages and benefits offered to local workers doing the same jobs, and intermediaries’ involvement, exploitation, and abuse are done away with,” she said.

Nguyen Van Duan, an automotive technician from the central Quang Nam province, said he went to Japan after learning of the opportunity through a recruitment agency. The higher salary was a draw, but so was the chance to learn technical skills, improve his Japanese and work in a more disciplined professional environment.

Like Ngoc, if he could earn a stable income back home, save money and continue his career growth, he would have seriously considered staying.

Duan hopes to use his experience and knowledge gained in Japan to build a career in Vietnam’s automotive repair industry upon his return.

“A workplace that offers opportunities to learn, fair treatment, job stability, and a clear career path is just as important,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] As mainland China tightens its tax rules, can Hong Kong remain a magnet for billionaires?
item.description:
For decades, Hong Kong has been a magnet for the rich.

From wealthy Chinese setting up family trusts to millionaires migrating from across Southeast Asia, all of them have been sucked in by the city’s promise of free capital flows, a trustworthy legal system and extensive financial expertise.

It is a winning combination that helped Hong Kong leapfrog Switzerland as the world’s biggest cross-border wealth hub last year, as the city rode a wave of blockbuster listings by Chinese technology companies.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, Hong Kong has been a magnet for the rich.

From wealthy Chinese setting up family trusts to millionaires migrating from across Southeast Asia, all of them have been sucked in by the city’s promise of free capital flows, a trustworthy legal system and extensive financial expertise.

It is a winning combination that helped Hong Kong leapfrog Switzerland as the world’s biggest cross-border wealth hub last year, as the city rode a wave of blockbuster listings by Chinese technology companies.

But some worry this model could now come under threat. Over the past few months, Beijing has launched a slew of measures to tighten controls over cross-border financial flows, seeking to prevent tax avoidance and capital flight.

Major brokerages have been punished for helping mainland investors illicitly buy overseas stocks, while banks have tightened checks for mainland customers applying to set up Hong Kong accounts.

Perhaps the most significant news came in late July, when Beijing announced that offshore trusts would now be subject to China’s personal income tax – closing a loophole that had allowed wealthy Chinese families to shield massive amounts of income from taxation.

In Hong Kong, some fear the new rules could disrupt – or even divert – capital flows into the city’s vast wealth management industry. But analysts said the city could benefit over the long term.

“In the short run, the new tax rules may push some mainland investors to adopt a wait-and-see approach,” said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University’s Guanghua School of Management.

However, “Hong Kong’s future competitiveness lies in compliance capabilities and the depth of its professional services, rather than simply the tax haven effect”.

Hong Kong’s Private Wealth Management Association (PWMA) – which counts 44 financial institutions in Hong Kong as full members – said Beijing’s new offshore trust tax rules provided “regulatory clarity and certainty for global wealth management” and that the city’s unique role as a “super-value adding connector” for global capital remained unchanged.

This move towards compliance will enhance the long-term credibility of Hong Kong’s trust industry

Tian Xuan, Peking University

A hub for Chinese wealth

In May, Hong Kong received a boost when a report by Boston Consulting Group (BCG) found the city had surpassed Switzerland last year to become the world’s largest centre for cross-border wealth.

The amount of cross-border wealth parked in Hong Kong grew by more than 10 per cent to US$2.95 trillion last year, driven by an initial public offering (IPO) bonanza and an influx of capital from mainland China, according to the report.

Hong Kong’s success was built on “cementing its role as China’s gateway to global markets”, with “mainland flows representing over 60 per cent of assets under management” in the city, BCG said.

But that same concentration also “ties its trajectory tightly to economic and regulatory developments on the mainland”, the report cautioned.

As of 2025, Hong Kong was home to 76 billionaires with combined wealth of US$328 billion, while mainland China housed 470 with a combined worth of some US$1.77 trillion, according to a report by UBS in December.

What’s more, the city’s wealth management industry is likely to benefit as an entire generation of Chinese entrepreneurs ages and prepares to transfer their wealth to their younger relatives.

Over the next 15 years, more than US$300 billion of wealth in mainland China and Hong Kong will be handed over to the next generation, according to UBS.

Behind Beijing’s clampdown

But the new tax rules, announced by China’s Ministry of Finance last month, could complicate that process.

The policy – which took effect immediately – will levy a 20 per cent tax on the gains from offshore trusts with mainland Chinese beneficiaries or whose underlying assets are from the mainland.

The levy will apply to each major part of a trust’s lifespan, from set-up to termination, as well as the distribution of any income. It will also affect any gains dating back to as early as January 1, 2023.

To encourage voluntary reporting, Beijing offered a 90-day grace period for individuals who put their domestic assets – ranging from corporate equities to properties – into offshore trusts between 2023 and 2025 to declare them.

The rules raised concerns in Hong Kong, which has long been a destination of choice for affluent – and often high-profile – Chinese investors to set up offshore trusts, drawn by its low tax rate and strong privacy protections.

The issue became a hot topic in China recently, when children of the late Zong Qinghou – the billionaire founder of drinks company Wahaha Group – launched a legal battle for control over offshore trusts containing assets worth about US$2 billion.

For Beijing, such offshore trusts are a serious issue, as they have allowed the country’s wealthiest families to avoid paying tax on vast amounts of assets.

With Chinese government revenues under pressure amid a prolonged property market downturn, Beijing urgently needs to raise more money from taxes – and clamping down on tax avoidance is a key part of that effort.

Last year, Chinese authorities collected 1.62 trillion yuan (US$240 billion) of income-tax revenues – a steep 11.5 per cent increase over 2024 – as officials stepped up enforcement and closed tax loopholes.

The new rules on offshore trusts are the latest step in that drive. “Not only existing loopholes in tax administration will be plugged, but also a comprehensive cross-border personal income tax system will be established,” lawyers at multinational law firm King & Wood said in a report released on July 26.

For China’s billionaires, the campaign could be painful. As the report noted, a significant proportion of high-net-worth individuals’ overseas income is linked to offshore trusts.

What the rules mean for Hong Kong

The offshore trust tax marks a sharp escalation in China’s tax clampdown, but analysts stressed that the policy was in line with international practices.

“[It] will only eliminate non-compliant ‘grey-area’ practices, without undermining Hong Kong’s status as a global wealth centre,” said Tian of Peking University.

“Indeed, this move towards compliance will enhance the long-term credibility of Hong Kong’s trust industry.”

China is far from alone in fighting tax avoidance. In 2021, members of the G20 agreed to introduce a global corporate minimum tax rate of 15 per cent as part of an effort to prevent large companies from shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions.

Key Chinese policies such as the country’s tax residency rules – which define anyone living in China for more than 183 days a year as tax resident – are closely modelled on overseas systems such as the US Internal Revenue Service.

To prosper under the new regime, Hong Kong needs to proactively drive the transition of the local offshore trust business towards greater compliance and allay mainland clients’ compliance concerns, according to Tian, who also serves as a Chinese government adviser and a deputy to the National People’s Congress.

Meanwhile, the city should further optimise its tax rules on share-based incentive schemes and trust isolation services to reduce cross-border tax costs for executives at artificial intelligence (AI) firms, Tian added.

That would help attract start-ups to set up related funds in Hong Kong, allowing the city to continue riding China’s tech boom.

Tapping China’s new tech elite

Hong Kong’s ability to serve China’s growing class of billionaire tech entrepreneurs will be key for the future of the city’s wealth management industry, analysts said.

Since early 2025, when the emergence of AI start-up DeepSeek reignited global investor interest in the Chinese tech sector, more than 200 companies have gone public in Hong Kong, raising nearly HK$500 billion between them, according to data from Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing.

The wave of blockbuster listings is being driven primarily by mainland start-ups, which are increasingly choosing to go public in Hong Kong rather than Western markets such as New York amid rising US-China geopolitical frictions.

These IPOs, in turn, are minting an entire new generation of super-rich tech founders, who have their own asset-allocation needs.

For example, Liu Debing, chairman of Chinese AI firm Knowledge Atlas Technology – also known as Zhipu AI – saw his net worth skyrocket after his firm’s Hong Kong IPO at the start of the year.

Liu’s wealth swelled from about US$1 billion in mid-January to US$16.2 billion as of early August, after Zhipu AI’s stock price rose more than sixfold, data from Hurun Group and Forbes showed.

Zhu Yiming, chairman of Chinese chipmakers ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and GigaDevice Semiconductor, has also seen his net worth inflate from US$2 billion in mid-January to US$15.4 billion as of early August.

As cross-border tax reporting becomes inevitable, compliance might help Hong Kong gain more support from Beijing

Liu Jing, Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

Hong Kong is well-placed to continue benefiting from the Chinese AI boom – bringing more talent and capital to the city – even as Beijing presses ahead with tighter offshore tax rules, according to Liu Jing, director of the investment research department at the Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business.

“As cross-border tax reporting has become inevitable, compliance might help Hong Kong gain more support from Beijing,” Liu said.

Hong Kong’s proximity to the mainland should help it maintain its competitiveness as an offshore wealth management hub for affluent Chinese investors, he added. After all, rival hubs such as Singapore will also need to deal with the stricter tax rules.

If it can do so, the rewards will be lucrative. With optimism rising regarding China’s ability to overcome US tech sanctions, Chinese AI start-ups have surged in value this year, propelling at least 20 domestic entrepreneurs onto the Hurun Global Rich List 2026.

Though US tech billionaires still dominate the list, Hurun Group’s CEO and co-founder, Sinclair Lyu, said the wave of AI-driven wealth creation had just begun, and China was primed to become a major driver of it.

“With the exciting Hong Kong IPO market and China’s reserves of young talent, we would definitely see more Chinese AI entrepreneurs stand at the top of the future global billionaire rankings,” Lyu said.

Deepening central support

Meanwhile, Beijing is backing Hong Kong to strengthen its role as an international asset and wealth management centre, with a related target included in China’s latest five-year plan.

Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), reaffirmed that support in early August.

“Hong Kong has become the world’s largest cross-border wealth management centre,” Wu said at an event to mark the launch of China’s first offshore government bond futures in the city.

“We will deepen cooperation with Hong Kong counterparts across the board – spanning markets, institutions and products – and spare no effort in injecting new vitality and momentum into the development of the capital market.”

Financial institutions are also expanding their operations in Hong Kong.

HSBC, the city’s top lender, said in May that it would continue to expand the front desk of its wealth management team, with a goal of becoming Asia’s largest wealth manager.

Last month, Sun Life joined the race by launching an integrated wealth management platform to meet rising cross-border demand from high-net-worth individuals.

The PWMA – Hong Kong’s wealth management association – said the enhanced cross-border policies, coupled with accelerating wealth creation driven by the AI boom, would “inject fresh energy and momentum into cross-boundary wealth management, reinforcing Hong Kong’s position as a leading global wealth management hub”.

item.title: [SCMP] How Southeast Asia’s monarchies stay relevant in a volatile region
item.description:
When Brunei’s Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah recently stripped his daughter-in-law of a royal title, the move drew attention for its unusually public glimpse into discipline inside one of the world’s few remaining absolute monarchies.

But it also offered a small example of what analysts who study Southeast Asia’s royal families describe as a wider challenge for the region’s monarchies: how to preserve authority through tradition and adaptation as public expectations change.

An official announcement dated August 7 said Pengiran Raabi’atul ‘Adawiyyah’s conduct had tarnished the monarchy’s reputation and shown disrespect towards the sultan, Queen Saleha and the royal family, but did not offer details.
item.content:encoded:
When Brunei’s Sultan Hassanal Bolkiah recently stripped his daughter-in-law of a royal title, the move drew attention for its unusually public glimpse into discipline inside one of the world’s few remaining absolute monarchies.

But it also offered a small example of what analysts who study Southeast Asia’s royal families describe as a wider challenge for the region’s monarchies: how to preserve authority through tradition and adaptation as public expectations change.

An official announcement dated August 7 said Pengiran Raabi’atul ‘Adawiyyah’s conduct had tarnished the monarchy’s reputation and shown disrespect towards the sultan, Queen Saleha and the royal family, but did not offer details.

A contrasting example came on May 25, when Cambodian Senate president Hun Sen, acting as head of state during King Norodom Sihamoni’s medical absence in China, signed a royal decree pardoning former opposition leader Kem Sokha.

One case involved hierarchy and discipline inside an absolute monarchy; the other showed the working of constitutional authority in a monarchy with limited governing power.

Across the region, the models differ sharply. Brunei’s sultan rules as both head of state and government, Malaysia’s king is elected every five years from among nine hereditary rulers, Cambodia’s crown remains largely symbolic and Thailand’s monarchy occupies a prominent but highly sensitive place in national life.

Yet analysts told This Week in Asia that all four faced a common test: whether they could keep adapting as politics, institutions and public expectations evolved.

Pavin Chachavalpongpun, a professor at Kyoto University’s Centre for Southeast Asian Studies, said monarchies endured partly by presenting themselves as inseparable from the nation and as “primary custodians of order, continuity and moral authority”.

Religion, history and state-sanctioned accounts of nation-building also allowed crowns to exercise influence beyond their formal constitutional roles, said Pavin, a prominent critic of Thailand’s royalist establishment who has lived in self-exile in Japan since Thailand’s 2014 military coup.

In moments of political crisis, he said, some political actors might look to royal institutions as sources of external legitimacy or arbitration.

But such reliance was “a double-edged sword”, Pavin said, because it could deepen institutional dependency and reinforce the idea that elected civilian leadership was secondary to royal guardianship.

Public discussion of the Thai monarchy remains constrained by Section 112 of the Penal Code, commonly known as the lese majeste law, which carries prison terms of three to 15 years for defaming, insulting or threatening the king, queen, heir apparent or regent. Pavin himself was charged under the law in 2014.

In Pavin’s view, Thailand’s royal institution had moved away from the informal “network monarchy” associated with previous eras towards a more formalised structure of authority.

The youth-led protests of 2020 and 2021, he said, showed that royal authority was not uncontested and that some younger Thais wanted more open discussion of the institution’s place in the country’s political system.

Malaysia offers a contrast in design, with royal power dispersed among nine houses whose rulers are heads of Islam in their respective states.

“The monarchy itself is tied very closely to identity and the position of Islam within the nation-state,” said Ahmad Fauzi Abdul Hamid, a political scientist at Universiti Sains Malaysia.

The kingship rotates among the houses, preventing permanent authority from accumulating in one royal line, while the Conference of Rulers helps resolve differences within the system. Ahmad Fauzi credited the arrangement with helping Malaysia navigate successive governments and a hung parliament between 2020 and 2022.

Malaysia’s larger, multi-ethnic population and competitive elections have also required its rulers to accommodate constitutional government and wider public expectations, Ahmad Fauzi said. Members of state royal families maintain direct public contact and have also entered the civil service.

Brunei presents the opposite model. Hassanal Bolkiah has fused the state with Sunni Islam and Melayu Islam Beraja (MIB), or Malay Islamic monarchy, while retaining sweeping authority. Oil wealth is central to the system’s legitimacy, Ahmad Fauzi said: “Most of the wealth goes to the royal and elite families, but the public still benefits.”

Frank Fanselow, a sociologist at the Singapore University of Social Sciences who spent years in Brunei, has called this arrangement a “rentier bargain”, where energy revenues fund education, healthcare, subsidies and public-sector employment, while citizens reciprocate with loyalty.

Fanselow said that Brunei’s durability rested on a welfare-based social bargain, MIB ideology, royal ritual and the sultan’s cultivated image as a paternal “caring monarch”, while the ruler also projected accessibility through visits to mosques, schools, offices and markets.

Longer-term pressures, however, include reliance on hydrocarbons, youth employment, economic diversification and succession after a reign that has become closely identified with the state, Fanselow added.

Ahmad Fauzi said the sultan was aware that the welfare system could not depend on oil indefinitely. “That is why you have initiatives to diversify the economy away from just petroleum,” he said.

“Few Bruneians can remember their country without him at the helm. In some ways, he is bigger than the monarchy itself, and his absence would leave a huge vacuum not only in the institutions but also in the collective consciousness of his subjects,” Fanselow added.

If Brunei shows monarchy fused with executive power, religion and welfare, Cambodia presents a much more constrained model.

The monarchy was restored in 1993 after the Khmer Rouge era and years of civil conflict, with the king expected to “reign but not govern”.

That limited constitutional role was visible in May, when King Norodom Sihamoni was in China for medical treatment and Hun Sen, as acting head of state, signed a royal decree pardoning former opposition leader Kem Sokha.

Kem Sokha had been under house arrest after receiving a 27-year sentence for treason.

Cambodia has no automatic hereditary succession, although Sihamoni is unmarried and has no children. When the throne becomes vacant, a nine-member Royal Council of the Throne elects a new king from eligible members of the royal family.

The episode illustrated the monarchy’s primarily constitutional and symbolic role in contemporary Cambodia. While the king remains an important national figure, the institution operates alongside political offices and governing structures led by the Cambodian People’s Party.

For Ou Virak, founder and president of Future Forum, an independent Phnom Penh-based think tank, that political imbalance has not erased the monarchy’s legitimacy.

“The very notion of Cambodia as a nation, as a kingdom, comes from long ago,” Virak said, pointing to the ancient Khmer empire and its god-kings, as well as the legacy of the late King Norodom Sihanouk, who is closely associated with Cambodian independence.

“We are always going to look at the role of the monarchy as a source of Cambodian identity,” he said.

The decline of royalist parties after the political turbulence of the 1990s also enabled the palace to be presented more readily as above party politics, Virak said. But he described its relationship with the ruling establishment as an “uneasy marriage”, with Buddhism and the monarchy remaining as cultural anchors whose endorsement could lend legitimacy to a centralised political system, even though “the ruling class holds most of the cards”.

After the Cambodia National Rescue Party’s dissolution in 2017, the monarchy increasingly became another source of legitimacy for the country’s rulers alongside economic growth and rising living standards, Virak said.

Oh Ei Sun, a senior fellow at the Singapore Institute of International Affairs, said Sihanouk’s legacy had made the monarchy a symbol of continuity for a population shaped by the Khmer Rouge era.

Sihamoni’s distance from day-to-day politics had also helped preserve the institution. “Realistically, it is very symbolic nowadays. The real power is with Hun Sen and Hun Manet,” he said. “It is this sort of flexibility and, in a sense, harmlessness which renders the monarchy quite durable in Cambodia.”

Taken together, the four monarchies suggest that endurance depends not only on tradition but also on how far each crown can bend with political, economic and social change without weakening the authority it seeks to preserve.

“A monarchy which is able and willing to adapt to changes according to the times, according to modern developments, will fare better,” Ahmad Fauzi said.

item.title: [SCMP] Shaoxing wine goes upmarket: Dongqu’s luxury touch elevates the Chinese pantry staple
item.description:
For a small city of three million people, Shaoxing stands as a giant in the global Chinese collective consciousness. After all, the name of the eastern Chinese city is emblazoned on the quintessential bottles of cooking wine that are found in Asian households and restaurants the world over, with which numerous Chinese regional cuisines – from the complex braises of Shanghai and Zhejiang (the province where Shaoxing is found) to the spicy marinades of Sichuan province and the subtle steamed seafood of Cantonese fare – would be nigh on impossible to cook without.

Shaoxing wine is one of China’s oldest grain ferments, evolving from ancient rice ales into a polished yellow wine poured at rites and family banquets for more than two millennia. First linked to early ritual offerings in the Spring and Autumn period (770BC to 476BC) and Han era (206BC to AD220), it later soaked the verses of Tang and Song dynasty poets, becoming a favoured pour at riverside feasts and scholarly gatherings. By the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), it had settled into its role as a symbol of longevity and good fortune, especially around autumn and winter festivals.

The character of Shaoxing wine is defined by three markers of terroir: the base grain of glutinous rice, Jianhu lake water fed by the Kuaiji Mountains and the qu (a wheat-based starter) that seeds fermentation with a complex microbiome. Today, Shaoxing is protected as a geographical indication, so any bottle bearing the name must be born of this landscape.
item.content:encoded:
For a small city of three million people, Shaoxing stands as a giant in the global Chinese collective consciousness. After all, the name of the eastern Chinese city is emblazoned on the quintessential bottles of cooking wine that are found in Asian households and restaurants the world over, with which numerous Chinese regional cuisines – from the complex braises of Shanghai and Zhejiang (the province where Shaoxing is found) to the spicy marinades of Sichuan province and the subtle steamed seafood of Cantonese fare – would be nigh on impossible to cook without.

Shaoxing wine is one of China’s oldest grain ferments, evolving from ancient rice ales into a polished yellow wine poured at rites and family banquets for more than two millennia. First linked to early ritual offerings in the Spring and Autumn period (770BC to 476BC) and Han era (206BC to AD220), it later soaked the verses of Tang and Song dynasty poets, becoming a favoured pour at riverside feasts and scholarly gatherings. By the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), it had settled into its role as a symbol of longevity and good fortune, especially around autumn and winter festivals.

The character of Shaoxing wine is defined by three markers of terroir: the base grain of glutinous rice, Jianhu lake water fed by the Kuaiji Mountains and the qu (a wheat-based starter) that seeds fermentation with a complex microbiome. Today, Shaoxing is protected as a geographical indication, so any bottle bearing the name must be born of this landscape.

Yet, for an industry that produces more than 600,000 tonnes annually, only a fraction of Shaoxing wine is intended for table-drinking, and just a hair’s sliver of that is produced by boutique wineries at the luxury end of the market.

Chen Zhi is looking to change that. In his late 30s, the boisterous, bespectacled businessman is a rare presence in a slow-moving, tradition-bound industry that is closely tied to the state, where the cultural concept of guanxi (connections) still reigns supreme.

In 2017, suffering from spontaneous nerve spasms that paralysed one side of his face, Chen was on his way to an acupuncture appointment when he chanced upon a fair organised by the China Alcoholic Drinks Association, where he was roped into a tasting of Shaoxing wine from the historic Pagoda Brand, leading him down a rabbit hole into which he has “been sinking deeper and deeper ever since, right up to this day”, he says.

Chen went on to launch Dongqu in 2019, defying many of the norms associated with Shaoxing wine.

First, there’s the price: at a starting price of HK$600 (US$77), even its most affordable bottling, the 2009 vintage, is almost triple the price of other high-quality sipping Shaoxing wines, such as the 10-year-aged bottling from the famed Nu’er Hong brand. This is largely a result of Dongqu’s laborious production processes, which depart from the industry practice of blending different wines for a consistent flavour. Instead, Dongqu opts for single-year vintages drawn directly from the earthenware jars they’re aged in – all the better to bring out the unique growing and fermentation conditions of each particular season.

Then there’s the move-fast-and-break-things approach that Chen has cultivated at Dongqu that, despite falling under the umbrella of the vast Pagoda Brand Winery, functions like a start-up.

“The mission of state-owned enterprises is not to make mistakes,” Chen tells me over a sumptuous dinner at the one-Michelin-star, Taizhou fine-dining restaurant Wild Yeast in Hangzhou. “There’s a slang term – mo yu [to stroke a fish] – which means to slack off and do nothing. Doing well isn’t necessarily a good thing, and doing badly also doesn’t really matter – you just have to guarantee a tiny bit of growth every year.”

In contrast, Dongqu has done everything but rest on its laurels. In just seven years, the boutique brand has expanded to more than 200 Michelin- and Black Pearl-awarded establishments across China, which have found it to be a perfect food pairing.

Like sake production, the brewing process for high-end Shaoxing wine takes place over the colder winter months, to prevent spoilage and allow for careful control of fermentation. On an overcast day in early November, the brewing halls at the Pagoda Brand Winery, on the shores of the Jianhu, are in full swing, pumping billowing, rice-scented columns of steam onto osmanthus-lined roads of the compound. There are 15 shifu (brewmasters) in charge of the process, each responsible for the operations of a brewing hall. Despite the sheer physicality of the job, experience is crucial here, with the youngest shifu already well into their 50s.

Mao-capped brewmaster Ni Xingjun is already working up a sweat despite the chill in the air, as he rakes a mixture of yeast, glutinous rice and Jianhu lake water in a large earthen jar – a labour-intensive task that must be repeated every four to five hours around the clock over four days for the hundreds of jars on the main brewing floor.

The winemaking is highly technical: the rice must be soaked and steamed to kick-start the brewing process, and the temperature of the grains meticulously controlled throughout by calibrating the steaming time to the temperature of the water as well as the ambient environment to ensure proper fermentation later. The shifu combines his intuition and years of experience with hard data to tease out the best qualities of the rice grains, a varietal from Anqing, Anhui province, that is allowed a longer growth cycle to increase its stores of starch, resulting in a wine with bolder flavours.

“If you’d like, lean in and take a deep breath of this aroma,” says Ni, pulling me towards a freshly raked vat. I breathe in, filling my nostrils with a milky, malty scent that is both gentle and all-encompassing, comforting and intoxicating all at once; a scent that is instantly nostalgic to anyone for whom a freshly steamed bowl of rice was a fixture at the dinner table.

Today, Dongqu is spearheading a return to dinner tables not just in homes, but across some of the most in-demand restaurant tables across the country. In Hong Kong, the brand’s layered, umami-forward pours have been featured in traditional-leaning pairings, such as with braised vermicelli with hairy crab at neo-Cantonese restaurant Jee and spritzed atop a crispy stuffed sea cucumber at Vea, to more left-field match-ups as with the signature king crab arroz caldoso at one-Michelin-star Ando, and even transformed into a Shaoxing wine ice cream to cap off an Edomae omakase meal at Sushi Kumogaku.

“Compared to sake, Dongqu offers a richer and more complex flavour profile, which is fully released when heated, making it particularly suited to grilling and simmering,” says Kumogaku’s head chef, Chan Wing-kin. He believes that it adds a deeper aroma to seafood that is difficult to find in Japanese cuisine.

This boundary-crossing milieu is all part of Chen’s mission to refashion the image of Shaoxing wine as a marker of Chinese haute gastronomy, rather than a cheap pantry staple relegated to the status of a mere condiment. He likens the winemaking process – tending to the yeast, keeping watch around the clock – and growing the brand as being akin to the process of raising his first daughter.

“As everyone knows, newborn babies need constant care, and what I saw at the brewing site was the same,” Chen recalls. “It’s like watching a child grow up. You don’t know what they’ll become; you can only wait patiently from the sidelines.”

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong-style cha chaan teng cafes thrive globally as Gen-Z embraces nostalgic dining
item.description:
When a cha chaan teng in Busan, South Korea, made it into this year’s Michelin Guide, it was a sign of how far the Hong Kong tea restaurants have come since the 1950s and 60s. Both at home and abroad, cha chaan teng are hotter than boiling-hot Ceylon tea poured through a milk-tea cotton “stocking”. In Hong Kong, long queues form outside Milk Cafe branches, while social-media buzz surrounds the ramshackle Lan Fong Yuen on Gage Street, Central. Overseas, these cafes have spread to cities such as Seattle and New York.

A popular working-class mealtime fixture since the mid-20th century, cha chaan teng have long been a Hong Kong mainstay. So why, in 2026, are they drawing fresh attention in culinary circles online and off?

A marriage of Cantonese and Western fare, cha chaan teng can ply a hungry guest with a macaroni soup starter, a satay beef noodle main and an egg tart for dessert, blending cuisines from far-flung places in one meal. And then there’s the speed at which the food is served. Hong Kong’s diners-cum-cultural landmarks are still as fast, furious and familiar as they ever were. Some, such as the Jordan institution Australia Dairy Company, are so brisk, in fact, that they have drawn criticism from tourists (notably, rarely from unfazed locals) for rushing customers into seats, through their order and back out the door.
item.content:encoded:
When a cha chaan teng in Busan, South Korea, made it into this year’s Michelin Guide, it was a sign of how far the Hong Kong tea restaurants have come since the 1950s and 60s. Both at home and abroad, cha chaan teng are hotter than boiling-hot Ceylon tea poured through a milk-tea cotton “stocking”. In Hong Kong, long queues form outside Milk Cafe branches, while social-media buzz surrounds the ramshackle Lan Fong Yuen on Gage Street, Central. Overseas, these cafes have spread to cities such as Seattle and New York.

A popular working-class mealtime fixture since the mid-20th century, cha chaan teng have long been a Hong Kong mainstay. So why, in 2026, are they drawing fresh attention in culinary circles online and off?

A marriage of Cantonese and Western fare, cha chaan teng can ply a hungry guest with a macaroni soup starter, a satay beef noodle main and an egg tart for dessert, blending cuisines from far-flung places in one meal. And then there’s the speed at which the food is served. Hong Kong’s diners-cum-cultural landmarks are still as fast, furious and familiar as they ever were. Some, such as the Jordan institution Australia Dairy Company, are so brisk, in fact, that they have drawn criticism from tourists (notably, rarely from unfazed locals) for rushing customers into seats, through their order and back out the door.

And yet, despite the complaints, the number of tourists adding cha chaan teng to their itinerary grows. The draw, perhaps, is less the fare than the feeling of sentimentality and the yearning for simpler times.

It’s likely that the “Chinamaxxing” social media trend has had a hand in this, adding fuel to the proverbial fire and increasingly pushing Gen-Z audiences into the bosom of Chinese nostalgia. With their wooden booths, mosaic floors and colourful melamine tableware, cha chaan teng are catnip to influencers, and their authentic vintage interiors make for the perfect background in just about any frame. With the wide availability of ring lights, garish, washed-out lighting is no longer a problem. So popular are cha chaan teng among content creators that staff at Mido Cafe in Yau Ma Tei have had to restrict photography so that they can keep serving – rather than swerving selfies.

As a symbol of Hong Kong’s East-meets-West fusion, as well as of the resilience of local culture and egalitarian social spaces, the cha chaan teng embodies the softer side of a city often thought of as sharp-edged. Theirs is a social-media-friendly aesthetic – think idiosyncratic and worn at the edges – and businesses stand ready to capitalise.

Brands such as Adidas and Marathon Sports have launched cha chaan teng-themed clothing lines, keeping this strand of wistfulness on the right side of chic.

Last October, a photography exhibition at K11 Art Mall featured five artistic takes on the tea restaurant. Airside, too, has taken note: an exhibition curated by architectural historian Charles Lai Chun-wai and product designer Kay Chan Wan-ki – running until the end of July – examines the cha chaan teng from table to tile.

Its visual appeal, it turns out, travels. Spreading through the Chinese diaspora to the United States, Canada, Australia and Britain, modern interpretations of the Hong Kong-style cafe are attracting young customers worldwide. Fok Noodles in New York has become the go-to spot for Hong Kong cart noodles, and Cafe No 12 in Penang’s George Town often sees queues out the door for its egg tarts.

Following waves of migration, cha chaan teng have become cultural touchstones for Chinese communities everywhere. So far is their reach and influence that a cha chaan teng pop-up opened at Art Basel in Paris in 2024.

Home-grown cha chaan teng without an online presence – but keen to cash in on the whims of “food-fluencers” or film aficionados eager to recreate their own Wong Kar-wai scene – are tapping their young customer base for social-media savvy.

Tai On Coffee and Tea Shop was a Kowloon landmark for more than 50 years, before closing in 2019 when its owners emigrated. The current owner, Tiffany Yeung Chiu-yi, bought and reopened the cha chaan teng in 2022, harnessing social media to amass a new following.

“We have had a lot more tourists in the past year, mainly due to the internet. Instagram is now a key source of marketing for us,” says Yeung. “All kinds of dining options dropped off over the past two years in terms of demand in Hong Kong. But through Instagram, we found out what customers expected from us and were able to adjust our offerings to meet those expectations. It’s about differentiating from others, and Instagram helped us to do that.”

The desire for nostalgia increases in places going through rapid social change, says Dr Veronica Mak Sau-wa, associate professor of anthropology at Hong Kong Shue Yan University. It’s no secret that the city has gone through monumental shifts in recent years, so this craving for all things old school could be seen as a reaction and the younger generations’ way of connecting with the city’s history, while forging a new cultural identity in the process. From an anthropological standpoint, Mak says, “it’s a very human craving, one that helps us to feel connected to other people and establish a clear sense of self. For some, it can even be a form of escapism”.

For ArChan Chan Kit-ying, head chef of modern Cantonese restaurant Ho Lee Fook, nostalgic dining is a celebration of local culture: “With fewer heritage restaurants left, there is a growing need for spaces that preserve the essence of Hong Kong while continuing to create new memories.”

Mak goes further, suggesting that eating at a cha chaan teng is not just a means of honouring the past, but of expressing what we would like to see in our future. “Dining out is always a form of identity, a differentiator,” she says. “Whether that’s the place we go after work or class to build community, a type of food that speaks to our heritage, or just a place to see and be seen, it’s all doing that very same thing: helping us to define and individualise ourselves in society.

“The noisiness of a cha chaan teng establishes an informality that allows people to speak more freely, in ways they couldn’t at a fine-dining restaurant. If you go to these places a lot, they remember you and they remember your order. A sense of community comes from that.”

Snapping photos of our food before we tuck in, or shooting a video of a plate, embeds it with meaning of our own making. A young person posting content from a traditional cha chaan teng is, perhaps unknowingly, lending it a modern significance. As Hong Kong’s F&B market continues its unpredictable roller-coaster ride, that significance may be key to the institution’s survival.

Now well into their seventies, cha chaan teng show no sign of slowing, even establishing themselves as a major tourism draw. How’s that for off-menu?

item.title: [SCMP] Delcy Rodriguez’s Castro tribute tests Venezuela’s balancing act between US and China
item.description:
Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez’s tribute to Fidel Castro has drawn a blistering rebuke from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, highlighting the political tensions surrounding Caracas’ rapprochement with Washington even as China seeks to preserve its economic interests in the South American country.

Rodriguez marked the centenary of the late Cuban leader’s birth this week by praising Castro as a figure who “transcends time” and invoking his commitment to sovereignty, social justice and Latin American unity.

Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants and a long-time critic of the communist government in Havana, responded sharply.
item.content:encoded:
Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez’s tribute to Fidel Castro has drawn a blistering rebuke from US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, highlighting the political tensions surrounding Caracas’ rapprochement with Washington even as China seeks to preserve its economic interests in the South American country.

Rodriguez marked the centenary of the late Cuban leader’s birth this week by praising Castro as a figure who “transcends time” and invoking his commitment to sovereignty, social justice and Latin American unity.

Rubio, the son of Cuban immigrants and a long-time critic of the communist government in Havana, responded sharply.

“Fidel Castro was a complete failure at everything except destroying Cuba and impoverishing, jailing and murdering his own people,” Rubio wrote on social media.

The exchange came as Chinese President Xi Jinping also commemorated Castro’s centenary, praising his contribution to relations between Beijing and Havana and describing him as a founder and promoter of China-Cuba ties.

But analysts said Rodriguez’s embrace of Castro should not necessarily be read as evidence that Venezuela is returning to the geopolitical alignment that characterised the Nicolas Maduro era.

Instead, it may underscore the delicate balancing act facing Rodriguez as she accommodates an increasingly influential Washington while attempting to reassure elements of the Chavista movement at home.

US substantially reduces Beijing’s strategic influence in Venezuela

Parsifal D’Sola, founder and executive director of the Andres Bello Foundation-China Latin America Research Centre, said the United States had “without a doubt” substantially reduced China’s strategic influence in Venezuela since Maduro’s removal in January.

The direct channel that once existed between Chinese decision-makers and the presidential palace in Caracas had effectively disappeared, D’Sola said, pointing to the absence of even mid-level Chinese official visits to Venezuela since January 3.

That retreat, however, began well before Maduro’s removal.

Chinese lending to Venezuela stopped in 2017, D’Sola said, while major Chinese oil companies largely withdrew, Huawei reduced its operations, and the seniority of Chinese officials engaging with Caracas declined over the years.

Venezuela nevertheless remains important to Beijing because of its geography and vast natural resources, he said, describing China before January as keeping “one foot inside” Venezuela while waiting to see how events developed rather than seeking to recreate the intense relationship of the Hugo Chavez era.

R. Evan Ellis, a Latin America research professor at the US Army War College Strategic Studies Institute, offered a different assessment of how much China had lost.

“China’s economic and strategic position in Venezuela has actually changed very little since January 3,” Ellis said.

China continues to buy significant quantities of Venezuelan oil, although it must now pay market prices, while its positions in oil joint ventures have not been substantially affected, he said.

Ellis estimated that of roughly US$104 billion China had lent Venezuela over the years, all but about US$10 billion had been repaid, with no indication that the remainder would not be recovered.

“What China appears to have lost is face and certain prospects for non-economic relationships in the future,” he said, arguing that concerns about the damage to Beijing’s economic interests had been overstated.

The distinction points to a potentially significant shift in the China-Venezuela relationship: Beijing may retain substantial commercial interests while losing some of the political access and strategic importance it enjoyed when Caracas was more isolated from Washington.

Before Maduro’s removal, Ellis said, the relationship was not simply one of Chinese influence but of Venezuelan “dependency”, with most Venezuelan oil ultimately flowing to China and Beijing and Moscow playing important roles in the country’s energy sector.

That dependency has diminished as Rodriguez’s accommodation with the Trump administration has reopened other options for Caracas, including access to Western oil companies and markets.

The share of Venezuelan oil going to China has consequently fallen significantly, Ellis said.

Rodriguez defends Venezuela’s right to maintain relations with China, Russia

Rodriguez has nevertheless publicly defended Venezuela’s right to maintain relations with China, Russia, Iran and Cuba while simultaneously rebuilding ties with the United States.

Beijing, for its part, has continued to describe Venezuela as an “all-weather” strategic partner and has signalled its intention to maintain economic cooperation with Caracas.

But analysts questioned how much latitude Rodriguez now has to restore the broader strategic relationship with China.

D’Sola said he saw little possibility of Caracas substantially expanding relations with Beijing given what he described as Washington’s “marked tutelage” over the Rodriguez government, particularly because China’s principal interests in Venezuela – oil and mining – are also critical priorities for the United States.

Chinese investment and participation in Venezuela were already at “historic lows”, he said, giving Beijing little incentive to risk creating another point of friction with Washington.

Ellis saw somewhat greater room for continued commercial engagement.

Rodriguez probably has latitude to continue selling oil to China and doing business with Chinese companies, he said, provided Venezuela remains open to US companies and avoids activities that Washington would view as threatening its strategic interests.

A renewed Chinese military or security presence, for example, would likely cross a very different line, he said.

Both analysts were sceptical that Rodriguez’s praise for Castro indicated a renewed foreign policy turn towards China or Cuba.

D’Sola said he viewed the rhetoric primarily through the lens of Venezuela’s domestic politics, noting dissatisfaction among ideological Chavista hardliners with Rodriguez’s accommodation with Washington, the restoration of relations with Israel, and softer rhetoric towards the West.

Ellis similarly described the Castro tribute as an attempt to signal Rodriguez’s continued fidelity to the Chavista movement while her government pursued markedly different policies.

He suggested Washington was ultimately likely to place more weight on Rodriguez’s actions than her rhetoric.

The episode nevertheless illustrates the competing pressures confronting the Venezuelan leader seven months after Maduro’s removal: maintaining the support of a movement built partly around resistance to US influence while governing under dramatically altered relations with Washington.

For China, meanwhile, the emerging arrangement could prove more complicated than a straightforward loss of Venezuela to the United States.

Beijing may retain access to Venezuelan oil, investments and commercial opportunities even as Washington constrains the political and security dimensions of a relationship that was once among China’s closest in Latin America.

The US State Department and the Chinese embassies in Washington and Caracas were contacted for comment.

item.title: [SCMP] The US’ future policymakers are questioning the standard ‘China threat’ playbook
item.description:
For years, the conventional wisdom in Washington was that America’s China policy was moving in one direction: tougher.

But walk into a classroom at Georgetown, Rice or another US university where the next generation of diplomats and foreign-policy professionals is being trained, and the picture looks less settled.

A generation that has grown up with China’s rise is increasingly sceptical of the idea that Beijing should be treated primarily as America’s great strategic rival.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the conventional wisdom in Washington was that America’s China policy was moving in one direction: tougher.

But walk into a classroom at Georgetown, Rice or another US university where the next generation of diplomats and foreign-policy professionals is being trained, and the picture looks less settled.

A generation that has grown up with China’s rise is increasingly sceptical of the idea that Beijing should be treated primarily as America’s great strategic rival.

That matters because many of these students are likely to enter the US State Department, Congress, think tanks, intelligence agencies and the national security bureaucracy.

The question is what they will take with them. Are younger Americans beginning to see China differently from the policymakers who shaped the current consensus – or are their views simply a response to the political and economic moment?

The experts observing the shift agree that something is changing, but differ over whether it will endure, whether it will survive the pressures of Washington, and how China’s own behaviour could shape what comes next.

“There is a shift in attitudes among students between the time I began teaching in 2016 and today,” said Dennis Wilder, a professor at Georgetown University’s Walsh School of Foreign Service and a former CIA China analyst. The change, he added, crossed disciplines.

Wilder said his recent students were “much more sceptical of the [Donald] Trump administration’s concentration on the ‘China threat’”.

Increasingly, he noted, they were questioning the adversarial logic that had shaped American foreign policy for generations. “Many see US foreign policy as always requiring an adversary,” Wilder said, pointing to the Soviet Union, the war on terror, and now China.

He added that his students ask “why did the long wars occur in the Middle East and what was the point”, while noting that China, despite tensions with its neighbours, had not been at war since 1979.

At Rice University, Steven Lewis, who teaches both first-year undergraduates and graduate students in global affairs, said he was seeing “a change towards a more positive view of China”.

“My students just know they are faced with traditional media that portray China almost exclusively negatively, according to political interests that don’t necessarily align with those of their generation,” Lewis said. “There’s also a broad cynicism about the motives and beliefs of older generations.”

That scepticism is showing up beyond the classroom. A Searchlight Institute survey published in March found that 62 per cent of Americans aged 18 to 34 favoured “cooperating with China and improving US-China relations”, compared with 29 per cent who preferred to “stand up to China”.

China looks different to them

Ali Wyne, a senior research and advocacy adviser for US-China relations at the International Crisis Group, sees the shift as part of a wider generational change.

“Younger Americans are more accustomed to a resurgent China,” Wyne said.

But he identified another important factor: economic anxiety.

Because younger Americans were more pessimistic about their economic prospects, Wyne said, they were more likely to regard strategic competition with China as “a distraction from – rather than a cause of – their cost-of-living concerns”.

He added that young people were “more likely to engage with digital media platforms, which offer a wider glimpse into everyday life in China than traditional ones”.

Lewis also attributed much of the shift in attitudes to a combination of social media exposure and deep scepticism of traditional coverage.

Many of his American students had never been to China, he noted, and after years of default-negative media portrayals, were increasingly turning to social media platforms for glimpses of everyday life there. “Many express surprise and great interest in travelling to and enjoying the PRC,” Lewis said, using the acronym for the People’s Republic of China.

Wilder agreed that social media was giving young Americans a wider window into everyday life in Chinese cities than previous generations had.

But he warned that this could also produce blind spots.

Limited reporting on human rights abuses, religious repression and restrictions on free speech in China creates an unduly favourable impression of the country, according to Wilder. “The views [young Americans] see on TikTok and Twitter are largely pro-China, and US propaganda is very limited,” he said.

Still, the broader effect is difficult to miss: China is increasingly something young Americans experience, rather than simply something they are told about.

Wilder said more students learned Chinese from a young age, and many had met Chinese students or Chinese Americans. “They find them polite and friendly,” he added.

He also cited “disenchantment” with US institutions, adding that young Americans “do not see the US system as that much better than China’s”.

Can the shift reach Washington?

As many of these students begin careers in government, Congress, think tanks and the national security establishment, the question is whether their views will follow them into Washington.

Wyne believes “the shift is likely to appear in the views of aspiring foreign policy professionals overall”.

But he cautioned that any lasting change would be slow. Given the foreign policy bureaucracy’s prevailing centre of gravity, “any enduring change in America’s approach to China would likely unfold slowly, across several presidential administrations”.

That institutional consensus, Wyne said, would also put pressure on Trump’s successor to “get tough”, amid an expanding range of disputes with Beijing and congressional criticism of the current administration’s China policy.

For now, there was “a marked gap between how many policymakers frame US-China relations and how a significant share of young Americans do”. That gap could gradually narrow, he said, as a new generation moved into more influential roles in Washington.

But whether this generation actually reshapes China policy may depend as much on what happens next as on what it believes now. Wyne said younger Americans’ views could harden if US-China tensions escalated – whether in the wake of a tougher White House approach or a serious security crisis between Washington and Beijing.

Wilder said his students’ views were similarly shaped by concerns about Taiwan, as well as Beijing’s increasingly assertive behaviour towards Japan and the Philippines. “In general, students have the most positive feelings about Japan, and are more eager to visit there and Taiwan than China,” he said.

At the same time, he said, “They know that China is modernising its military, but they are tired of endless conflicts.”

So could this generation of Americans ultimately weaken the bipartisan China consensus?

“Much depends on Beijing’s approach to the US and the world,” Wilder cautioned, adding that young Americans’ views of China would become more negative if Beijing adopted a more confrontational approach abroad.

At the same time, however, recent years have witnessed a noticeable decline in student interest in public service and diplomacy careers, according to Lewis.

“My feeling is that our students are exhausted by and discouraged by the political atmosphere here in the US, at least for the next few years … When there are few opportunities for advancement or internships at State, they naturally turn elsewhere, especially [to] foreign study,” he added.

Whether the more open attitudes towards China that he observed would ultimately shape policy remained unclear, he said. “I think it’s far too early to say … Few policies or debates in [Washington] DC … seem to be directed at the interests and beliefs of anyone under 30 or 40.”

item.title: [SCMP] Indonesian families of Lion Air crash victims suffer again, ‘predatory’ lawyer evades jail
item.description:
For Indonesian families who lost loved ones in the 2018 Lion Air crash that killed 189 people, the latest development in the US courts has deepened their pain that justice remains out of reach.

Keith Griffin, a Californian lawyer who worked with disgraced Hollywood celebrity lawyer Tom Girardi in compensation suits related to the crash, was sentenced by a federal court in Chicago last week to one day in prison with credit for time served, meaning he avoided any further time behind bars.
