Alberto Moel, a professor of practice in finance at the University of Hong Kong, said it would be harder for young entrepreneurs such as Wong and Mochizuki to grow businesses built from their own ideas in the city, as the government and universities dominated the local start-up ecosystem.

“We are in a stage in Hong Kong where university research projects are the ones driving the pool of innovation,” he said.

“If your idea is outside that pool, then you are basically up against the usual headwinds in venture capital that have been around for a long time, namely that it is difficult to get capital and difficult to put together a team.”

Moel added that Hong Kong’s risk-averse culture was also reflected in the investment behaviour of venture capitalists, resulting in limited capital for very early stage start-ups or those taking on more risk.

In contrast, funding for such companies in the US was much broader because the culture there was more inclined to “try things and see what happens”, while there was much more capital in the country, he said.

Hong Kong’s young entrepreneurs would stand a better chance of success if they looked at opportunities arising from university research projects, Moel said.

“If the policy is not focused on [independent ideas], you are more likely to fail, and it is going to discourage you,” he said.

“I would recommend young entrepreneurs look at the existing platforms and work within them because you will find much better chances and opportunities to monetise [ideas] into a company.”

The government should do more to publicise and create opportunities for building businesses from research projects by linking tech-minded businesspeople with innovative ideas, he added.

Derek Chim, HKSTP’s head of start-up ecosystem and development, agreed that access to early-stage capital remained important in helping innovative ventures scale up, and said the park had teamed up with the private sector to catalyse start-up growth.

“While different investors naturally have different risk appetites and return expectations, we are seeing growing interest in deep-tech and innovation-driven companies that require longer development horizons,” he said.

The Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau said the government attached importance to encouraging and cultivating a thriving I&T ecosystem for start-ups, and acknowledged that its sustainability relied heavily on private sector participation.

It said the government would launch an HK$10 billion Innovation and Technology Industry-Oriented Fund this year to channel more social capital into “emerging and future industries of strategic importance”, benefiting companies at different stages of development.

Despite the growing range of start-up funding options in Hong Kong, Mochizuki and Wong agreed the city’s cautious culture still made it hard for young entrepreneurs to strike out on their own.

“In Hong Kong, the culture drives most people down a very traditional path – primary school, high school, graduating from college, working in a full-time job – and it is very hard to pivot if you want to change your profession based on your interests,” Wong said.

“Everything is laid out for you, and this sense of security is embedded into young Hong Kong people growing up.”

item.title: [SCMP] The best guest shifts in Hong Kong and Macau amid Asia’s 50 Best Bars 2026
item.description:
All of Hong Kong and Macau are gearing up for a week of mixology festivities as Asia’s 50 Best Bars looks to descend on our sister SAR for its second year, announcing this year’s list next Tuesday.

In the days before and after, both Macau and Hong Kong will be flush with the region’s top mixologists, either here to receive awards or soak in the cities – or to take over many of our city’s world-class bars. From mega shifts like at Argo or Wing Lei Bar to unique one-off shifts featuring bars from Mongolia, Nepal, Phnom Penh and, of course, Singapore, Bangkok and Seoul, here are the guest shifts this week you don’t want to miss.

Friday, July 24
item.content:encoded:
All of Hong Kong and Macau are gearing up for a week of mixology festivities as Asia’s 50 Best Bars looks to descend on our sister SAR for its second year, announcing this year’s list next Tuesday.

In the days before and after, both Macau and Hong Kong will be flush with the region’s top mixologists, either here to receive awards or soak in the cities – or to take over many of our city’s world-class bars. From mega shifts like at Argo or Wing Lei Bar to unique one-off shifts featuring bars from Mongolia, Nepal, Phnom Penh and, of course, Singapore, Bangkok and Seoul, here are the guest shifts this week you don’t want to miss.

Friday, July 24

Green Room x Three x Co

Ranked the No 15 best bar in Asia last year, Kuala Lumpur’s Three X Co is heading all the way up to the 49th floor of Upper House to take over Green Room for one night only. Represented this time by bar manager Rachel Hor and senior bartender Chris Ang, Three X Co focuses on contemporary cocktails such as those from its IndiVDuality menu. The Quiet Quinn riffs on the martini with a Tanqueray 10 base, a chrysanthemum infusion and Yzaguirre Dry Reserva Spanish vermouth, topped with orange bitters and grapefruit zest.

Where: Green Room, 49/F, Upper House Hong Kong, Admiralty

When: 6.30pm-9.30pm

The Local Pour – Dara x Flair Up

Dara, celebrated for its modern Filipino dishes and vibrant neighbourhood atmosphere, is teaming up with “flairtender” Washam Limbu for a special collaboration titled The Local Pour.

Limbu is the co-founder of Flair Up and frequently participates in the Young Chef, Young Waiter, Young Mixologist (YYY) competitions. He took home the 2026 YYY Story Teller Global title and was named the Young Mixologist of the Year in 2025, when he was also crowned champion in the 2025 Ichiko Cocktail Competition Hong Kong event.

Guests can expect high-energy performance, artisanal craft cocktails and a commitment to locally produced ingredients.

Where: Dara, Shop 3, Soho 189, 189 Queen’s Road West, Sai Ying Pun

When: 7pm until sold out

Saturday, July 25

The Road Less Travelled – Wing Lei Bar x Nomad Lab x Barc x Kiki Lounge

Even though Wynn Palace and Wing Lei Bar start their festivities earlier in the week, one of our favourites on the itinerary has to be this one – gathering bars from Mongolia, Nepal and the Isle of Man.

All three bars are represented by their co-founders. Nomad Lab’s Awaraa Awarzed is coming in from Ulaanbaatar as the self-proclaimed “first cocktail lab in Mongolia”, while Barc’s Abhishek Tuladhar is arriving from Nepal. The latter won the 2025 Michter’s Art of Hospitality award from Asia’s 50 Best Bars last year. Rounding out the takeover is Drew Fleming from Kiki Lounge in Isle of Man, the winner of the Spirits Business Awards Bar of the Year in 2024.

Where: Wing Lei Bar, West Esplanade, G/F, Wynn Palace, Avenida da Nave Desportiva, Coloane-Taipa, Macau

When: 5pm-8pm

25:00 x Thaipioka

Bartenders Hope Narawut and Supawit Thinpitayanurat, also known as Miguel, are arriving from Bangkok to take over 25:00 Twenty Fifth Hour, representing Thaipioka, which focuses on equal parts cocktails and music. Back home, Thaipioka offers fruit-centric cocktails like the Kyoho Balsamic Negroni, adding vinegar, shiso bitters and kyoho grapes to the traditional profile, or the Orange Thai Milk Tea, which soups up the citrus drink with rum, coffee, caramel and fresh orange.

Where: 13/F, Luk Yu Building, 24-26 Stanley Street, Central

When: 9pm-1am

Sunday, July 26 (early)

C108 celebrates its second anniversary with Sora Bar

C108’s second anniversary on Old Bailey Street is coming hot on the heels of its updated menu earlier in the month. Taking centre stage for Sunday’s anniversary party is a guest shift by Jonas Vittur, director of bars at Rosewood Phnom Penh’s rooftop bar, Sora, and its head bartender Phirun Lek.

Last year, the sky bar was ranked No 65 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars list and won the Ketel One Sustainable Bar Award. C108 is also working with Good Stuff to have four DJs play music all night long.

Where: 15 Old Bailey Street, Central

When: 7pm-10pm

The Old Man x AABBCC

Start your Sunday night at the top of the alphabet as AABBCC arrives from New Delhi to take over The Old Man on Aberdeen Street. The “retro-futuristic archive” bar sends co-founders Jairaj Singh Solanki and Aditi Singh, who are bringing cocktails such as a twist on the Godfather with dandelion, a Bellini using cacao butter, a caprese salad rendered in alcohol form, and a drink called the Mushroomisu.

Solanki’s former concept, Lair, also based in New Delhi, was ranked the 8th best bar in Asia last year.

Where: The Old Man, LG/F, 37 Aberdeen Street, Soho, Central

When: 6pm until sold out

Sunday, July 26 (late)

Dio x Bar Woody

There’s so much happening on Sunday and Monday that it’ll be easy to catch an early shift and a late shift on either night. Bar Woody has made a name for itself in Chengdu by anchoring its concept on the complexity of wood and herbs, with its signature cocktails such as the Cedar, the Benzoin and Sandalwood. Now there is a chance to try those earthy sips at Dio on Sunday, when Bar Woody’s Keith Lo and Austin Guo serve their wood-forward creations supported by Mizunara, featuring The Hachi Shochu and Wakshio 424 Gin.

Where: Dio, 8 Aberdeen Street, Central

When: 8pm till sold out

The Diplomat x Offtrack

Singapore’s Offtrack, last year’s No 23 best bar in Asia and known for its high-energy music and equally excellent focus on cocktails and food, arrives in Hong Kong to take over The Diplomat for one night only. At home, Offtrack’s co-founder Aslam Zainal and his team serve straightforward, inventive drinks like the Cora Middleton, combining raspberry, white almond, rum, lime, hibiscus and egg white. It makes perfect sense for Zainal to stage a guest stint at one of Hong Kong’s best bars for martinis, Irish coffees and burgers.

Where: The Diplomat, LG/F, H Code, 45 Pottinger Street, Central

When: 8pm till sold out

Monday, July 27 (early)

Quinary x Native x Milli x Chanel Adams

Hong Kong’s first home of molecular mixology, Quinary, is starting the party early on Monday with a triple-header featuring Singapore’s Native and Milli, alongside a special guest. Native is represented by co-founder Vijay Mudaliar and mixologist Amillie Chan, who are showcasing their unique approach to obscure and foraged ingredients, while Danny is bringing a menu of playful cocktails from Milli, a rooftop bar atop Singapore’s National Gallery. Rounding out the line-up is Chanel Adams, who most recently worked at the Mandarin Oriental Bangkok, and at Please Don’t Tell in Hong Kong before that.

Where: Quinary, 56-58 Hollywood Road, Central

When: 7pm-10pm

Tell Camellia x Gong-Gan

Gong-Gan, famed for its zero-waste philosophy, arrives from Seoul to take over tea-inspired cocktail joint Tell Camellia. Ranked No 74 on Asia’s 50 Best Bars this year, Gong-Gan is represented by co-founders Evan Noh and Willy Park. Their signature cocktails include the Si-Jang, featuring the premium Korean spirit Igangju alongside bourbon, lemon juice, roasted rice and banana beer.

Where: Tell Camellia, 45 Pottinger Street, Central

When: 8pm onwards

Monday, July 27 (late)

Kinsman x Bar Truce x Bar Notes

Wong Kar-wai-inspired Kinsman brings together Indonesia and South Korea in a double header featuring Bar Truce from Jakarta and Seoul’s Bar Notes. The former is grounded in Japanese mixology tradition with a twist, serving cocktails like the Ogura Dream as a clarified twist on the Alexander. Meanwhile, Bar Notes puts its focus on storytelling – its owner Ricky is also a freelance writer – serving concoctions like the Ssanghwa, inspired by the portmanteau “halmae-nial” – a combination of “halmae”, meaning granny, and “millennial”, referring to millennials enjoying foods normally associated with the elderly – containing rum, cream, egg and the eponymous bitter tea.

Where: Kinsman, 65 Peel Street, Central

When: Bar Truce: 8pm-10pm; Bar Notes: 10pm-12am

Socio x Modernhaus

One of Jakarta’s best – Modernhaus – arrives to take over Socio, Hong Kong’s main venue focused on upcycling community ingredients. Modernhaus was named the No 12 best bar in Asia last year and focuses on conceptual, minimalist cocktails. At home, they serve drinks like the Turmeric, which involves a turmeric gin, coconut chai milk, cream, salted tamarind and lemonade soda, and the Apple, which spotlights smoked manalagi apple brandy, koji, umami bitters and apple miso.

Where: Socio, 17 Staunton Street, Central

When: 8.30pm onwards

Tuesday, July 28

Campari x Wynn Palace Asia’s 50 Best Bars after-party

Tuesday is the day we’ve all been waiting for. After our region’s most excellent bars get their flowers, Wynn Palace is joining hands with Campari to host an all-out after-party in Macau. Responsible for the vibes are some of the region’s best. Look out for veterans of the list to host this get-together: Singapore’s Cat Bite Club (No 86, 2026); The Cocktail Club (No 12, 2024) and Carrots (No 34, 2025), both from Jakarta; Opium from Bangkok (No 43, 2025); and Bengaluru’s Soka (No 28, 2025).

Where: Palace Reserve Club, Wynn Palace, Avenida Da Nave Desportiva, Cotai, Macau

When: Post-ceremony till late

Wednesday, July 29

Argo Mega Friends Takeover

Argo plays host to an exceptional night of mixology as Argo Mega Friends returns with three new regional names. This collaboration brings together teams from three of Asia’s top-ranked bars. Bangkok’s Bar Us is represented by co-founders Aum Veerach and Taln Sudarat; Dry Wave Cocktail Studio sends founder Supawit “Palm” Muttarattana and bartender Ammie Suparada; and Taipei duo William Wu and Cloris Huang of The Public House round out the line-up.

Expect a vibrant atmosphere where these master mixologists serve up inventive, culinary-forward cocktails, such as Bar Us’ famous Jackfruit & Sticky Rice.

Where: Argo, Four Seasons Hotel Hong Kong, 8 Finance Street, Central

When: 6pm-9.30pm

Terrible Baby x Moebius Milano

Moebius Milano, ranked No 7 on the World’s 50 Best Bars last year, is housed inside a Milanese textile warehouse where Michelin-starred gastronomy, live jazz and avant-garde mixology collide.

For one night only, Moebius’ owner Lorenzo Querci and bartender Andrea Giraldo are taking over Eaton HK’s Terrible Baby. On the menu are cocktails like the Cocco & Salvia Negroni, which contains Bulldog gin and Del Professore Vermouth Rosso, as well as the aperitif Raspberry Lavorato Secco, which contains Campari and Rabarbaro Zucca.

Where: Terrible Baby, 4/F, Eaton Hong Kong, 380 Nathan Road, Kowloon

When: 7pm till sold out

item.title: [SCMP] Asia’s AI boom has a dirty secret: the coal that powers it
item.description:
Asia sits atop vast amounts of coal, nearly three-fifths of the world’s known reserves by some estimates.

Cheaper and more reliable than imported oil and gas, and far less vulnerable to disruptions caused by foreign wars, coal is also dirty, polluting – and the region’s No 1 “stopgap source” to power the AI infrastructure roll-out.

“AI demand is materialising faster than clean energy generation can be commissioned,” said Alexander Kheder, a market research analyst at BMI who tracks global AI infrastructure spending and data centre expansion.
item.content:encoded:
Asia sits atop vast amounts of coal, nearly three-fifths of the world’s known reserves by some estimates.

Cheaper and more reliable than imported oil and gas, and far less vulnerable to disruptions caused by foreign wars, coal is also dirty, polluting – and the region’s No 1 “stopgap source” to power the AI infrastructure roll-out.

“AI demand is materialising faster than clean energy generation can be commissioned,” said Alexander Kheder, a market research analyst at BMI who tracks global AI infrastructure spending and data centre expansion.

Solar and wind, for all their recent progress, still could not deliver the relentless, round-the-clock baseload that the data centres powering artificial intelligence demanded, he said.

In Malaysia’s pioneering smart city of Cyberjaya, dozens of data centres are already in operation, with more planned for the future.

“The impact is going to be very, very visible,” said Adit Rahim, 49, a local resident and communications executive who worries about the strain all this development is placing on utilities.

“What no one is really addressing is whether resources like water and electricity are keeping pace,” he said.

Data centres never sleep. Their servers hum around the clock, training and running the artificial-intelligence models that are transforming the global economy – and their appetite for electricity is voracious.

That hunger has been a boon for companies such as Johnson Controls, whose Asia-Pacific vice-president for project delivery and data centre solutions, Ali Badreddine, has been fielding a flood of urgent requests from his base in Singapore.

“Customers are telling us they need everything faster,” he told This Week in Asia.

His company’s backup power systems – essential to prevent catastrophic data loss at AI data centres, where an unexpected power outage can destroy months of model-training progress – used to ship within months, but now come with waiting times of two years or more.

“Even if you are willing to pay, there simply isn’t enough manufacturing capacity available,” Badreddine said.

Southeast Asia’s AI workload demand will, in all likelihood, continue outpacing renewable energy supply for some years yet, according to Kheder, which is why coal has become the No 1 “stopgap source to bridge this gap”.

War woes

Asia imports the bulk of its oil and gas, much of it through a chokepoint strait that has been largely sealed off amid the US-Israel war on Iran.

Oil prices have whipsawed this year from lows of around US$60 a barrel in January to nearly US$120 at the height of the conflict in April. A ceasefire agreed in June helped stabilise the market for a few weeks until US President Donald Trump declared the truce “over” on July 8 following a fresh round of tit-for-tat attacks, sending prices rising again.

Soaring natural gas prices, meanwhile, have driven electricity tariffs to all-time highs of nearly 35 cents (27 US cents) per kilowatt-hour in Singapore, while sky-high prices in the Philippines have pushed households towards solar and Vietnam has rolled out peak-hour energy pricing to manage the strain.

Malaysia’s rates have held steady so far, largely thanks to government subsidies, but those living in the shadow of Cyberjaya’s server farms are nervous about the future.

“At the end of the day, there will be a choke point in electricity supply,” Rahim said of Malaysia’s proliferating data centres. “And there will definitely be an impact on water supply.”

Big data centres had two key questions when it came to power, said Ashwin Balasubramanian, a partner at management consultancy firm McKinsey: how soon can we get it and how reliable is the supply?

“That is much more important than just green power. Less than 40 per cent have actually made those [green] commitments,” he said, predicting a short‑term increase in fossil fuel emissions.

Mayank Maheshwari, an energy analyst for India and Southeast Asia at multinational investment bank Morgan Stanley, said the priority for policymakers across the region would be securing steady energy supplies.

“Energy consumers worldwide are price-sensitive and discerning. They always gravitate towards the most affordable and reliable forms of energy,” he said – adding that Asia, with its enormous coal reserves, had an easily accessible option close at hand.

Morgan Stanley projects that the region’s coal consumption will climb by 130 million tonnes between now and 2030, which equates to an 8-10 per cent increase.

It also forecasts Asia’s annual energy spending will double over that same period, with more than US$5 trillion being spent on clean and fossil fuel investments, making it the region’s second-largest funding destination after AI itself.

Separately, Asian buyers are expected to snap up a decent chunk of the more than 100 million tonnes of natural gas that analysts predict the US will release onto global markets this year alone.

“Asia is preparing to absorb the supply, as it is expected to be cheaper than the imported natural gas prices Asian consumers have paid in recent years,” Maheshwari said.

In a coal hole?

Fossil fuels offer a quick fix to power the AI boom when demand outstrips supply, but not everyone is convinced that a full-blown coal revival is inevitable.

“A major new coal wave would be a blunt and expensive answer to a more complex problem,” said Aditya Lolla, interim managing director at energy think tank Ember.

He argues that the sums simply do not add up, as new coal plants take years to build and would not come online until long after the current AI-driven demand spike has passed.

In the longer term, Lolla said more coal and gas would only lead to increased air pollution while saddling the region with power plants ill-suited to grids increasingly built for renewables.

Renewables are certainly more cost efficient, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency, which found that more than 90 per cent of all newly commissioned utility-scale renewable projects globally last year delivered power cheaper than the lowest-cost new fossil-fuel alternative.

In Indonesia, Thailand and the Philippines alone, renewable generation has already displaced an estimated US$5.7 billion of coal and gas imports that would otherwise have been bought, the agency found in a recent report.

“In many markets, it is already the most cost-competitive source of new electricity generation and is increasingly the preferred procurement option for major technology and industrial companies,” said Joe Phelan, executive director for the Asia-Pacific at the World Business Council for Sustainable Development.

Yet analysts say there exists a divergence between the region’s most advanced, supply-constrained economies such as Singapore – which is increasingly positioning itself as a regional hub for clean-power imports – and less constrained markets that tend to lean more heavily on coal and gas because they are so readily available.

Michael Goh, vice-president and general manager for the Asia-Pacific and other regions at Iron Mountain Data Centres – one of the world’s largest operators, with a facility in Singapore – said higher electricity costs had indeed affected the industry, though he credited the city state’s government with working to contain them.

He said his own group had focused on boosting energy efficiency and tapping resources otherwise considered waste output, such as heat recovered through the regasification of liquefied natural gas, rather than drawing more heavily on water and power.

Singapore had also met additional demand through partnerships with Indonesia and Australia to import renewable energy, he added.

Cross-border connectivity may be the key to solving the region’s energy challenge, according to specialist project management consultancy TBH.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ long-stalled integrated power grid plan, first sketched out decades ago, could offer such a path to sharing surplus clean power across borders rather than each country going it alone.

“Southeast Asia’s energy transition is entering a new phase,” said Ali Nami, a director and energy lead at TBH.

“The ability to coordinate these investments and translate them into reliable outcomes will play a major role in shaping the region’s long-term energy future.”

Additional reporting by Ushar Daniele

item.title: [SCMP] US accuses 9 Latin American countries of helping China avoid Trump’s tariffs
item.description:
Three Latin American governments that moved against Chinese commercial interests over the past year were named in a White House report on Thursday, which accused Chinese exporters of routing goods through third countries to evade US tariffs.

Mexico, Panama and Colombia now join Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic among more than 40 countries the report says carry elevated risk of illegal transshipment, the practice of moving goods through an intermediate country so they enter the US under a different origin and a lower duty.

Previously, the three Latin American countries appeared to support the Trump administration during the relentless US-China trade war.
item.content:encoded:
Three Latin American governments that moved against Chinese commercial interests over the past year were named in a White House report on Thursday, which accused Chinese exporters of routing goods through third countries to evade US tariffs.

Mexico, Panama and Colombia now join Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic among more than 40 countries the report says carry elevated risk of illegal transshipment, the practice of moving goods through an intermediate country so they enter the US under a different origin and a lower duty.

Previously, the three Latin American countries appeared to support the Trump administration during the relentless US-China trade war.

Mexico imposed tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Chinese cars in December, ahead of the review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Panama’s Supreme Court annulled the concessions held by Hong Kong’s CK Hutchison at both ends of the canal in January, drawing an arbitration claim of more than US$2 billion and a freeze on Chinese state investment.

Colombia applied a 35 per cent duty in March on steel and metalworking imports from countries without a trade agreement, the ceiling permitted under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and aimed principally at its largest supplier, China.

Countries identified as engaging in illegal transshipment face concrete costs at the US border.

Washington has included anti-transshipment clauses in its recent trade agreements. Executive Order 14326, signed in July, 2025, applies a 40 per cent penalty duty to goods that US Customs and Border Protection determines were diverted to evade tariffs, in place of the reciprocal rate that would otherwise apply.

The order also requires the US Commerce and Homeland Security departments to publish a list every six months that names countries, entities and facilities involved in transshipment.

Chinese exporters accused of moving shipments through third countries

The Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy, the White House unit run by Peter Navarro, produced the 25-page document titled “The Great Transshipment Scam”. It argues that Chinese exporters responded to the 2018 tariffs by shifting shipments through third countries, where light assembly, relabelling, or changes in paperwork could disguise the goods’ origin.

That the rerouting is happening is not what specialists on regional trade dispute. Diego Marroquin Bitar, a fellow with the Americas Programme at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and on the USMCA initiative, said the practice does real damage.

“Transshipment is a genuine threat to US industrial capacity, to American jobs, and to revenue collection. That case does not need to be argued,” he said.

But his disagreement begins at the next step, where the report treats the size of a country’s trade as grounds for calling it an accomplice.

It places Mexico and Canada in a tier of large trading partners, where it says the risk is embedded within broad, legitimate trade flows, a classification Marroquin Bitar said describes scale rather than conduct.

What separates the two countries from others on the list, he said, is the rule book they already trade under.

“Mexico and Canada operate inside a framework with the United States that carries strict regional content thresholds, labour provisions, and wage requirements,” he said, adding that Central American partners work under comparable terms in their own agreements.

No comparable set of content and labour rules covers the South American countries on the list, whose trade has tilted the other way over the same period.

China took 28.7 per cent of Brazil’s exports last year, worth US$100 billion and more than two and a half-times what Brazil shipped to the US, according to trade ministry figures. It is also the leading buyer from Chile and Peru.

Chinese capital has also moved with the trade, from the US$1.3 billion of Chinese investment in the deep water port at Chancay in Peru to the plants Chinese carmakers are building across the region.

The report was released six weeks before US President Donald Trump is due to host Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington next month.

The USMCA review is under way after Washington declined an automatic extension, and Brazil filed for consultations at the WTO last month over US tariffs that its trade ministry says amount to 23.1 per cent of Brazilian exports to the American market.

The report sorts the countries it names into three tiers of risk, and the region is spread across all of them.

Mexico ranks at the top, alongside Canada, the European Union, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. Brazil sits in the middle tier with countries like Turkey and Vietnam. The other seven fall into a lower tier of what the report calls “opportunistic targets” defined by free zones, port access, bonded warehousing, or limited customs enforcement capacity.

Only three of the nine are tied to particular goods anywhere in the document. Mexico’s Guanajuato-Queretaro corridor is matched to electric motors, generators, transformers and static converters under tariff headings HS 8501 to 8504, set against Detroit, Grand Rapids and Indianapolis.

Costa Rica’s Limon-Moin corridor appears under heading HS 850300, covering electric motor and generator parts, opposite Dallas-Fort Worth and Oklahoma City.

And the Dominican Republic’s Caucedo-Haina corridor covers insulated conductors and cable assemblies, weighed against Portland, Seattle and Spokane.

Report claims US loses whenever the foreign hub wins

The report calls these pairings the ugly sisters of a zero-sum trading system and argues that the US loses whenever the foreign hub wins. Marroquin Bitar said the arithmetic rests on an assumption that does not hold.

“That only holds if you assume every motor built in Queretaro would otherwise have been built in Michigan, and it would not have been. The realistic alternative is Asia, not Detroit,” he said.

Roughly three-quarters of every dollar of Mexican manufactured exports to the US originates in North America, he said, describing US labour and US value returning home inside goods that are counted as imports.

“The job in Michigan depends on the one in Queretaro,” he said.

The report applies the same reasoning to Central America, counting permissive free-zone rules among the weak-link advantages that draw Chinese rerouting.

In Costa Rica, those zones are the core of its export economy. The regime accounts for about 15 per cent of national output, three-quarters of foreign direct investment and more than 265,000 jobs, according to 2024 figures from the state trade agency Procomer.

San Jose concluded talks in May to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, part of a push to widen its export markets.

Panama is named without any product line, grouped with Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic in a category of maritime gateways alongside Malaysia, Oman and the United Arab Emirates.

The report said only that Panama and Costa Rica offer maritime access, free-zone logistics, and re-export platforms, and did not identify any Panamanian facilities, products, or volumes.

The five South American countries named are placed in a category the report calls Latin American Corridors, its function given as Pacific and Atlantic re-routing, bonded warehousing and regional assembly.

Brazil singled out in document as US ramps up pressure

The largest economy in the group, Brazil, appears four times in the document, three of which are in lists that name it and nothing more. The single descriptive sentence says it serves, with Turkey, as a larger regional platform capable of supporting re-routing or transformation claims in selected product categories. Which categories, the report does not say.

Mexico is the only economy in the region carrying a dollar figure. The report ranks it among three leading hubs worldwide, with India and Vietnam, through which the US Commerce Department traced about US$67 billion in Chinese goods into the American market last year.

The report qualifies its own figures in several places in the text. It said the shift in US import sourcing after 2018 does not prove that all displaced Chinese trade was illegally diverted.

It also puts the annual value of the trade anywhere between US$40 billion and US$303 billion across five analyses it says are not directly comparable; and presents its estimates of 450,000 American jobs and up to US$150 billion in output as model-based illustrations.

Navarro said on a call with reporters that anti-transshipment terms would form part of the administration’s trade negotiations and that countries found to be rerouting goods would face penalties.

Those qualifications point to where Marroquin Bitar said the document is on firmer ground: the difficulty of knowing what is actually inside a shipment.

“What needs closing is the visibility gap,” he said, describing the distance between what customs authorities can assume about a good crossing a border and what they can verify.

“Closing that gap is a technical problem with a technical answer, and the partners best positioned to solve it alongside Washington are the ones already building things with US firms.”

item.title: [SCMP] ‘India’s biggest corporate decision’: Tata Group chair’s exit raises hard succession questions
item.description:
The sudden announcement that N Chandrasekaran will not seek another term as chairman of Tata Sons has raised a pressing question for India: who can steer one of the country’s most powerful and influential conglomerates through its next phase?

The answer matters well beyond the group’s boardroom. Tata’s businesses span salt, software, cars, steel, airlines and hi-tech manufacturing, with annual revenue equivalent to about 5 per cent of India’s gross domestic product and more than a million employees, giving the trust-controlled empire an outsize role in the country’s economic ambitions.

Chandrasekaran, 63, said on Wednesday that he had informed the board he would not seek reappointment once his tenure ended in February next year, after directors failed to reach a decision on his future role.
item.content:encoded:
The sudden announcement that N Chandrasekaran will not seek another term as chairman of Tata Sons has raised a pressing question for India: who can steer one of the country’s most powerful and influential conglomerates through its next phase?

The answer matters well beyond the group’s boardroom. Tata’s businesses span salt, software, cars, steel, airlines and hi-tech manufacturing, with annual revenue equivalent to about 5 per cent of India’s gross domestic product and more than a million employees, giving the trust-controlled empire an outsize role in the country’s economic ambitions.

Chandrasekaran, 63, said on Wednesday that he had informed the board he would not seek reappointment once his tenure ended in February next year, after directors failed to reach a decision on his future role.

His announcement sparked a rout in the shares of Tata Group companies on Wednesday, eroding billions of dollars in a single day amid investor concerns about a leadership crisis at the iconic group.

Tata Sons is the principal holding company of the Tata Group, whose foundations date back to before India’s independence from British rule and whose controlling shareholder, Tata Trusts, gives the charitable trusts unusual influence over one of Asia’s most prominent business empires.

The Tata Group comprises 31 key mainstream companies operating across 10 distinct business verticals, though the broader ecosystem includes over 100 operating and subsidiary companies globally.

Chandrasekaran’s move reportedly followed disagreement among board members over issues including losses at some group companies.

The dispute leaves Noel Tata, head of the influential Tata Trusts and half-brother of late chairman Ratan Tata, to manage the transition after he pushed back against a Chandrasekaran-led spending spree amounting to US$120 billion over the next five years.

Suresh Prabhu, a former Indian minister and a chartered accountant, articulated investor concerns in a social media post, pointing out that the group had become “India’s flag bearer with substantial global presence”.

“I sincerely hope (that) the resignation of N Chandrasekaran, a seasoned professional, will lead to a smooth leadership transition,” he said.

Chandrasekaran, who was chief executive of the group’s flagship information technology company Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) before being appointed as chairman of Tata Sons in 2017, currently oversees the management of dozens of major companies, including Tata Motors and Air India.

Under Chandrasekaran, the Tata Group saw its revenue nearly triple, while its net profit and listed market capitalisation grew roughly fivefold and threefold, respectively, over his tenure from 2017 to 2026.

The group also pushed into hi-tech manufacturing such as semiconductors, digital enterprises including online grocery app BigBasket, and aerospace and defence equipment manufacturing, embellishing his reputation that he once described in an interview as a “man in a hurry”.

Chandrasekaran’s exit could mean that many of the conglomerate’s current and planned projects could slow down, according to a Bloomberg report.

Lloyd Mathias, a leading New Delhi-based angel investor and business strategist, said Chandrasekaran’s resignation was not “all that surprising” given reports about concerns over lack of profitability in some of the group’s ventures.

Tata Group “virtually has its leg in every aspect of the Indian economy” and the “immediate priority will be to find a successor,” Mathias said, but noted that finding a new chairman before February could prove difficult.

“It is easily India’s biggest corporate decision to be made in the next six months. There are challenges ahead.”

The development comes as TCS, the group’s largest profit generator, is under pressure from a slowdown in global technology spending. The company is also grappling with threats from generative AI software and its shares have fallen more than 20 per cent in the past year.

The Tata Group’s efforts to revive the loss-making Air India have suffered setbacks following the crash of a London-bound flight last June and reports last week that a pilot of a flight to Phuket, which experienced severe turbulence, had smoked marijuana.

Vijay Govindarajan, distinguished professor of management at the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth, said on social media that Chandrasekaran’s successor “will inherit a paradox”.

TCS, the cash machine that funds the empire, including Air India’s planned turnaround, is “staring down the most disruptive force it has ever faced” because its legacy IT services model catering to Fortune 500 companies is being threatened by generative AI, according to Govindarajan.

Vaibhav Kakkar, senior partner at law firm Saraf and Partners, said the end of Chandrasekaran’s tenure “should primarily be understood as a leadership transition at Tata Sons, rather than a sign of potential operational instability across the Tata Group’s diversified businesses”.

“He has been instrumental in shaping the group’s growth trajectory over the past decade, but one must bear in mind that institutions such as Tata are built over decades on governance, professional management and continuity – and those foundations do not change overnight,” Kakkar said.

The institutional depth of the group companies was often underappreciated during times of transition, he added.

Looming uncertainty

Amritraj Kaushal, a lawyer at the Supreme Court of India, said the priority “should be a swift and transparent succession process”.

An extended period of uncertainty could slow down distribution of finance, group initiatives and coordination, which are particularly important for businesses like Air India that are still in transformation, according to Kaushal.

He pointed out that Chandrasekaran was closely involved in Air India’s integration and turnaround after Tata reacquired it in 2022 from the government, 69 years since it was brought under state control from its founder, the Tata Group.

“So continuity of vision matters here more than most group companies,” Kaushal said.

The implications for Air India’s business go beyond India because Singapore Airlines has faced direct shareholder questions regarding its 25.1 per cent equity stake in the carrier.

Mayur Patel, regional commercial and industry affairs leader for Asia-Pacific, Middle East and Africa at OAG, a travel data and aviation analytics firm, said Singapore Airlines had consistently viewed its investment as a long-term strategic play to participate in India’s significant domestic market and international growth.

“While Air India is undergoing a significant transformation and faces near-term challenges, Singapore Airlines has continued to emphasise the strategic rationale behind the investment,” he said.

Chandrasekaran’s departure was unlikely to make much of a difference to Air India, Patel noted.

Earlier this month, Air India appointed aviation veteran Tewolde Gebremariam, former group head of Ethiopian Airlines, as its new CEO and managing director. He succeeds Campbell Wilson, who previously led Scoot, Singapore Airlines’ low-cost subsidiary.

item.title: [SCMP] China’s STEM students turn to Singapore as Western study options shrink
item.description:
For generations, China’s brightest science and technology minds followed a well-worn path: board a Westbound flight and claim a seat at a globally renowned university.

That once-reliable trajectory has fractured. Escalating US-China tech competition and tightening immigration policies across the “big four” study destinations – Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States – have redrawn the map for global student mobility.

As Western nations impose ever-stricter access controls and security protocols on their laboratories, a less conspicuous but significant shift is gathering momentum. A growing number of China’s top STEM talent – scientists, technologists, engineers and mathematicians – are quietly redirecting their ambitions southwards, with Singapore emerging as one of the primary destinations.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, China’s brightest science and technology minds followed a well-worn path: board a Westbound flight and claim a seat at a globally renowned university.

That once-reliable trajectory has fractured. Escalating US-China tech competition and tightening immigration policies across the “big four” study destinations – Australia, Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States – have redrawn the map for global student mobility.

As Western nations impose ever-stricter access controls and security protocols on their laboratories, a less conspicuous but significant shift is gathering momentum. A growing number of China’s top STEM talent – scientists, technologists, engineers and mathematicians – are quietly redirecting their ambitions southwards, with Singapore emerging as one of the primary destinations.

Singapore’s China scholarship pipeline

Among the pull factors is a decades-long, state-backed scholarship programme aimed at channelling top Chinese science students to Singapore: the Senior Middle 2 (SM2) scholarship programme.

Launched in 1997 as a joint initiative between the Singaporean and Chinese ministries of education, the programme recruits high-achieving second-year high school (Grade 11) youngsters from China to study at the city state’s top institutions, including the National University of Singapore and Nanyang Technological University (NTU).

The Singapore government offers fully funded undergraduate education in science and engineering, along with living allowances. In return, recipients commit to working in Singapore for six years after graduation.

Singapore previously operated the Senior Middle 1 or SM1 programme, recruiting about 300 top-performing mainland Chinese secondary students annually to attend high school and junior college in the city state.

Chinese students and their families are asking where an overseas education can still deliver academic prestige, employability and long-term security

Liu Jiaqi, Singapore Management University

In 2024, that programme was succeeded by a scholarship managed by Business China – a non-profit organisation launched by Singapore’s founding prime minister Lee Kuan Yew in 2007.

These long-running schemes have found renewed relevance as Chinese families pivot towards study destinations perceived as safer and more politically stable.

In many cases, plans for Western higher education have been thrown into disarray by visa crackdowns, rising anti-China sentiment, restrictive immigration policies and the looming threat of policy reversals, prompting families to look elsewhere.

Education experts say Singapore’s scholarship schemes are drawing academically gifted Chinese students into the city state’s educational system during their formative years, absorbing them into its universities and eventually, its highly skilled workforce.

American education dream crumbles

The catalyst for a global shift in mobility remains the US, where the American education dream for Chinese families has faced political headwinds. A significant deterrent is Proclamation 10043, signed in 2020 during Donald Trump’s first term and strictly maintained across successive administrations.

It restricts Chinese graduate students and scholars in STEM fields with ties to certain institutions in the country, on the grounds of national security.

“With that change, Singapore has become more attractive to mainland [Chinese] students who previously might have considered going to the West,” said Yang Peidong, an NTU associate professor whose research focuses on educational mobility.

Lin Xiongji, an SM2 scholarship holder who arrived in Singapore in the mid-2010s, views the scheme as increasingly appealing.

“This can safely shield Chinese students from the growing uncertainty of studying in Western countries and offer a pathway to integrate into Singaporean society,” he said.

The restrictions extend beyond American shores.

Canada’s immigration ministry introduced a hard cap on international study permits, slashing targets significantly year on year through 2026, while postgraduate STEM students from China have faced prolonged, multi-month visa background checks for Australia in recent years.

At the same time, the UK government has moved to curb net migration. Policy changes include a 2024 restriction preventing most international students from bringing their family members, and a decision to shorten the post-study Graduate Route work visa from two years to 18 months, effective January 2027.

Singapore benefits from the uncertainty surrounding studying in the West because it offers a middle position: it is not China, but it is also not perceived as hostile to China

Denis Simon, Quincy Institute

According to Liu Jiaqi, assistant professor of sociology at Singapore Management University (SMU), Chinese students now see overseas study largely through the lens of risk management, with Singapore emerging as a “lower-risk and high-value alternative”.

“Chinese students and their families are asking where an overseas education can still deliver academic prestige, employability and long-term security without the political uncertainty now attached to some Western destinations.”

Nearly 266,000 Chinese students studied in the US in the 2024-25 academic year, a 4 per cent decrease from the previous year, according to the Institute of International Education’s latest annual survey of higher education institutions, published last November and sponsored by the US State Department.

That figure represents a 28 per cent decline from the peak of 369,548 in the 2018-19 academic year.

Meanwhile, Singapore ranks second among 28 popular study-abroad destinations for Chinese students, according to a 2025 report jointly published by China’s Ministry of Education and the Beijing-based think tank Centre for China and Globalisation.

Singapore as a STEM talent hub

After being suspended for four years during the Covid-19 pandemic, Singapore’s scholarship programmes resumed in 2024 on a smaller scale. Interest among Chinese families has remained strong since the relaunch.

Numerous prospective applicants and their families continue to exchange application tips and seek information about the scholarship on the Chinese social media platform RedNote.

Denis Simon, a senior fellow at the Quincy Institute in Washington, said Singapore’s scholarship framework functioned as an early-stage talent pipeline.

“It brings academically strong Chinese students into Singapore’s system before university, socialises them into Singaporean institutions, and potentially directs them into Singapore’s universities, research ecosystem and technology labour market,” he said.

Lin, who is nearing the end of his six-year work bond and recently attained Singapore permanent residency, said he would stay on.

“These programmes are great and predictable pathways for kids from ordinary families to rewrite their destinies, and are highly suited to those who do not want to spend a fortune studying abroad,” he said.

Simon said Singapore was positioning itself as a “talent arbitrage hub” in the era of US-China rivalry.

“As Washington narrows access for some Chinese STEM talent, Singapore can absorb a portion of that mobility and convert it into long-term human-capital advantage.”

But he cautioned against viewing the scholarships purely through the lens of geopolitical rivalry, noting they were fundamentally about sustaining Singapore’s workforce, innovation base, and bridge role linking China, Southeast Asia and the global economy.

“Singapore benefits from the uncertainty surrounding studying in the West because it offers a middle position: it is not China, but it is also not perceived as hostile to China,” Simon said.

A tougher job market at home

Another strong pull factor for Singapore’s scholarship programmes is China’s increasingly cutthroat job market.

Yang of NTU said applicants’ motivations had remained largely unchanged over the years, but the circumstances surrounding their decisions had shifted.

Singapore, he said, still offered “a much more advanced and globally connected higher education system and labour market” than many Chinese students perceived at home, where slowing economic growth, fierce competition and worsening employment anxieties had made the city state’s schemes increasingly appealing.

Yang has also observed that many students remain in Singapore after completing their six-year employment bond, with some eventually becoming permanent residents or citizens.

Others return to China, where their international study experience and bilingual abilities give them a clear advantage in the job market.

Even so, many do not settle permanently in mainland China, instead becoming what Yang describes as “very mobile, highly skilled professionals whose careers take them to different places”.

Liu of SMU cautioned that the meaning of overseas study was shifting in China, where its value was now “far more conditional”.

In recent years, studying abroad has become a politically double-edged sword, with China’s Ministry of State Security warning the public that students were prime targets for foreign intelligence recruitment. A prominent Chinese business leader sparked controversy last year by saying her company would not cultivate foreign-educated talent over spying fears.

Government departments, state-owned enterprises and politically sensitive industries are increasingly wary of foreign-educated candidates, fearing ideological divergence or security liabilities.

Liu said students and families were navigating “a fractured global education market, a difficult Chinese job market, and a political climate in which mobility itself has become more sensitive”.

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore’s provision shops struggle to keep shutters open in HDB heartlands
item.description:
Surrounded by a clutter of carton boxes, bottles of dishwashing liquid and rows of dry snacks, Ramasamy Vellasamy holds court behind a cashier. For nine hours a day since 1986, he has been running a provision shop on the ground floor of a housing block in northern Singapore and knows the neighbourhood and its residents like the back of his hand.

Despite Samy Provision Shop’s enduring presence, it was barely breaking even, said Ramasamy, who lamented the struggle of adapting to the ever-shifting preferences of his customers.

The racks of vegetables and spices which used to front his store have disappeared over the years. “Nowadays, nobody cooks and everybody just presses buttons on their phones to order delivery or dabao [takeaway],” the 75-year-old said.
item.content:encoded:
Surrounded by a clutter of carton boxes, bottles of dishwashing liquid and rows of dry snacks, Ramasamy Vellasamy holds court behind a cashier. For nine hours a day since 1986, he has been running a provision shop on the ground floor of a housing block in northern Singapore and knows the neighbourhood and its residents like the back of his hand.

Despite Samy Provision Shop’s enduring presence, it was barely breaking even, said Ramasamy, who lamented the struggle of adapting to the ever-shifting preferences of his customers.

The racks of vegetables and spices which used to front his store have disappeared over the years. “Nowadays, nobody cooks and everybody just presses buttons on their phones to order delivery or dabao [takeaway],” the 75-year-old said.

When Ramasamy first raised his shutters in the 1980s, there were about over 560 standalone provision shops but the number has now dwindled to under 250, according to local media, citing data from the Housing Development Board (HDB).

Increased competition, high rents and the lack of successors have snuffed out many such stores, according to industry observers.

Sales at retail stores stocking daily and other items in Singapore have reportedly been falling in recent years, with online competition cited as a major factor. Within this retail segment, shops run by the likes of Ramasamy are facing strong competition from minimarts and convenience stores.

Such shops, which operate on thin margins and small transaction values, lose out to larger retailers who are better positioned to negotiate wholesale prices and spread business costs across outlets, according to Lee Kwan Ok, professor of real estate and deputy head at the National University of Singapore Business School.

Chen Liang, an associate business professor at the Singapore Management University, said delivery options from minimart chains and convenience stores operating around the clock had further piled the pressure on small shops.

“The final issue is that a lot of these shops only work because the family isn’t really paying itself. The next generation can earn far more elsewhere, so nobody takes over,” he added.

The surge in oil prices amid the ongoing conflict in the Middle East has also worsened the situation, with suppliers and delivery companies increasing costs.

Abdul Rawoof, who has been running a provision shop in the eastern estate of Marine Parade for 11 years, said his profit margin had been cut significantly because he had been absorbing most cost increases instead of passing them on to customers.

“Now I sell a big bottle of soft drink at S$2.80 [US$2.20], and there’s no way I can raise it to S$3 because that’s a lot of money for some people,” the 52-year-old said.

Provision shops also face succession issues, with some operators’ children indicating that they have no wish to carry on the trade.

“My children are not learning the business, they don’t want to take over, they are doing their own thing,” Ramasamy said. “Here, I earn about S$100 to S$150 a day, and they can earn much more in their jobs.”

More than just retail

Twice a week, Gani Idris hangs out at Ramasamy’s shop as he waits for his wife to finish her physiotherapy session. The two men chat about family matters and the frequent aches in their legs, which seem to worsen during the rainy season.

The 88-year-old, who has lived in the estate for a decade and is one of Ramasamy’s regular patrons, said the shop was a lifeline for elderly residents. “It’s a good way for us old people to talk to each other. Sometimes youngsters at home don’t want to talk to us.”

The shop, a mere lift ride away from Gani’s house, also meant that he did not have to take a bus to the nearest supermarket, a routine that would tire him.

Provision shops, which are typically located on the ground level of public housing blocks and are known colloquially as mama shops for generations of Singaporeans, serve a broader purpose beyond customer engagement, according to retail experts.

The name mama, meaning “uncle” in Tamil, stemmed from the Indian ethnicity of its owners, said Yeo Kang Shua. The associate professor of architecture and sustainable design at the Singapore University of Technology and Design noted that provision shops run by other ethnic groups have also sprouted in the city state.

These shops act as informal social spaces and help foster familiarity and a sense of belonging, according to Yeo. “From an urban perspective, mama shops help animate public spaces, bringing activity and informal oversight to residential areas.”

“Although many traditional shops have declined due to competition from larger retailers, the need they fulfil has not disappeared,” Yeo said. “Culturally, they reflect Singapore’s history of small-scale entrepreneurship and neighbourhood life.”

Lee noted that the shops’ proximity to residents helped support a more walkable urban lifestyle by reducing car journeys. The short distance also becomes more important as Singapore’s population ages, according to Lee.

Megan Ng, a 36-year-old insurance agent, recalled visiting a now-defunct shop near her childhood home to buy snacks for her siblings after school. “I didn’t go to the supermarket since it was all the way across the road. The mama shop was a lot less intimidating because you couldn’t get lost in one,” Ng said.

Whenever she came up a few cents short, the shopkeeper would grant her a credit line. “Instead of making me put the item back, she said she trusted me and told me it was OK to pay the next time I saw her.

“They are definitely disappearing, and it’s a loss because they really contribute to the sense of community.”

Targeted support?

To boost his earnings, Rawoof has diversified his income stream by using his shop as a collection point for e-commerce orders, while Ramasamy has leased his space to other businesses such as claw machine companies.

In his latest move to boost sales, the owner of Samy Provision Shop on Tuesday spent more than S$1,000 on Pokemon cards, which now sit proudly at his storefront. “The children flock to them. They are flying off the shelves,” he said.

While the number of provision shops is expected to continue falling, they are unlikely to disappear from Singapore’s heartlands, according to analysts, who note that some stores have found ways to stay afloat.

“Realistically, we’re not getting back to the 1980s,” SMU’s Chen said. Instead, a smaller number of shops with multiple income streams and specialised products, such as rolling paper and henna, would have a chance to remain in business, he said.

While there is a case for targeted government support, it should not be implemented to shield these shops from bigger players, analysts say.

Lee suggested small grants for digital payments, inventory management and modest shop improvements, as well as succession programmes to match current owners with young entrepreneurs.

“The objective should be to help viable businesses adapt and preserve socially valuable neighbourhood functions. It should not be to compensate every shop indefinitely for declining demand,” she said.

Last September, Sun Xueling, senior minister of state at the Ministry of National Development, told parliament that the rent for 90 per cent of shops held by the HDB had remained largely unchanged over the last five years.

As of August last year, there were around 15,500 HDB shops, of which about 8,500 were privately owned and 7,000 leased out by the HDB, including those owned by Ramasamy and Rawoof. To keep rents low, HDB had the option of acquiring privately owned shops and leasing them out if there was a need to meet demand in existing estates, Sun said.

Chen suggested setting aside some units in each precinct for provision shops and charging rent based on turnover instead of area. “And then pay the shops for community work: such as parcels collected or helping elderly residents with their phones or their government apps,” he said.

Yeo said Singapore should strive to sustain a diverse retail ecosystem and avoid having standardised neighbourhoods and shop space dominated by larger operators.

“We should not only pay attention to mama shops when one is about to close. What is often lost is not just a business, but also the long-standing relationships between the owner and the neighbourhood,” he said.

“The key question is whether future neighbourhoods will continue to make room for small, independent businesses that are closely connected to the communities they serve.”

item.title: [SCMP] AI threatens nearly a quarter of Southeast Asia’s workforce but not all is lost
item.description:
Fears of a new industrial revolution in which artificial intelligence replaces manual labour have yet to materialise in Southeast Asia – but white-collar workers should brace themselves.

Nearly one in four workers in the region face generative AI (GenAI) disrupting or affecting their jobs, according to a July report by the International Labour Organization (ILO).

Clerical, administrative and professional positions were most at risk, the report stated. Manual trades, craft and agricultural work remain relatively insulated, with the effects of AI varying across the region based on economic development, digital infrastructure and labour policies.
item.content:encoded:
Fears of a new industrial revolution in which artificial intelligence replaces manual labour have yet to materialise in Southeast Asia – but white-collar workers should brace themselves.

Nearly one in four workers in the region face generative AI (GenAI) disrupting or affecting their jobs, according to a July report by the International Labour Organization (ILO).

Clerical, administrative and professional positions were most at risk, the report stated. Manual trades, craft and agricultural work remain relatively insulated, with the effects of AI varying across the region based on economic development, digital infrastructure and labour policies.

But being most “exposed” to GenAI does not mean that entire professions will be replaced – just that some could move up the value chain or evolve, analysts say.

“Our understanding of automation and its impact on jobs has become more nuanced than in the early forecasts surrounding the Fourth Industrial Revolution,” Phu Huynh, senior employment specialist at the ILO, said.

GenAI exposure among craft and trades workers and skilled agricultural workers “is generally low”, he added. Only 3.3 per cent of Southeast Asian workers were in occupations within the highest exposure category, while around 67 per cent had jobs with no identified exposure to GenAI.

“These patterns suggest that, while GenAI has the potential to affect a sizeable share of workers across Asean, occupations with the highest levels of exposure still account for a relatively small share of total employment,” Huynh said.

Nearly 80 million women and men across the region are employed in jobs exposed to GenAI. There were twice as many women (4.8 per cent) as men (2.3 per cent) – reflecting the concentration of women in “clerical, administrative and selected professional occupations”, according to Huynh.

The gender gap was most pronounced in Thailand and the Philippines, where women are around three to four times more likely than men to work in highly exposed occupations.

Singapore has the highest share of workers exposed to Gen AI – at 42.2 per cent – which the brief said might partly “reflect the country’s highly knowledge-intensive occupational structure”.

The Philippines follows at 28.1 per cent, reflecting the country’s service-oriented economy and prominence of its information technology and business process management sector. Indonesia (21.7 per cent), Vietnam (20.8 per cent), and Thailand (20.6 per cent) also recorded significant levels of exposure.

Transforming jobs

Despite the scale of AI exposure, there was limited evidence of large-scale job losses associated with GenAI.

“In Asean, widespread labour market disruption is not yet visible,” Huynh said. “Nevertheless, continued monitoring of job impacts is critical, especially among young workers in countries [showing] slower growth or declining employment in selected entry-level administrative and clerical jobs.”

Across the region, GenAI remains dominant over agentic AI and is used for tasks such as drafting, translation, coding and clerical and administrative work. GenAI operates on prompts to create content or data, while agentic AI can plan and execute deeper steps towards goal with higher autonomy.

The emerging consensus is that the impact of this technological transition will be greater on the transformation of jobs and tasks, rather than outright displacement.

“GenAI is likely to reshape white-collar jobs because many routine cognitive tasks can be automated or augmented. However, the key issue is less about jobs disappearing and more about jobs evolving,” Huynh said.

“Ensuring that workers have the skills to use AI effectively will be critical to supporting economic upgrading and sustaining the region’s transition up the value chain.”

ILO’s findings mirror similar research conducted on India and Indonesia by Aapti Institute.

“Our study notes that AI systems are likely to amplify demand for advanced digital and cognitive skills while reducing the demand for routine and clerical activities,” said Nighat Nighat, an associate at the India-based institute.

“Also in greater demand will be skills that complement GenAI, such as critical thinking, creativity, and emotional intelligence.”

Entry-level white-collar roles were “precisely the tasks GenAI is best at automating”, she said, with workers and experts pointing out a decline in demand for simpler, repetitive tasks.

Readiness factor

Readiness across the board remains a primary concern.

“Young workers in advanced economies potentially face higher exposure because a larger share of jobs involves tasks that can be augmented or automated by AI. In developing economies, lower adoption may reduce immediate disruption, but it can also limit access to the related productivity gains from innovation and new opportunities,” Huynh said.

According to the report, Singapore was best positioned to harness AI opportunities due to its strong digital infrastructure and ecosystem, and whole-government approach.

Malaysia, Thailand, Brunei, Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam were next. At the bottom tier are Cambodia, Laos, Myanmar and East Timor, which “generally exhibit lower levels of readiness, reflecting more limited digital infrastructure, institutional capacity and technological capabilities”.

Analysts also stressed the importance of organisations supporting their workers through the shifts.

“While various forms of rule-based AI have been in use by businesses since the last two decades, the adoption of the newer GenAI and related technologies is dependent on the attitudes and belief systems of managers towards the effectiveness and cost-efficiency of these technologies,” said Ben Teehankee, president of the Responsible AI Council of the Analytics and Artificial Intelligence Association of the Philippines.

“More human capital strategic companies may leverage generative AI for reskilling their current workers for higher-value adding tasks but since this transition takes time, there will be significant AI-related job disruptions for some workers who cannot readily adapt or who are not provided transition support by their companies.”

AI adoption could widen the gap between high-skill, well-paying jobs and low-skill, low-paying jobs, Nighat said.

“When GenAI skills are mature enough to match or exceed human ability, they tend to substitute workers; but when jobs involve more complex workflows, disruption tends to be minimal,” she said.

“This creates a two-tier effect: workers doing routine tasks get substituted, facing downward wage pressure, while those whose jobs are AI-complemented gain productivity and see their skills become more valuable and in greater demand.”

Policy reforms and country support could help the transition process, Teehankee said. “Without significant policy reforms and government intervention, broad-based AI automation will tend to impact workers in advanced economies first but this will cascade to the value chains in developing countries, as companies look for cost efficiencies to stay competitive.”

The key determinant, Huynh said, would be “how effectively countries support workers and enterprises to prepare for and navigate the transition, including investments in skills, digital infrastructure, and inclusive and ethical AI adoption.”

item.title: [SCMP] Thai teen kills at least 5 in school, after shooting grandparents at home
item.description:
At least five people were killed at a school near Thailand’s capital Bangkok on Friday morning after a student went on a gun rampage, with the tragedy shocking the nation and reopening questions over access to firearms.

The 14-year-old suspect had killed his grandparents before opening fire at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, about an hour outside the capital, and then took his own life, officials said.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff, and police said the shooter fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that ‌belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found.
item.content:encoded:
At least five people were killed at a school near Thailand’s capital Bangkok on Friday morning after a student went on a gun rampage, with the tragedy shocking the nation and reopening questions over access to firearms.

The 14-year-old suspect had killed his grandparents before opening fire at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, about an hour outside the capital, and then took his own life, officials said.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff, and police said the shooter fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that ‌belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found.

Police said 23 people were wounded in the incident.

The boy appeared to have shot his grandparents first before attending school as normal, said Royal Thai Police spokesman Police Lieutenant General Trairong Phiwphan. After class started, the boy opened fire inside his classroom before walking out and continuing to shoot.

Trairong said the teen fired more than 20 shots and over 30 rounds were found on him after he shot himself.

Several family members of the alleged shooter told police the boy usually kept to himself and was a good student. They said they were unaware of any troubles he faced at home or school.

Harrowing video footage shared on social media, apparently filmed by a pupil during the shooting, shows children in blue uniforms cowering under wooden desks, as five shots ring out while the school’s automatic public address system announces the time is 10am.

One pupil in the clip extends an arm out to comfort another who is crying as the shots are fired in what appears to be a methodical manner.

“It’s really awful, this shouldn’t have happened,” Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters. “I’m not just sad about the people who died, I’m sad that something like this could happen in our country at all.

“This is exactly what I’ve been saying – the reason the government doesn’t allow people to carry guns, doesn’t allow ownership, doesn’t allow licence renewals, is because of exactly this kind of thing.”

Anutin confirmed reports that the shooter was 14 years old and killed himself, according to Associated Press. He said the boy, who lived with his grandparents, had shown signs of stress related to school.

The gun, described by police as small and compact, was legally registered to the boy’s grandfather, Anutin said.

The prime minister on Friday also vowed to introduce a new firearms control law.

Anutin, who previously tightened gun ‌laws when he was interior minister, will now propose a law to restrict the carrying of firearms by the public.

“The new law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns,” he told reporters on Friday, but did not provide any specifics for the envisaged legislation, including whether it would tighten gun ownership requirements.

Images shared by police showed what appeared to be the gunman’s weapon, a semi-automatic pistol with multiple rounds packed in a pouch, as questions emerged over his mental health and the motive behind the attack. Several pupils suggested the shooter had been bullied.

“Our school doesn’t check our bags when entering school,” Kittipat Choolert, 16, told This Week in Asia. “He fired several shots, I was two buildings away from him and I heard the gunshots, the entire school heard it and we were in shock.”

Tearful students in school uniforms held each other outside the school.

“I’m still in shock,” 16-year-old Thatchai Jaiyen told Agence France-Presse, expressing disbelief that a kind former teacher of his had been killed.

“She was such a good person. I thought that if she had encountered the shooter, she might have been able to reason with him. I never expected that the child would actually shoot her,” he said, his voice trailing away.

Student Purin Khumchoo said he felt depressed and bad for the people who were killed.

“The two teachers who were killed were lovely, and many students became better people because of them,” he said.

Emergency worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, 47, described arriving during the shooting and his team treating students with injuries to the back, ‌chest and arms. They found a teacher dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room a female teacher with chest and arm wounds.

Kiatikhun said he was called to treat the teenage shooter after hearing a final shot. “We rushed up ‌and found ‌that the perpetrator had shot himself in the right side of the head and collapsed. When we got up there, we checked his pulse, he still had one, so we started CPR.”

The school suspended all classes for next week and instructed staff to work from home during that time.

It is the latest shooting to stun a nation where millions of firearms are in circulation, many unlicensed and unregistered and where shootings are commonplace, but mass killings involving children are rare.

Last weekend, Anutin was at the scene of the killing of five people in Chonburi, including Russian siblings, one shot by an alleged robber.

In February, a teacher ‌died and a ‌student was injured in southern Thailand’s Hat Yai district after a gunman opened fire at a school.

In 2023, a shooting by a 14-year-old boy killed two – a Chinese and a Myanmar citizen – at Siam Paragon, one of Thailand’s most famous downtown malls.

It was a tragedy that spurred calls for stricter gun controls, yet killings have continued, with regular police raids unearthing large caches of heavy weapons and pistols.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia, second only to Pakistan but far surpassing its Southeast Asian neighbours.

Data collected in 2017 by the groups Small Arms Survey and GunPolicy.org in their last extensive international study found civilian gun ownership in Thailand was about 15.1 guns per 100 people, compared with fewer than one per 100 in neighbouring Malaysia.

Thailand had 3.49 deaths by firearms per 100,000 people, according to 2023 statistics published by World Population Review.

“I think we need to [look at] why we still haven’t learned from everything that’s happened,” Krisanaphong Poothakool, a leading criminologist and adviser to the Royal Thai Police on police reform, told Channel One News.

“Why do firearms in Thailand seem so easy to access? The fact that children and youth have access to guns and gun sets is really not something normal in Thai society.”

In the worst episode of its kind in living memory, Panya Khamrab, a 34-year-old former policeman with a history of drug abuse, massacred 37 people – 24 of them children – in a shooting and stabbing rampage at a day care centre in the northeastern province of Nong Bua Lam Phu in 2022.

Additional reporting by Associated Press, Reuters and Agence France-Presse

item.title: [SCMP] Chinatown Los Angeles memories: my father loved the place once, and now I remember why as an exhibition brings its history to life
item.description:
My father grew up just a few steps from where I am now on this shop-lined section of Chung King Road in Los Angeles, two flights of worn wooden stairs above his father’s general store.

The family flat was a heavenly slice of the homeland, the living room lined with silk-tasselled lanterns, Chinese landscapes on the walls and a custom red rug holding the room together. The cool, dark hallways smelled of camphor wood and soy sauce. A sizeable turtle roamed the kitchen like a king (until one day he disappeared – only to reappear in a soup).

The flat had a bank of tall windows that overlooked all of Chinatown, with LA’s art deco City Hall looming in the middle distance. Throughout his childhood, my father gazed out onto this dreamy mid-20th century tableau, a sparkling panorama of newly built pagodas and temples with tiled roofs curled up at the eaves, some lined in neon.
item.content:encoded:
My father grew up just a few steps from where I am now on this shop-lined section of Chung King Road in Los Angeles, two flights of worn wooden stairs above his father’s general store.

The family flat was a heavenly slice of the homeland, the living room lined with silk-tasselled lanterns, Chinese landscapes on the walls and a custom red rug holding the room together. The cool, dark hallways smelled of camphor wood and soy sauce. A sizeable turtle roamed the kitchen like a king (until one day he disappeared – only to reappear in a soup).

The flat had a bank of tall windows that overlooked all of Chinatown, with LA’s art deco City Hall looming in the middle distance. Throughout his childhood, my father gazed out onto this dreamy mid-20th century tableau, a sparkling panorama of newly built pagodas and temples with tiled roofs curled up at the eaves, some lined in neon.

Amid the constant bustle of tourists, Hollywood stars would often be seen pulling up in their Cadillac convertibles, while down on Hill Street lived any number of old Chinatown families who had known my father since he was born.
