Families like the Fongs, the Lees, the Moys and the Wongs, these were Cantonese who dared to immigrate to these shores when they were not at all embracing to arrivals from Asia.

In 1882, the Chinese Exclusion Act forbade most Chinese immigration to the United States, although the law did permit Chinese merchants like my grandfather, as well as diplomats and students and their families, into the country. For the Chinese already in the US, however, citizenship was disallowed, and the act would not be repealed until 1943.

Standing here again, after so many years since my last visit, I can understand why my father loved Chinatown and felt so deeply connected to its courtyards, banquet halls and backstreets. And yet, even though Chinatown seemed like a fantasy come alive for my grandparents’ generation, at some point in his time, the shine came off and my father wanted out. He was not the only one.

But before then, “your grandfather was like China­town’s mayor”, my mother would remind me – recalling a photograph of him showing then-US president Richard Nixon around his store in the 1970s – and my grandfather oversaw activities in Chinatown with such a big heart and open wallet that nobody ever wanted him to leave.

Throughout my childhood living in another part of LA, I knew Chinatown as the place where I could eat the most delicious siu mai and har gow, and reunite with my band of cousins, running through the alleys until we reached the statue of Dr Sun Yat-sen in Central Plaza, the area’s main dining and shopping courtyard.

Beyond that, Chinatown was a little dirty, a little dangerous, and almost always blazing hot. It was also the exotic backdrop for much Gee family drama: my father’s squabbles with my grandfather over his will; my nasty aunt’s public snubbings of my mother; and a sprawling funeral for my grandfather, for which an entire half-mile stretch of Hill Street was shut down, all of the Gee girls and female cousins dressed in matching black dresses, sewn in another aunt’s Chinatown factory.

This photograph marks such an accomplishment – to create something from scratch like these men did, merchants working together ... to offer an identity for ... the community

Richard Liu, who owns several Chinatown buildings

I did not realise back then how remarkable our little enclave was. Turns out, I did not know many things about my childhood’s special place of most welcome escapism. But suddenly, a few months ago, word began to spread about a kind of retrospective of the area and its people, and like it or not, it was my direct history, too, that was about to be put on public display.

And so this spring, the Huntington Library, Art Museum and Botanical Gardens, after having received a trove of mid-20th century Chinatown photos from the Chinese Historical Society of Southern California (CHSSC) and a number of local family albums, joined forces with the Los Angeles Public Library to celebrate and explore the legacy of LA Chinatown, the first community in North America planned and owned by people of Chinese descent.

The ongoing “Stories and Voices from LA China­town” exhibition, both online and wrapped around a fence on those streets sacred to my family, includes photographs of the founders of Chinatown, such as Peter SooHoo Snr and You Chung Hong, the first Chinese-American graduate of the University of Southern California Law School.

There are early renderings of Central Plaza by prominent LA architects Erle Webster and Adrian Wilson, and videos of China­town residents, past and present, waxing poetic about the area’s complex legacy.

The exhibition includes oral histories of descendants of Chinatown’s founders and former and current residents. Pat SooHoo Lem, daughter of SooHoo Snr, remembers walking up to tourists and offering to sell them a gardenia corsage or sing God Bless America for them. “We’d sing and they would give us a nickel or a dime,” she says in her twangy American accent.

Caitlin Bryant, great-granddaughter of SooHoo Snr, is a CHSSC board member, working to rejuvenate Central Plaza. In the exhibition video, Bryant tells the story of how her grandmother worried about her grandfather in a newly founded Chinatown, as he sweated out the summer as a busboy at the Golden Pagoda restaurant. “My grandma would go and throw popsicles up to him on the second-floor window.”

There is also Richard Liu, a Burma-born Chinese interior designer. “We left Burma when I was 12, in 1968, for an education and a better life,” Liu recalls. “We had big fears – that we would not be able to get Chinese food and spices, that we would just have to eat American food. Then we got to Chinatown and we realised everything was going to be OK. We could find everything we needed here.”

As a young man, the designer frequented the Chung King Road antique stores, ferreting out such treasures as hand-painted snuff bottles. Today, Liu owns several Chinatown buildings, including YC Hong’s original law office. He has set up his design firm in one of them, overlooking a graceful Chinese courtyard garden.

What I had not known during my childhood visits was that there had been an original Chinatown a few miles south of the new Chinatown site. Established in the 1800s, the old Chinatown was home to some 200 immigrants, many of whom crossed the ocean to work on the railroad. One black-and-white exhibition photograph captures the early Chinese settlers performing a lion dance in the middle of a dusty road.

“That photo really touched me,” says Li Wei Yang, curator of Pacific Rim collections at The Huntington and a collaborator on the exhibition. “Even though life was so hard for them, these Chinese immigrants made such an effort to stay connected to their culture.”

This original Chinatown had also been the scene of bleak events: an 1871 massacre in which some 500 rioting Anglos and Latinos stormed the area and mutilated and killed 18 Chinese men, including a respected doctor. A photograph of the massacre also appears in the exhibition.

“It was very disturbing to see,” says Todd Lerew, director of special projects for the Library Foundation of Los Angeles, who worked with Yang on the exhibition. “While we’ve come a long way from the horrific treatment and violence and overtly racist policies that earlier generations faced, it is clear that problems of racism and violent Sinophobia still persist today.”

In the 1930s, the area was razed to make way for Union Station, still the city’s main railway hub. Soon after the displacement, SooHoo Snr and Hong spearheaded plans to build the new Chinatown, which runs primarily along Hill Street and Broadway. Indeed, designer Liu’s favourite photograph is of the grand opening of the new Chinatown, an image capturing Chinese-American dignitaries, the LA mayor and a brass band, all beaming at this monumental achievement.

“To me,” says Liu, “this photograph marks such an accomplishment – to create something from scratch like these men did, merchants working together, building a shopping centre to attract tourists and to offer an identity for Chinatown and the community.”

One of the early residents, Doré Hall Wong, whose father built new Chinatown’s landmark Golden Pagoda restaurant, remembers the racism that she and her family faced throughout their early lives in LA. “When I was a child I had to wear a bracelet, a necklace, with my name, my address, and I also had a pin that said, ‘I am Chinese’,” she recalls in an exhibition video titled Exclusion. “I realised what was happening when I got older – that there was discrimination. There will always be a form of discrimination.”

Indeed, Chinese people in the US faced decades of harassment and violence throughout the 19th century and into the 20th, based primarily on resentment of China’s labour force. The men who arrived, often from southern China, were skilled and willing to work for lower wages. The Chinese Exclusion Act was, and remains, America’s only law established to prevent the immigration and naturalisation of an ethnic group.

This policy of exclusion, as well as widespread racist sentiment, resulted in the clustered living situations that created Chinatowns throughout North America.

That the founders of LA’s community were able to envision and manifest such a fantastical representation of China was a huge point of pride, especially given its proximity to Hollywood. Liu points out that while the architects Webster and Wilson, who designed the area, were Caucasian, they worked closely with Hong’s wife, Mabel, who provided examples of architectural and landscaping styles from books.

As a result, the buildings had strong symmetries, octagonal windows and evocative wooden screens. One architectural critic remarked that “it was the neon trim that followed the upturned eaves of the classical Chinese designs that gave these silhouettes a freshness and sparkle”.

Perhaps it was Chinese style with the “overlay of Westernness” – the vision of Webster and Wilson – that made LA Chinatown as dramatic as it was. “You could feel their passion, they fell in love with China and this project,” says Liu, whose favourite building is the former Golden Pagoda restaurant, later the bar Hop Louie (now closed). “The architecture was pretty much modelled after the Forbidden City and the Temple of Heaven. Chinatown evoked a fantasy, a place to escape.”

In fact, when Chinatown first opened, in 1938, “it was an exciting environment”, says Lerew. “It was clean and new with wide, brightly lit streets – in contrast to old Chinatown. The Chinese community in LA at that time knew that they could capitalise on the broader curiosity and interest in ‘Oriental’ culture, food and design.”

Indeed, even though Central Plaza opened during the Great Depression, “it was extremely popular in the years immediately following the 1938 grand opening and during the second world war”, says Lerew. “There was no Disneyland yet at that time. Chinatown was the place to go.”

My grandfather, whose American name was Sam Ward, was one of Chinatown’s pioneers. He ran his eponymous general store and an import/export business where you could get everything from bak choi to fancy vases and chopsticks to Chinese whiskey – a business that kept the family connected to their Guangdong homeland.

In the 1960s and ’70s, my grandfather was chairman of the Chinese Consolidated Benevolent Association, whose mission was to “advocate for democracy for the Chinese people and serve as a bridge between Chinese-American immigrants and the mainstream groups, diminish racial discrimination and promote peace among the people”, according to its website.

My parents met for the first time on a blind date arranged by their parents at Fong’s Cafe. My mother, the daughter of a Sacramento chicken farmer, remembers my father Peter’s first question to her, as she lunched on a hamburger: “Do you like onions?” My grandfather needed to get his favourite son married off quickly so that Peter could avoid the Korean war draft. Enter the simple farming family with an available 17-year-old daughter.

My mother could have been intimidated by the Gee family’s big busy store, but instead she felt an easy kinship, and life in Chinatown looked like fun. “I could have said no to the marriage,” my mother recalls, “but I looked around the store and everything looked OK. So, I said yes.”

My mother soon moved into the flat above the Sam Ward shop, where she learned to steam fish and make beef chow fun. She worked as a salesgirl during the day, tallying up the cost of ceramic bowls and oolong tea, and packing up goods for tourists. My mother loved the pretty buildings with their neon lights, and she loved hopping from banquet to banquet, celebratory meals thrown by the other Chinatown families.

“We always had lots of friends around,” she says. But my father, who was studying engineering at the University of California, Los Angeles, could not concentrate with so many people around him. He wanted a place of his own, somewhere to raise his family in peace.

And so it went. I would ride in the family estate car every weekend, my face pressed against the already-smudged window on the 15-minute drive to Sam Ward.

I could not wait to see the bright buildings, moon-shaped portals, and wishing wells with their Guanyin statues, penjing trees and koi fish, slicing through the water like gold ingots with fins. We sometimes followed my grandfather as he made the rounds of Central Plaza, where tourists shopped for silk fans and backscratchers.

Other times, we came dressed for one of his glamorous banquets where waiters in white jackets appeared in a line, holding big platters of sliced abalone, Peking duck and shrimp in lobster sauce. The sumptuous menu was always the same, but my five siblings (I was the second youngest) and I would still “ooh” and “aah” as each dish appeared. Then my grandfather would stand up, rising to his six-foot (183cm) height, corsage on his suit lapel, and give a speech that would have the whole room clapping wildly.

As I grew older, Chinatown remained a touchstone, a place I would sometimes go when I wanted to find home. As a junior in university, I returned to dance, swirl and smile for the Miss Chinatown pageant. I did not win but I still got to ride next to the then LA mayor Tom Bradley, waving to the crowds from a convertible in the annual Lunar New Year parade. Now I had a place in Chinatown history, too.

As it was for so many original families, Chinatown was a way station, a place for immigrants to gain their American footing and then carry on to live and work someplace else. Once housing restrictions for the Chinese eased in the ’60s, Chinese-Americans began to move to such enclaves as Monterey Park, Alhambra and San Gabriel, and create robust residential and commercial communities there, with Chinese characters gracing many signs among the main thoroughfares.

To leave Chinatown behind for these new suburbs, with their housing estates, McMansions and strip malls, became a Chinese-American measure of success. But such upwards and outwards mobility came with a cost.

Today, Chinatown has admittedly lost much of its original lustre. The beautiful buildings, once the colour of jewels, are faded and worn. Many of the best restaurants closed down during the pandemic, if not before.

Google “Most dangerous parts of LA” and Chinatown tops at least one list, not because of its own citizens committing crimes but the gangs that surround the area. “Chinatown has become so dirty, and it has got progressively worse – all the empty storefronts and the merchants leaving,” says Liu. “It’s hard to see.”

But Liu, for one, has a plan. He is renovating five of his storefronts and, this summer, these spaces will be showcasing paintings by some 30 famous artists who once exhibited in Chinatown. Opening day will be one big party. “It’s going to be a relaunch of Chinatown, post-Covid,” he says. “We’ll turn the neon lights on, the galleries and restaurants will be open. It’s going to be fun.”

As I stand on Chung King Road, a light breeze sends rows of faded red lanterns swaying, and I hear my grandfather’s voice: “Just look at everything that we Chinese built here.” Then I hear my dad’s voice: “Be grateful we got out.”

But with this exhibition bringing the vicissitudes of our history into one place, one timeline, Chinatown descendants such as Bryant, the great-granddaughter of Peter SooHoo Snr, feel hopeful about the enclave that has given so much to their families.

“My generation is looking back,” she comments in her exhibition video. “They are looking back to look forward. They only want to make it great. This is just the beginning.”

item.title: [SCMP] Singapore and South Korea eye science opportunities as last main US-China link shatters
item.description:
As President Xi Jinping prepares for summit talks with Donald Trump in Washington next month, the United States is closing one of the few remaining openings between the two countries by targeting scientific research.

This field has been one of the most durable links in the US-China relationship, but a series of new security-related restrictions on federally funded collaborations with Chinese institutions mark the latest, and arguably most consequential, step in a years-long shift away from cooperation.

Experts say the measures are unlikely to halt Chinese scientific progress. Instead, they are reshaping where international collaboration takes place – creating opportunities for intermediary research hubs while narrowing one of the most enduring channels of bilateral engagement.
item.content:encoded:
As President Xi Jinping prepares for summit talks with Donald Trump in Washington next month, the United States is closing one of the few remaining openings between the two countries by targeting scientific research.

This field has been one of the most durable links in the US-China relationship, but a series of new security-related restrictions on federally funded collaborations with Chinese institutions mark the latest, and arguably most consequential, step in a years-long shift away from cooperation.

Experts say the measures are unlikely to halt Chinese scientific progress. Instead, they are reshaping where international collaboration takes place – creating opportunities for intermediary research hubs while narrowing one of the most enduring channels of bilateral engagement.

The timing is striking. The latest restrictions arrive as Washington and Beijing prepare for a summit intended to manage an increasingly adversarial relationship.

But they also expose a growing contradiction. On paper, the diplomatic architecture of scientific cooperation remains intact. The US-China Science and Technology Agreement, first signed in 1979, was quietly renewed in late 2024.

In practice, however, the space for collaboration is shrinking under an expanding web of funding restrictions, blacklists and security rules.

For diplomats who spent decades managing US-China ties, the shift goes beyond science policy. It marks the erosion of one of the few long-standing areas of common interest.

“When I served in the Foreign Service, we always described our environment, health and science cooperation as the ballast of the relationship,” said Deborah Seligsohn, a former US diplomat who worked extensively on environmental and scientific cooperation with China.

Now an assistant professor at Pennsylvania’s Villanova University, Seligsohn said the field embodied the principle of “mutual benefit”, one of the founding principles of the two countries’ formal diplomatic relationship.

“We all benefited from advancing science and improving areas like public health, medical treatment and environmental protection,” she added.

This had provided a form of ballast in the relationship, but Seligsohn warned this was steadily being lost.

Scientific collaboration between the world’s two largest research powers was already slowing before Trump’s return to the White House last year.

Scientific papers with American and Chinese co-authors peaked between 2017 and 2019 before falling by roughly 20 per cent, according to analyses of National Science Foundation and Clarivate data.

The decline has been particularly steep in strategically sensitive fields such as artificial intelligence (AI), advanced engineering, telecommunications and quantum technologies.

The Australian Strategic Policy Institute estimates that the share of China’s international collaborations involving US researchers has fallen from nearly half in 2016 to just over a quarter in recent years.

This trajectory began under the first Trump administration’s China Initiative, which targeted alleged industrial spying and the theft of intellectual property. While the programme ended, the broader shift away from scientific cooperation continued throughout Joe Biden’s presidency.

Recent measures have accelerated this trend. Private sector research, non-federally funded academic work and collaborations in clearly non-sensitive basic science still occur, but even these have to overcome barriers such as rising compliance burdens, risk-averse universities and reputational concerns.

Visa scrutiny of Chinese students and researchers in sensitive fields, reciprocal access difficulties and intensifying global competition for scientific talent have further amplified this practical decoupling.

In July, the US defence department expanded its Section 1286 list of foreign institutions that engage in “problematic activities” to include leading civilian universities such as Fudan and Shanghai Jiao Tong. Previously it had mainly focused on universities seen as linked to the Chinese military.

The Pentagon has banned any funding that supports fundamental research involving collaboration with any institution on the list, while researchers receiving grants from the National Science Foundation are banned from collaborating with institutions appearing on US restricted-party lists or employing researchers affiliated with them.

The White House Office of Management and Budget has also proposed a government-wide ban on using federal grants to support collaborations involving “countries of concern”, including China.

Taken together, these measures mark a significant departure from previous efforts to balance scientific openness with targeted security safeguards.

“The risk-benefit equation has shifted fundamentally,” said Denis Simon, senior research fellow at the Quincy Institute and former executive vice-chancellor of Duke Kunshan University.

In the pre-Trump era, he said, researchers generally evaluated collaborations based on scientific merit and complementary expertise while federal agencies relied on disclosure requirements and oversight to manage risks.

“Today researchers must weigh export controls, sanctions lists, funding restrictions, compliance risks and potential reputational costs.”

The consequences extend beyond collaborations explicitly prohibited by law.

“The transaction costs of international collaboration have increased considerably,” Simon said. “Many principal investigators now avoid otherwise permissible collaborations because university compliance offices recommend caution, funding uncertainty threatens future grants and administrative burdens have increased substantially.”

As direct collaboration narrows, other countries are positioning themselves to capture some of the movement of talent, capital and international partnerships.

Singapore has emerged as perhaps the clearest beneficiary. Its combination of political neutrality, English-language universities, strong intellectual property protections, relatively predictable regulation and ability to attract international talent has drawn multinational research operations from both American and Chinese companies.

“Singapore has deliberately cultivated an ecosystem that remains scientifically open to both countries while offering world-class universities, biomedical research and multinational corporate R&D,” Simon said.

The Gulf states are pursuing a similar strategy. The United Arab Emirates has invested heavily in AI, advanced computing and international talent recruitment, while Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 programme has channelled its sovereign wealth into AI, biotechnology, clean energy and advanced manufacturing.

“Rather than replacing US-China scientific cooperation, these countries increasingly function as multinational hubs connecting researchers who might otherwise have collaborated directly,” Simon said.

He also said Australia, Canada, India, South Korea, Switzerland and parts of the European Union were emerging as new research hubs in an increasingly multipolar system.

Yet their emergence does not mean the global scientific system is simply relocating.

Seligsohn argued that while countries such as Singapore, the UAE and Switzerland could host international meetings and enable collaborations, they could not replicate the scale of the world’s two largest scientific powers.

She said their spending on research was not “anywhere near as great as the US and China”, adding: “The issue with third countries becoming research hubs is that they don’t solve the problems US researchers have with export controls and funding restrictions.”

“The advantage the US had was that it has been one of the two major funders – traditionally the largest – and it has been the most open: the place people from other countries could come to and traditionally wanted to come to.

“Now our funding is decreasing, but other than China there really aren’t any countries increasing spending on the same scale. And with all our visa restrictions, we simply aren’t as open as we were.”

Rather than shifting from one centre to another, she predicted global science would become increasingly fragmented.

“We will see other places become venues for meetings and the like,” she said. “But the reality is that overall science is going to become more fractured – with some in the US, some in China, some in Europe or Canada or Australia or other countries. The centrality that came from having one interconnected system that promoted rapid movement in global science is simply being lost.”

Sourabh Gupta, from the Washington-based Institute for China-American Studies, argued that the restrictions were unlikely to derail China’s scientific rise. China was already a near peer in high-quality, highly cited research, he said, and Chinese and American academics remained each other’s largest international collaborators.

“The US is welcome to drop out of the race of its own volition and cede its leadership spot,” Gupta said. “But that will not stop the Chinese side from powering ahead – by itself, and in collaboration with others.”

He expected tighter visa restrictions, weaker university partnerships and greater controls on research collaboration would be introduced in future, leaving both sides “poorer off, in relative terms”.

For Seligsohn, the biggest loss is not simply fewer joint papers or shared discoveries but the erosion of one of the last channels through which the world’s two most powerful countries could understand one another.

That carries both geopolitical and practical risks, she added, pointing to the mistrust that emerged during the Covid-19 pandemic. “Understanding each other is important for maintaining peace between the world’s two most powerful countries.”

item.title: [SCMP] North Korea missile launch hints at upgraded weapons exports to Russia for Ukraine war
item.description:
North Korea’s recent missile launch may be a test of upgraded exports to Russia, observers say, as the war in Ukraine gives Pyongyang opportunities to improve its weapons.

At about 6am on Wednesday, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected a missile launched from the North’s southeastern port city of Wonsan. It flew roughly 700km (435 miles) eastward before falling into the Sea of Japan, or East Sea.

The JCS conspicuously did not specify the missile’s launch angle or whether it should be classified as short- or long-range. Instead, it said South Korean, US and Japanese authorities had been tracking the launch from its early stages.
item.content:encoded:
North Korea’s recent missile launch may be a test of upgraded exports to Russia, observers say, as the war in Ukraine gives Pyongyang opportunities to improve its weapons.

At about 6am on Wednesday, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) detected a missile launched from the North’s southeastern port city of Wonsan. It flew roughly 700km (435 miles) eastward before falling into the Sea of Japan, or East Sea.

The JCS conspicuously did not specify the missile’s launch angle or whether it should be classified as short- or long-range. Instead, it said South Korean, US and Japanese authorities had been tracking the launch from its early stages.

A South Korean military official said further analysis was needed to determine its type.

The JCS said the military was “closely monitoring various developments in North Korea under a robust South Korea-US combined defence posture”. It stressed that Seoul was maintaining the capabilities and readiness to respond overwhelmingly to any provocation.

The latest launch came six days after Pyongyang fired what the South Korean military identified as a short-range ballistic missile towards the Sea of Japan.

North Korea usually reports its missile launches through state media a day or so after they occur. But it has yet to publish a report on last week’s launch, raising the possibility that it was unsuccessful or involved a top-secret new missile.

Product testing

North Korea operates KN-23, also known as Hwasong-11Ga, short-range ballistic missiles with a maximum range of about 700-800km.

At a military exhibition last October, it unveiled the Hwasong-11MA, a short-range hypersonic missile modelled after Russia’s Iskander-M system. The missile, which was test-fired later that month, is designed to perform a terminal “pull-up” manoeuvre during its descent, altering its trajectory shortly before impact to confuse missile-defence radars and evade interception.

“Given the growing need from Russia for the Ukraine war, it could be a test to improve existing missiles or develop a new type of missile,” said Cho Han-bum, a senior research fellow at the Korea Institute for National Unification (KINU).

On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Moscow was receiving additional military aid from North Korea in the war, now entering its fifth year.

Zelensky said Russian forces had used North Korean ballistic missiles in an overnight attack on the southeastern city of Zaporizhzhia that killed seven steel-plant workers.

A North Korean ballistic missile unit is also reportedly taking up positions in Russia’s Voronezh region, which borders Ukraine’s Luhansk region. The unit is believed to have six launchers and 120 ballistic missiles.

In Russia’s first reported use of North Korean missiles since last August, KN-23 ballistic missiles struck the village of Radushne, southeast of Kryvyi Rih in the Dnipropetrovsk region, on July 30.

Recent Russian missile attacks have put further strain on Ukraine’s air-defence network, including systems based on the US-made Patriot.

The pressure has prompted Zelensky to call on South Korea to provide air-defence systems – which it is unlikely to do as South Korean law prohibits the export of weapons to countries at war. Seoul is also seeking to avoid an escalation of tensions with Moscow.

Given the lack of details surrounding the August 6 launch, Wednesday’s test could have been a follow-up to a possible failure, said Yang Moo-jin, a professor at the University of North Korean Studies.

The launch appeared to have had multiple objectives, he said. “It may be aimed at improving a tactical ballistic missile for export to Russia, or at testing an upgraded version of the Hwasong-11 series.”

It may also be linked to recent developments on the battlefield, including Russia’s escalating missile strikes against Ukraine and call to North Korea to send additional troops.

Another possible objective is to accumulate technology for submarine-launched ballistic missiles. North Korea is constructing a new nuclear-powered submarine and preparing for underwater launch tests.

Response to Japan

Yang noted that Wednesday’s launch came about a week after Kim Yo-jong, sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, warned that Pyongyang would take military action in response to Japan’s test-firing of long-range cruise missiles and other military build-ups.

On July 30, the Japanese Aegis destroyer JS Chokai launched a Tomahawk cruise missile in the Pacific Ocean for the first time, with support from the US Navy.

Kim condemned that test-firing as well as Japan’s participation in a US-led joint exercise in the Philippines in May.

Japan’s acquisition of a pre-emptive strike capability had “entered the stage of actual action”, she said, while denouncing the United States as the force behind Japan’s military build-up.

The distance Wednesday’s missile flew was roughly that between Wonsan and Sasebo Port in Japan, host to a US military base, said Hong Min, a senior research fellow at KINU.

Sasebo, scheduled to become the home port of an Amphibious Readiness Group, is one of the key logistics bases for US reinforcements deployed to the Korean peninsula in the event of a contingency. It is also the home port of destroyer JS Chokai.

“The launch was a possible message of protest at Japan’s military moves,” Hong said.

If North Korea were to extend the missile’s range to around 1,000km by incorporating a glide phase, the system could potentially cover much of southwestern Kyushu as well as areas hosting US military bases in Japan, he said.

Lee Il-woo, a senior analyst at the Korea Defence Network, said North Korea could have been testing newly produced KN-23 missiles before shipping them to Russia.

“The North is possibly evaluating the missile’s performance with new warheads and checking the accuracy of new guidance systems,” he said.

North Korea has significantly improved its circular error probable, a measure of missile accuracy, over the past few years, aided by Russia, according to Lee.

“Most alarmingly, through the war, North Korea is gaining experience in penetrating US missile-defence systems, which are also deployed in South Korea,” he said.

The experts say the latest launch is also a possible show of force ahead of the South Korea-US joint military exercise Ulchi Freedom Shield, scheduled to take place from August 17 to 27.

North Korea has long denounced Ulchi as an “exercise for an invasion” and has responded to the drills with provocations, including ballistic missile launches.

item.title: [SCMP] Showdown in Indonesia’s Solo pits Widodo’s dynasty against Megawati’s machine
item.description:
The rivalry between two of Indonesia’s former presidents is moving onto the political ground where their alliance was first forged, with Joko Widodo’s youngest son preparing to contest the constituency held by Megawati Sukarnoputri’s daughter.

Kaesang Pangarep plans to seek a parliamentary seat in Central Java V in 2029. The constituency has been represented since 2009 by House Speaker Puan Maharani – one of the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle’s (PDI-P) most prominent figures and the offspring of the woman whose party carried Widodo from Solo’s city hall to the presidency.

Kaesang, who chairs the upstart Indonesian Solidarity Party (PSI), announced the plan at a party meeting in Solo on July 25. Central Java V covers Solo, Boyolali, Klaten and Sukoharjo, combining Widodo’s home base with one of PDI-P’s long-standing strongholds.
item.content:encoded:
The rivalry between two of Indonesia’s former presidents is moving onto the political ground where their alliance was first forged, with Joko Widodo’s youngest son preparing to contest the constituency held by Megawati Sukarnoputri’s daughter.

Kaesang Pangarep plans to seek a parliamentary seat in Central Java V in 2029. The constituency has been represented since 2009 by House Speaker Puan Maharani – one of the Indonesian Democratic Party of Struggle’s (PDI-P) most prominent figures and the offspring of the woman whose party carried Widodo from Solo’s city hall to the presidency.

Kaesang, who chairs the upstart Indonesian Solidarity Party (PSI), announced the plan at a party meeting in Solo on July 25. Central Java V covers Solo, Boyolali, Klaten and Sukoharjo, combining Widodo’s home base with one of PDI-P’s long-standing strongholds.

That makes the race a prospective proxy contest between two political families at very different stages of dynastic power. Analysts see it as part of Widodo’s broader challenge to Megawati and PDI-P – an effort to turn his family’s recent rise and PSI into a durable political machine capable of competing with a party rooted in the legacy of Megawati’s father, Indonesia’s first president Sukarno.

Marcus Mietzner, a professor of political and social change at the Australian National University and author of Ruling Indonesia, a recent study of Widodo’s decade in office, described Kaesang’s candidacy as “the boldest expression of this challenge so far”.

It is not necessarily a winner-takes-all duel – Indonesia’s proportional electoral system could allow both Kaesang and Puan to secure seats.

However, a strong showing by Kaesang and PSI would suggest Widodo can convert his personal popularity into lasting family influence, but a poor result could underline PDI-P’s political resilience at a time when it is also navigating an uncertain future outside President Prabowo Subianto’s governing coalition.

PDI-P had propelled Widodo from Solo mayor to a two-term presidency, but the partnership unravelled during the 2024 election after he backed Prabowo – who chose Widodo’s eldest son, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, as his running mate – rather than PDI-P candidate Ganjar Pranowo.

Kaesang’s challenge follows two major electoral clashes between the former allies. After Widodo helped Prabowo and Gibran secure a decisive presidential victory in 2024, including in Central Java, he openly endorsed Ahmad Luthfi, who defeated PDI-P’s candidate in the province’s gubernatorial race later that year.

PDI-P made the rupture formal that December, expelling Widodo, Gibran and Widodo’s son-in-law Bobby Nasution for defying the party line.

Widodo responded from Solo that he respected the decision, adding: “Time will tell.”

Home turf

Kristian Widya Wicaksono, an associate professor at Parahyangan Catholic University, said the overlap between Widodo’s political home base and PDI-P territory gave Kaesang’s choice both electoral logic and political symbolism.

“Choosing a constituency is not merely an administrative decision but part of an effort to send a political message to both opponents and supporters,” Kristian said.

A strong showing for Kaesang there, he added, would strengthen the argument that the Widodo family no longer needed PDI-P as its political vehicle.

Arya Fernandes, head of the politics and social change department at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in Jakarta, said Kaesang had “two main motivations” for choosing Central Java V.

The first was that it was already one of PSI’s stronger constituencies. The second, he said, was “to challenge PDI-P politically”.

Puan topped the constituency in 2024 with 297,366 votes, while PDI-P won 774,282 votes overall, compared with PSI’s 134,249.

But PSI was gaining ground. Its vote share rose from 1.3 per cent in 2019 to 5.8 per cent in 2024, while PDI-P’s fell from 36.8 per cent to 33.2 per cent and its seat tally dropped from four to three.

Arya said PSI’s 2024 support there was already strong enough to compete for a seat. But the young party, established in 2014, has never entered the national parliament and won only about 2.8 per cent of votes nationwide in the last election, short of the 4 per cent threshold then required.

The Constitutional Court has ordered lawmakers to revise both the threshold rules and the percentage before the 2029 election, although no new figure has yet been set.

To become one of PSI’s first national lawmakers, Kaesang would not need to defeat Puan personally. PSI would need to clear whatever national parliamentary threshold applies in 2029 and win a seat in Central Java V, while Kaesang would have to rank among the party’s highest-polling candidates there.

“All of this is doable, but it doesn’t substitute for PDI-P’s long-entrenched network and ideological rootedness,” Mietzner said.

Yoes Kenawas, a political analyst at the Indonesian Survey Institute who specialises in dynastic politics, said the drama surrounding the two families could exaggerate the immediate threat to Puan.

PDI-P’s deep cultural and organisational roots in Central Java made its dominance difficult to dislodge, he said, but the rivalry still served PSI by helping it “grab national attention, pump up PSI’s popularity” and showing that Widodo’s influence was far from over.

The real objective, Yoes said, was likely to use Kaesang’s strongest natural base to secure PSI a foothold in parliament rather than defeat Puan personally.

Arya was less confident that PDI-P would escape unscathed, saying its representation in Central Java V could fall from three seats to two unless it strengthened its local organisation.

Both parties have downplayed the idea of a personal showdown between the political scions. PDI-P’s Ganjar last month described Central Java V as a natural choice for Kaesang, who is from Solo, while PSI political affairs chief Bestari Barus similarly denied that Widodo’s son was specifically challenging PDI-P.

This Week in Asia has reached out to both PSI and PDI-P for comment.

Family capital

Widodo, whose approval rating stood at about 75 per cent in a poll during his final weeks as president, has remained politically active since leaving office, meeting allies and throwing his weight behind PSI as it tries to enter parliament for the first time.

But the question remains whether his appeal can be transferred first to his children and then to a party capable of surviving without him.

Gibran’s vice-presidential victory offers an early test case. In an analysis of the 2024 election, Mietzner argued that the electoral significance of Gibran’s nomination lay less in his own popularity than in the signal it sent to Widodo’s supporters that Prabowo was the outgoing president’s preferred successor.

Mietzner said that distinction posed a risk for Kaesang.

“The case of Gibran shows that while voters still like Jokowi, they are much cooler on his sons,” he said, referring to Widodo by his popular nickname.

Mietzner said PSI was also important to Widodo because it could give him “other options” if Gibran was not chosen again as Prabowo’s running mate in 2029.

Kristian cautioned that even a Kaesang victory would not necessarily mean PSI had become a durable political force.

“The victory of a popular figure does not always lead to the strengthening of the party organisation,” he said.

For PSI to become more than a vehicle for the Widodo family, Kristian said it would need strong local networks, its own cadre base and support that could be sustained between elections and beyond candidates with famous family names.

PDI-P had vulnerabilities of its own, Kristian said, including highly centralised leadership under Megawati, which he said risked slowing leadership renewal and limiting opportunities for new leaders.

But it also has advantages that would be difficult for PSI to reproduce quickly: structures reaching down to the village level, decades of electoral experience and a relatively loyal voter base.

Arya said 2029 could be a crucial window for PSI, predicting that Widodo would campaign seriously for both the party and Kaesang.

“The 2029 election is the window PSI has left to qualify, especially while Jokowi remains a strong figure,” he said. “By 2034, Jokowi’s stature will have diminished.”

For Kristian, the real test for PSI will be whether it can attract support independent of the Widodo family.

“Long-term success will not be determined by the extent of the Widodo family’s influence,” he said, “but by PSI’s ability to build a strong organisation, produce quality cadres, maintain ideological consistency and gain political legitimacy through performance and public trust.”

item.title: [SCMP] Thailand’s rising body count reveals a nation unable to curb gun crime
item.description:
The cremations of the victims of the Debsirin school shooting in the Thai province of Nonthaburi had barely begun when another body was added to the country’s rising toll from gun violence.

On Monday morning, a former MP for Nonthaburi fired four rounds at a local official inside a car – then calmly strode away, the pistol tucked back into his belt.

Police Colonel Thongchai Yenprasert was shot over an alleged money dispute by 71-year-old Chalong Riewrang, a three-time lawmaker with deep political influence, who then called a television host to confess his alleged crime.
item.content:encoded:
The cremations of the victims of the Debsirin school shooting in the Thai province of Nonthaburi had barely begun when another body was added to the country’s rising toll from gun violence.

On Monday morning, a former MP for Nonthaburi fired four rounds at a local official inside a car – then calmly strode away, the pistol tucked back into his belt.

Police Colonel Thongchai Yenprasert was shot over an alleged money dispute by 71-year-old Chalong Riewrang, a three-time lawmaker with deep political influence, who then called a television host to confess his alleged crime.

Thongchai, 71, was the 12th victim of gun killings in under three weeks in Nonthaburi alone, a small province of a quarter of a million people just outside Bangkok.

On July 21, a young man was gunned down by a masked gunman on a motorbike in Pak Kret. A week later, a former bank manager killed two relatives and injured four others in a bullet-strewn dispute over land.

But most of the lives were taken by a 14-year-old student who allegedly shot his grandparents before going on a killing spree at Debsirin school on Friday morning. By the next day, the death toll was nine and included the shooter, who apparently took his own life.

Over 20 people were shot dead nationwide in that period, according to an estimate from local media reports. But that is not a definitive tally in a country where conflict, gang disputes, robberies, debts, broken hearts and mental health breakdowns are often resolved in a hail of bullets.

No control

It is a gun violence problem everyone knows exists, but no one seems able to control.

“I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve repeated this, but let me say it again: no one has the right to carry a firearm around in public, especially not in public places,” Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Monday.

He vowed to drive through new law to get on top of the illegal guns in circulation and make sure that only active personnel were allowed to carry weapons in public. There would be searches, roadblocks and harsh punishments for anyone who breached the law, he added.

“The last public-carry permit was issued three years ago. These carry permits are valid for only one year. Therefore, [right now] no one can carry a gun unless they are an official actively on duty.”

On Tuesday, Anutin suspended the issuance ⁠of permits to buy firearms and said existing licences would be reviewed, Reuters reported.

In the fallout from the school killings, gun control arguments have split along predictable lines: those calling for further tightening of laws and those who say it is not legal guns to blame but the individual who pulls the trigger.

It is already a complex process to obtain a gun legally in Thailand, according to Pat Hakimi, vice-president of the Firearms Traders Association of Thailand.

“Before you can buy a gun from a shop, there has to be a background check … the government does the checking. There’s fingerprinting, it gets sent to the district officer for review, and then another signature for approval,” he said.

“My family has been selling guns for 90 years, since my grandmother’s time. As far as I know, not a single one of our guns has ever been used to commit a crime.”

Instead, he said the overwhelming majority of gun crimes are committed with unlicensed, black market weapons – over one million of which may be in circulation.

Those include blank guns illegally altered to fire real bullets or so-called welfare weapons – bought via a cut-price quota scheme allowing civil servants to buy subsidised guns – that slip onto the black market. “Prevention starts by controlling guns in the wrong hands – they’re sold openly all over online marketplaces,” Pat said.

Sporadic Thai police raids on criminal gangs often uncover alarming evidence of the firepower on the streets: caches of military-grade weapons including automatic rifles and machine guns.

‘Flawed society’

Thailand is often cited as having the highest rate of gun ownership in Southeast Asia with the last data point, compiled in 2017 by the Small Arms Survey, reporting over 10.3 million firearms were in civilian hands, or around 15 guns per 100 people.

Experts say that abundance is partly to do with Thailand’s militarised culture as well as its location as a smuggling route between two active war zones: in the south, where insurgents battle authorities, and in civil war-torn Myanmar.

The school shooting has highlighted the complexity of gun control, as the weapon used was licensed to the shooter’s grandfather.

Kisanaphong Poothakool, a police lieutenant-colonel and leading criminologist, said firearms laws should be updated to require “periodic renewal and reassessment” for licensed gun holders.

He also called for tougher illegal firearm control, better databases and tracing for risk assessment and mandatory safe-storage requirements “especially in homes where children or other vulnerable persons are present”.

“Every society has conflict. The issue is why a firearm is available at the moment the conflict escalates,” he said. “If we can reduce the intersection between conflict, anger and access to firearms, we can reduce the number of disputes that end in death.”

In the absence of comprehensive data or government findings, those who regularly see the outcomes of violence are left to make their own diagnosis of the ills plaguing Thailand.

Ekkapop Luangprasert, founder of the Sai Mai Tong Rod, a leading volunteer group that members of the public often contact before the police, receives complaints of violence, including shootings, “almost daily”.

“I think what we’re seeing overall stems from a flawed belief embedded in Thai society – a culture that glorifies violence,” he said. “Whenever something goes wrong, Thai society has taught us that the answer is punishment.”

Old-school parenting and wider power values leave children ill-equipped to deal with anger and frustration, he said. “By the time they grow up and enter society, they end up defaulting to violence as the way to solve problems.”

“We need to take a hard look at what’s actually happening in Thai society today. Thai society is built on authoritarianism: you must listen to your teachers, you must listen to your elders. That era is over now. It doesn’t work any more in this day and age.”

item.title: [SCMP] For China’s aspiring foreign workers, getting a job is only half the battle
item.description:
Even as an undergraduate in his native Barcelona, Aitor knew he wanted to work in China.

The young finance major reckoned an economy of such scale and speed had more to offer someone with his skill set than the market waiting for him closer to home.

After moving to Shanghai to complete a master’s degree, he had what he came for: a supply-chain job in the bustling financial centre. What Aitor – a nickname, requested to protect the identity of his employer – did not expect was that getting a job would be the easy part.
item.content:encoded:
Even as an undergraduate in his native Barcelona, Aitor knew he wanted to work in China.

The young finance major reckoned an economy of such scale and speed had more to offer someone with his skill set than the market waiting for him closer to home.

After moving to Shanghai to complete a master’s degree, he had what he came for: a supply-chain job in the bustling financial centre. What Aitor – a nickname, requested to protect the identity of his employer – did not expect was that getting a job would be the easy part.

Being hired at firms in China is already difficult for foreign graduates: employers barely give applications a look, given the number of qualified local candidates.

But Aitor’s Chinese language proficiency provided a way around this hurdle. He could search on Boss Zhipin, one of the country’s largest recruitment apps, which Aitor said was “not very friendly for foreigners” and not known to most expats.

Then came the real challenge: the visa. A points-based system for qualification, the overlapping categories and the volume of documentation involved have made obtaining a work permit a longer-running problem than the job search ever was.

“Visa applications are complicated, especially working visas, and I’m still in the process six months after my application,” Aitor said. “The amount of papers needed makes it very complicated.”

Yet as a degree holder from a Chinese university, he said he considered himself lucky, noting that others had it worse.

“I know many valuable and well-educated individuals are struggling to find ways to formalise their work in China, since family reunion visas are not flexible at all and working visas are very hard to get and [it is] hard to be sponsored by local companies; they are caught in between,” he said.

As China’s economy has grown in scale and its influence across global supply chains has expanded, more international graduates and professionals are eyeing opportunities in the world’s second-largest economy.

However, unlike traditional immigration destinations such as the United States and Canada, China has historically relied less on foreign workers to fill labour shortages, leaving the country to build a foreign talent system relatively slowly.

Many foreign workers in China are transferred there by multinational companies, with visa processing, housing and relocation costs typically covered by their employers. This provides a markedly different experience from younger candidates attempting to enter China’s job market independently.

At the same time, the country has been facing rising employment pressure, particularly among young workers, adding another layer of complexity to efforts to attract overseas talent. Its youth unemployment reached 21.3 per cent in June 2023, before the National Bureau of Statistics revised its calculation method. The rate stood at 14.9 per cent in June.

Last year, China introduced the “K visa”, targeting young science and technology professionals as it competes globally for engineers, researchers and innovators.

For most foreign workers, however, the standard “Z visa” remains the main route, requiring employer sponsorship, qualifications, work experience and extensive administrative procedures.

“In reality, we have not yet handled any K visa applications. The visa is still very new and at least from my experience, I have not heard of any successful cases so far,” said Anna Chen, a visa consultant based in Shenzhen.

Chen said the K visa, which attracted significant attention overseas when it was introduced, mainly targets young foreign scientists, engineers and other highly skilled technology professionals.

“The target group is quite narrow. Most foreigners coming to China for work do not meet that threshold,” she said. “And those who do often choose the United States instead, since salaries there are generally more attractive, based on my conversations with clients.”

Meanwhile, the Z visa is divided into three categories: A, which targets high-level talent such as leading researchers, executives and recognised experts; B, which covers most skilled professionals who must meet requirements related to education, work experience and salary; and C, a less common category reserved for seasonal or temporary employees.

“Most of the foreign workers I deal with are still applying for Category B work permits,” Chen said.

The visa agent said that compared with the US, China’s work visa system was generally less competitive for high-skilled applicants, as it did not have a lottery system like the H-1B programme in the US.

“But the process can still be complicated, since China requires employers to sponsor visas and most Chinese companies do not lack workforce domestically anyway, making them less likely to look overseas for talent,” she added.

Unlike China, countries such as the United Kingdom and US offer post-study work routes for international graduates.

In the UK, new degree holders can apply for a graduate visa, allowing them to work without employer sponsorship, usually for two years before switching to a skilled worker visa with an approved employer.

In the US, graduates can seek Optional Practical Training – temporary employment related to their field of study – before seeking employer-sponsored visas such as the H-1B.

China, by contrast, generally does not offer a similar transition route. Foreign graduates typically need to secure a job offer and employer sponsorship before applying for a work visa, even after studying at a Chinese university.

China has not released updated nationwide figures on foreign employment, but data showed that authorities issued 711,000 residence permits to foreign nationals in 2023, about 15 per cent below pre-pandemic levels.

Around 237,000 of these were work-related residence permits, according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data.

Chen said China had tightened scrutiny of work visa applications in recent years, following cases in some cities where foreigners obtained permits through fake employment arrangements or shell companies.

“The process now takes longer, employers also face stricter documentation requirements and applicants are asked to provide more financial records. Overall, work visa approvals have slowed,” she added.

Marshall Ma, a former recruiter based in Shanghai, said demand for foreign professionals in the city – widely regarded as China’s largest market for overseas talent – has declined sharply in recent years.

“The last time I heard a company specifically asking to hire foreigners was in 2021,” Ma said. “After the pandemic, competition in Shanghai’s job market intensified.

“Foreign candidates [are] often seen as having higher expectations, not only in terms of salaries but also benefits such as annual leave.”

Ma said demand for foreign workers remained relatively strong mainly in English teaching roles, while many other white-collar positions could now be filled by younger Chinese jobseekers at lower cost and with native language proficiency.

Another factor discouraging companies from hiring foreigners, he said, was the additional administrative burden, including visa applications and social insurance requirements.

“Many that traditionally hired large numbers of foreigners were Asia-Pacific regional headquartered firms, but lots of them began scaling back their China operations since 2023. Naturally, demand for foreign workers declined as well,” Ma added.

China has taken steps to make everyday digital services more accessible for foreigners, initially targeting overseas visitors but also benefiting foreign residents living and working in the country.

Since 2023, authorities have expanded mobile payment options by allowing more international bank cards to link with platforms such as Alipay and WeChat Pay, while simplifying registration and identity verification procedures.

However, challenges remain for some foreigners navigating China’s digital ecosystem.

“Digital and internet services work very well for the most part, but as foreigners, we often encounter small issues with many apps because we need to use our passports or provide other information that can sometimes cause problems,” Aitor said.

“Since I came to China three years ago, I think things have been moving in a positive direction, but there is still work to be done in some internet services so that foreigners can have a smoother experience.”

The reason why I decided to stay in China is because I knew my skill set would be more valuable here

Marcos Sabio, British-Spanish dual citizen

Yet not all foreigners encounter the same visa hurdles. For British-Spanish dual citizen Marcos Sabio, the transition into China’s workforce was relatively smooth. He found his software industry role in Beijing through the career-oriented social media platform LinkedIn, where his employer handled the work permit application.

“Luckily, for the visa applications and all the administration and bureaucracy, everything was handled by the HR team in the company,” he said.

“The reason why I decided to stay in China is because I knew my skill set would be more valuable here. Being able to speak Chinese, English, Spanish and some Russian is a real asset,” said Sabio, who has lived in China for 12 years.

Despite the hurdles, China’s appeal among foreign professionals appears to be recovering. According to a 2025 survey from InterNations – an online platform for people living and working abroad – China ranked sixth out of 46 destinations, with respondents expressing relatively high satisfaction with career opportunities, personal finances and daily convenience.

However, the survey also highlighted persistent challenges, including language barriers, administrative procedures and adaptation to the domestic digital ecosystem.

For Malaysian citizen Jens Lee, his China career journey involved less adaptation than others. His ethnic background and previous study experience in the country meant that adjusting to daily life and workplace culture came relatively naturally. After completing his master’s degree, he moved smoothly into a full-time role at a European-backed consultancy.

But familiarity with China did not necessarily make the bureaucracy easier.

Lee turned to a visa agency to handle the process, but found the experience less than smooth. The agency was relatively inexperienced, partly because he chose a cheaper provider that charged 6,000 yuan (US$886).

He said the intermediary handled most of the application, leaving him with limited understanding of the points-based system and other requirements.

Despite the administrative obstacles, Lee said, “China’s scale, economic dynamism and fast-paced working environment offer significant opportunities for professional learning and personal growth, which is something I value tremendously at the current stage of my career.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why was a US Yale graduate hounded out of his job promoting Chinese culture?
item.description:
In just two months, Yale graduate Edward Kuperman went from being praised by Chinese state media to being bombarded by public accusations that he was a spy.

It began with a June 18 article from state news agency Xinhua, in which he was described as an eager 24-year-old sinophile who made the unconventional choice of spurning China’s eastern metropolises to live in Dunhuang, an oasis in the country’s northwestern Gansu province.

His interest in China started with a Chinese language class in junior high school, as well as books and films about China, Xinhua reported. At 17, he was an exchange student in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. After returning to the United States, his parents hired a Chinese tutor for him, it said.
item.content:encoded:
In just two months, Yale graduate Edward Kuperman went from being praised by Chinese state media to being bombarded by public accusations that he was a spy.

It began with a June 18 article from state news agency Xinhua, in which he was described as an eager 24-year-old sinophile who made the unconventional choice of spurning China’s eastern metropolises to live in Dunhuang, an oasis in the country’s northwestern Gansu province.

His interest in China started with a Chinese language class in junior high school, as well as books and films about China, Xinhua reported. At 17, he was an exchange student in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. After returning to the United States, his parents hired a Chinese tutor for him, it said.

Kuperman, who also goes by the Chinese name Gu Aihua – “Loving China” – started his first job as an intern live-streamer at the Dunhuang Culture International Communication Centre (DCICC) in April, the article said, adding that he believed the city was a “unique entryway to observing China, understanding China and telling China’s stories”.

Dunhuang was for centuries a stop along the Silk Road and in the article Kuperman’s life there is presented as typically rosy. One anecdote describes how he spent three hours helping a Dutch tourist find their lost backpack. “Kuperman told the relieved tourist, ‘In China, nothing gets lost.’ The tourist nodded in agreement,” the article said.

The DCICC’s Instagram account featured Kuperman in three videos in May and June, interviewing participants at the Third World Conference of Sinologists and introducing the city’s Crescent Lake, one of its main attractions.

Dressed in a buttoned-up waistcoat and trousers, he walked in the sand around the lake, introducing it as a place lovers flocked to. “I don’t know about romance for me, but I will say that I love this place,” he said.

But Kuperman’s problems began in July, when he was hired by the Dunhuang Convergence Media Centre, an outlet run by the local government.

The hiring notice, which was picked up by Chinese media, showed that Kuperman was the only foreigner among three new hires. The other two women, both Chinese, had studied translation and communications at British universities.

Posts questioning Kuperman’s qualifications soon emerged on Chinese social media. Some claimed that he received an annual salary of 900,000 yuan (US$133,000), and questioned the pay. “Aren’t they using taxpayers’ money to pamper foreigners?”

That salary would far exceed what a Western graduate would usually expect to be paid in China. For a fresh Chinese graduate, that wage would be astronomical. According to the Hong Kong-based MyCOS Research Institute, the average starting salary for Chinese bachelor’s graduates in the class of 2025 was 77,220 yuan a year.

Online rage and suspicion were further inflamed by the discovery that Kuperman had studied Chinese at National Taiwan University and had interned at the conservative American Enterprise Institute’s Coalition Defence of Taiwan programme.

Hu Xijin, the former editor-in-chief of state-run tabloid Global Times, which has an English edition, waded into the controversy.

He wrote in a now-deleted online post that most foreigners employed by Chinese organisations had “complex experiences”, such as previously working in American media or think tanks, where they may have written reports viewed as unfavourable by the Chinese.

Hu said netizens wanted to “spoil his job” using spy accusations, because they were unhappy Kuperman was paid so much.

Kuperman has said that his interest in East Asia is cultural, not political. He previously wrote on Yale’s website that he studied the region “because of its unique combination of ancient tradition and dialogue with the West”.

Regardless of netizens’ intentions, their furious posting got results.

By Friday, Kuperman had decided not to take the job, state broadcaster CCTV reported. The local authorities clarified that he was only offered an annual salary of about 330,000 yuan – not 900,000 yuan – with various allowances on top. An investigation had been launched to see if there were any problems with the hiring, it said.

A salary of 330,000 yuan is within the normal range for Western graduates working in China.

Kuperman could not be contacted for comment, while the DCICC and local media centre did not respond to interview requests.

Einar Tangen, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and chairman of Asia Narratives, said that while Dunhuang was a city of just 200,000 people, it had more than 20 million visitors annually, with its Mogao Caves representing shared heritage spanning Buddhist, Persian, Greek, Indian and Chinese civilisations.

Dunhuang has been using this identity to try to tell its story to global audiences through what it calls the “innovative Dunhuang model”. A 2025 article from the city’s propaganda department said the DCICC was an important part of that effort, with 28 global social media accounts, 800,000 fans, 5,100 posts and more than 65 million cumulative views.

“We will make Dunhuang an important window for the world to understand China and feel Chinese civilisation,” it said.

The Chinese authorities are keen to win foreigners’ praise for the country’s heritage and modern technology. In 2025, when American influencer IShowSpeed visited Beijing and Shanghai, the Chinese embassy in the US said he was “bridging cultural gaps” and multiple state media outlets ran glowing pieces praising the trip.

Governments often actively invite foreign influencers to China. In June last year, the Hainan provincial tourism board invited 19 influencers from 12 countries to explore the southern island and produce content.

Despite this, a political scientist who wished to stay anonymous acknowledged that in recent years Chinese public opinion had become increasingly sensitive when it came to any issue involving foreigners. He said the resolution of any controversy depended on the style of the decision-maker.

“If you have an open mind or do not think [such backlash] matters, then this will boost cross-cultural exchanges,” he said.

Tangen added that he was worried by the instinct to build walls rather than bridges.

“Dunhuang’s entire model is built on openness. It processes visa-on-arrival for international tourists, has established sister-city ties with cities abroad and hosted over 600 global events in 2025,” he said.

“China is extending visas and inviting the world to see the country as it is, not as hostile or ignorant media portray it. If Kuperman had genuine issues in his background, then they should be addressed – through proper channels.”

item.title: [SCMP] CJ Hendry brings Juju World to Hong Kong with exclusive collectibles
item.description:
The Australian artist Catherine Jenna Hendry, best known to the world as CJ Hendry, first entered the public consciousness through social media, by sharing her hyperrealistic interpretations of luxury items on Instagram. The ink drawings gained Hendry a following of almost a million, and celebrity collectors of her works include Kanye West, Vera Wang, Floyd Mayweather and Pharrell Williams – an impressive feat for someone without formal training or gallery representation.

The New York-based artist has expanded her drawing practice from black and white to colour. But not one to stay confined to a single medium, Hendry has also made waves with her viral plush “flower markets”.

She has also created Juju, a kawaii collectible with floppy ears and a flower for an eye. Running until August 16, Pacific Place is hosting “Juju World”, a fluffy and fun exhibition inspired by the character. Giant Jujus, swings and a chamber filled with 400 plushies await.
item.content:encoded:
The Australian artist Catherine Jenna Hendry, best known to the world as CJ Hendry, first entered the public consciousness through social media, by sharing her hyperrealistic interpretations of luxury items on Instagram. The ink drawings gained Hendry a following of almost a million, and celebrity collectors of her works include Kanye West, Vera Wang, Floyd Mayweather and Pharrell Williams – an impressive feat for someone without formal training or gallery representation.

The New York-based artist has expanded her drawing practice from black and white to colour. But not one to stay confined to a single medium, Hendry has also made waves with her viral plush “flower markets”.

She has also created Juju, a kawaii collectible with floppy ears and a flower for an eye. Running until August 16, Pacific Place is hosting “Juju World”, a fluffy and fun exhibition inspired by the character. Giant Jujus, swings and a chamber filled with 400 plushies await.

There’s also a pop-up store selling iridescent Jujus, created exclusively for Pacific Place. In this line, there are nine standard versions and five additional “secret” versions, which come in limited-edition blind boxes. Visitors can also unlock surprise accessories at the Capsule Toy Station and customise their Juju with interchangeable flower eyes, outfits and more.

At the launch of “Juju World”, we meet an energetic Hendry for a conversation about art, artificial intelligence and what it takes to make it in the industry today.

Describe your routine.

I have studios in Hong Kong and New York, so we’re here every other month. In the studio, every day is different. With three children aged between one and five, it’s mostly chaos. We are just piecing it together and there’s a lot we want to create and achieve, and that comes a little bit chaotically sometimes.

How has that influenced your art?

A lot of my artistic concepts are childlike and have a lot of whimsy. I’m not sure if that’s because I have children and I’m surrounded by childlike wonder, but creating ideas that appeal to both adults and kids is what I want to do. Sometimes, there’s no rhyme or reason to it.

You’ve tackled various mediums. Is there a thread that ties them all together?

Over the past three years, I have started to use this very feminine flower shape. Because I had so many unusual, different concepts, the flower shape allowed me to connect them all together. That has become a branding moment for everything. Even with the Juju logo, there’s a flower on top of the letter J.

Why the pivot from ink drawings to the kawaii collectibles realm?

My drawing practice is very labour-intensive, focused and intimate. I was finding it frustrating because those works are only available to a few people, as they are expensive and hard to come by. I was uncomfortable with that. I still draw, but maybe one-tenth of the time I used to. It has allowed me to spend time creating these other, kooky concepts, such as Juju and the flower markets.

I’ve created these concepts so that more people can appreciate and experience them. You don’t need money to appreciate the flower market: people can access it for free and even their first flower is free. Juju is not necessarily the same, but this fun, friendly character is appealing to many.

How would you explain Juju?

Juju is a fun character with a flower over their eye and no mouth, so they can’t talk back. They are a character that can take you through the happiest of times and the darkest of times, one who is with you no matter what.

How did Juju come about?

Juju’s name comes from my mother. Her name is Judy and my kids call her Juju. My mum is a very elegant lady who wears all white. So the rarest Jujus are always white.

I used AI to help design Juju in early 2025. AI is interesting because everyone kind of belittles it. But as an artist, it’s important to use different tools. I used AI for a very small portion of the design process.

AI is controversial, especially in art because it draws from existing works. Tell us more about your position on it

AI can be used very cleverly, and it can be used very poorly. It depends on what you want to do and the story you want to tell. Anyone can design anything in AI in seconds, but designing something and then making it a reality is a totally different skill set. My artistic process is more in bringing it to life and rolling it out.

I’ve been an artist for 15 years and I’ve been plagiarised for much of that time. So, I’ve become confident enough in my practice to know that no ideas are original, even before AI. Everyone’s referencing everyone else. AI is just speeding that up.

Art is all about collaboration and moving forward. If your entire practice is based on AI, I don’t think you’ll get very far. Mine is based pretty much entirely on design and creativity and using AI only for very small parts.

So, in the age of AI, do you see the role of an artist as more of a curator of sorts?

Yes, absolutely. It’s important to have your own voice. You can use AI to perhaps start a concept, but to build and develop that takes a lot of energy and thought.

Because I’ve been doing this for so long, I feel very comfortable talking about AI. People want to pretend it’s not there. But I’m like, “It’s here, you’ve got to go with it.” I’ve used AI and I will continue to use AI.

Building real-life experiences is so important to me. Like with “Juju World” in Pacific Place, for example, you can only buy these Jujus in person. I’ve purposely taken this offline. Also, we haven’t made many of them. So, when they sell out, they sell out. They’ll never be made again. We never revisit it and we never will.

Like Takashi Murakami, Kaws and others, you seem instinctively aware of how social media, branding and merchandising works. How important is that for an artist today?

It’s hard to be an artist nowadays. Everyone pines over the old days, but they are not coming back. Technology is a beautiful tool, if you can use it in a clever way. But because everyone has social media, it has become oversaturated. I’m interested in in-person experiences. When I build concepts and installations, it’s important to create something unique for people to experience.

That said, I also think there are so many ways to be an artist. I see my job as creating and starting discussions. I’m a commercially successful artist, but that’s not for everyone. Not everyone wants to have merch at their art exhibition. Some people just want to have one extraordinary painting that they’ve taken two years to make. That’s special and important. It depends on the artist you want to be. I’m just one type of artist. Art comes in so many ways, in so many voices.

Who inspires you?

I don’t think, for me, there are people who are inspirations. Like I said before, nothing is original any more. Everything’s being built on something else.

I’ve always interpreted my concepts off other things, blended them, meshed them, reinterpreted them in my own voice, in my own way. Actually, a lot of my ideas come from runway shows, which are extraordinarily inspiring in the way they bring together worlds to showcase concepts and clothing.

When we launched Juju at Phillips West Kowloon (in late 2025), a lot of that inspiration came from the Chanel runway show at the Grand Palais, in Paris, where they did it like a Chanel supermarket.

What do you want people to take away from this particular exhibition?

I’ve always been pretty open with the fact that when I build ideas and exhibitions, I don’t expect anything from anyone. That’s not my job. I believe, as an artist, you’re meant to build something and what people experience is none of my business. A lot of artists might put a plaque on the wall explaining the idea, but I’ve never done that and I never will. I build the idea and people can come and experience it however they want.

What’s next for you?

Gosh, I genuinely don’t know. It’s too hard to predict the future. My art could crash and burn, or I could reach the stars. You never know.

What I do know is that I’m relatively creative. I have a lot of energy, a lot of excitement and a lot of really kooky ideas. I love executing, building and creating. There’s no shortage of ideas. I just love working with my team to come up with stupid stuff all the time.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity
